policies.title: Conserve Forests
policies.bcr_basis: Anchor: the only randomized trial with a benefit-cost calculation. Jayachandran et al. (2017, Science) paid Ugandan forest owners not to clear forest in 60 of 121 villages; tree-cover loss was 4.2% in treatment vs 9.1% in control villages, with no detectable local leakage, and the value of delayed CO2 was 2.4 times programme cost. HIGH 2.4: the trial's published central ratio. Its cost already includes monitoring and administration of the at-scale programme; carbon-market certification costs do not apply to a government payments programme. The working paper gives the sensitivity range: programme cost ~$0.57/tCO2 delayed (payments plus administration), valued at a $39 SCC; 0.7 with immediate catch-up after payments stop, 12.3 with permanent delay, a case the authors call very tentative. LOW 0.09 (full-cost case for credit-based delivery, with leakage): programme cost per credited tonne = Kindermann et al.'s upper average cost $18.7/t (28.0/1.5) + MRV/certification $1.46/t (Merger et al. 2012) = $20.2/t; West et al. (2023, Science) find only ~6.1% of credits from voluntary REDD+ projects reflect additional reductions, so cost per real tonne = 20.2/0.061 = $331; at the $51 US IWG SCC, 51/331 = 0.15. Payments are counted as programme cost, as Jayachandran et al. do. Leakage: Gan & McCarl (2007) estimate 42-95% of one country's or region's conservation effort is displaced elsewhere (as summarised by Hu et al. 2024); payments flow to countries one at a time, so cross-border displacement applies, and at the lowest figure 0.15 x (1 - 0.42) = 0.09. Cross-checks: Kindermann's $6.4-18.7/t gives 2.7-8.0 at $51 and 9.9-29 at $185 (Rennert et al. 2022) if every paid tonne is real; Brazil's DETER enforcement breaks even at $0.76/t (Assuncao et al.); Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015 rated halving forest loss at ~10, McVittie 2-3. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; the whole cost behind the ratio is public outlay; LOW = 0.09 / 3.00 = 0.03; HIGH = 2.4 / 1.34 = 1.79.
policies.grade_reason: A randomized controlled trial published in Science reports a benefit-cost ratio (2.4, range 0.7-12.3), backed by a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study of Brazilian enforcement (AEJ: Applied 2023) and a peer-reviewed global cost curve (PNAS 2008). The low end is built from a peer-reviewed synthetic-control evaluation of REDD+ credits (West et al. 2023, Science). Not A+ because only one RCT computes a BCR and the offset evidence is negative.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost = results-based payments $28.0bn/yr (Kindermann et al. 2008, upper estimate for a 50% cut in deforestation; equal to landholders' opportunity costs) + MRV/transaction/capacity administration ~$4.7bn/yr (Merger et al. 2012, up to $1.46/tCO2 x 2.7 Gt; Eliasch Review $4bn over 5 years) + private compliance 0 (compensated opportunity cost, not added twice) + GDP loss null. See cost_components.
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained funding scale-up with working precedents: Norway's results-based payments, the Amazon Fund, and Brazil's DETER enforcement system, which cut deforestation sharply after 2004-2008 (Assuncao et al. 2023). No new treaty is needed, but delivery depends on enforcement capacity in tropical-forest countries.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Payments flow to rural forest-owning households in low-income tropical countries (Uganda trial); climate benefits are global. Caveat: Jayachandran et al. note reduced firewood access for landless neighbours and possible widening of within-village inequality.
policies.summary: Paying landowners or governments in tropical countries to keep forests standing is often presented as one of the cheapest ways to cut CO2. The best evidence, a randomized trial in Uganda, found $2.40 of climate benefit per $1 while payments lasted, and the authors call longer-lasting gains very tentative. Where the money buys carbon credits like those in voluntary REDD+ projects, only about 6% reflected real reductions, and 42-95% of protection in one place is offset by more clearing elsewhere, leaving about 9 cents per $1. Full cost of halving deforestation: about $33bn a year including monitoring and administration.
policies.selected_by: Peoples' Climate Vote 2021 (#1 of 18, 54%); Dechezleprêtre et al. 2025

policies.title: Renewable Energy Subsidies
policies.bcr_basis: Evaluated as the subsidy/mandate itself: BCR = social value of CO2 avoided (SCC) / social resource cost per tonne abated. The per-tonne abatement costs used are resource costs (generation, backup, transmission and fuel, or observed retail-price effects), so they already contain firms' and ratepayers' compliance costs; tax credits are transfers and are not added again. LOW 0.024: the highest published ex-post cost, Abrell, Kosch & Rausch (2019, J. Public Economics; weather-driven natural experiment): solar subsidies in Germany and Spain cost EUR 411-1,944 per tCO2 in the short run; 1,944 x ~1.1 $/EUR = $2,138; at the $51 US IWG SCC, 51/2,138 = 0.024. HIGH 0.75: Bistline, Mehrotra & Wolfram (2023, BPEA) IRA power-sector abatement cost when both costs and emissions are discounted (the consistent comparison with a per-tonne SCC), $88-94/t, valued at the DICE-2023 social cost of carbon, $66/t (Barrage & Nordhaus 2024): 66/88 = 0.75. Their headline $36-87/t discounts costs but not tonnes, and they note costs 'would be higher if distortions associated with financing the incentives were included'. Intermediate: RPS (Greenstone & Nath 2026, $86-211/t) 0.24-0.59 at $51; wind subsidies (Abrell, EUR 82-276 = $90-304/t) 0.17-0.57 at $51; Copenhagen Consensus rates doubling the renewable share below 1. Sensitivity: at Rennert et al.'s $185/t, the low end would be 0.087 and the high end 185/88 = 2.10 (RPS 0.88-2.15). System costs of intermittency: Gowrisankaran, Reynolds & Samano (2016, JPE) find intermittency adds $46/MWh to a $138.4/MWh social cost at 20% solar; Idel (2022) finds full-system costs of wind and solar serving a whole market far above LCOE. These costs are inside the ex-post estimates (observed prices) but can be understated in LCOE-based models. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies. The credits are transfers, but the deadweight of the taxes that pay for them is a real cost (Bistline et al. note costs 'would be higher if distortions associated with financing the incentives were included'); weighted by the tax-financed share of cost_bn, (197 + 1.0) / 237.7 = 0.833 (the rest is ratepayers' mandate costs): LOW = 0.024 / (1 + 2.0 x 0.833) = 0.009; HIGH = 0.75 / (1 + 0.34 x 0.833) = 0.58.
policies.grade_reason: The end points come from a peer-reviewed natural experiment (Abrell et al. 2019, weather variation) and a model-based estimate published in Brookings Papers (Bistline et al. 2023), with a quasi-experimental working paper (Greenstone & Nath, revised 2026) in between, converted to BCRs with published SCC values. Results differ in sign by technology and SCC, so not A-range.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost = public outlay $197bn/yr (Cato PA 992 high-end IRA energy-subsidy cost, $1.97T over 2025-2034) + administration ~$1.0bn (IRS cost of collection 0.53%) + private compliance ~$39.7bn (RPS retail-price effect of 11%, Greenstone & Nath, on RPS states' ~70% share of $514bn US retail electricity revenue, EIA) + GDP loss: no estimate (null). Fiscal outlays are transfers whose resource content is the abatement cost, so they are not added to the BCR denominator (see bcr_basis). See cost_components.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: needs ordinary budget or tax legislation (or state RPS statutes), with abundant precedent (IRA 2022, EU and German feed-in laws, 29 US state RPS laws). Durability is the weak point: the July 2025 OBBBA cut back most federal wind, solar and EV credits within three years of enactment.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Borenstein & Davis (2016, Tax Policy and the Economy) find the top income quintile received ~60% of US clean-energy tax credits and the bottom three quintiles ~10%; mandates raise retail electricity prices 11-17% (Greenstone & Nath), a cost that weighs more on low-income households. Health co-benefits are broad.
policies.summary: Subsidies, tax credits and mandates for wind and solar cut emissions, but at very different costs per tonne of CO2. Solar subsidies in Germany and Spain cost up to about $2,100 per tonne, returning about 2 cents per dollar at the former US government carbon value, while US state mandates cost $86-211 per tonne and model estimates of the Inflation Reduction Act's power-sector credits about $88 per tonne on a consistent basis. Overall range: about 2 to 75 cents per dollar. Counting full costs, the federal credits (up to about $200bn a year) plus higher electricity bills from state mandates (about $40bn a year) cost around $238bn a year.
policies.selected_by: Peoples' Climate Vote 53%; Dechezleprêtre et al. 69.5%

policies.title: Climate Adaptation
policies.bcr_basis: Package = early-warning systems (EWS) plus flood defences, including nature-based ones (mangroves, marshes, reefs). Range: the Global Commission on Adaptation (2019, 'Adapt Now') finds benefit-cost ratios of 2:1 to 10:1 across its five priority adaptation investments ($1.8tn over 2020-2030 generating $7.1tn net benefits; average 'almost 4'), and both components of this package sit inside that span: EWS 'save lives and assets worth at least ten times their cost', mangrove preservation and restoration benefits are 'up to 10 times' costs. LOW 1.7: the published ratios are computed on project costs; adding programme management at FEMA's 15% cap lowers a ratio by 1/1.15, applied to the low end, where the highest cost estimate belongs: 2/1.15 = 1.74, rounded to 1.7. HIGH 10: the GCA's top ratio, which is stated on total investment. Central ~4: Mechler (2016, Natural Hazards), a peer-reviewed review of risk-based disaster-risk-management BCAs, finds benefits average about four times costs. Component checks: Hallegatte (2012, World Bank WP 6058) estimates that bringing hydro-met services and EWS in all developing countries to developed-country standard costs ~$1bn/yr and yields $4-36bn/yr (avoided asset losses $0.3-2bn, 23,000 lives/yr valued at $0.7-3.5bn, $3-30bn of wider economic benefits), BCR 4-36; GCA: $800m on EWS avoids $3-16bn/yr of losses (3.75-20). US flood mitigation: NIBS (2019) finds federal riverine-flood mitigation grants return ~7:1 and all federal mitigation grants 6:1. Coastal: Hinkel et al. (2014, PNAS) find dike costs of $12-71bn/yr by 2100 are far below the damages they avoid (0.3-9.3% of world GDP/yr without adaptation); Narayan et al. (2016, PLoS ONE) find marshes and mangroves 2-5 times cheaper than submerged breakwaters for low waves. The upper EWS figures (up to 36) are not used as the package high end because EWS are ~1-3% of package cost, so the blended ratio is dominated by the defences (2-10). Ward et al. (2017, Nature Climate Change) caution that dyke investment is economically attractive in many but not all urban areas. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; the whole cost behind the ratio is public outlay; LOW = 1.74 (2/1.15) / 3.00 = 0.58; HIGH = 10 / 1.34 = 7.46.
policies.grade_reason: The central value comes from a peer-reviewed review of risk-based BCAs (Mechler 2016) and is consistent with peer-reviewed coastal (Hinkel et al. 2014 PNAS) and nature-based-defence (Narayan et al. 2016) studies; the range end points are official estimates (GCA, World Bank, NIBS). No randomized or quasi-experimental BCR for the package.
policies.cost_basis: Built from component estimates: EWS ~$1bn/yr for all developing countries (Hallegatte 2012; the UN Early Warnings for All plan budgets $3.1bn over 2023-2027, ~$0.6bn/yr); coastal dikes $12-71bn/yr (Hinkel et al. 2014, end-century, midpoint ~$40bn) with river and nature-based defences partly overlapping. Bounds: the full five-area GCA programme is ~$180bn/yr ($1.8tn over 2020-2030) and UNEP (2023) puts all adaptation needs of developing countries at $215-387bn/yr, so this package is a subset of those. Programme management/administration at FEMA's statutory cap of 15% of grant awards (DRRA Section 1215) adds ~$6bn/yr, for a total of ~$46bn/yr. See cost_components.
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained funding scale-up with clear precedents: Bangladesh's cyclone warning and shelter programme, FEMA mitigation grants, and the UN Early Warnings for All initiative endorsed by 50 countries. No treaty or constitutional change is needed, but large defences need multi-year capital budgets and maintenance.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Disaster mortality falls hardest on low-income countries; the UN notes countries with limited early-warning coverage have disaster mortality eight times higher than those with high coverage, and Hallegatte's estimate targets developing countries. Mangrove protection also supports coastal fisheries livelihoods (GCA).
policies.summary: Early-warning systems and flood defences, including mangroves and marshes, protect people and property from storms and floods. Official and peer-reviewed reviews consistently find benefits of about $2 to $10 per $1 spent, with around $4 typical. Early warnings alone score higher, $4 to $36 per $1, because they are cheap (about $1bn a year for all developing countries). The case is strongest where exposure is high and protection is currently weak.
policies.selected_by: Peoples' Climate Vote 45% + 45% (Protecting People group)

policies.title: Ocean Protection
policies.bcr_basis: Benefits counted: fisheries spill-over, tourism and recreation, coastal protection, biodiversity and carbon sequestration (blue carbon) from coral reefs, mangroves and coastal wetlands; costs: MPA establishment and management plus fisheries opportunity costs (~90% of total cost). Fisheries management outside MPAs is excluded by the policy definition. HIGH 2.7: the peer-reviewed global bio-economic model (Brander et al. 2020, Marine Policy) finds global benefits exceed costs by a factor of 1.4-2.7 across six expansion scenarios; its ratios already include establishment, management and fisheries opportunity costs. Brander's Copenhagen Consensus assessment of MPA expansion for the EEZs of Africa's 38 coastal countries ('Identifying best buys for Africa' series) gives 9.2 for protecting 10% of EEZs and 1.16 for 30% (5-year build, 30 years of benefits), the ratio falling as coverage expands into lower-value, higher-fishing-cost areas. A non-peer-reviewed version of the global model for WWF/IVM (Brander et al. 2015) reported 3.2-19.8 (PV costs $45-47bn for 10% and $223-228bn for 30% coverage, 2015-2050) and is superseded by the 2020 paper. Full-cost check: replacing Brander's management cost with Balmford's high-end $19bn/yr (PV 19 x 21.83 = $414.8bn) in the 2015 global 30% scenarios gives E2E30: 719.2/(227.0 - 23.8 + 414.8) = 1.16 and P2P30: 1,145.2/(228.0 - 24.4 + 414.8) = 1.85 (Balmford's cost covers 20-30% of all seas, more than 30% of EEZs, so this overstates cost). LOW 0.12: Brander's 1.16 for 30% coverage assumes protected areas work as designed; Edgar et al. (2014, Nature) find only 9 of 87 MPAs had four or five of the features that make them effective and 'most of the remainder of MPAs were ecologically indistinguishable from non-MPAs', and Gill et al. (2017, Nature) find only 9% had adequate staff. Benefits accruing only to effective MPAs (9/87 = 10%) give 1.16 x 0.10 = 0.12. The modelled benefits are also contested: Ovando et al. (2023, Nature) find a more realistic model cuts the food benefits of priority MPAs by 62%; Hilborn & Kaiser (2022) note that fishing effort moves rather than disappears; Hiddink et al. (2023) find trawling-carbon claims biased upward 'by several orders of magnitude'; and blue-carbon removal is 'uncertain and unreliable' (Williamson & Gattuso 2022). Fishers bear most of the cost: lost fishing access is about 90% of total costs in Brander's model, and Hawaii longline revenue per trip fell 9% after the Papahanaumokuakea expansion (Chan 2020). Blue carbon: GCA (2019) finds mangrove preservation and restoration benefits up to 10 times costs. Not used: Sala et al. (2021, Nature) map where protection would yield the most biodiversity, food (>8 Mt extra catch) and carbon benefits but report no BCR, and their trawling-carbon estimate is disputed by Hiddink et al. (2023, Nature), who argue it is 100-1,000 times too high. Waldron et al. (2020) find benefits at least 5:1 for 30% of land and sea combined (not ocean-specific, not peer-reviewed). Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; in Brander's ratios about 90% of cost is fishers' lost access (private), so only the remaining ~10% (establishment and management) is tax-financed: LOW = 0.12 / (1 + 2.0 x 0.10) = 0.1; HIGH = 2.7 / (1 + 0.34 x 0.10) = 2.61.
policies.grade_reason: The range rests on one global bio-economic model (Brander et al. 2020, peer-reviewed), whose benefit inputs are disputed in Nature (Ovando et al. 2023; Hilborn & Kaiser 2022; Hiddink et al. 2023), and on field evidence that most MPAs do not deliver (Edgar et al. 2014; Gill et al. 2017). No randomized or ex-post global BCA exists.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost = establishment ~$0.36bn/yr + management and enforcement $19bn/yr (Balmford et al. 2004 high end) + fisheries opportunity cost ~$9.0bn/yr (Brander et al. 2015, 30% scenario, PV $195.8bn over 2015-2050 at 3%) = ~$28.4bn/yr. Waldron et al. (2020) put all protected areas (land and sea, 30%) at ~$140bn/yr. See cost_components.
policies.difficulty_reason: Each country can designate and enforce MPAs in its own waters under ordinary law (many have, e.g. the US Papahanaumokuakea monument); the global 30x30 target is agreed under the 2022 Kunming-Montreal framework, but high-seas protection needs the multilateral BBNJ treaty, and enforcement against fishing is costly.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Benefits (coastal protection, tourism, fish spill-over, biodiversity, carbon) are widely shared, and Balmford et al. estimate a global network would support about one million jobs; but the main cost, lost fishing access, falls on fishing communities, some of them poor, so distribution is mixed.
policies.summary: Marine protected areas close parts of the ocean to fishing and other uses to protect reefs, mangroves and fish stocks. The most complete global cost-benefit model finds $1.40-2.70 of benefit per $1, but it assumes the protected areas work as designed: a Nature study of 87 of them found only 9 had the features that make them effective, and most were ecologically indistinguishable from unprotected waters. Counting benefits only where protection works gives about 12 cents per $1. Lost fishing access is about 90% of the cost, borne mostly by fishers, and the claimed food and carbon benefits have been cut sharply by later studies.
policies.selected_by: Peoples' Climate Vote 45%

policies.title: Combustion Car Ban
policies.bcr_basis: Scope: a global ban on sales of new combustion-engine cars (by 2030) and trucks, on the schedules of California's Advanced Clean Fleets/Advanced Clean Trucks rules (100% zero-emission truck sales) and the EU's 90% heavy-duty CO2 cut for 2040. No study evaluates it directly, so the ends come from the closest priced analyses. No published benefit-cost ratio covers trucks on the pessimistic side, so the range is anchored on the car evidence. LOW -0.07: Holland, Mansur, Muller & Yates (2016, AER) value the full environmental benefit of an EV over a gasoline car (CO2 plus power-plant and tailpipe local pollution) at a mean of -$1,095 per vehicle on the 2010-12 US grid (+$2,785 California to -$4,964 North Dakota). Their 2020 update (AEJ: Policy) finds EVs cleaner than gasoline cars on the 2017 US average grid, but a 2030 global ban puts most new EVs on grids like China's (58% coal) and India's (75%) (Ember 2025), and Ji et al. (2012, EST) find e-car PM2.5 health impacts in Chinese cities 3.6x those of gasoline cars. Full cost per forced EV: battery premium $10,000 (Mills 2023) + grid and charging $6,250 (Brattle: $75-125bn for 20m EVs = $3,750-6,250) = $16,250. -1,095 / 16,250 = -0.07 (-0.11 with the battery premium alone; a larger denominator moves a negative ratio toward zero). HIGH 0.19: the Cebr analysis for the APPG for Fair Fuel of the UK's 2030 car ban, benefits GBP 76bn against costs GBP 400bn: 76/400 = 0.19. Used-car leakage of 13-16% of expected fuel savings (Jacobsen & van Benthem 2015) would lower the high end further. Cross-checks: McKitrick (CJE 2024) general-equilibrium cost of Canada's mandate $2,700-4,700/t: 185/2,700 = 0.07, 51/2,700 = 0.02, 36/4,700 = 0.008; the same model finds Canada's mandate cuts real GDP by 2.8% in 2030 and 7.0% in 2035 when parity arrives in 2050; Gillingham & Stock static EV-subsidy cost 36/640 = 0.06 to 185/350 = 0.53. Trucks: a battery-electric Class 8 tractor costs over $400,000 against about $180,000 for diesel; electrifying the US commercial fleet needs nearly $1 trillion of charging ($620bn) and utility grid ($370bn) investment, about $145,000 of charging per heavy-duty vehicle, excluding vehicle costs (Roland Berger for the Clean Freight Coalition, 2024); ATRI (2022) puts the payload loss at about 13,800 lb per truck and finds an all-electric US fleet would need more than 40% of current US electricity generation, plus 6.3-34.9 years of current world output of cobalt, graphite, lithium and nickel. IEA (2024): announced projects meet only 70% of copper and 50% of lithium needs in 2035 under national climate goals. The regulators' own appraisals (UK DfT ZEV mandate 1.31; CARB ACF 1.5; EU heavy-duty impact assessment net savings) are listed as counter-evidence. Tax-finance check: each $1 of public outlay or public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); administration is $0.3bn of $1,043.2bn (0.03% of cost_bn); the penalty changes neither end at two decimals and is not applied (negligible).
policies.grade_reason: The low end rests on peer-reviewed environmental-damage models (Holland et al. 2016 AER, with the 2020 AEJ: Policy update; Ji et al. 2012 EST) and the main cross-check on a peer-reviewed CGE model of an actual mandate (McKitrick 2024 CJE); the high end is a government self-appraisal (B- alone), and the cost inputs are industry and think-tank figures (Brattle, Mills). No ex-post or quasi-experimental BCR of an ICE sales ban exists.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, US$bn per year once the ban binds (high end): public outlay 0 + administration 0.3 (DfT administrative share 0.0275% of total cost) + private compliance 1,043.2 [cars, global: 56m ICE buyers outside China x $10,000 battery premium (Mills 2023) = 560; 68m extra EVs x $6,250 grid, storage and charging per EV (Brattle) = 425; trucks, US only: $990bn of charging and grid investment (Roland Berger 2024) over the 17 years to 2040 = 58.2] + GDP loss not estimated globally (national auto-sector losses: McKitrick, Canada, up to C$1.2T over 2025-2050; CLEPA/PwC, EU, net 275,000 jobs) = ~1,043. Low end of the car components: 280 + 255 = ~535 (593 with trucks). Fuel and maintenance savings are counted inside the ratio, not netted here.
policies.difficulty_reason: Each market can ban sales of new combustion-engine vehicles through ordinary legislation or regulation, with no treaty required, and the EU has adopted a 2035 rule. Meeting a 2030 date across major markets still needs zero-emission sales to rise from about 20% in 2024 to 100% within about five years, and precedents have slipped: the UK moved its 2030 ban to 2035 in 2023, and the US EPA moved in 2026 to rescind its 2024 vehicle standards.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Up-front premiums fall on car buyers, and lower-income and rural households face the largest relative burden and the least access to home charging; Borenstein & Davis (2016) find ~90% of US EV tax credits went to the top income quintile. Offsetting: lower running costs (EPA: ~$6,000 lifetime fuel savings per vehicle) and cleaner urban air where grids are low-carbon are broadly shared; on coal-heavy grids local pollution shifts toward communities near power plants (Holland et al. 2016: 91% of EV local damages are exported across state lines).
policies.summary: Requiring every new car and truck sold to be zero-emission (cars by 2030 worldwide; trucks on California's and the EU's schedules) would cut oil use, but on coal-heavy grids, like most of Asia's, an electric car can do more pollution damage than the gasoline car it replaces (about minus 7 cents per dollar), and an analysis of the UK's 2030 car ban puts costs at five times benefits (19 cents per dollar). Battery trucks cost more than twice as much as diesel, carry about 13,800 lb less, and electrifying US trucking alone needs nearly $1 trillion of chargers and grid; a general-equilibrium model of Canada's mandate finds GDP up to 7% lower by 2035. Battery premiums, grid upgrades and chargers for cars cost about $535-985bn a year, plus about $58bn a year for US truck charging and grid.
policies.selected_by: Only policy asked in all three surveys (PCV, Dechezleprêtre, EIB)

policies.title: Global Carbon Tax
policies.bcr_basis: $135/t in 2030 is the bottom of the IPCC SR1.5 price range for 1.5 C pathways ($135-5,500/t; Niskanen summary), so the range uses full-cost benefit-cost studies of Paris/1.5 C-strength policy. Their costs are general-equilibrium GDP losses, which already contain firms' compliance spending, so nothing is counted twice. Induced deaths are subtracted from benefits, as in the Green New Deal entry; costs are the GDP loss plus administration ($22bn). World GDP ~$105T. Energy-poverty mortality: IMF (2019) finds $75/t raises electricity prices ~45%, so $135 implies ~81% (linear); Chirakijja et al. (2024) find a 42% heating-price change shifts ~11,000 US winter deaths a year; 11,000 x 81/42 = ~21,200 deaths x HHS VSL $13.1m = ~$278bn/yr (US only). Poor-country infant deaths: Baird, Friedman & Schady (REStat 2011) find +0.24 to 0.40 infant deaths per 1,000 births per 1% fall in GDP per person, on ~119.9m births a year in low- and middle-income countries (World Bank), each valued at $198,000. HIGH 0.55: Tol (2023), central 1.5 C comparison against the SSP5-8.5 baseline, benefits 3.1% vs costs 5.6% of GDP: (3,255 - infant deaths 30.0) / 5,902 = 0.55. LOW 0.16: Tol's 1.5 C benefits of 2.2% of GDP ($2,310bn) when the no-policy baseline is SSP3-7.0 (3.9 C by 2100), with Tol's own statement that real-world policy imperfections such as unequal national carbon prices 'would readily double' costs, so costs become 11.2% of world GDP ($11,760bn) plus administration: (2,310 - energy-poverty deaths 278 - infant deaths 100.1 [world GDP -10.5% x 0.40 x 119.9m births = 505,498 deaths at $198,000]) / 11,782 = 0.16. A Paris-style global price is set and enforced country by country, so unequal prices are the realistic case. Sensitivities: Tol's least-cost 1.5 C costs (5.6%) against the SSP3-7.0 baseline, (2,310 - 278 - 50.0) / 5,902 = 0.34; Tol's most favourable pairing of his reported ranges (benefits 3.2% vs costs 3.8% of GDP), (3,360 - 21.7) / 4,012 = 0.83; Tol 2 C 2.8/3.8 = 0.74. Optimal-price comparison: DICE-2023 (Barrage & Nordhaus 2024) gives a social cost of carbon on the cost-benefit optimal path of $59/t in 2025 rising to $125 in 2050 (Table 2; about $69 in 2030 by geometric interpolation: 59 x (125/59)^(5/25)), while its optimal carbon price must rise to $115/t by 2050, so $135 in 2030 is roughly twice the optimal-path SCC and above the optimal price the model reaches only in 2050; the same model finds the 1.5 C limit 'infeasible' (SCC on that path $4,185/t in 2025). Revenue use is unspecified; Parry, Williams & Goulder (1999) show that spending rather than recycling revenue raises costs, which points toward the low end. Counter-evidence (counter_sources): DICE-2023 finds a 2 C-limited path raises global wealth by ~$107T versus current policy, and Rennert et al.'s $185/t SCC would pass a $135 tax. Lost-income mortality: income lost to a policy costs lives. Broughel & Viscusi (Mercatus 2017) put it at about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed; valued at the HHS VSL of $13.1m, each $1 of net income lost carries 13.1/99.3 = $0.132 of mortality cost (and each $1 gained saves the same). This adjustment is applied uniformly to every policy after the published range is drawn. Tax-finance check: each $1 of public outlay or public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); the only public cost is tax collection, $22bn of $5,902bn (0.37% of cost_bn); the penalty changes neither end at two decimals and is not applied (negligible). Additional study (below the range, not used to set it): Tol's (2012) Copenhagen Consensus III paper models global carbon taxes in FUND; a tax of $250/tC ($68/tCO2) in 2010 rising at the 5% discount rate, which holds CO2 below 450 ppm (about the EU's long-term target), costs $47.6 trillion in present value with a benefit-cost ratio of 0.02 (Table 2), or 0.01-0.12 after Tol's own corrections for equity weighting, uncertainty and model bias (Table 3). Its price path ($68 x 1.05^20 = ~$181/tCO2 by 2030) is stricter than $135 in 2030 and its damages come from an older model version, so it brackets the low end from below rather than redefining it.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost results for Paris/1.5 C-strength carbon pricing (Tol 2023, Climate Change Economics; Nordhaus DICE, AER 2019 and PNAS 2024) with the cost side taken from the high end of peer-reviewed and IPCC-assessed GDP-loss estimates, plus a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental mortality adjustment (Chirakijja et al. 2024). Not A: no controlled or quasi-experimental study of a global tax at this level, none scores $135/t exactly, and DICE-2023 reports that a 2 C path passes a cost-benefit test.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost = public outlay $0 (revenue is a transfer) + administration ~$22bn/yr (IRS cost of collection 0.53% applied to $4,185bn of revenue from 31 GtCO2e x $135 in IPCC AR6 1.5 C pathways) + GDP loss $5,880bn/yr (Tol 2023: 1.5 C target costs ~5.6% of GDP, the highest published central estimate; applied to ~$105T world GDP). Private abatement spending is inside the GDP-loss measure and is not added again. Lower published GDP-loss estimates: IPCC AR6 2.6-4.2% of 2050 GDP for 1.5 C pathways ($2.7-4.4T), Nordhaus (2019) ~1% of output for a 50% cut ($1.05T). See cost_components.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: needs a binding agreement among many countries. Carbon pricing covers only ~24% of global emissions and prices 'continue to fall short' of Paris levels (World Bank 2024); the IMF's own proposal is a differentiated floor among large emitters only (Parry, Black & Roaf 2021), and the IMF put the global average price at $2/t in 2019.
policies.who_benefits_reason: IMF (2019): a $75/t tax alone raises electricity prices ~45% and gasoline ~15% over a decade, hitting poorer households and fossil-dependent developing countries hardest; higher heating costs raise winter deaths (Chirakijja et al. 2024). Only lump-sum rebates reverse this (Tax Foundation: bottom quintile +6.8% after-tax income), and the policy as defined does not require them.
policies.summary: A $135-per-tonne global carbon tax by 2030 is a 1.5 C-strength price, about twice the social cost of carbon on the cost-benefit optimal path in the latest Nordhaus model and above the $115 optimal price that model reaches only by 2050, which also finds the 1.5 C path infeasible. Published cost-benefit studies put its cost at 5.6% of world output, roughly $5.9 trillion a year, and its author says uneven national implementation 'would readily double' that, against climate benefits of 2.2-3.1% of world output. Higher energy prices add winter deaths, and a world economy 5-11% smaller means an estimated 152,000-505,000 more infant deaths a year in poor countries. Each dollar returns about 0.16 to 0.55 dollars of benefit.
policies.selected_by: Paris-aligned carbon price; IMF international carbon price floor

policies.title: Global Plastic Ban
policies.bcr_basis: Net-damage construction: BCR = (regulator-monetised benefit per $ of cost) - (extra environmental damage from heavier substitutes per $ of cost), with cost = $869bn/yr (cost_components). HIGH 0.30: Canada's RIAS (2022) monetised benefits C$616m vs costs C$1,990m = 0.31; its costs already include administration, enforcement, substitution and manufacturers' costs, so no full-cost adjustment is needed. It does not monetise substitutes' emissions, so the smallest published substitution penalty is subtracted: Meng, Brandao & Cullen (2024) find plastics emit 10-90% less than alternatives in 15 of 16 applications, so alternatives emit at least 1/0.9 = 1.11x; plastics are ~4.5% of 57.1 GtCO2e = 2.57 Gt; 11% of that = 0.28 Gt x $36/t (Nordhaus) = $10bn; 10/869 = 0.012; 0.31 - 0.012 = 0.30. LOW -0.42: Defra's straw-ban IA lowest case 2.4/77.7 = 0.03 (already counts paper-straw CO2) minus the monetised environmental cost of replacing plastics: Trucost (2016, commissioned by the American Chemistry Council) values the natural-capital cost of plastics in consumer goods and packaging at $139bn/yr and of functionally equivalent alternatives at $533bn/yr; (533 - 139)/869 = 0.45; 0.03 - 0.45 = -0.42. Supporting life-cycle evidence: Franklin Associates (2018, for ACC) find substitutes for US plastic packaging weigh ~4.5x as much and plastic's global-warming potential is 26.2% of the substitutes' (substitutes ~3.8x); UK Environment Agency (2011): paper, LDPE, non-woven PP and cotton bags must be reused 3, 4, 11 and 131 times to match a single-use HDPE bag's global-warming potential; Danish EPA (2018): cotton 7,100-20,000 uses across all indicators; Taylor (2019, JEEM): ~30% of California's bag-ban plastic reduction offset by extra trash-bag purchases. Sensitivity with only the peer-reviewed Meng penalty at $185/t: 0.28 x 185 = $53bn; 0.03 - 53/869 = -0.03. Counter-evidence: UNEP (2023) and Lau et al. (2020) find net savings for reuse- and recycling-led packages, not bans. Tax-finance check: each $1 of public outlay or public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); government compliance and enforcement is C$0.9m of Canada's C$234m (0.4%; $0.12bn of $869bn globally, 0.01% of cost_bn); the penalty changes neither end at two decimals and is not applied (negligible).
policies.grade_reason: Built from regulators' own impact analyses (Canada RIAS, UK Defra IA) adjusted with a peer-reviewed life-cycle study (Meng et al. 2024) and peer-reviewed substitution evidence (Taylor 2019); the low end uses an industry-commissioned natural-capital valuation (Trucost 2016), which on its own would rate C+. No study monetises a global ban.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost = public outlay $0 + administration ~$0.12bn + private compliance ~$28.9bn (Canada RIAS per-capita cost of its single-use ban, ~C$5/person/yr, scaled to 8.0bn people) + GDP loss ~$840bn (OECD 2022: 0.8% of world GDP for its most ambitious plastics package, applied to ~$105T). See cost_components for arithmetic and the double-counting check.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: needs a binding international agreement among many countries. UN plastics-treaty talks (INC-5.2, Geneva, August 2025) adjourned without consensus, with production limits among the contested issues (UNEP), and the resumed one-day INC-5.3 session on 7 February 2026 was organisational only (electing a new Chair after the previous Chair resigned), with no substantive negotiation.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Bag bans and fees weigh most on low-income shoppers (Reason, Morris & Seasholes 2014), Defra expects 60% of the higher substitute costs to pass through to consumers, and the OECD (2022) finds costs of ambitious action concentrated in non-OECD countries.
policies.summary: Governments that have banned single-use plastics measured costs well above the benefits they could put a number on: Canada's ban returns about 31 cents per dollar and England's straw ban as little as 3 cents. Life-cycle studies find that the substitutes (paper, glass, metal, cotton) usually weigh more and emit more greenhouse gas, so a general ban can add environmental damage; one valuation puts the extra damage at about $394bn a year. Counting compliance and a GDP cost of about 0.8% of world output (~$870bn a year), the return ranges from about minus 42 cents to plus 30 cents per dollar.
policies.selected_by: UN plastics treaty negotiations (UNEA resolution 5/14)

policies.title: Green New Deal
policies.bcr_basis: Scored as if every Western nation (US, Canada, EU-27, UK, Norway, Switzerland, Iceland, Australia, New Zealand) adopts the US Green New Deal package. Their combined 2024 GDP is $58,287bn, 1.99x the US (World Bank WDI), and their fossil CO2 is 8,669 Mt, 1.77x the US (Global Carbon Project). US figures per year (AAF outlays, Heritage GDP loss, CEI compliance, Chirakijja et al. winter deaths) are scaled by 1.99. Cross-checks on the scaling: Canada's PBO finds 2030 real GDP 1.4% lower. Form: the same net-damage form as the UBI, student-loan and Social Security entries. Health-care outlays are transfers worth $1 to recipients per $1; job-guarantee pay is worth about half the gross wage to participants, because they give up other income and time (Jalan & Ravallion 2003, Argentina's Trabajar public-works programme). The deadweight of the taxes that fund all outlays, the GDP loss, induced deaths and poor-country infant deaths are subtracted from benefits. Financing at this scale: at the peak of the Laffer curve the US can raise at most about 7.4% of GDP in extra tax revenue and the EU-14 about 3.1% (Trabandt & Uhlig 2012, Table 7). New tax-financed outlays larger than that cannot be raised at the 34-cent marginal burden measured for small changes (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985). Policies whose new tax-financed outlays exceed 7.4% of GDP therefore use Feldstein's (1999) estimate, which 'may exceed $2 per $1 of revenue', at both ends of the range. The Green New Deal's outlays are about 32% of Western GDP, over four times the US Laffer maximum and ten times the EU-14's. Climate benefit: Western-only cuts leak to other countries through trade and lower world fuel prices. Leakage estimates run from a 12% mean (EMF 29, Böhringer, Balistreri & Rutherford 2012) to 130% (Babiker 2005), where global emissions rise. The low end uses Babiker's 130% at Nordhaus's $36/t; the high end uses the 12% mean at the DICE-2023 social cost of carbon of $66/t (Barrage & Nordhaus 2024), the most recent estimate from the model's authors. LOW = (health transfers 7,164 + job-guarantee value 4,438 [0.5 x 4,460 x 1.99] + climate -93.6 [8.669 Gt x $36 x (1 - 1.30)] - winter deaths 204.8 - GDP loss 1,421 [Heritage 714 x 1.99] - deadweight 36,974 [2.0 x outlays 9,290 x 1.99] - infant deaths 32.4) / (outlays + admin + compliance 20,220) = -1.34. HIGH = (health transfers 7,164 + job-guarantee value 677 + climate 503.5 [8.669 Gt x $66 x 0.88] - winter deaths 204.8 - deadweight 20,338 [2.0 x 5,110 x 1.99]) / (10,227) = -1.19. Infant deaths: the GDP loss is 2.44% of Western GDP; a 1 pp US growth shock moves developing-country growth by 0.6 pp (Kose et al. 2017) and a G7 shock by about 1.4 pp (Huidrom, Kose & Ohnsorge 2017, Figure 3), so developing-country GDP falls 1.5-3.4%; at 0.24-0.40 extra infant deaths per 1,000 births per 1% fall in GDP per person (Baird, Friedman & Schady, REStat 2011) on ~119.9m births a year in low- and middle-income countries (World Bank), that is 42,088-163,676 infant deaths a year, valued at $198,000 each. Output produced by job-guarantee workers is not valued; no published estimate exists for a national job guarantee. Lost-income mortality: income lost to a policy costs lives. Broughel & Viscusi (Mercatus 2017) put it at about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed; valued at the HHS VSL of $13.1m, each $1 of net income lost carries 13.1/99.3 = $0.132 of mortality cost (and each $1 gained saves the same). This adjustment is applied uniformly to every policy after the published range is drawn. Tax finance (net-damage form): each $1 of public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); as for the other net-damage entries, the burden is subtracted from benefits; the outlays already carry Feldstein's $2 per $1 at both ends, but administration ($382bn a year at the low end, 1.25% of cost_bn) did not; adding it: LOW = (-27,123.8 - 2.0 x 382) / 20,220 = -27,887.8 / 20,220 = -1.38. The high end's non-outlay cost is at most 10,227 - 10,169 (5,110 x 1.99) = $58bn; even if all of it were administration, 2.0 x 58 = 116 would move the high end only from -1.19 to -1.20, so it is left at -1.19.
policies.grade_reason: The parameters that drive the ratio are peer-reviewed (SCC: Nordhaus 2019, Barrage & Nordhaus 2024; mortality elasticity: Chirakijja et al. 2024; marginal deadweight of taxation: Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985, Feldstein 1999), combined in a published-model framework (Tol 2023). The cost quantities themselves (AAF, Heritage, CEI) are think-tank estimates (C+ level), and no study computes a BCR for the GND, so B is the ceiling.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost for all Western nations, US$bn a year (US high-end components x 1.99): public outlays 18,487 + administration 382 + private compliance 1,351 + GDP and welfare loss 10,295 (Heritage GDP loss plus tax deadweight at 48 cents per $1) = 30,515, about half of Western GDP. Most of the outlay is health-care and job-guarantee transfers.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: no precedent anywhere; it would replace the US fossil-fuel energy system and add federal outlays of $5-9 trillion a year (AAF), and the resolution failed 0-57 in the Senate on 26 March 2019 (NBC News).
policies.who_benefits_reason: The energy core raises household electricity spending ~30% (Heritage 2019) and costs a typical household >$70,000 in year one in most states studied (CEI 2019); cheaper heating measurably saves lives among the poor and elderly (Chirakijja et al. 2024), so higher energy prices fall hardest on them. The job guarantee, health care, worker-transition payments and foreign clean-energy finance are transfers toward lower-income groups, and Galvani et al. (2020) find single-payer financing would give the most relief to lower-income households; no study models the net distribution once the energy costs and the taxes that fund the package are included.
policies.summary: The Green New Deal bundles a crash net-zero energy programme with a job guarantee, universal health care, worker-transition support and clean-energy money for poor countries; here every Western nation adopts it. Its outlays alone come to about a third of Western GDP, more than four times the most extra tax revenue the US could raise at the peak of its Laffer curve, so it cannot be financed without very large losses from taxation. Because only Western nations cut, part or all of the reduction leaks abroad: published estimates run from 12% to 130%, the last meaning world emissions rise. Job-guarantee pay is worth about half its cost to the workers, and the GDP loss slows developing economies, which means an estimated 42,000-164,000 more infant deaths a year. Each dollar spent destroys about $1.19-1.38 of value.
policies.selected_by: H.Res.109, US Congress 2019

policies.title: 15-Minute Cities
policies.bcr_basis: Annual flows at C40 scale (523m people in 2017, ~25% of world GDP = $26,250bn; 240 private vehicles per 1,000 = 125.5m), C40/Arup/Leeds (2019) ambitious targets as mandates. Form: the caps are rationing, so they are scored in the same net-damage form as price controls: lost consumer value, lost output and induced deaths are subtracted from benefits, and the cost base is the money spent to carry the rule out (administration plus mandatory retrofits). Benefits. Climate: the report's ambitious interventions save ~32 GtCO2e over 2017-50 (0.97 Gt/yr); the low end counts only the mandated categories (food 10.5, clothing 4.3, private transport 3.8, aviation 1.9 = 20.5 Gt, Fig. 15) less the report's one-third rebound = 0.41 Gt/yr x $36/t (Nordhaus 2019) = $15bn; the high end values 0.97 Gt at the DICE-2023 $66/t (Barrage & Nordhaus 2024) = $64bn, plus operational CO2 of banned cars 125.5m x 4.6 t (EPA) x $66 = $38bn (excluded at the low end because the C40 baseline already electrifies cars). Car externalities (Parry et al. 2007): 125.5m x 11,026 mi (FHWA) x 5-10 c/mi = $69-138bn. Retrofits: Fowlie et al. (2018) BCR 0.37-0.94 x $571bn = $211-536bn. Total benefits $295bn (low) and $776bn (high). Diet changes are not credited with any health benefit. Costs (cost_basis) run from $1,896bn (low) to $8,042bn (high), including the loss of city productivity from slower travel once private cars are removed. LOW = (benefits 295 - meat 3,420 - car access 1,405 - slower travel 1,932 - aviation 130 - trade 560 - infant deaths 5.1) / (admin 23.8 + retrofits 571) = -12.03. HIGH = (benefits 776 - meat 273 - car access 276 - slower travel 708 - aviation 21 - trade 36 - infant deaths 0.20) / (admin 11.6 + retrofits 571) = -0.92. Unpriced items would lower both ends: dairy and restaurant-meat welfare, the clothing consumer-surplus loss, leisure-flight consumer surplus, replacement transit capital, and trips other than the journey to work. Flows are steady-state annual values, so the ratio of flows approximates the ratio of present values. Infant deaths: lost trade lowers world income by 0.034-0.53% (560/105,000 at the high end); at 0.24-0.40 extra infant deaths per 1,000 births per 1% fall in GDP per person (Baird, Friedman & Schady, REStat 2011) on ~119.9m births a year in low- and middle-income countries (World Bank), that is 987-25,563 infant deaths a year, valued at $198,000 each. Scope: C40's report states the consumption interventions come on top of the cities' Deadline 2020 sector commitments (zero-carbon buildings, renewable energy, zero-emission transport): 'A more explicit focus on urban emissions from a consumption perspective does not supplant previous C40 efforts to reduce production-based emissions; the two agendas are complementary' (pp. 60-61). Those sector plans are scored separately under the Green New Deal entry, so they are not added here. The main published estimate for cities' sector plans (Coalition for Urban Transitions 2019) projects savings above investment, but measured programmes realise only about half of projected energy savings (Christensen et al. 2023, 51%; Fowlie et al. 2018, 38%), which turns its projected saving into a net cost of about $0.4-0.8tn a year (see counter_sources). Measured local effects of car restrictions: Madrid Central cut affected consumers' in-person spending in the zone by 21% (Galdon-Sanchez et al. 2023, JEEA). Lost-income mortality: income lost to a policy costs lives. Broughel & Viscusi (Mercatus 2017) put it at about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed; valued at the HHS VSL of $13.1m, each $1 of net income lost carries 13.1/99.3 = $0.132 of mortality cost (and each $1 gained saves the same). This adjustment is applied uniformly to every policy after the published range is drawn. Tax-finance check: each $1 of public outlay or public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); administration of the allowance system is $23.8bn of $8,042bn (0.30% of cost_bn); the penalty changes neither end at two decimals and is not applied (negligible).
policies.grade_reason: No study prices this bundle and per-person caps on meat, dairy, clothing, flights and car ownership have never been applied at scale outside wartime rationing, so the ratio is built by scaling component estimates to the C40 network. The dominant cost terms come from peer-reviewed work but are extrapolations: Lusk & Norwood (2009) describe their 100% meat-removal figure as far outside the data, and Moody et al. (2021) is a stated-preference survey in four US metros. The travel-speed loss applies a cross-city productivity elasticity (Prud'homme & Lee 1999) to a change far larger than those observed. Aviation and auto footprints come from industry-commissioned studies (ATAG/Oxford Economics, CAR), the trade term applies cross-country elasticities (Frankel & Romer 1999; Feyrer 2019) to a demand shock, and the emission savings are the proposer's own model. Individual components have stronger evidence (Fowlie et al. 2018 retrofit BCA from a randomized encouragement design; Wolff 2014 LEZ natural experiments), which would grade A-/B+ on their own.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, US$ bn a year at C40 scale; HIGH-end sum shown. Admin $23.8bn (Defra 2008 personal carbon allowance, scaled per person). Private compliance $5,396bn: meat elimination $3,420bn (Lusk & Norwood 2009, 13.0% of GDP applied to C40's ~$26.25T GDP), car-ownership ban $1,405bn (Moody et al. 2021, $11,197 per vehicle x 125.5m vehicles), mandatory retrofits $571bn (EU Renovation Wave, 2.17% of GDP). GDP loss $2,622bn: slower travel without private cars $1,932bn (Prud'homme & Lee 1999 productivity-speed elasticity; Census commute times; Prieto-Curiel & Ospina 2024 car share), aviation $130bn (ATAG/Oxford Economics $4.1T footprint x C40 share 10.2% x 31% cut) and lost trade $560bn (Frankel & Romer 1999 upper elasticity on lost clothing and meat exports). Public outlay: none estimated (replacement transit not priced). Low-end readings give $1,896bn.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: low-emission zones and building renovation rules have precedents (German LEZs, EU building directives), but binding personal caps on meat and dairy (0 kg), clothing (3 items a year), flights (one short-haul return trip every 3 years) and private car ownership (zero) have no modern peacetime precedent and would need a ration-tracking system; Defra's 2008 pre-feasibility study put even a simpler personal carbon allowance at GBP 1-2bn a year to run for the UK alone, and the scheme was not pursued. C40 itself 'does not advocate' the ambitious targets (C40/Arup/Leeds 2019), and the median US resident makes only 14% of consumption trips locally (Abbiasov et al. 2024).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Abbiasov et al. (2024) find that higher local-trip usage goes with higher experienced segregation for low-income residents; travel confined to the neighbourhood cuts access to city-wide job markets (Prud'homme & Lee 1999); LEZs and car bans force owners of older vehicles to replace them first (Wolff 2014). Outside the cities, lost clothing and meat demand falls on exporters .
policies.summary: The 15-minute city is a planning idea (daily needs within a short walk); this version adds the C40 'ambitious' consumption targets as mandates (no meat or dairy, 3 new clothing items a year, no private cars, one short-haul return flight every three years) plus low-emission zones and mandatory retrofits, targets C40 itself does not advocate. Priced at C40-city scale, the full cost runs from about $1.9 trillion to $8.0 trillion a year: lost consumer value from removing meat (Lusk & Norwood 2009) and private cars (Moody et al. 2021), retrofit spending, output lost from smaller aviation, tourism and trade, and up to $1.9 trillion of lost productivity as commutes that took 24 minutes by car take 48 by transit. Benefits from avoided emissions, cleaner and safer streets and fewer energy-wasting buildings come to about $0.3 trillion to $0.8 trillion a year. Priced as rationing, in the same way as price controls, every dollar spent carrying it out destroys between $0.92 and $12 of value, before about 81,000 deaths a year from lost income and up to 26,000 infant deaths a year in poor countries from lost trade. These caps come on top of the cities' own energy and building plans.
policies.selected_by: C40 Cities 'Future of Urban Consumption' (city governments)

policies.title: Innovation Prizes
policies.bcr_basis: No study measures the return on privately funded prizes, so each sub-area takes the best published R&D return. Energy technology: Galiana & Green (Copenhagen Consensus 2012) find more low-carbon R&D yields benefits '3 to 11 times' its cost; their 2009 Copenhagen Consensus paper put ~$100bn/yr of R&D at ~11 (Lomborg 2009). Agricultural yields: low 7.5, the lowest ex-ante BCR across the three adoption/technology scenarios for an advance market commitment aimed at either of the two most cost-effective targets, West African maize (8.7/22.6/7.5) and East African sorghum (10.4/25.7/7.7) (Glennerster et al. 2024, Table 3, PDF p.11; weaker targets run as low as 0.3, Table A9, PDF p.26); high 33, Rosegrant et al. (2023, JBCA) for +$5.2bn/yr of Global South ag R&D (bracketed by Alston et al. 2011, 21-32). Geoengineering research: low 25 (Bickel & Lane 2009, stratospheric aerosols, deployment: 'on the order of 25 to 1', as reported by Pielke 2009, p.6), high ~1,000 per research dollar (Bickel & Lane 2012) for a programme 'on the order of a billion dollars' in total. Weighting: the three sub-areas are weighted equally, because a prize pool is an expected-return allocation: the money is paid only for results, so it flows to whichever innovations succeed, and a funder can direct it toward the highest-return areas rather than in proportion to existing R&D budgets. LOW = (3 energy + 7.5 agriculture + 25 geoengineering)/3 = 11.8. HIGH = (11 + 33 + 1,000)/3 = 348. The high end is driven by Bickel & Lane's ~1,000:1 return on geoengineering research, a Copenhagen Consensus estimate that other researchers dispute (Pielke 2009, 'precision without accuracy'; Goes et al. 2011); the evidence grade (B) shrinks the range toward 1:1 in the ranking. Sensitivity: weighting by the size of each source's R&D programme ($100bn energy, $5.2bn agriculture, ~$0.1bn geoengineering) gives LOW = (100 x 3 + 5.2 x 7.5 + 0.1 x 25)/105.3 = 3.2 and HIGH = (100 x 11 + 5.2 x 33 + 0.1 x 1,000)/105.3 = 13.0; the raw span is 3-1,000. Prize mechanism: historical prizes raised high-quality patenting (Brunt, Lerner & Nicholas 2012); the $1.5bn pneumococcal AMC saved ~700,000 lives at ~$83/DALY (Kremer, Levin & Snyder 2020). Williams (2012) warns prizes are hard to evaluate and best seen as a complement to grants. Administration: the source ratios are per research dollar; competing teams typically spend far more than the purse (Ansari X Prize: $10M purse, >$100M of team spending, McKinsey 2009), so administration equal to the purse adds roughly 10/110 = ~9% to the social resource cost, which would give 11.8/1.1 = 10.7 to 348/1.1 = 316. If instead the purse were treated as the only research input, administration equal to the purse would halve the ratios (5.9-174). The range is stated per research dollar.
policies.grade_reason: The weighted range rests mainly on Galiana & Green's Copenhagen Consensus models (published in the Cambridge University Press volume 'Global Problems, Smart Solutions'), with a peer-reviewed JBCA estimate for ag R&D (Rosegrant et al. 2023) and peer-reviewed evidence that prizes and AMCs induce innovation (Brunt et al. 2012; Kremer et al. 2020). Not A-: no study measures the return on prize money itself, and the geoengineering figures are contested think-tank estimates.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost = public outlay $0 + private prize administration ~$0.14bn/yr (XPRIZE rule of thumb: operating costs equal the purse, applied to ~$0.14bn/yr of current private climate prize and AMC funding). Voluntary private prize money, so no government spending or mandate: $0 public cost. For scale, existing private pull funding: XPRIZE Carbon Removal $100M awarded April 2025 (Musk Foundation); Frontier advance market commitment $925M over eight years from Stripe, Alphabet, Shopify, Meta and McKinsey (April 2022, ~$0.12bn/yr); a heat-resilient-crop AMC costs $50-376M per crop target (Glennerster et al. 2024). Large-prize philanthropy totalled only ~$375M over the decade to 2009 (McKinsey 2009).
policies.difficulty_reason: Easy: a single philanthropic or corporate funder can do it under existing law, and it has been done many times (Ansari X Prize, XPRIZE Carbon Removal 2025, Frontier AMC 2022, pneumococcal AMC).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Agricultural-yield prizes are pro-poor (Rosegrant et al. 2023 project 35% less hunger and 16% lower food prices in the Global South after 35 years, 2022-2056), while cheaper clean energy and climate-risk research benefit everyone; no source measures the distribution across the combined programme.
policies.summary: Privately funded prizes and advance market commitments pay out only when someone delivers a defined result: higher crop yields, cheaper clean energy, or answers about geoengineering. No study measures the return on prize money itself, but the research they would fund has some of the best returns in the literature: about $3-11 per dollar for clean-energy R&D (Copenhagen Consensus), $9-33 for agricultural R&D, and very high but contested figures for geoengineering research. Weighting the three areas equally, on the view that prize money flows to the highest-return results, gives about $11.80 to $348 of benefit per dollar, with no cost to taxpayers; weighting by the size of each research programme gives about $3 to $13.
policies.selected_by: Mission Innovation (governments' clean-energy R&D pledge, Paris 2015); Copenhagen Consensus R&D findings

policies.title: Rent Control
policies.bcr_basis: No study publishes a single benefit-cost ratio for rent control, so the ratio is built from two peer-reviewed or NBER natural experiments as: value reaching protected tenants, net of the harm the rule does to everyone else, of administration and of misallocation, per $1 taken from property owners and other renters. Supply effects, LOW base 0.34: Diamond, McQuade & Qian (2019, AER), San Francisco's 1994 expansion. The NBER conference draft puts benefits to the covered 1994 tenant cohort at $7.62bn over 1995-2012 (about $423m a year, 2010 dollars, of which roughly a third are landlord buyout payments, i.e. transfers). The 15% cut in rental supply by treated landlords raised citywide rents (7% in the draft; 5.1% in the NBER abstract) and caused about $5bn of welfare losses to all renters, which the authors say is 'almost as large' as the gains. (7.62 - 5.0) / 7.62 = 0.34: only about 34 cents of each $1 of tenant benefit survives as a net gain for renters as a class, before counting landlords' own losses (which would push it lower). Supply effects, HIGH base 0.67: Ahern & Giacoletti (2022, NBER w30083), St. Paul's 2021 rent-control law: property values fell 6-7%, an aggregate $1.57bn, of which their model attributes 67% to direct capitalisation (the transfer to tenants) and 33% (at least $518m) to deadweight externalities. 1 - 0.33 = 0.67 is an upper bound, since even the 'transfer' share reaches tenants only to the extent they stay. Cross-check: Autor, Palmer & Pathak (2014, JPE) find that ending rent control in Cambridge, MA added about $1.8bn to property values over 1994-2004, nearly a quarter of the city's total residential price appreciation, mostly on never-controlled properties, confirming that controls depress neighbouring values (an externality not counted in the high case). Administration: San Francisco's Rent Board costs $13.8m a year (FY2024-25) against the $423m a year of benefits to the 1994 cohort alone, so administration is at most 13.8 / 423 = 3.3% of the transfer (an upper bound, since the board also serves earlier-controlled units and the budget is in 2024 dollars while the transfer is in 2010 dollars). HIGH: 0.67 - 0.033 = 0.64. LOW, using the high-end published per-unit cost (Berkeley ~$324 vs SF ~$59.5 per unit, 5.4 times higher): 3.3% x 5.44 = 17.8% of the transfer, so 0.34 - 0.18 = 0.16. Landlords' own compliance time is not counted (no estimate), so the true ends are slightly lower. Misallocation: Glaeser & Luttmer (NBER w6220, 1997; AER 2003) put the cost of controlled apartments going to the wrong households in New York City (1993 Housing and Vacancy Survey) at a best estimate of $200 per regulated apartment a year, with a lower bound of more than $40 (observable characteristics only) and an upper range of $200-2,000. Scale of the transfer: Mildner (1987 data, as tabulated by Turner & Malpezzi 2003) puts the landlord's cost of the subsidy on a New York rent-controlled unit at $122 a month, $1,464 a year; at 1993 prices (CPI-U 144.475 / 113.617 = 1.272) that is $1,862. Misallocation as a share of the transfer: LOW, best estimate 200 / 1,862 = 10.7%; HIGH, lower bound 40 / 1,862 = 2.1%. LOW = 0.16 - 0.107 = 0.05. HIGH = 0.64 - 0.021 = 0.62. Both ends are below 1. Dividing by the rent-controlled subsidy (the largest category; Mildner finds stabilized units at or above market rent in 1987) keeps these shares conservative. No double counting: Diamond et al. measure the supply cut and its effect on market rents, and Ahern & Giacoletti measure property-value externalities; neither measures which households occupy the controlled units. The transfer from owners is counted at $1 for $1, with no extra weight for tenants. Not added (no conversion to dollars per $1 of transfer): Gyourko & Linneman (1990) find Manhattan units under the older controls had a 9 percent higher probability of being in unsound condition; Sims (2007) finds Massachusetts controls moved units out of the rental market (condominium conversion) and lowered quality; and Early (2000), as summarised by Turner & Malpezzi, finds that once higher uncontrolled rents are counted the average benefit to tenants in regulated New York units was negative, which would place the low end below zero (about -0.83); it is not used because the figures come from a review table and the tenant-benefit measure may already include part of Diamond et al.'s rent effect. Glaeser & Luttmer's upper misallocation range ($200-2,000) would also push the low end well below zero. Cross-check: Olsen (1972) finds New York tenants valued a $406 a year subsidy at $213, a transfer efficiency of 0.52, and Turner & Malpezzi's cross-country table shows 0.45-0.99, so a large share of each $1 is lost even before effects on other renters. Tax finance (net-damage form): each $1 of public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); as for the other net-damage entries, the burden is subtracted from benefits; rent boards are funded by registration fees charged to landlords (San Francisco: 'funded by the Rent Board fee'; Berkeley: about $6.88m + 5,700 x $212 = $8.09m of fees against an $8.33m budget, 97%), and fees are part of the transfer already counted, so at most 2.9% of administration is tax-financed. HIGH (San Francisco, fee-funded): no change, 0.62. LOW (Berkeley cost level): 0.34 - 0.178 - 0.107 - 2.0 x (0.029 x 0.178) = 0.055 - 0.010 = 0.04.
policies.grade_reason: The numbers come from peer-reviewed and NBER natural experiments that measure the size of gains and losses (Diamond, McQuade & Qian 2019 AER; Autor, Palmer & Pathak 2014 JPE; Ahern & Giacoletti 2022 NBER), converted into a ratio by direct arithmetic. No published benefit-cost study exists, so A-level grades do not apply. Expert consensus (Clark Center 2012 and 2024) and a 2024 peer-reviewed literature review (Kholodilin, JHE) point the same way. The misallocation term uses a peer-reviewed estimate (Glaeser & Luttmer 2003 AER) converted with a published subsidy figure; the conversion mixes data years (1987 subsidy, 1993 misallocation) and cities, which keeps the grade at B+.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: $0 (no budget transfer; rent boards are usually fee-funded). Administration: rent boards' budgets per covered unit, scaled to the 46.8m US renter-occupied units (Census HVS, Q2 2026). Berkeley's FY2024-25 Rent Board budget ($8.33m, ~25,700 units, ~$324 per unit) gives $15.2bn a year, the high end used here; San Francisco's FY2024-25 budget ($13.83m, 232,263 units, ~$59.5 per unit) gives $2.8bn. Private compliance: no published estimate (landlords' registration fees are the board budgets already counted). GDP loss: supply and welfare losses are inside the ratio and are not published at national scale. The transfer from owners to tenants is not a cost and stays inside the ratio. cost_bn = 0 + 15.2 = $15.2bn a year.
policies.difficulty_reason: Ordinary legislation at city or state level, with many precedents (New York, San Francisco, St. Paul 2021; Clark Center's 2024 poll concerns a proposed national 5% cap on corporate landlords). A national cap would need an act of Congress, but no constitutional change.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Ahern & Giacoletti (2022) find the St. Paul tenants who gained most had higher incomes and were more likely white, while the owners who lost most had lower incomes and were more likely minorities. Diamond, McQuade & Qian (2019) find the lost rental supply raised market rents for later (often younger, poorer) renters and fuelled gentrification. Benefits go to incumbent tenants regardless of need.
policies.summary: Rent control caps how fast rents can rise on covered apartments. It is very popular: over 85% of about 5,000 voters supported capping rents in Elmendorf, Nall & Oklobdzija's 2024 survey experiment (and 73.9% of US GSS/ISSP respondents say government should 'keep prices under control'). Economists disagree: 89% of the Clark Center panel in 2012 and 80% in 2024 rejected the claim that rent caps help. Natural experiments in San Francisco and St. Paul show covered tenants gain, but landlords pull 15% of units off the rental market, raising rents for everyone else and destroying a third or more of the value transferred; New York evidence adds that controlled apartments end up with the wrong households (about $200 a unit a year) and decay faster. Rent boards also cost about $60-324 per covered unit a year, roughly $3-15bn a year nationally. Counting these costs, each $1 taken from owners and renters yields roughly $0.04-0.62 of net benefit, a ratio below 1.
policies.selected_by: ~85% support (survey experiment n≈5,000); ISSP price-control items

policies.title: Price Controls
policies.bcr_basis: A binding price ceiling transfers money from sellers to buyers who still get the good, and destroys value three ways: the Harberger triangle (trades that no longer happen), misallocation (goods go to people or places that value them less), and queuing (buyers burn time to get the cheap goods). Ratio = (transfer - queuing - Harberger - misallocation - administration and compliance) / transfer, i.e. net value to buyers per $1 taken from sellers, the same net-damage form used for other transfer policies. Calibration from Albrecht, Tabarrok & Whitmeyer (2026, arXiv working paper), using station-level data from the 1973-74 US gasoline controls: ceiling 20% below baseline price, 9% quantity shortfall, Harberger triangle 2.0% of baseline spending, misallocation 2.2-17.7% of spending (1.09-8.75 times the triangle). Transfer = 0.20 x 0.91 = 18.2% of spending. Queuing: Deacon & Sonstelie (1989, Economic Inquiry), using the US gasoline controls, estimate that rent seeking (time in queues plus the waste from buying more per purchase) 'exhausts an estimated 116 percent of the rent transferred'. Buyers' net gain is then 18.2 - 1.16 x 18.2 = 18.2 - 21.11 = -2.91 points of baseline spending. Frech & Lee (1987, QJE) and Deacon & Sonstelie (1985, JPE), as summarised by Albrecht et al., likewise find queuing costs could exceed the whole transfer. Administration and compliance: Blinder & Newton (1981) find the 1971-74 controls had cut the non-food, non-energy price level by 3-4%; applied to 1973 GDP ($1,425bn) the transfer was at most $43-57bn a year (an upper bound on the base, since controls did not cover all output, so the cost share is if anything understated). Admin $0.08bn + compliance $2.0bn a year = $2.08bn / $42.8bn = 4.9% of the transfer, or 0.89 points on the 18.2-point gasoline scale. LOW = -1.29, with the highest misallocation: (-2.91 - 2.0 - 17.7 - 0.89) / 18.2 = -23.50 / 18.2 = -1.29. Albrecht et al. state that their misallocation (stations or regions receiving nothing) is a distinct loss that 'exists even in a hypothetical world with zero queuing costs', so the two are added. HIGH = -0.44, with the lowest misallocation: (-2.91 - 2.0 - 2.2 - 0.89) / 18.2 = -0.44. Albrecht et al. note that their upper-bound shadow prices correspond to queuing equilibria, so some overlap between queuing and misallocation is possible; pairing the measured queuing loss with the lowest misallocation allows for it. No measured case shows zero queuing cost. Cross-checks: Henderson's 1979 arithmetic (controlled price 80c, DOE market-clearing price $1.00, effective price including waiting $1.20) gives buyers -20c per gallon against a 20c transfer, about -1.0. Davis & Kilian (2011, JPE) find allocative losses from US natural-gas ceilings averaged $4.6bn a year (1950-2000) and 'effectively triple' the net welfare loss: MacAvoy's $6.9bn transfer against $9.3bn deadweight plus $5.9bn allocative cost a year in 1968-77 gives (6.9 - 9.3 - 5.9) / 6.9 = -1.20. Tarr (1994, World Bank Economic Review) finds that Polish price controls on colour televisions, with rents dissipated, cost 0.46% of GDP, 112% of producers' sales, and about ten times the Harberger triangle (rectangle 116bn zlotys, triangle 14bn), i.e. (116 - 116 - 14) / 116 = -0.12 per $1 transferred before any misallocation term. Short, disaster-only price-gouging laws sit inside this range: the CRA International study for ACCF estimated a $1.9bn welfare loss had a federal law applied after Katrina and Rita (Sept-Oct 2005). Enforcement scale: the WWII Office of Price Administration imposed 259,966 sanctions in 1941-47, and one business in fifteen was charged with illicit transactions (Higgs 2009, citing Rockoff 1984 and Lingeman); Rockoff notes black markets left poor statistical records, so they are not priced here. Tax finance (net-damage form): each $1 of public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); as for the other net-damage entries, the burden is subtracted from benefits; only the Cost of Living Council's administration ($80m a year, 0.19% of the transfer, 0.034 points on the 18.2-point scale) is tax-financed; compliance is private. LOW = (-23.50 - 2.0 x 0.034) / 18.2 = -1.295, still -1.29; HIGH = (-8.00 - 0.34 x 0.034) / 18.2 = -0.440, still -0.44. Negligible at two decimals.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed historical natural experiments measure the losses (Frech & Lee 1987 QJE; Deacon & Sonstelie 1985 JPE; Davis & Kilian 2011 JPE; Blinder & Newton 1981 JME; Cavallo et al. 2014 RIW), and a 2026 working paper (Albrecht, Tabarrok & Whitmeyer) supplies the bounds used in the arithmetic. No published benefit-cost ratio exists. Expert consensus is strong (Clark Center 2012 and 2024). Both ends use a peer-reviewed queuing estimate (Deacon & Sonstelie 1989), with Tarr (1994, WBER) as a cross-check.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, for general price controls on the 1971-74 model. Public outlay: $0. Administration: Dunlop's estimate that the 1971-74 controls cost taxpayers nearly $200m over about 2.5 years ($80m a year, 0.0056% of 1973 GDP) scales to $1.7bn a year at 2025 GDP ($30.9T, FRED). Private compliance: Dunlop's industry estimate was $721m-$2bn for the whole period, while other sources cited by Bleiberg put it at about $2bn a year; the high end, 0.14% of 1973 GDP, scales to $43.3bn a year (the low end would be $6.2bn). GDP loss: shortages, queues and misallocation sit inside the ratio and have no modern economy-wide estimate. Seller-to-buyer price cuts are transfers. cost_bn = 0 + 1.7 + 43.3 = $45.0bn a year. Disaster-only anti-gouging laws would cost a small fraction of this.
policies.difficulty_reason: Ordinary legislation. Many US states already have price-gouging statutes (CRS R47072 reviews federal and state authority), and the 1971-74 Nixon programme shows economy-wide controls under an act of Congress. No constitutional change needed.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The transfer goes to whoever obtains the price-capped good, not specifically to the poor. Queuing favours people with low time costs, misallocation sends goods to lower-value users, and Cavallo et al. (2014) show that stable prices after disasters came with 17-32% fewer goods on shelves. No source shows a clear progressive or regressive tilt.
policies.summary: Price Controls & Price Gouging caps prices, either during emergencies (anti-price-gouging laws) or generally (economy-wide or grocery price controls). It polls well: 65% of likely voters backed cracking down on grocery price gouging (Data for Progress, April 2026), and 73.9% of US GSS/ISSP respondents say government should keep prices under control. Economists are close to unanimous against it: 88% of the Clark Center panel in 2024 agreed that widespread price controls create substantial distortions, and most opposed Connecticut's 2012 anti-gouging bill. Evidence from the 1970s US gasoline controls shows queues alone burning about 116% of the money moved from sellers to buyers, on top of shortages and misallocation, and the 1971-74 controls cost about $45bn a year in today's economy to run and comply with. Counting all of this, each $1 shifted from sellers to buyers destroys between 44 cents and $1.29 of value.
policies.selected_by: Data for Progress 2026: 65%

policies.title: Open Borders
policies.bcr_basis: Benefit = the rise in world output when workers can move to where they are most productive; cost = the real resources spent on moving, as in the free-trade entry, where the denominator is the adjustment cost. Borjas (2015, JEL) gives both from one model. With pre-migration world GDP of $70tn and a North/South productivity ratio of 4, Table 2 reports the gross gain and the gain net of migration costs (cost = 10 times a Southern worker's initial salary, 5% discount) for different shares (lambda) of origin-country productivity carried by migrants. HIGH: lambda = 0, gross gain $40.1tn, net $28.1tn, so migration costs are $12.0tn: 40.1 / 12.0 = 3.34. LOW: lambda = 0.25, gross $24.2tn, net $12.9tn, costs $11.3tn: 24.2 / 11.3 = 2.14. Lambda of 0.5 cuts the gross gain to $8.8tn (as quoted by Clemens & Pritchett 2019), below the migration costs, so the net gain turns negative in Borjas's table; Clemens & Pritchett (2019, JDE) find that evidence for migrants carrying large fractions of origin productivity is unsupported, which bounds lambda at about 0.25 and sets the low end. Scaled to 2025 world GDP of $118,350bn (World Bank), migration costs are 12.0 / 70 x 118,350 = $20,289bn a year at the high-cost end and $19,105bn at the low-cost end; the gross gain is $40.9-67.8tn. Cross-checks: Clemens (2011, JEP) reports full-removal gains 'often in the range of 50-150 percent of world GDP' before moving costs; Docquier, Machado & Sekkat (2015, SJE), with estimated migration and visa costs and about 400 million movers, find world GDP rises 7.0-17.9%; Kennan (2013, RED) finds a net gain of $11,046 per worker a year against average income of $8,382 in 40 less-developed countries. Context, not part of the range: the reverse policy, strict border controls applied by every country, scores as the mirror image. Counting everyone affected, including the people kept out, per migrant kept out and per $ of enforcement: US natives +$20,500 (low-skill +$9/yr) and -$79,000 (high-skill -$21/yr) from the 2006-10 wall that deterred about 311,000 migrants (Allen, Dobbin & Morten 2024); the migrant's lost earnings of PPP$10,523/yr over a 20-year working life, $156,600 (or $285,200 at 2024 prices) (Clemens, Montenegro & Pritchett 2019); a fiscal saving of $231,000 (Hall 2016, reading NAS 2017) or a forgone contribution of $57,000 (Nowrasteh, Eckhardt & Howard 2023); enforcement of $10,600 per migrant deterred for the wall to $533,400 under H.R. 1 ($170.7bn / CBO's 320,000 fewer residents in 2035); and the lost-income mortality step of $0.132 per $1 (Broughel & Viscusi 2017; HHS VSL $13.1m). Each $1 of enforcement destroys between 97 cents and $1.31 (ratio -1.31 to -0.97), on a cost of about $143.4bn a year (US 2025-26 build-up: H.R. 1 and the Secure America Act). This does not change the open-borders range.
policies.grade_reason: The range comes from a peer-reviewed general-equilibrium model (Borjas 2015, JEL) that prices both the gain and the moving cost, cross-checked by peer-reviewed estimates (Clemens 2011, JEP; Kennan 2013, RED; Docquier, Machado & Sekkat 2015, SJE). All are calibrated simulations of a policy never tried at world scale, and the result depends on how much productivity migrants carry, so B.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, $bn a year: migration costs of 12.0 / 70 of world output (Borjas 2015, Table 2, lambda = 0) applied to 2025 world GDP of $118,350bn = $20,289bn. Repealing entry restrictions needs no new public outlay; administration and private compliance fall rather than rise.
policies.difficulty_reason: Requires every high-income country to repeal entry and work restrictions, with no modern precedent outside regional zones such as the EU single market.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Most of the gain goes to migrants and their origin countries: Borjas (2015) finds Southern wages rise 143% while Northern wages fall 39.3% and capital owners gain $12.0tn; Docquier, Machado & Sekkat (2015) find sending-country natives gain 26-79% and natives of the US and EU 0.3-2.1%. Restriction runs the other way: the 2006-10 US border wall raised low-skill US workers' pay by $9 a year and cut high-skill workers' pay by $21 a year (Allen, Dobbin & Morten 2024), while the migrants kept out give up at least PPP$10,500-13,600 a year (Clemens, Montenegro & Pritchett 2019).
policies.summary: Letting people live and work in any country moves workers to where they are far more productive; identical low-skill workers earn about four times as much in the US as at home. Published models put the gain at roughly 35-57% of world output before moving costs, the largest of any policy on this list. Moving several billion people is also very costly, about $19-20 trillion a year, so each $1 spent returns about $2.14 to $3.34. Most of the gain goes to migrants and poor countries, while wages of workers already in rich countries fall in the largest-scale model. The reverse policy, strict border controls in every country, scores as the mirror image: counting the people kept out, each $1 of enforcement destroys between 97 cents and $1.31, on a cost of about $143.4 billion a year.
