policies.selected_by: Gallup World Poll 2021: nearly 900 million adults would like to migrate permanently (opposite view: CES 2024, 79% of Americans backed more border patrols)

policies.title: Student Loan Forgiveness
policies.bcr_basis: Forgiveness is a transfer from taxpayers to borrowers, so it uses the same net-damage form as the UBI entry: ratio = (value to recipients - excess burden x net fiscal cost) / net fiscal cost. Value to recipients: $1 per $1 of present-value debt cancelled (CBO and PWBM already score cancellation in present value, which accounts for loans that would never have been repaid; Catherine & Yannelis 2023 show balances overstate present value most for low earners). Net fiscal cost per $1: administration and lender paperwork add about $0.02bn a year, 0.05% of the $40bn outlay. In the low case it also includes the extra borrowing that expected future forgiveness induces, a fiscal externality, the same way the Social Security (15) and UBI (18) entries add behavioural responses. Penn Wharton Budget Model (Chen & Smetters, July 2023) estimate the SAVE repayment plan's 10-year cost at $342bn with no behavioural response, $475bn with its medium borrowing response and $559bn with its maximum response; induced borrowing therefore adds (475 - 342) / 342 = 39% to (559 - 342) / 342 = 63% of the static cost. HIGH = 0.67: no induced borrowing, excess burden at Ballard, Shoven & Whalley's (1985) central 33 cents per $1 raised: (1 - 0.33 x 1.0005) / 1.0005 = 0.67. LOW = -1.39: Feldstein (1999) finds a proportional rise in all income-tax rates costs nearly $2 of deadweight loss per extra $1 of revenue; with the maximum induced-borrowing response, net fiscal cost = 1 + 0.63 + 0.0005 = 1.635, and (1 - 2.0 x 1.635) / 1.635 = -1.39. With the medium 39% response the low end is (1 - 2.0 x 1.39) / 1.39 = -1.28; with no induced borrowing it is (1 - 2.0 x 1.0005) / 1.0005 = -1.00. Applying a permanent repayment plan's borrowing response to a one-off cancellation is reasonable only to the extent borrowers expect forgiveness to recur; Sallie Mae's 2024 survey found 48% of student borrowers expect their debt to be forgiven. Lucca, Nadauld & Shen (2019) indicate where much of the induced borrowing goes: about 60 cents of each $1 of extra subsidised loan capacity passes into tuition; that share is part of the same fiscal externality and is not added again. Catherine, Perez Clanton & Yannelis (2024) warn of school-level moral hazard. The financing deadweight (the GDP-loss cost component) is counted in the ratio only, not twice. Debt financing: CBO's $400bn is a present value, so interest on the borrowing that funds it is not added separately; the financing distortion is covered by the excess-burden term. Not added: the behavioural gains found by Di Maggio, Kalda & Yao (NBER 2019/2020), where borrowers whose private loans were voided became more mobile and earned about $3,000 more over three years, which would nudge the high end up slightly via extra taxes. No study publishes a BCR or MVPF for broad forgiveness. Additional study (inside the range, corroboration): Dinerstein, Earnest, Koustas & Yannelis (2025, NBER w33462) follow the $132bn of federal student loans actually cancelled from 2021 and find forgiven borrowers' earnings fell, with a marginal propensity to earn of -0.49 and a marginal change in labour-income taxes (MPT) of -0.117 per $1 of the annuitized wealth shock (Table 9; -0.088 without their expectations adjustment). Treating the lost tax as a fiscal externality of 0.117 per $1 forgiven, in this entry's form: (1 - 0.33 x 1.1175) / 1.1175 = 0.56 and (1 - 2.0 x 1.1175) / 1.1175 = -1.11, both inside the range. Adding it to the induced-borrowing response at the low end would give (1 - 2.0 x 1.7475) / 1.7475 = -1.43; that combination is shown only as a sensitivity.
policies.grade_reason: Built from peer-reviewed estimates of the excess burden of taxation (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985 AER; Feldstein 1999 REStat) applied to official cost estimates (CBO 2022; PWBM 2022), with peer-reviewed distributional evidence (Catherine & Yannelis 2023 JFE). There is no direct benefit-cost study or experiment on broad forgiveness, so B+ or above does not apply. The low end adds a think-tank estimate of induced borrowing (PWBM 2023) applied by analogy from a repayment plan to one-off cancellation.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: CBO (Sept 2022) ~$400bn present value for the 2022 plan, ~$40bn a year over a 10-year window (PWBM: $47-52bn a year). Administration: the Education Department's own regulatory impact analysis for its 2024 debt-relief rule put one-time administrative costs at $31m ($13.0m systems and contractors + $18.0m waiver processing) for about $147bn of relief, or 0.021%; at $400bn that is ~$84m, about $0.008bn a year. Private compliance: that RIA's paperwork cost for guaranty agencies and FFEL lenders, $0.012bn a year. GDP loss: the excess burden of the taxes needed, at Feldstein's ~$2 per $1 (the high end used for the ratio's low end), $80bn a year. cost_bn = 40 + 0.008 + 0.012 + 80 = $120.0bn a year.
policies.difficulty_reason: Biden v. Nebraska (June 30, 2023, 6-3) held that the HEROES Act does not authorise mass cancellation, so broad forgiveness now needs ordinary legislation from Congress. Narrower discharges (income-driven repayment, Public Service Loan Forgiveness) show precedent for the mechanism.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Catherine & Yannelis (2023, JFE), measuring debt in present value, find full or partial forgiveness is regressive: the top income decile gains as much as the bottom three deciles combined. PWBM's balance-based table for the capped 2022 plan is more even (about two-thirds of benefits to households earning $88,000 or less; top 5% almost nothing), which is noted as the main counter-reading.
policies.summary: Broad student-loan forgiveness cancels federal student debt for most borrowers, as in the 2022 plan of up to $10,000-20,000 each. It has majority support: 55.1% backed forgiving up to $20,000 per person in the 2024 Cooperative Election Study (weighted, researcher-computed). CBO put the 2022 plan at about $400bn, roughly $40bn a year over a decade; running it costs very little extra, but the taxes needed to fund it could cost the economy up to about $80bn a year more. If borrowers come to expect more forgiveness, they borrow more: a Penn Wharton model of a related plan finds this adds 39-63% to the cost, and other work shows much of extra student lending ends up in higher tuition. Peer-reviewed work finds the benefits tilt toward higher earners. As a transfer, each $1 is worth $1 to borrowers but costs taxpayers $1 or more plus the economic drag of raising it, so the ratio runs from about -1.39 to 0.67.

policies.title: Block Social Security and Medicare Changes
policies.short: Block Social Security and Medicare Changes
policies.bcr_basis: Blocking any rise in eligibility ages or cut in benefits means paying scheduled benefits after the trust funds run out (OASDI 2034, HI 2033), so the extra money must be raised by taxes or borrowing. Benefits are a transfer, valued at $1 per $1 to retirees, so the net-damage form of the UBI entry applies: ratio = (1 - excess burden x net fiscal cost) / net fiscal cost, where net fiscal cost includes administration and the fiscal externality (FE) of lower work. FE from age changes: CBO (2012) finds raising the full retirement age from 67 to 70 cuts Social Security spending about 13% and enlarges the economy by slightly more than 1% in the long run; 13% of today's 5.3%-of-GDP programme (2026 Trustees) is 0.69% of GDP; CBO's rule of thumb (as reported by CRFB) is about 0.25 of extra GDP returning as revenue (0.5% of GDP on 2% more GDP), so blocking the age rise forgoes 0.25 x 1.0 = 0.25% of GDP of taxes per 0.69% of GDP of benefits kept: FE = 0.36. Mastrobuoni (2009, JPubE) confirms the behaviour: when the 1983 law raised the normal retirement age, mean retirement ages rose by about half the increase. Administration adds 0.53% of benefits. HIGH = 0.66: blocking across-the-board benefit-formula cuts (little labour-supply response, FE about 0) with the Ballard-Shoven-Whalley central excess burden of 0.33: (1 - 0.33 x 1.0053) / 1.0053 = 0.66. LOW = -1.27: blocking an age rise (FE 0.36, net fiscal cost 1.365) financed at Feldstein's (1999) nearly $2 marginal deadweight loss: (1 - 2.0 x 1.365) / 1.365 = -1.27. Middle case (age rise blocked, BSW 0.33): (1 - 0.33 x 1.365) / 1.365 = 0.40. The financing deadweight is subtracted in the ratio and the work-loss effect enters through the FE, so neither is added again; the GDP-loss figure in cost_components is output, which overstates the welfare loss. The choice of cost base (75-year gap, current annual deficit or post-2034 shortfall) changes cost_bn but not the ratio. Poverty-reduction value (Engelhardt & Gruber) is not weighted.
policies.grade_reason: Combines a peer-reviewed natural experiment on retirement behaviour (Mastrobuoni 2009, JPubE), CBO macro estimates and the Trustees' official fiscal gap, with peer-reviewed excess-burden estimates (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). No published benefit-cost ratio exists for keeping current-law benefits, and the labour-supply feedback is from CBO's model rather than a measured welfare change, so the grade is below B+.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: the 2026 Trustees' 75-year actuarial deficits (OASDI 4.42% and HI 0.56% of payroll) come to about 1.67% of GDP, ~$535bn a year. Administration: SSA spends 0.4% of OASDI cost on administration (CY2025, $6.95bn) and Medicare HI 1.3% ($5.9bn of $444.2bn, CRS 2026); applied to the extra benefits that is about $2.8bn a year (an upper bound). Private compliance: none identified. GDP loss: (a) CBO (2012) finds raising the full retirement age to 70 would enlarge the economy by slightly more than 1%, so blocking it gives up about $320bn a year of output (output, not welfare, since retirees gain leisure); (b) the excess burden of the taxes needed at Feldstein's ~$2 per $1, $1,070bn a year. cost_bn = 535 + 2.8 + 1,390 = $1,927.8bn a year (75-year average). With only the 2026 cash deficit (0.8% of GDP) and Ballard-Shoven-Whalley's 33 cents, the total would be far smaller (about $340bn).
policies.difficulty_reason: Keeping current benefit rules needs no change, but paying full scheduled benefits after 2034 (OASDI) and 2033 (HI) needs ordinary legislation to raise payroll taxes or transfer general revenue; Congress has done this before (1977 and 1983 amendments). No constitutional change.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Benefits go to nearly all retirees and disabled workers; Engelhardt & Gruber find a roughly unitary elasticity of elderly poverty with respect to benefits, so cuts would raise poverty, which favours the poor. But benefits rise with lifetime earnings and the cost falls on current workers through payroll taxes, so the net effect is broad rather than clearly pro-poor.
policies.summary: This policy blocks any rise in the Social Security or Medicare eligibility ages and any cut in scheduled benefits, so the trust-fund shortfalls must be filled with new taxes or borrowing. It is among the most popular ideas tested: 87.5% of US GSS/ISSP respondents say government should provide a decent living for the old, and protecting both programmes from cuts or age increases had net support of +72 in a 2024 YouGov poll of 4,038 voters. The 2026 Trustees put the gap at about $535bn a year on average over 75 years; at the high end, the taxes to fill it and the work forgone could cost the economy more than twice that again. As a transfer, each $1 is worth $1 to retirees, but raising it costs $1 plus the drag of higher taxes, and blocking higher retirement ages also forgoes extra work and tax revenue. The ratio runs from about -1.27 to 0.66.
policies.selected_by: ISSP 88-99%; YouGov net +72

policies.title: Billionaire Wealth Tax
policies.bcr_basis: A 2% global minimum tax on billionaires' wealth (Zucman 2024) moves money from about 2,800 billionaires to governments. That money is a transfer, counted at $1 on both sides, so the ratio takes the net-damage form used for the other transfer policies: ratio = (transfer - excess burden - administration - private compliance) / transfer, all per $1 of wealth tax collected. Base: billionaires owned $14.2 trillion in 2024 and already pay tax equal to 0.3% of wealth, so the minimum tax adds 1.7% of wealth: $242bn with perfect enforcement (Zucman, Table 1). Excess burden: the same convention as the student-loan (14) and Social Security (15) entries, whatever the size of the transfer. HIGH uses Ballard, Shoven and Whalley's (1985) marginal welfare cost of 34 cents per $1 of revenue (range 34-48 cents); LOW uses Feldstein's (1999) 'nearly two dollars per incremental dollar of revenue'. Feldstein's measure is built on the response of the taxable base, which is the same channel through which wealth is hidden, moved or valued down, and on the resulting loss of revenue, so the wealth-tax base response and the revenue lost from other taxes are not added on top. Revenue is about 0.22% of world GDP, far inside the capital-tax Laffer limit (Trabandt and Uhlig: US 2.3% of GDP), so the convention that applies Feldstein at both ends to very large programmes does not apply. Administration (wealth-specific, both ends): Wealth Tax Commission, government cost for a one-off 5% UK tax scaled to a 1.7% rate (fixed costs over a smaller take): HIGH Burgherr's central 1% x 5/1.7 = 0.029; LOW 1.4% at the GBP 10m threshold x 5/1.7 = 0.041. Private compliance (valuation, filing, disputes): HIGH 0.06% of taxable assets at GBP 10m / 1.7% = 0.035; LOW 0.13%, the highest in the Commission's Table 6, / 1.7% = 0.076. HIGH = 1 - 0.34 - 0.029 - 0.035 = 0.60. LOW = 1 - 2.0 - 0.041 - 0.076 = -1.12. No double counting: the GDP loss (Penn Wharton 2021: -1.2% of GDP in 2050 for revenue of 0.735% of GDP, 1.63 per $1) is the output counterpart of the excess burden, so it is reported in cost_components and not subtracted again, as in entries 14, 15, 17 and 18. Sensitivity, built from wealth-tax evidence instead of the income-tax excess burden (exponential base W = W0 x e^(-s x 0.017)): HIGH, Advani and Tarrant's (2021) 7% base loss for a 1% tax (s = 7.26, revenue $213.9bn, average excess burden 0.064) plus Penn Wharton's macro feedback ((2,390 - 2,025)/2,390 = 0.153): 1 - 0.064 - 0.153 - 0.029 - 0.035 = 0.72. LOW, Brülhart et al.'s (2022) Swiss response net of the 21% due to house prices (s = ln(1.43) x 0.79/0.01 = 28.3, revenue $149.7bn, marginal excess burden x/(1 - x) = 0.924) plus Trabandt and Uhlig's (2011) 51% US capital-tax self-financing: 1 - 0.924 - 0.51 - 0.041 - 0.076 = -0.55; with the average excess burden 0.09, with the EU-14 share (79%) -0.83, and with Penn Wharton's full output loss in place of both terms -0.75. Cross-check: Jakobsen et al.'s long-run elasticity of 1.15 for the very wealthy, with the net return cut from 7.2% to 5.5%, implies a long-run base of (5.5/7.2)^1.15 = 0.73 of its untaxed level. Lost-income mortality: income lost to a policy costs lives. Broughel and Viscusi (Mercatus 2017) put it at about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed; valued at the HHS VSL of $13.1m, each $1 of net income lost carries 13.1/99.3 = $0.132 of mortality cost. This adjustment is applied to every policy after the range shown here is computed. Poor-country infant deaths from lower world income use Baird, Friedman and Schady (REStat 2011): +0.24 to 0.40 infant deaths per 1,000 births per 1% fall in GDP per person, on about 119.9m births a year in low- and middle-income countries (World Bank). Tax finance (net-damage form): each $1 of public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); as for the other net-damage entries, the burden is subtracted from benefits; the wealth-tax revenue is counted in full as the transfer, so the government's administration cost must be funded from other taxes and carries the same penalty. LOW = 1 - 2.0 - 0.041 - 0.076 - 2.0 x 0.041 = -1.20; HIGH = 1 - 0.34 - 0.029 - 0.035 - 0.34 x 0.029 = 0.59. Additional study (above the headline range, not used to set it): Londoño-Vélez & Ávila-Mahecha (2024, NBER w32134) find Colombian taxpayers' reported wealth has an elasticity of 2 with respect to the net-of-tax rate (3.1-4.0 in alternative estimates), costing up to a fifth of revenue under Colombia's higher, recurrent rates. In this entry's exponential-base form (s = 2/(1 - 0.017) = 2.03, x = 0.035) the marginal excess burden of a 1.7% tax is x/(1 - x) = 0.036 (0.074 at an elasticity of 4); with the high-end administration and compliance: 1 - 0.036 - 0.029 - 0.035 - 0.34 x 0.029 = 0.89 (0.85 at an elasticity of 4). This is above the high end and close to the Advani-Tarrant sensitivity case above; the headline keeps the income-tax excess-burden convention shared with entries 14, 15 and 18, and Colombia's moderately wealthy filers had fewer cross-border options than billionaires (Brülhart et al.; offshoring in the same paper), so the range is not extended.
policies.grade_reason: The two ends rest on peer-reviewed estimates of the cost of raising tax revenue (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), the same as the other transfer entries, applied to the proposal's own revenue estimate. The wealth-tax responses behind the sensitivity come from peer-reviewed natural experiments in Switzerland, Denmark and Sweden and a peer-reviewed review that reconciles them (Brülhart et al. 2022; Jakobsen et al. 2020; Advani and Tarrant 2021); administration and compliance costs come from a UK commission's costing. No peer-reviewed benefit-cost study of a wealth tax exists, and no country has taxed billionaires at this scale, so the grade is B.
policies.cost_basis: Full annual cost = $0 public outlay (the tax collects revenue, a transfer) + $10.0bn administration (4.1% of revenue, the Wealth Tax Commission's highest government cost scaled to a 1.7% rate) + $18.5bn private compliance (0.13% of $14.2 trillion of billionaire wealth for valuation, filing and disputes) + $395.1bn lost output (Penn Wharton 2021: 1.63 of GDP per $1 of US wealth-tax revenue by 2050, x $242bn) = $423.6bn a year, all at full enforcement. The output loss is an upper bound and is the counterpart of the excess burden in the ratio, so it is not subtracted twice.
policies.difficulty_reason: It needs a binding agreement among many countries, and the 2024 G20 declaration commits only to 'engage cooperatively ... with full respect to tax sovereignty'. Twelve OECD countries had net wealth taxes in 1990 and only four in 2017, with repeals justified by efficiency costs, capital flight and high administrative costs (OECD 2018). No country has applied a 2% annual tax to billionaires.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The tax is paid by about 2,800 billionaires, whose effective tax rate would rise from about 22% to 39% of pre-tax income (Zucman 2024). The $193-242bn a year of revenue (depending on how much is lost to avoidance and evasion) can be spent on anything, so its benefits are as broad as the spending. Part of the cost reaches workers: Penn Wharton (2021) projects average hourly wages 1.2% lower by 2050 as less capital is accumulated.
policies.summary: A coordinated 2% minimum tax on the wealth of the world's roughly 3,000 billionaires, as proposed to the G20 in 2024, would raise $242bn a year if perfectly enforced. The revenue is a transfer; the costs are the extra burden of raising it, the costs of valuing and collecting the tax, and the output lost as less capital is built. Scored like the other transfer policies, each $1 collected delivers between a net loss of $1.20 and a net 59 cents of value; lost-income mortality lowers both ends. Evidence specific to wealth taxes gives a similar range, -0.55 to 0.72.
policies.selected_by: Ipsos 2024 G20 survey (Earth4All): 68%

policies.title: Medicare for All
policies.bcr_basis: No published BCR exists for single payer. It is scored in the same transfer form as the UBI and Social Security entries: new federal spending replaces premiums and out-of-pocket costs, so it counts $1 to households per $1 in both benefit and cost; the excess burden of tax financing and the waiting-time cost are subtracted from benefits; the cost base adds any rise in national health spending. Life-years are valued at ICER's $100,000-150,000 per QALY thresholds. Financing at this scale: at the peak of the Laffer curve the US can raise at most about 7.4% of GDP in extra tax revenue and the EU-14 about 3.1% (Trabandt & Uhlig 2012, Table 7). New tax-financed outlays larger than that cannot be raised at the 34-cent marginal burden measured for small changes (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985); near or past the peak the marginal burden rises without limit (Browning 1987: up to more than 300% of marginal revenue). Policies whose new tax-financed outlays exceed 7.4% of GDP therefore use Feldstein's (1999) estimate, which 'may exceed $2 per $1 of revenue', at both ends of the range. New federal spending of $1.5-2.8T is 5-10% of US GDP, at or beyond the 7.4% maximum, so both ends use Feldstein's $2 per $1. The CEA's (2018) estimate that tax financing would cut GDP by 9% ($2,778bn at 2025 GDP) measures the same tax distortion and is not added; it is an output measure and assumes about $2.4T of new taxes in 2022. Waiting: Blahous (2019 testimony) notes that first-dollar coverage would raise demand by about 11% for the privately insured and 16% for the uninsured while provider payments would be cut by more than 40% in the lower-bound design, the setting in which queues arise. Canada's single-payer system had a median wait of 30.0 weeks from GP referral to treatment in 2024 (Fraser Institute, Waiting Your Turn), and Moir & Barua (Fraser Institute 2024) value patients' lost time at C$10.6bn a year (all waking hours). Scaled per person to the US and converted at 1.3973 C$ per US$: $65.0bn a year, subtracted at both ends. LOW = -0.76: Urban Institute (2019) finds its comprehensive single payer raises national health spending by $720bn and federal spending by $2.8T in 2020 (administration is inside these figures). Lives saved: Galvani's 1.73m life-years at $100,000 = $173bn, which generously assumes Galvani's mortality gain. LOW = (2,800 + 173 - 2.0 x 2,800 - 65.0) / (2,800 + 720) = -0.76. HIGH = -0.57: Galvani et al. (2020, Lancet) estimate single payer saves 13%, about $450bn a year (net of single-payer administration), and 1.73 million life-years (68,000 lives) a year, valued at $150,000 = $259.5bn; federal cost $1.5T, the low end of CBO's 2030 range for new federal subsidies (which includes administration). HIGH = (1,500 + 450 + 259.5 - 2.0 x 1,500 - 65.0) / 1,500 = -0.57. CBO's five options span national-spending changes of -$0.7T to +$0.3T in 2030, which falls between these cases. Blahous (Mercatus 2018) puts added federal spending at $32.6T over 2022-31 and says even that assumes providers accept payment cuts of more than 40%, which points to the low end; his alternative estimate without provider cuts ($38.8T) is an outlay figure, a transfer in this ratio, so it does not change the ends. Not priced: health losses from delayed treatment (no published US-applicable dollar estimate found) and physician-supply responses to 40% payment cuts (Blahous: 'We do not know how providers would respond'), both of which would lower the ends further. Benefit and cost years differ (2017-2030 dollars); that is a stated simplification. Lost-income mortality: income lost to a policy costs lives. Broughel & Viscusi (Mercatus 2017) put it at about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed; valued at the HHS VSL of $13.1m, each $1 of net income lost carries 13.1/99.3 = $0.132 of mortality cost (and each $1 gained saves the same). This adjustment is applied to every policy after the range shown here is computed. Poor-country infant deaths from lower world income use Baird, Friedman & Schady (REStat 2011): +0.24 to 0.40 infant deaths per 1,000 births per 1% fall in GDP per person, on ~119.9m births a year in low- and middle-income countries (World Bank).
policies.grade_reason: The range rests on official CBO estimates and think-tank models (Urban Institute, Mercatus), plus one peer-reviewed modelling study (Galvani et al., Lancet) whose savings CBO and Urban do not replicate. Health effects of coverage are backed by quasi-experimental and randomized evidence (Miller et al. 2021 QJE; Oregon experiment), but no peer-reviewed BCA of single payer exists. The waiting-list cost is a think-tank estimate for Canada applied by analogy.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: CBO (Dec 2020) finds federal subsidies rise by $1.5-3.0T in 2030; the design closest to current bills (Option 5) is about $3.0T, used here (Urban Institute: +$2.8T in 2020; Blahous 2018: $32.6T over 2022-31). Most of this replaces private premiums and out-of-pocket spending (a transfer). Administration: shown separately within the $3.0T, at Medicare fee-for-service's ~2% administrative rate, about $60bn (CBO assumes 1.5-1.6%; critics say that is too low, supporters say billing savings shrink total admin). Private compliance: provider billing is inside national health spending, already in the ratio. GDP loss: the CEA (2018) estimates tax-financed Medicare for All would cut GDP by 9%, about $2,778bn a year at 2025 GDP, the high-end published estimate. Private cost of waiting: Canada's waiting-list time cost (Fraser Institute 2024, all waking hours, C$10.6bn) scaled per person to the US, $65.0bn a year. cost_bn = 2,940 + 60 + 65.0 + 2,778 = $5,843.0bn a year.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate by the rubric: ordinary federal legislation, with modern precedents abroad (e.g., Canada, Taiwan's 1995 single payer). Politically it is near the hard end, because it replaces employer insurance for about 150 million people and needs roughly $1.5-3T a year in new federal revenue.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Gains go mostly to the uninsured and underinsured, who are disproportionately low-income: covering low-income adults through Medicaid cut their mortality (Miller, Johnson & Wherry 2021) and cut their medical debt (Oregon experiment). Financing through broad taxes is typically more progressive than premiums.
policies.summary: Medicare for All would replace private insurance with one government plan covering everyone. It is popular, with 66% support in the CES 2022. Official and think-tank estimates agree it would add $1.5-3.0 trillion a year in federal spending, but they disagree about whether total national health spending would rise or fall, and one government estimate says the taxes to pay for it could shrink GDP by 9%. If US waiting lists grew to Canadian levels (a 30-week median wait), patients' lost time would cost about $67bn a year. Counting lives saved, waiting time and the economic drag of the extra taxes leaves each $1 destroying 0.57 to 0.77 dollars of value, because taxes on this scale sit at or past the peak of the Laffer curve: the optimistic end uses a Lancet study projecting $450bn in savings and 68,000 lives saved a year, and the pessimistic end uses an Urban Institute estimate that national spending rises by $720bn, with taxes on this scale costing about $2 of lost output per $1 raised (Feldstein 1999).

policies.title: Global Universal Basic Income
policies.bcr_basis: Treated as a full, permanent, tax-financed global UBI. Net-damage construction per $1 paid out: BCR = (value to recipients - excess burden x net fiscal cost) / net fiscal cost. Value to recipients: $1 (a transfer is worth its face value to the person receiving it). Net fiscal cost = $1 + the fiscal externality of reduced earnings + delivery cost. Fiscal externality: the NBER version of the OpenResearch trial (Vivalt et al. 2024, w32719) finds treated households received an extra $950 a month ($11,400 a year) over the control group; household income excluding transfers fell by $4,215 a year in the raw survey measure (0.37 per $1) and by $3,228 in the authors' preferred adjusted measure (0.28 per $1); partners cut hours about as much as participants. Daruich & Fernández find a labour-tax-financed UBI raises the average labour tax from 22% to about 27.8%. Delivery cost per $1 delivered (excluded from the ILO costing): $0.041 (PROGRESA, Caldes, Coady & Maluccio) to $0.25 (GiveDirectly). Financing at this scale: at the peak of the Laffer curve the US can raise at most about 7.4% of GDP in extra tax revenue and the EU-14 about 3.1% (Trabandt & Uhlig 2012, Table 7). New tax-financed outlays larger than that cannot be raised at the 34-cent marginal burden measured for small changes (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985); near or past the peak the marginal burden rises without limit (Browning 1987: up to more than 300% of marginal revenue). Policies whose new tax-financed outlays exceed 7.4% of GDP therefore use Feldstein's (1999, REStat) estimate, which 'may exceed $2 per $1 of revenue', at both ends of the range. A global UBI costs about 32.7% of world GDP, so both ends use $2 per $1. HIGH: preferred household response 0.28 at the pre-reform 22% rate, FE = 0.28 x 0.22 = 0.062; net fiscal cost = 1.062 + 0.041 = 1.103; BCR = (1 - 2.0 x 1.103) / 1.103 = -1.09. LOW: raw household response 0.37 at the post-reform 27.8% rate, FE = 0.370 x 0.278 = 0.103; net fiscal cost = 1.103 + 0.25 = 1.353; BCR = (1 - 2.0 x 1.353) / 1.353 = -1.26. A universal, untargeted government scheme would probably deliver at nearer PROGRESA's 4 cents, which would give a low end of about -1.13. A global scheme costing 32.7% of world GDP would need far higher tax rates than Daruich & Fernández's US scheme, so the low end's fiscal externality is likely understated. The Daruich-Fernández GDP loss is the output counterpart of the excess-burden term already in the ratio, so it is reported in cost_components but not subtracted again. Cross-checks: Hendren & Sprung-Keyser (2020, QJE) score the randomized US Negative Income Tax at an MVPF of -0.01; Daruich & Fernández's dynamic GE model finds a labour-tax-financed UBI cuts steady-state GDP 12.9% and costs future generations over 9% of lifetime consumption, i.e. net damage. Excluded (the counter-evidence list): the GiveDirectly Kenya UBI RCT (Banerjee et al. 2023), which is donor-funded with no financing distortion; the Kenya local multiplier (~2.4) for a one-off transfer into poor villages, and Finland's unemployed-only pilot, neither of which is a permanent tax-financed universal payment. Additional study (just above the range, not used to set it): Jones & Marinescu (2022, AEJ: Economic Policy) find Alaska's universal, permanent dividend had no effect on employment and raised part-time work by 1.8 points; with no fiscal externality and the lowest delivery cost in this entry, (1 - 2.0 x 1.041) / 1.041 = -1.04, slightly above the high end of -1.09. The dividend is paid from oil-fund returns rather than taxes and is a few percent of income, far smaller than a full basic income, so it does not test the labour response or the financing this entry prices; the range is not extended.
policies.grade_reason: Built from a modern RCT (Vivalt et al. 2024), a peer-reviewed MVPF for the randomized NIT experiments (Hendren & Sprung-Keyser 2020, QJE) and peer-reviewed excess-burden and dynamic GE estimates (Feldstein 1999; Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Daruich & Fernández 2024); no study scores a global UBI directly.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: ILO (Ortiz et al. 2018) puts a global poverty-line UBI at 32.7% of GDP, about $34.3T a year at ~$105T world GDP; the ILO excludes administration. Administration: delivery costs per $1 delivered range from $0.041 (PROGRESA's steady-state cost-transfer ratio, Caldes, Coady & Maluccio) to $0.25 (GiveDirectly, ~80% of large-programme spending reaching recipients; GiveWell finds ~83% overall); the high end gives $8,575bn a year. Private compliance: none identified. GDP loss: Daruich & Fernandez's dynamic model finds a labour-tax-financed UBI cuts steady-state GDP 12.9%, $13,545bn a year on world GDP. cost_bn = 34,300 + 8,575 + 13,545 = $56,420bn a year (with low-end admin, $35,706bn before GDP loss).
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: a global scheme needs binding commitments across many countries, and the ILO puts a poverty-line UBI at 32.7-39.4% of GDP on average and 62-79% of GDP in low-income countries.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Payments go to everyone rather than being targeted, so most spending reaches the non-poor, and financing creates high implicit marginal tax rates on middle earners (Henderson 2019). Daruich & Fernandez (2024) find the long-run losses fall on future generations through lower capital and human capital.
policies.summary: A universal basic income pays every adult a regular, unconditional cash amount. It splits opinion: 45% of Americans favoured a $1,000-a-month UBI in Pew's 2020 survey, while 68% of EU respondents said they would vote for one in Dalia's 2017 poll. A randomized US trial (OpenResearch) found every $1 paid out cut recipients' household earnings by 28-37 cents, with partners cutting work as much as recipients, and delivering the money costs about 4-25 cents per $1 on top. Once that and the excess burden of the taxes needed to fund it are counted, each $1 returns between about minus $1.26 and minus $1.09, because a scheme costing a third of world GDP is far beyond what taxes can raise without very large losses, and a dynamic model finds such a scheme would shrink GDP by about 13%. Kenya's 12-year GiveDirectly UBI trial shows strong local gains in poor villages, but it is donor-funded, so the ILO's estimate of roughly a third of world GDP for a global poverty-line UBI (before delivery costs) is the relevant scale.
policies.selected_by: Pew 2020: 45% US support for $1,000/month UBI; Dalia 2017: 68% EU

policies.title: Digital ID Mandate
policies.bcr_basis: Built from the two randomized evaluations of biometric ID in welfare delivery (both Muralidharan, Niehaus & Sukhtankar, India). LOW before tax finance (-1.0): making Aadhaar biometric authentication compulsory for food rations in Jharkhand (NBER 2020; RESTAT 2025). Benefit = change in leakage, which rose by an insignificant Rs 14 per ration card per month. Cost = extra transaction costs to government, dealers and beneficiaries, Rs 13.6 per card per month (+7.8%). BCR = -14 / 13.6 = -1.03, about -1.0. HIGH before tax finance (1.05): the Andhra Pradesh biometric smartcard payment system (AER 2016), which was rolled out carefully alongside the old system. Beneficiaries' time savings alone ($4.3m) exceed the government's cost of implementation and operation ($4.1m), so BCR = 4.3/4.1 = 1.05. Its large leakage reductions (NREGS leakage down $32.8m a year, eight times the cost) are mostly a transfer from corrupt officials to the state and are not counted. The spread reflects the authors' own conclusion that results depend on how the mandate and transition are managed. Platform costs: the Jharkhand low end already counts the extra costs to government, ration dealers and beneficiaries of compulsory authentication; adding the platform's own running cost to the denominator would mechanically pull a negative ratio toward zero, which would understate the harm, so it is not done. The Andhra Pradesh high end compares time savings with the smartcard system's full delivery cost, which paid for enrolment and payments through the bank commission; a share of a national ID platform's recurrent cost (0.06-0.1% of GDP) is not included and would lower the high end somewhat. Exclusion: in the Jharkhand trial the 23% of households not 'seeded' at baseline lost Rs 49 a month (12.6%), an average of 0.23 x 49 = Rs 11.3 per ration card a month, and nearly 300,000 people lost benefits; but value received by the average household was unchanged and disbursement rose slightly, so these losses are already inside the measured Rs 14 rise in leakage (disbursed minus received), and adding them again would double count. With an equity weight on excluded poor households (losses not offset by small gains to others), they would add, giving -(14 + 11.3) / 13.6 = -1.86. Not priced: surveillance and data-breach risk (Cato, EFF) and business identity-verification (KYC) costs; no published estimate attributes these to a digital ID mandate per $1 of programme cost, and all would lower both ends. Excluded (the counter-evidence list): McKinsey's 3-13% of GDP projection for consent-based 'good ID'; India's correlational DBT savings claim; and Defra's 2008 appraisal of carbon-allowance tracking (BCR 0.07-0.22), which applies only if the ID is used for personal carbon tracking. Additional study (outside the range, different basis, not used to set it): the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy's cost-benefit analysis of Aadhaar (NIPFP 2012, Table 1, constant prices) puts costs of building Aadhaar and linking it to welfare schemes at Rs 37,187 crore and benefits at Rs 109,806 crore over 2010-11 to 2020-21 (real IRR 52.85%), a ratio of 59,517 / 23,351 = 2.55 at an 8% discount rate (2.95 undiscounted). Its benefits are fiscal savings from reduced leakage, which this entry treats as transfers (as with the Andhra Pradesh leakage figures above), so the ratio is on a fiscal rather than a social basis; it is above the high end and does not set the range. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; the cost behind each end is partly or wholly public. HIGH: the Andhra Pradesh government's $4.1m implementation and operating cost is all public (share 1.0): HIGH = 1.05 (4.3/4.1) / (1 + 0.34 x 1.0) = 0.78. LOW: in the Jharkhand trial the government's share of the Rs 13.6 extra transaction cost is the ePOS deployment cost, Rs 6.2 per ration card per month (0.456 of the total; the rest falls on beneficiaries, Rs 7, and dealers). Because the low end is negative, the excess burden is subtracted from the benefit in the net-damage form used for entries 14-16 rather than added to the denominator, which would pull a negative ratio toward zero: with -14 ÷ 13.6 = -1.03 before tax finance and a public share of 0.456 (Rs 6.2 of Rs 13.6), LOW = (-14 - 2.0 x 6.2) ÷ 13.6 = -1.03 - 2.0 x 0.456 = -1.94.
policies.grade_reason: Both ends are converted directly from peer-reviewed randomized evaluations (RESTAT 2025; AER 2016) that report costs and benefits. Applying evidence from Indian welfare delivery to a worldwide mandate is by analogy, and the two trials point in opposite directions, so the grade is B+ rather than A.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, illustrative global extrapolation, using the median of published estimates. Build/enrolment: published per-registrant costs are $1.16 (Aadhaar), ~$5 (poor-country schemes), $7 (Gelb's low-income model) and $4-11 (Gelb & Diofasi Metz, midpoint $7.5); median $6.0 for ~8.0bn people over 10 years = $4.8bn a year. Operation and administration: published recurrent costs are 0.06-0.1% of GDP (midpoint 0.08%), 0.065% (Peru's RENIEC) and 0.11% (Gelb's steady state); median 0.08% of ~$105T world GDP = $84bn a year. Cross-check: the OBR's provisional UK cost (GBP 1.8bn over three years, ~GBP 0.6bn a year) scales per person to ~$90bn a year globally. Mostly budget-financed, so treated as tax-financed. Private compliance: no published estimate. GDP loss: none published. cost_bn = 4.8 + 84 = $88.8bn a year. If the ID were also used for personal carbon-allowance tracking, Defra's GBP 52 per person a year implies about $420bn more.
policies.difficulty_reason: Each country can mandate a digital ID through ordinary legislation, and India's Aadhaar shows enrolment of more than a billion people is possible. A worldwide mandate still needs action in nearly every country, and rich democracies have retreated: the UK dropped compulsory right-to-work use in January 2026, and the incoming prime minister moved to scrap the scheme in July 2026.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Exclusion risk falls on the poor. About 45% of the poorest quintile in low-income countries lack ID, against 28% of the richest (ID4D 2019), and 1.5-2 million Indian welfare beneficiaries lost access at some point during the biometric authentication rollout (Muralidharan, Niehaus & Sukhtankar 2025).
policies.summary: A digital ID mandate would require everyone to hold and use a government digital identity. Public support is lukewarm: a September 2025 YouGov poll found 42% of Britons for and 45% against the UK plan. The best evidence comes from two randomized trials in India. When biometric checks were made compulsory for food rations, corruption did not fall, costs rose about 8% and hundreds of thousands of legitimate recipients lost benefits, a return of about minus $1 per dollar before tax costs. A carefully managed biometric payment system in Andhra Pradesh roughly paid for itself through time savings alone (about $1.05 per $1). Building and running a national ID costs governments real money (a median of about $6 per person to enrol and 0.08% of GDP a year to run, roughly $89bn a year worldwide), and counting the excess burden of the taxes that pay the public share puts the range at about -1.94 to 0.78, before counting privacy and surveillance risks.
policies.selected_by: YouGov 2025: 42% support (UK); Ipsos UK 2025: 57% support a national ID card

policies.title: Medicare Drug Price Negotiation
policies.bcr_basis: Lower negotiated prices are mainly a transfer from drug makers to Medicare and its enrollees. They are scored in the same form as the other transfer policies: savings to taxpayers and enrollees, plus health gains from lower out-of-pocket costs, are the benefit; lost innovation is subtracted as a health harm; the transfer from manufacturers plus administration is the cost base. BCR = (savings + health gains - lost innovation) / (manufacturer revenue loss + administration). Savings: CBO puts negotiation's deficit reduction at $98.5bn over 2022-31 and $25bn in 2031, which is also the manufacturers' revenue loss. Cogan, Heil & Mulligan (Hoover 2025) model a fully phased-in IRA in which brand revenue falls $10.9bn a year after manufacturers' launch-price response. Administration: the $3bn appropriation spread over 10 years is $0.3bn a year; manufacturer reporting (about $0.013bn a year) does not change either end at two decimals. Lost innovation: CBO expects 13 fewer of about 1,300 new drugs over 30 years (about 1%), or 0.43 a year; valuing each lost drug at the $2.5bn of revenue needed to bring one new chemical entity to market (Dubois et al. 2015, peer-reviewed) gives $1.1bn a year. This treats revenue as the value of a drug, a floor, since patients usually gain more than the seller's revenue. The Hoover paper's own (Mulligan) method gives $4.5bn a year. The Philipson & Durie method ($196.3bn a year; 135 fewer drugs and 331.5m US life-years lost through 2039 under H.R. 5376) implies about ten times CBO's projected loss of drugs and is not used. Health gains: lower out-of-pocket costs keep patients on their medicines. Chandra, Flack & Obermeyer (2024, QJE) find Medicare patients facing smaller drug budgets 'consume fewer drugs and die more: 0.0164 percentage points per month (13.9%) for each $100 per month budget decrease', i.e. about one death per $610,000 of out-of-pocket cost (1.64e-4 / $100 a month). CMS estimates enrollees save $1.5bn in out-of-pocket costs in 2026 on the first 10 drugs and $685m in 2027 on the next 15 ($2.185bn a year). $2.185bn / $610,000 = 3,583 deaths averted a year, valued at the HHS VSL of $13.1m = $46.9bn. Chandra et al. study a sharp loss of coverage at age 65; applying it to lower negotiated prices is an extrapolation. LOW = (10.9 - 4.5) / (10.9 + 0.3) = 0.57, with no health gains, because CBO has not assessed patients' health outcomes. HIGH = (25 + 46.9 - 1.1) / (25 + 0.3) = 2.80. Without the health gains the high end would be (25 - 1.1) / (25 + 0.3) = 0.94. Lost innovation is valued as a health harm, so the lost-income mortality adjustment applies only to the administration cost. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; CMS's implementation appropriation ($0.3bn a year) is tax-financed; manufacturers' reporting cost is private. The tax-financed share of the cost base is 0.3 of 11.2 (0.0268) at the low end and 0.3 of 25.3 (0.0119) at the high end. Applied conservatively: the policy saves Medicare far more than it costs to run, and the savings are not credited with the same excess burden. LOW = 0.571 (6.4/11.2) / (1 + 2.0 x 0.0268) = 0.54; HIGH = 2.80 (70.8/25.3) / (1 + 0.34 x 0.0119) = 2.79.
policies.grade_reason: The high end rests on official CBO and CMS estimates, converted with peer-reviewed estimates (Dubois et al. 2015, RAND Journal, for the value of a lost drug; Chandra, Flack & Obermeyer 2024, QJE, for health gains, applied by extrapolation). The low end rests on think-tank modelling (Hoover), so the best sources are official estimates, which makes it B-.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, US$bn a year: administration $0.3bn (IRA appropriation of $3bn over 10 years) + manufacturer reporting $0.013bn + lost innovation $4.5bn a year (Cogan, Heil & Mulligan 2025, Mulligan method; CBO's projection of ~13 fewer drugs in 30 years implies about $1.1bn a year at Dubois et al.'s $2.5bn per new drug). Lower prices are a transfer of about $10.9-25bn a year from manufacturers to Medicare and enrollees, so they are not a cost to society.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: it needed ordinary federal legislation (the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022) and is now run by CMS. Expanding the number of drugs, or extending negotiation to commercial insurance, would again need legislation.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Savings are spread across Medicare enrollees and taxpayers. Hoover's modelling finds Part D households save about $51 (middle income) to $65 (upper income) a year, under 0.1% of income. Costs from fewer future drugs fall on future patients generally.
policies.summary: Medicare negotiates prices for some high-spend drugs, and about 85% of Americans support it (KFF 2024; CES 2022 85.9%). Lower prices move money from drug makers to Medicare and its enrollees, and enrollees save about $2.2bn a year out of pocket on the first 25 drugs (CMS). A Quarterly Journal of Economics study finds Medicare patients who face higher drug costs take fewer medicines and die sooner; applied to these savings, that is about 3,583 deaths averted a year. Against CBO's small estimated loss of new drugs (13 of 1,300 over 30 years), each $1 returns between 54 cents and $2.79 once the excess burden of the taxes that pay for CMS administration is counted.
policies.lives_basis: High: Chandra, Flack & Obermeyer (2024, QJE) find one extra death per about $610,000 of out-of-pocket drug cost (0.0164 percentage points a month per $100 a month); applied to CMS's estimated enrollee savings of $2.185bn a year ($1.5bn in 2026 on the first 10 drugs + $685m in 2027 on the next 15) = 3,583 deaths averted a year, as in bcr_basis. Low: 0, because the low end of the ratio counts no health gains (CBO has not assessed patients' health). This is an extrapolation from a loss of coverage at age 65 to lower negotiated prices. Fewer new drugs are valued in dollars ($1.1-4.5bn a year) in the sources, not in deaths, so no death count is added for them; deaths caused stay the lost-income deaths on the $0.3bn administration cost.

policies.title: Childhood Immunization
policies.bcr_basis: All figures are aid-programme scale-ups in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The Copenhagen Consensus 2023 'Halftime' package raises 2022 coverage to 2030 targets for 9 vaccines (pentavalent, HPV, JE, measles, MR, MenA, PCV, rotavirus, yellow fever) in 80 LMICs; Patenaude, Sriudomporn & Mak (2023, JBCA) give benefits $762.2bn / costs $7.58bn (present value, 8% discount, VSLY valuation) = 100.5, reported as 101 in Best Things First. Ozawa et al. (2016, Health Affairs) find a net return about 16 times cost for 10 vaccines in 94 LMICs when only cost of illness (treatment costs and lost productivity) is counted, a benefit-cost ratio of 16 + 1 = 17; their full-income value of life gives a net return of 44, a ratio of 45. Sim et al. (2020, Health Affairs) get 19.8 (cost of illness) and 52.2 (value of statistical life) for 2021-30. The Post-2015 Consensus panel gave expanded immunization $60 per $1, and Copenhagen Consensus 2012 (Jamison et al.) gave 20. Cost-of-illness methods therefore give 17-26 and value-of-life methods 45-101. US programme studies (BCR 7.5-10.9) are a different setting and are listed as counter-sources. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 14.4: Ozawa et al. (16 + 1) / 1.178 = 14.4 (all of its cost is programme spending, so the full 17.8% Gavi non-direct share is added). HIGH = 94 (lower overhead rate): CCC 100.5 / (1 + 0.075 x 0.882) = 94.3, rounded 94, where 0.882 = 1.5/1.7 is the programme (non-time) share of the CCC cost. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies. LOW (Ozawa et al., all programme spending) = 14.43 (17/1.178) / 3.00 = 4.81. HIGH: only the programme share of the CCC cost (0.882, plus its 7.5% overhead) is tax-financed; parents' time is not: 100.5 / (1 + 0.075 x 0.882 + 0.34 x 0.882 x 1.075) = 100.5 / 1.3885 = 72.4.
policies.grade_reason: Several independent peer-reviewed benefit-cost/ROI studies (Patenaude et al. 2023 JBCA; Ozawa et al. 2016 and Sim et al. 2020 in Health Affairs) agree that benefits are many times costs, and each vaccine's efficacy rests on randomized controlled trials. The results are consistent across methods, datasets and decades.
policies.cost_basis: Copenhagen Consensus Best Things First leaflet (2025 web version): $1.7bn a year, of which $0.2bn is parents' time. The government/donor programme cost is therefore about $1.5bn a year; parents' time belongs inside the BCR, not in cost_bn. Cross-check: Patenaude et al. (2023) give a present-value cost of $7.58bn for 2023-2030 (8% discount), about $0.95bn a year in discounted terms. GiveWell's New Incentives programme costs about $146 per vaccinated infant at the margin in northern Nigeria, which shows the last children are expensive to reach. cost_bn = public outlay $1.5bn + administration/overhead $0.27bn + private (household) cost $0.2bn = $1.97bn/yr. Patenaude et al. (2023) cost vaccines (procurement, injection supplies, freight) plus immunization delivery costs that explicitly include labour, cold chain and its overheads, transport, buildings/utilities overheads and 'program management, short-term training, IEC/social mobilization, disease surveillance' (Section 4.1.1); Ozawa/Sim also cost vaccines, supply chain and service delivery. Country-level administration is therefore already included. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (Gavi: Secretariat implementation, partners' (WHO/UNICEF/CSO) technical assistance and overhead). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: a sustained donor and government funding scale-up through national immunization programmes on the proven Gavi model. Nothing new has to be invented, but global DTP3 coverage has stalled at 85% with 14.3 million zero-dose infants in 2024 (WHO/UNICEF), and those children are in conflict-affected and remote areas.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Zero-dose children are concentrated in the poorest households and fragile states (WHO/UNICEF 2025). The averted deaths, which dominate the benefits, are mostly young children in low-income countries (Patenaude et al. 2023).
policies.summary: Paying for routine childhood vaccines (measles, pneumococcal, rotavirus, HPV and others) in poor countries is one of the best-documented high-return investments in health. Every major study finds benefits far above costs: about 17-26 times when only medical costs and lost work are counted, and 45-101 times when lives saved are valued. The Copenhagen Consensus 2023 package costs about $1.5bn a year in programme spending and saves about 523,000 lives a year. The hard part is reaching the last 10-15% of children in conflict zones and remote areas. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $1.97bn a year and the ratio range is 14.4-94.
policies.lives_basis: Copenhagen Consensus 2023 immunization package (9 vaccines, 80 low- and lower-middle-income countries, 2023-2030 average), costing $1.7bn a year including $0.2bn of parents' time, the same programme as cost_bn: 'saves 523,000 lives each year' (Best Things First leaflet); Lomborg (2023) Table 3.1 gives 0.5 million.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3 + WHO/GiveWell

policies.title: Blood Pressure and Heart Drugs
policies.bcr_basis: WHO 'Saving lives, spending less' (2018), using the Bertram et al. (2018, Lancet) method, gives $3.29 per $1 for drug therapy and counselling for people at high cardiovascular risk in low- and lower-middle-income countries. This counts only economic output and averted health spending, not the value of lives saved, so it is a floor. Nugent's Post-2015 paper gives 3-17 for multi-drug secondary prevention (DALY at $1,000 vs $5,000, 3% discount). The Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015 expert panel put aspirin therapy for heart attacks at $63 per $1. The same panel gave high-blood-pressure medication $47 and a stroke/heart-attack pill (polypill) $7. Nugent's Post-2015 assessment gives aspirin for heart attack 31-153 and hypertension management 7-34. The full 'best investment' NCD package scored 23. So cheap acute aspirin is the top item, routine antihypertensives sit around 7-47, and multi-drug or polypill regimens sit lowest (3-17). Before overhead, the policy's components span 3.3-63. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 3.1: WHO 3.29 / 1.08 = 3.05, rounded 3.1. HIGH = 59 (lower overhead rate): Post-2015 panel 63 / 1.07 = 58.9, rounded 59. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; the whole cost behind the ratio is public outlay; LOW = 3.05 (3.29/1.08) / 3.00 = 1.02; HIGH = 58.9 (63/1.07) / 1.34 = 44.0.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Watkins et al. 2023 in JBCA; Bertram et al. 2018 in the Lancet; Nugent & Brouwer 2015 in Global Heart), with effect sizes taken from randomized-trial meta-analyses of aspirin, antihypertensives and statins, and polypill RCTs (TIPS-3, PolyIran). It is not A+ because the published BCRs for each component vary by an order of magnitude and depend heavily on the DALY value.
policies.cost_basis: Watkins, Ahmed & Pickersgill (2023, JBCA): scaling up the 'best-investment' NCD interventions in LICs and LMCs (including aspirin for heart attack, CVD primary prevention and heart-failure care in LMCs, plus near-zero-cost taxes and regulations) costs US$19bn over 2023-2030, about US$2.4bn a year. This is used as the annual government cost for the CVD drug scale-up. It is a rough proxy: it also covers a few non-CVD clinical items (e.g., early breast cancer, epilepsy) but leaves out lower-BCR CVD drugs. Cross-checks: the WHO HEARTS package costs about US$18-44 per person treated per year (Moran et al. 2022). The CCC NCD bundle is $4.4bn/yr (leaflet), and Nugent's five Post-2015 NCD interventions cost about $8.5bn/yr. cost_bn = public outlay $2.4bn + administration/overhead $0.19bn + private (household) cost $0bn = $2.59bn/yr. Watkins et al. (2023) clinical unit costs already carry a 17% above-facility (programme management) markup plus ancillary facility costs (replication data: cost-adjustment multipliers 1.17, 1.257 and 1.488 by platform). WHO's $3.29 return uses the OneHealth Tool, which costs drugs/supplies plus related health-system costs (WHO/UNDP 2019 guidance note). A larger programme markup (70% of direct service costs, used for TB by Pretorius et al. 2023) was not applied because it is specific to vertical TB programmes. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (UN agency (WHO/UNICEF/UNDP) standard cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor funds). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: needs a sustained funding scale-up of primary-care hypertension and CVD treatment, with precedent in the WHO HEARTS programme in dozens of countries. The drugs are generic and cheap. The hard parts are screening, follow-up and adherence (in TIPS-3, 43% of participants had stopped taking the pill by the end of the trial).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Benefits go to adults with hypertension or heart disease across all income groups in LICs and LMICs. Programmes funded by government or donors help poorer patients who cannot pay for drugs, but diagnosis and continuing care reach better-off, urban patients first, so the sources do not show the benefits are concentrated on the poorest.
policies.summary: Cheap generic drugs (aspirin at the time of a heart attack, blood-pressure pills, and combination 'polypills' with a statin) prevent heart attacks and strokes, now the leading killers in many poor countries. Copenhagen Consensus panels put aspirin for heart attacks at about $63 per $1 and blood-pressure medication at about $47. WHO's narrower economic-only estimate is $3.29, and long-term multi-drug regimens score lower (about 3-17). A primary-care scale-up costs roughly $2.4bn a year across poor countries. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $2.59bn a year and the ratio range is 3.1-59.
policies.lives_basis: Watkins, Ahmed & Pickersgill (2023) best-investment NCD package, LICs + LMCs, annual average over 2023-2030, from the paper's replication output (output/cost_outputs.csv). Low: the cardiovascular drug items only (aspirin for suspected heart attack, CVD primary prevention in LMCs, chronic heart-failure treatment in LMCs) = 9,035,849 deaths over 8 years = 1,129,000 a year. High: the whole best-investment package that cost_bn pays for (12.14m deaths over 2023-2030; the paper's Table 2 gives 12 million), less tobacco and alcohol excise taxes, which are counted under #25 = 10,510,011 / 8 = 1,314,000 a year. Copenhagen Consensus's chronic-disease item gives 1.5 million a year for the package including taxes.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3 + WHO Best Buys

policies.title: Malaria Prevention
policies.bcr_basis: Shretta & Anye (2023, JBCA) cost a 10-percentage-point scale-up of insecticide-treated nets in 29 African countries at $5.7bn present value (8% discount) for 2023-2030. Benefits are $275.4bn (mortality $225.9bn, productivity $41.7bn, health-system savings $7.7bn), giving BCR 48, which is the Copenhagen Consensus 2023 figure. Middle: the Post-2015 Consensus panel put 'halve malaria infections' at $36 per $1, and Copenhagen Consensus 2012 (Jamison, Jha, Laxminarayan & Ord) gave the ACT treatment subsidy a BCR of about 35. Hallett et al. (2025, Lancet) find that an optimal HIV/TB/malaria investment returns up to $19 of health value per $1. This is a whole-portfolio figure across three diseases, so it is a conservative floor for malaria's highest-value tools. The same paper gives $3.50 if only direct economic benefits are counted (see counter-sources). Seasonal malaria chemoprevention has no published BCR in these sources. Its cost-effectiveness is similar to nets: GiveWell estimates about $4,000 per life saved for SMC versus $5,500 for nets. ACCESS-SMC (2020, Lancet) found 88% protective effectiveness within 28 days at about $3.63 per child per season. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 17.4: Hallett et al. 19 / 1.090 = 17.4. HIGH = 45 (lower overhead rate): Shretta & Anye 48 / 1.067 = 45.0. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; the whole cost behind the ratio is public outlay; LOW = 17.43 (19/1.090) / 3.00 = 5.81; HIGH = 45.0 (48/1.067) / 1.34 = 33.6.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Shretta & Anye 2023 in JBCA; Hallett et al. 2025 in the Lancet) built on randomized-trial evidence for nets, SMC and ACTs, with large-scale observational confirmation (Bhatt et al. 2015; ACCESS-SMC 2020). It is not A+ because there is essentially one BCA per component rather than several independent BCAs.
policies.cost_basis: Costed scale-ups behind the BCRs: Copenhagen Consensus 2023 net scale-up $1.1bn a year (leaflet), plus about $0.3bn a year for the ACT treatment subsidy (Jamison et al. 2012) = about $1.4bn a year. SMC adds little: about $3.63 per child per season (ACCESS-SMC). The full funding gap is larger: WHO World Malaria Report 2025 says US$3.9bn was spent in 2024 against a US$9.3bn target, a shortfall of about US$5.4bn a year. Filling all of it would likely have a lower marginal BCR than the costed scale-ups. cost_bn = public outlay $1.4bn + administration/overhead $0.13bn + private (household) cost $0bn = $1.53bn/yr. Shretta & Anye (2023) cost nets, their distribution and social-behaviour-change communication from country and literature unit costs (Table 3); the authors state that active-surveillance costs are not included. Jamison et al. (2012) price the ACT subsidy at delivered cost. National programme management is not itemised separately, so only the funder overhead is added. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (Global Fund Secretariat operating expenses). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: a sustained donor funding scale-up (only 42% of the required funding was attained in 2024) through proven channels: the Global Fund, PMI, national malaria programmes, AMF and Malaria Consortium. Precedent: SMC grew from 170,000 to 54 million children per cycle between 2012 and 2024, and several countries have been certified malaria-free.
policies.who_benefits_reason: About 95% of malaria deaths are in the WHO African Region and about 75% of those are children under five (World Malaria Report 2025). The burden falls on the poorest rural households. Sarma et al. (2019) find larger income effects from reduced malaria in poorer, high-burden countries.
policies.summary: Insecticide-treated bed nets, seasonal preventive drugs for young children in the Sahel, and cheap combination treatment are the core tools against malaria, which still kills about 610,000 people a year, mostly African children. Peer-reviewed benefit-cost studies put the return at about $19-48 per dollar when lives saved are valued, and GiveWell estimates $4,000-5,500 per life saved. Costed scale-ups need about $1.4bn a year, while the global funding gap is about $5.4bn a year. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $1.53bn a year and the ratio range is 17.4-45.
policies.lives_basis: Low: bed-net scale-up, Shretta & Anye (2023): 1,337,069 deaths averted over 2023-2030 = 167,000 a year at $1.1bn a year (Copenhagen Consensus leaflet: 'saving 167,000 lives'). High: adds the ACT treatment subsidy costed in cost_bn, Jamison, Jha, Laxminarayan & Ord (2012): 'spending $300 million a year would save 300,000 child deaths' = 467,000 a year. The ACT figure is older and was estimated when drug resistance was rising, so it is the upper end.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3 + GiveWell

policies.title: Micronutrient Supplementation
policies.bcr_basis: Component BCRs: (1) Multiple micronutrient supplements (MMS) replacing iron-folic acid for pregnant women: BCR 37.5 at 8% discount (Larsen, Hoddinott & Razvi 2023, JBCA). This sets the high end. MMS plus calcium is 19-24 (the CCC leaflet's nutrition item), and the whole CCC nutrition package (MMS, calcium, complementary feeding, SQ-LNS) is 18. (2) Staple-food fortification: iron fortification of flour about 8 (Horton, Alderman & Rivera 2008: 8 at 3% discount, 7 at 6%; Copenhagen Consensus guide: $1,336M benefits / $167M cost = 8.0). Horton & Ross (2003, Food Policy) give a median of 6 for iron fortification counting physical productivity only, which sets the low end, rising to 36 with cognitive benefits. Salt iodization is about 30 ($570M / $19M; GAIN cites 28). GAIN (Garrett et al. 2019) gives 27 for fortification overall. (3) Child vitamin A supplementation: no published BCR was found. A Cochrane review of 19 trials (Imdad et al. 2022) shows 12% lower all-cause child mortality, and GiveWell estimates about $3,500 per life saved, its most cost-effective top charity. The Post-2015 panel's 45 for 'reduce child malnutrition' is a broader stunting package and is not used. Before overhead the range is 6 (iron fortification, productivity only) to 37.5 (MMS). Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 5.6: Horton & Ross 6 / 1.08 = 5.6. HIGH = 35 (lower overhead rate): Larsen et al. 37.5 / 1.07 = 35.0. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; the whole cost behind the ratio is public outlay; LOW = 5.56 (6/1.08) / 3.00 = 1.85; HIGH = 35.05 (37.5/1.07) / 1.34 = 26.2.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Larsen et al. 2023 in JBCA; Horton & Ross 2003 in Food Policy) backed by randomized trials and meta-analyses (Cochrane review of vitamin A supplementation, 19 trials, 1.2 million children, high-certainty evidence). It is not A+ because a large trial (DEVTA) found a non-significant mortality effect for vitamin A, and no BCA covers the exact iron-zinc-vitamin A fortification bundle.
policies.cost_basis: Sum of costed components: iron flour fortification at 50% coverage in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa $167M/yr, plus salt iodization at 80% coverage $19M/yr (Copenhagen Consensus guide), plus MMS for pregnant women about $84M/yr and calcium about $216M/yr (Larsen et al. 2023). Total = 0.167 + 0.019 + 0.084 + 0.216 = $0.486bn, rounded to $0.5bn a year. Not included: zinc/vitamin A in fortification (no separate cost found) and scaling up child vitamin A supplementation (~$2 per child-year per GiveWell; existing programmes already reach many children). Much of fortification's cost is borne by millers and passed to consumers rather than paid by government. The CCC nutrition package as a whole is $1.4bn/yr including $0.2bn of time costs. cost_bn = public outlay $0.5bn + administration/overhead $0.04bn + private (household) cost $0bn = $0.54bn/yr. Larsen, Hoddinott & Razvi (2023) include an incremental delivery cost of US$0.50-1.45 per pregnant woman for MMS through antenatal care. The fortification cost lines (Copenhagen Consensus guide; Horton et al. 2008) are total resource costs, including the share borne by millers and salt producers, so industry compliance cost is already counted in public outlay rather than added again. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (UN agency (UNICEF/WFP/WHO) standard cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor funds). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Easy: one health ministry or food regulator can mandate fortification under existing food-standards law, and over 60 countries already have 70%+ household coverage of iodized salt. Supplements in pregnancy and vitamin A capsules can be funded by a single donor or health ministry through existing antenatal and child-health days. The total cost is about $0.5bn a year.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Micronutrient deficiency is concentrated among poor households that rely on cheap, nutrient-poor staples. 80% of undernourished children are in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa (Copenhagen Consensus), and vitamin A and pregnancy supplements are delivered through public programmes that reach low-income mothers and children.
policies.summary: Adding iron, zinc and vitamin A to flour, salt and oil, giving pregnant women a daily multiple-micronutrient tablet, and giving young children vitamin A capsules all cost cents to a few dollars per person a year. Peer-reviewed benefit-cost studies put the return at about 6-8 per dollar for iron fortification counting only productivity, about 30 for iodized salt, and about 37 for prenatal multiple micronutrients. Vitamin A capsules cut child deaths by about 12% in trials and are among GiveWell's most cost-effective programmes. The costed package is about $0.5bn a year. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $0.54bn a year and the ratio range is 5.6-35.
policies.lives_basis: Larsen, Hoddinott & Razvi (2023) Table 12: calcium for pregnant women averts 0-8,470 maternal deaths a year (pre-eclampsia/eclampsia; Hofmeyr et al. 2018 find no significant effect on maternal mortality, hence the low end of 0); multiple micronutrients show no significant effect on neonatal or infant mortality and none is counted. The 127,785 stillbirths a year the two supplements avert (46,857 + 80,928) are not counted as deaths in that source. Iron flour fortification and salt iodization are valued by productivity and cognition, with no death count in their sources.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + GiveWell (+DCP3)

policies.title: Tobacco and Alcohol Taxes
policies.bcr_basis: HIGH = 100: Watkins, Ahmed & Pickersgill (2023, JBCA, Copenhagen Consensus Halftime), replication data, 8% discount, 2023-30, LICs+LMCs: tobacco excise tax gross benefits $51.31bn PV against incremental implementation cost $0.045bn and a forgone-consumer-surplus charge of $0.462bn = 101.2 (LMCs 102, LICs 94). Alcohol excise tax: $2.94bn / ($0.029bn + $0.026bn) = 53.3 (LICs 53). The implementation cost includes tax administration (WHO/UNDP 2019 costing convention: programme costs at the administrative level), and the marginal administrative cost of raising an existing excise rate is reported to be small (India: US$5.7m/yr), so no further cost is added at the high end. Without any consumer-surplus charge the tobacco BCR would be 620 (LICs) to 1,300 (LMCs); that is not used. Middle: the Post-2015 panel gave 'increase tobacco prices 125%' $22 per $1; Nugent (Post-2015) gave tobacco tax 10-52; WHO 'Saving lives, spending less' (2018) gives $7.43 (tobacco package) and $9.13 (alcohol) counting only output and averted health spending. LOW = 2.9: base-case tobacco-tax benefits reduced by 10% for illicit substitution (World Bank 2019: illicit trade is about 10% of global consumption; tax increases add little to it) divided by Watkins' cost and surplus charge plus the upper-bound annual costs in cost_components (collection $0.80bn + enforcement $0.45bn + secure stamps $1.21bn = $2.46bn/yr) over 8 years: 0.9 x 51.31 / (0.045 + 0.462 + 6.206 x 2.46) = 46.18 / 15.79 = 2.9. WHO's 7.4 lies inside the range. Note on the consumer-surplus charge: the paper text describes offsets of 0.9 (tobacco/alcohol) and 0.5 (salt) of health benefits, but the replication code applies 0.009 and 0.001; if the paper's stated 90% offset were subtracted from benefits, the tobacco BCR would be 0.1 x 1,134 = 113, above the published 101, so the high end is not overstated on that account. Tax revenue is a transfer and is not a benefit. Elasticities behind the health effects: tobacco about -0.4 (Jha & Peto 2014); alcohol -0.51 (Wagenaar et al. 2009). Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; the public costs are Watkins et al.'s implementation cost ($0.045bn PV) and, at the low end, tax collection ($0.80bn a year) and illicit-trade enforcement ($0.45bn a year); consumer surplus and industry-paid tax stamps are private. The tax-financed share of the cost base is 7.80 (0.045 + 6.206 x 1.25) of 15.79 (0.494) at the low end and 0.045 of 0.507 (0.0888) at the high end. Applied conservatively: the tax raises far more revenue than it costs to collect. LOW = 2.92 (46.18/15.79) / (1 + 2.0 x 0.494) = 1.47; HIGH = 101.2 (51.31/0.507) / (1 + 0.34 x 0.0888) = 98.2.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Watkins et al. 2023 in JBCA; Bertram et al. 2018 in the Lancet, underlying WHO's ROI figures), built on price elasticities from meta-analyses of many quasi-experimental and econometric studies (Wagenaar et al. 2009; Jha & Peto 2014). It is not A+ because the BCR depends heavily on how lost consumer surplus is treated (100 vs 1,300) and no RCTs exist.
policies.cost_basis: cost_bn = public outlay $0 + administration/enforcement $1.26bn + industry compliance $1.21bn = $2.47bn/yr (upper bound; details in cost_components). Tax revenue is a transfer, so only administrative, enforcement and compliance costs count. Watkins et al. (2023) put full implementation of India's tobacco tax increase at US$5.7m a year, and their replication data give a PV implementation cost of $0.045bn (tobacco) + $0.029bn (alcohol) for all LICs and LMCs over 2023-30 (~$0.012bn/yr). Chisholm et al. (2018) put alcohol excise tax implementation below I$0.10 per capita. Tax collection, illicit-trade enforcement and secure tax stamps are costed from WHO (2021) and World Bank (2019) ratios. Funding status: tax administration and enforcement are carried out and paid for by national governments; donors (e.g., Bloomberg Philanthropies, WHO FCTC programmes) fund technical assistance. Costs here are government administration plus industry compliance.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: needs ordinary tax legislation in each country, with many precedents (the Philippines, Turkey, South Africa and others have raised tobacco excise sharply). Industry lobbying and smuggling concerns are the main obstacles. Progress on tobacco taxes has stalled partly because of tobacco-industry political influence.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Global Tobacco Economics Consortium (2018, BMJ): in 13 middle-income countries, a 50% cigarette price rise gives the poorest 20% 6.7 times more life-years than the richest 20%, averts 8.8 million men's falls into extreme poverty, and the poorest pay only about 10% of the extra tax. Measured as a share of cash spent, the tax is regressive for poor smokers who do not quit (Remler 2004).
policies.summary: Raising excise taxes on cigarettes and alcohol pushes up prices, which cuts smoking and heavy drinking, especially among the young and the poor, and raises revenue. Copenhagen Consensus analysis puts the return at about 53-100 per dollar of social cost; WHO's narrower economic-only estimates are $7.43 for tobacco and $9.13 for alcohol. Counting the full cost of collecting the tax, policing smuggling and secure tax stamps (up to about $2.47bn a year across poor countries) a 10% loss of benefit to illicit cigarettes, and the excess burden of the taxes that pay the public collection and enforcement costs, lowers the bottom of the range to about 1.5; the top is about 98. Jha and Peto estimate that doubling real cigarette prices could cut smoking by about a third.
policies.lives_basis: Watkins, Ahmed & Pickersgill (2023) replication output (output/cost_outputs.csv), LICs + LMCs. Low: tobacco and alcohol excise taxes average 203,000 deaths averted a year over 2023-2030 while the tax rises (1,553,547 + 72,253 over 8 years). High: 443,000 a year in 2030 at full implementation (425,916 + 17,298). The paper's India example: 'saving 910,000 lives in India'.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3 + WHO Best Buys

policies.title: School Deworming
policies.bcr_basis: LOW = 6: Copenhagen Consensus best-practice paper (Hall & Horton), 'each dollar spent results in about $6 of benefits' for preschool children. HIGH = 100: DCP3 (Ahuja et al., Vol. 8 Ch. 29) reports the long-run benefits from the Kenyan Primary School Deworming Project (Baird et al. 2016, QJE) as 'more than 100 times the cost', with an annualised internal rate of return of 32-51%; Copenhagen's own high-prevalence figure is 'up to 60 times' the costs. The 20-year follow-up (Hamory et al. 2021, PNAS) gives a conservative annualised social internal rate of return of 37% (40.7% on earnings gains, 36.7% on consumption gains); at a 10% discount rate the social net present value is US$ PPP 230.71 (earnings) to 467.90 (consumption) per child. Cost is about $0.30 per child per treatment; treating most of the 870 million at-risk children costs under $0.3bn a year (DCP3 p. 419). The evidence is disputed: the Cochrane review (Taylor-Robinson et al. 2015) finds no effect on many outcomes from mass drug administration, which is why the low end uses the conservative Copenhagen figure. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; the whole cost behind the ratio is public outlay; LOW = 6 / 3.00 = 2.0; HIGH = 100 / 1.34 = 74.6.
policies.grade_reason: Built on a long-run cluster-randomized trial with peer-reviewed economic returns (Baird et al. 2016, QJE; Hamory et al. 2021, PNAS) and a Copenhagen Consensus best-practice paper, but the wider trial evidence is contested (Cochrane review), so B+ rather than A.
policies.cost_basis: About $0.30 per child per treatment; under $0.3bn a year to treat most of the 870 million at-risk children in low- and middle-income countries (DCP3 Vol. 8 Ch. 29, p. 419). Drugs are largely donated.
policies.difficulty_reason: Delivered through existing schools once or twice a year with cheap, largely donated drugs.
