policies.who_benefits_reason: Children in poor, high-infection areas; the Kenyan trial's long-run gains in earnings and consumption accrue to them as adults.
policies.summary: Giving schoolchildren a cheap pill once or twice a year clears intestinal worms that sap nutrition and school attendance. A long-running randomized trial in Kenya found the treated children earned and consumed more as adults twenty years later, an annual social return of 37%, and the development-economics handbook DCP3 puts the long-run benefits at more than 100 times the cost. Copenhagen Consensus's conservative figure is about $6 per $1. The wider evidence is disputed, so the range is wide, but at about $0.30 per child the whole programme costs under $0.3bn a year.
policies.lives_basis: No deaths averted are counted. The Cochrane review (Taylor-Robinson et al. 2015; three trials, 1,005,135 children) finds 'May be little or no effect on death' (risk ratio 0.95, low-quality evidence); the ratio's benefits are adult earnings and consumption (Hamory et al. 2021), not lives.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3

policies.title: Contraception & Family Planning
policies.bcr_basis: Main policy = universal access to modern contraception. Kohler & Behrman (Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015) give 120 for meeting the unmet need of 214 million women at ~$3.6bn/yr; about 40 of this comes from health benefits (640,000 fewer newborn and 150,000 fewer maternal deaths a year) and the rest from a $288bn/yr demographic dividend (Lomborg 2019). Madise et al. (2023, JBCA, 8% discount) give 22 for the 'family planning' package alone in 55 LICs/LMICs (Figure 3). In between, Ghana Priorities (Amporfu et al. 2020, 8%) gives 33.6 (married women, +10 pp contraceptive prevalence) and 29.3 (unmarried women). The spread reflects how much demographic-dividend benefit is counted and the discount rate (Post-2015 work used lower rates than the 8% of the Halftime/Ghana studies). Sub-policy (girls' full secondary education) is not folded into the range because its returns are lower and differently measured: the Ghana scholarship RCT (Duflo, Dupas & Kremer 2021; Duflo, Dupas, Spelke & Walsh 2026, AER) gives a conservative $4.1 per $1 of long-run government cost, rising to 10-110x when targeted at girls and counting their children's survival (VoxDev summary); Copenhagen Post-2015 puts secondary completion at ~4 and girls' schooling/later marriage programmes at ~5. If the sub-policy were bundled at its cost (~$15bn/yr upper bound) the combined ratio would fall to roughly (3.6x22 + 15x4.1)/18.6 = 7.6 at the low end and (3.6x120 + 15x10)/18.6 = 31 at the high end. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 20.4: Madise et al. 22 / 1.08 = 20.4. HIGH = 112 (lower overhead rate): Kohler & Behrman 120 / 1.07 = 112.1, rounded 112. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; the whole cost behind the ratio is public outlay; LOW = 20.37 (22/1.08) / 3.00 = 6.79; HIGH = 112.1 (120/1.07) / 1.34 = 83.7.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimate including family planning (Madise et al. 2023, JBCA) consistent with Copenhagen Post-2015 and Ghana Priorities BCRs, backed by quasi-experimental evidence (Matlab, Bangladesh: Joshi & Schultz 2013 Demography; Colombia: Miller 2010 Economic Journal). The girls'-education sub-policy rests on a 15-year randomized trial with a peer-reviewed BCR (Duflo et al. 2026, AER).
policies.cost_basis: $3.6bn a year to provide modern contraception to the 214 million women with unmet need (Kohler & Behrman, Copenhagen Consensus, as reported by Lomborg 2019); donor funding for family planning was only ~$1.27bn in 2017. Funding: government/donor spending. The girls' secondary-education sub-policy is costed separately and not included: ~$505 per girl for four years of senior high school including forgone wages (VoxDev summary of the Ghana trial) = ~$126/yr; x 122 million out-of-school girls (UNESCO) = ~$15bn/yr, an upper bound since many are primary-age. cost_bn = public outlay $3.6bn + administration/overhead $0.29bn + private (household) cost $0bn = $3.89bn/yr. The $3.6bn/yr Kohler & Behrman figure comes from the Guttmacher 'Adding It Up' costing, whose method adds 'programs and systems costs' (program management, supervision, M&E, training, outreach, supply systems, HMIS) to direct costs; Madise et al. (2023) cost staff, consumables, overheads and supervision. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (UNFPA standard cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor funds). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Needs a sustained donor/government funding scale-up (~$3.6bn a year vs ~$1.27bn donor funding in 2017; Lomborg 2019) with working precedents, e.g. Bangladesh's Matlab outreach programme (Joshi & Schultz 2013) and Colombia's Profamilia (Miller 2010). The girls'-education sub-policy is a larger, budget-heavy scale-up with a tested model in Ghana's scholarships.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Unmet need is concentrated among poorer women in high-fertility low-income countries (Kohler & Behrman; Madise et al. 2023 cover 55 LICs/LMICs). Matlab showed long-run gains in women's and children's health in rural Bangladesh (Joshi & Schultz 2013). The Ghana scholarships were means-tested; female recipients gained 20-30% in earnings and their children's mortality fell (J-PAL; Duflo et al. 2026).
policies.summary: Fund modern contraception (pills, injectables, implants, IUDs, counselling) for the roughly 214 million women in poor countries who want to avoid pregnancy but lack access, at about $3.6bn a year. Copenhagen Consensus estimates $22-120 of benefit per $1, depending on how much of the 'demographic dividend' from smaller families is counted; health benefits alone give about $40. A sub-policy, paying for girls to finish secondary school, is backed by a 15-year randomized trial in Ghana (Duflo, Dupas, Kremer and co-authors): it delayed childbearing, raised women's earnings and halved infant mortality among their children, returning at least $4 per $1 of government cost, more if targeted at girls. The headline ratio is for family planning; the schooling sub-policy is valuable but lower-return and costs far more. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $3.89bn a year and the ratio range is 20.4-112.
policies.lives_basis: Kohler & Behrman (Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015), as reported by Lomborg (2019): universal access to modern contraception for 214 million women at about $3.6bn a year 'would result each year in 640,000 fewer newborn deaths, 150,000 fewer maternal deaths' = 790,000.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3

policies.title: Maternal and Newborn Care
policies.bcr_basis: To avoid double counting with #27, this item is defined as facility obstetric and newborn care only (no family planning). Madise et al. (2023, JBCA, 55 LICs/LMICs, 8% discount, coverage raised from 68% to 90%) report by package (Figure 3): BEmONC alone = 83 and comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care (CEmONC, adds caesarean capacity) = 65; these set the high and low ends before overhead. The CCC headline of 87 (Lomborg 2023; leaflet) is BEmONC + family planning and includes a $25bn/yr demographic dividend, so it is not used. Wider packages score lower (entire continuum of care 36; antenatal 7) and are reported as counter-evidence. Benefits are mostly newborn lives: the BEmONC+FP package averts 1.20m newborn and 161,000 maternal deaths a year (newborn lives worth $238bn of $281bn benefits, VSLY $2,983). Valuing stillbirths averted would raise the bundle's BCR to 159. On the '65%' target: universal coverage of existing interventions would avert 71% of neonatal deaths, 82% of that through facility-based care (Bhutta et al. 2014); Madise's 1.2m of 2.16m LIC/LMIC neonatal deaths is about 56%. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 62: 65 / (1 + 0.08 x 0.571) = 62.2, rounded 62, where 0.571 = 2.8/4.9 is the financial share of the CCC cost (the rest is mothers' time). HIGH = 80 (lower overhead rate): 83 / (1 + 0.07 x 0.571) = 79.8, rounded 80. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; only the financial share of the cost (0.571, plus its overhead) is tax-financed, mothers' time is not: LOW = 65 / (1 + 0.08 x 0.571 + 2.0 x 0.571 x 1.08) = 65 / 2.2790 = 28.5; HIGH = 83 / (1 + 0.07 x 0.571 + 0.34 x 0.571 x 1.07) = 83 / 1.2477 = 66.5. Additional study (below the range, not used to set it): the Malawi Priorities cost-benefit analysis of basic emergency obstetric and newborn care (National Planning Commission, Copenhagen Consensus Center and AFIDEP 2021; Madise is a co-author), at the same 8% discount rate, finds a benefit-cost ratio of 15 for the full 15-intervention BEmONC package and 31 for a targeted five-intervention package (Table 14). With this entry's overhead and tax-finance adjustments these become 15 / 2.2790 = 6.6 and 31 / 1.2477 = 24.8, below the low end. Benefits are valued for Malawi, one of the poorest countries, whereas the range uses the 55-country estimate, so the single-country result is reported but the range is not extended. Other single-country Copenhagen Consensus studies of facility births are also lower (Bangladesh facility births 8; Ghana EmONC 5.6-8.3 at 8%).
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost analysis (Madise et al. 2023, JBCA; Lomborg 2023 JBCA summary) whose intervention effects come from the trial-based Lives Saved Tool evidence summarised in the Lancet Every Newborn series (Bhutta et al. 2014).
policies.cost_basis: Lomborg (2023) Table 3.1 / CCC leaflet: maternal & newborn package costs $4.9bn/yr (2023-30 average), of which $2.1bn is mothers' time (non-financial), leaving $2.8bn of financial (government/donor) cost. That package includes family planning; Madise et al. (2023) Table 2 costs FP at 68.6m extra women x ($2.89 + $2.14 + $0.65 + $0.75 = $6.43) = ~$0.44bn/yr. Facility care excluding FP therefore ~$2.8bn - $0.4bn = ~$2.4bn/yr (approximate, since it mixes 2020 and 2023 dollar bases). Cross-check: Bhutta et al. (2014) put facility-based care at $3.66bn of a $5.65bn/yr incremental running cost for universal coverage. cost_bn = public outlay $2.4bn + administration/overhead $0.19bn + private (household) cost $2.1bn = $4.69bn/yr. Madise et al. (2023) include provider costs (staff, consumables, equipment, overheads), a 15% supervision add-on, beneficiary costs (travel) and demand-generation costs. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (UN agency (UNICEF/UNFPA/WHO) standard cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor funds). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: Needs a sustained government/donor scale-up to staff, equip and supply birth facilities in 55 countries (Madise et al. 2023), plus demand-generation payments for facility births on the model of India's Janani Suraksha Yojana, which Madise et al. use for costing. Precedent exists, but it is a health-system build-out, not a single-agency switch.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The 55 low- and lower-middle-income countries modelled carry about 90% of global maternal and neonatal deaths; the welfare loss from these deaths is ~5.5% of their GDP (Madise et al. 2023).
policies.summary: Upgrade basic hospitals and health centres in poor countries so every birth has trained staff, clean delivery, drugs to stop bleeding, antibiotics, newborn resuscitation and steroids for preterm labour. Peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus analysis finds $65-83 of benefit per $1 for these facility packages, mainly from newborn lives saved, at roughly $2.4bn a year in public cost. Existing interventions could prevent about 71% of newborn deaths, most of them through better care at birth. The often-quoted ratio of 87 also includes family planning, which is counted separately under policy 27. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $4.69bn a year and the ratio range is 62-80.
policies.lives_basis: Madise, Nandi, Wong & Razvi (2023): raising basic emergency obstetric and newborn care from 68% to 90% coverage in 55 countries averts '1.20 million newborn deaths and 161,000 maternal deaths' a year = 1,361,000 (Copenhagen Consensus leaflet: 161,000 maternal deaths and 1.2 million newborns; Lomborg 2023 Table 3.1: 1.4 million). These figures are for the package with family planning added; the source does not report deaths for facility care alone, so some of these deaths overlap with #27.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3

policies.title: Tuberculosis Treatment
policies.bcr_basis: Pretorius et al. (2023, JBCA, Copenhagen Consensus Halftime) cost-benefit analysis of the Stop TB Global Plan 2023-2030 (modern diagnostics, screening, treatment, prevention) in LICs/LMICs, without new vaccines, vs standard baseline, 8% discount, effects to 2050: incremental costs $56.4bn and benefits $2,595bn (PV, 2020 US$) = 46.0; 27.3m deaths averted (~1m/yr) at ~$2,063 per death averted. The paper's own sensitivity range is 28-84: about 28 with vaccines and R&D costs included (27.7) and about 84 against the disruption baseline at a 5% discount (83.9); these set the low and high ends before overhead. Other cells: 55.4 at 5%, 36.6 at 12%, 34.0 including R&D, 71.0 vs the COVID-disruption baseline. Consistent with Copenhagen Post-2015 (Vassall): cut TB deaths 95% and incidence 90% for $8.1bn/yr, BCR 43. The older World Bank estimate of 9-15 (Laxminarayan et al. 2007) is below this range and listed as counter-evidence. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 26: 27.7 / (1 + 0.090 x 0.839) = 25.8, rounded 26, where 0.839 = 5.2/6.2 is the financed share of the total cost. HIGH = 79 (lower overhead rate): 83.9 / (1 + 0.067 x 0.839) = 79.4, rounded 79. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; only the financed share of the cost (0.839, plus its overhead) is tax-financed, the $1.0bn non-financial enabler cost is not: LOW = 27.7 / (1 + 0.090 x 0.839 + 2.0 x 0.839 x 1.090) = 27.7 / 2.9045 = 9.54; HIGH = 83.9 / (1 + 0.067 x 0.839 + 0.34 x 0.839 x 1.067) = 83.9 / 1.3606 = 61.7. Additional study (below the range before adjustment, not used to set it): Vassall's (2016) Bangladesh Priorities analysis for the Copenhagen Consensus Center prices treating 90% of all TB cases in Bangladesh (expanded case detection through community and private-sector channels plus treatment), about 120,000 extra cases a year: BCR 20.60 at 3%, 17.86 at 5% and 12.91 at 10% (results table, p.10). These are below the 27.7-83.9 that set this range before overhead and tax finance (12.91 / 2.9045 = 4.4 and 20.60 / 1.3606 = 15.1 with this entry's adjustments). They value one country's low-income DALYs and do not use the 8% Halftime convention, like the World Bank estimate in the counter list, so the range is not extended; the Andhra Pradesh study (Arinaminpathy, 108-117 at 5%) lies far above it, so single-country results bracket the global range on both sides.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus benefit-cost analysis (Pretorius et al. 2023, JBCA), consistent with Post-2015 (43) and with positive older World Bank estimates, built on the trial-established efficacy of standard TB treatment and diagnostics.
policies.cost_basis: Lomborg's Best Things First Table 3.1 lists TB 'Total cost $6.2 billion' and, in a separate column 'whereof non-financial cost', '$1.0 billion enabler cost'. Total social cost = $6.2bn/yr (2023-30 average; used in the BCR) and the part that governments/donors must finance = $6.2bn - $1.0bn = $5.2bn/yr. This matches Pretorius et al.'s year-by-year incremental costs: $4.4bn in 2023, peaking at $7.1bn in 2027, $5.2bn in 2030. Post-2015 (Vassall) costed a 95%-death / 90%-incidence target at $8.1bn/yr. cost_bn = public outlay $5.2bn + administration/overhead $0.47bn + private (household) cost $1.0bn = $6.67bn/yr. Pretorius et al. (2023) state that costs 'include health system costs and substantial markups beyond patient costs such as program costs and enablers'; programme (above-patient) costs are a 70% markup on direct service costs, based on expenditure data reported to WHO. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (Global Fund Secretariat operating expenses). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained funding scale-up with precedent: national TB programmes already treat 8.3m people a year with 88% success for drug-susceptible TB, but only US$5.9bn was available in 2024 against a US$22bn annual target for 2027 (WHO 2025).
policies.who_benefits_reason: TB deaths (over 1.2m in 2024; WHO 2025) are concentrated in low- and lower-middle-income countries, and the modelled ~1m deaths averted a year are in LICs/LMICs (Pretorius et al. 2023).
policies.summary: Find and treat far more TB cases in poor countries: rapid molecular tests, screening of high-risk groups, full treatment courses, prevention for contacts, and work with private clinics. A peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus study puts the return at about $46 per $1 (range 28-84), saving close to a million lives a year at roughly $2,000 per death averted. Governments and donors would need to find about $5.2bn a year (about $6.2bn including patients' non-financial costs). Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $6.67bn a year and the ratio range is 26-79.
policies.lives_basis: Low: Copenhagen Consensus leaflet, $6.2bn a year 'saves 554,000 lives per year' (2023-2030 average; Lomborg 2023 Table 3.1: 0.6 million). High: Pretorius et al. (2023): 27.3 million deaths averted 'over the 28-year period between 2023 and 2050 inclusive: almost 1 million averted deaths per year' (27.3m / 28 = 975,000), since treatment and prevention keep cutting deaths after 2030.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3

policies.title: HIV Prevention
policies.bcr_basis: Geldsetzer, Bloom, Humair & Bärnighausen (2015, Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015) model raising male circumcision coverage to 90% of HIV-negative adult men in the five hyperendemic countries (Botswana, Lesotho, South Africa, Swaziland, Zimbabwe), 2015-2030. Their BCR tables: 7.4 (5% discount, $1,000 per life-year), 11.3 (3%, $1,000), 37.0 (5%, $5,000) and 56.4 (3%, $5,000); the lowest and highest set the range before overhead. The Copenhagen summary headline is 28 (annual benefits $818m / annual costs $30m = 27.3). These value only life-years gained; health-system savings alone are also large: scaling VMMC to 80% in 13 countries costs $2bn (2011-2025) and yields $16.51bn net savings in averted HIV care (Njeuhmeli et al. 2011), and each circumcision at age 20 in South Africa saves a net $617 at 5% (Haacker et al. 2016). Returns fall as HIV incidence falls: a five-model comparison found continued VMMC cost-effective in 68% of settings (Bansi-Matharu et al. 2023), so the low end is the safer guide where incidence is now lower. Full-cost adjustment: the source costs already include country-level delivery and programme management (see cost_components), so only the international channel overhead is added to the denominator. LOW = 6.8: Geldsetzer et al. 7.4 / 1.090 = 6.8. HIGH = 53 (lower overhead rate): Geldsetzer et al. 56.4 / 1.067 = 52.9, rounded 53. The adjustment applies to costs only; benefits are not adjusted. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; the whole cost behind the ratio is public outlay; LOW = 6.79 (7.4/1.090) / 3.00 = 2.26; HIGH = 52.86 (56.4/1.067) / 1.34 = 39.4.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed economic evaluations (Njeuhmeli 2011 and Haacker 2016, PLOS Medicine; Bansi-Matharu 2023, Lancet Global Health) and a Copenhagen Consensus BCR, all built on randomized controlled trials showing ~60% protection against HIV acquisition (Auvert et al. 2005, ANRS 1265; Kenya and Uganda trials).
policies.cost_basis: Copenhagen Post-2015 summary: $30m a year (outcome document $35m). Geldsetzer et al. (2015) Table 1: additional cost over maintaining current coverage = $451.9m (3% discount) to $524.7m (5%) over 2015-2030, i.e. ~$30-35m a year. Unit cost $65.85-$95.15 per circumcision (Njeuhmeli et al. 2011). Funding: government/donor spending (PEPFAR, Global Fund). cost_bn = public outlay $0.03bn + administration/overhead $0.0027bn + private (household) cost $0bn = $0.033bn/yr. Njeuhmeli et al. (2011) unit costs, used by Geldsetzer et al. (2015), include direct costs (consumables, staff, training) and indirect costs (capital, maintenance, utilities, support overhead and management overhead) plus waste-management and supply-chain costs; they exclude demand-creation costs, for which no global estimate was found. The added administration is the overhead of the donor channel (Global Fund Secretariat operating expenses (used as the rate for the PEPFAR/Global Fund channel)). Funding status: this programme is currently financed by national governments and donors (bilateral aid and multilateral funds); costs here are aid-programme (government/donor) costs, not market transactions.
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained donor-funded scale-up with precedent (national VMMC programmes across 13 eastern and southern African countries modelled by Njeuhmeli et al. 2011). Cost is small, but prevention depends on aid: international assistance funds 80% of HIV prevention programmes in LMICs, and 2025 cuts put it at risk (UNAIDS 2025). Demand creation among adult men is the practical bottleneck.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Targets hyperendemic Southern African countries (adult HIV prevalence >15%) where HIV is a leading cause of lost life and income; women also benefit over time as fewer male partners are infected (Geldsetzer et al. 2015).
policies.summary: Offer free, voluntary medical circumcision to HIV-negative adult men in the Southern African countries with the highest HIV rates. Three randomized trials found it cuts men's risk of acquiring HIV by about 60%, and it is a one-off procedure costing under $100. Copenhagen Consensus puts the return at about $28 per $1 (range 7-56 depending on discount rate and how a life-year is valued), for only $30-35 million a year; it also saves more on future HIV treatment than it costs. Returns are falling where HIV incidence has declined. Counting the donor channel's own overhead and any household time costs, the full cost is about $0.033bn a year and the ratio range is 6.8-53.
policies.lives_basis: Derived from the same source. Geldsetzer, Bloom, Humair & Barnighausen (2015) Table 1: raising male circumcision coverage to 90% gains 3,886,000 (5% discount) to 5,101,000 (3%) life-years over 2015-2030; the paper states an average of 33.5 undiscounted life-years gained per death averted. 3,886,000 / 33.5 / 16 years = 7,250 and 5,101,000 / 33.5 / 16 = 9,520 deaths averted a year. Because the life-years are discounted and the 33.5 is not, this understates deaths averted.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + GiveWell

policies.title: Privatize Social Security
policies.bcr_basis: The ratio compares what later generations gain from funded personal accounts with what the transition generations pay to keep honouring benefits already promised. HIGH = 2.0: Feldstein & Samwick (1998, NBER volume Privatizing Social Security) simulate a shift to Mandatory Individual Retirement Accounts. In the long run, about 2.04-2.1% of payroll in accounts replaces the 12.4% payroll tax, and deadweight loss falls by 1.57% of payroll (a combined gain of 11.92% of payroll). In the early decades, workers pay an extra 0.82% of payroll in year 1, rising to 1.58% by year 15. In their worked family example (3% discount rate), two 45-year-old parents lose $11,680 in present value and their two children gain more than $23,000: 23,000 / 11,680 = 1.97, rounded to 2.0. Feldstein (1996, AER P&P) puts the net present-value gain above $15 trillion, about 3% of future GDP a year. LOW = 1.0: Geanakoplos, Mitchell & Zeldes (1998) show that once the debt to current retirees and workers is paid (about a permanent 3% of payroll), the higher return on accounts disappears; without extra saving, privatization moves money between generations rather than creating it. Kotlikoff (1998) finds the pure efficiency gain, after fully compensating transition generations, ranges from 7.23% of lifetime income (cold-turkey) and 4.33% (consumption-tax financing) down to 1.08% (payroll-tax financing). It turns into a 1.22% loss with income-tax financing and strong benefit-tax linkage, so the ratio can dip slightly below 1 under some designs. Caveats: Feldstein & Samwick credit accounts with the return on capital, and their own sensitivity case (5.4% return) raises the long-run contribution to 3.31% of payroll. Feldstein & Samwick also find the summed present value for everyone aged 20-65 at the switch is negative, so the gains go mainly to the young and the unborn. Both ends already include the costs counted in cost_bn. The transition financing is the denominator of the high end (the parents' $11,680 present-value loss in Feldstein & Samwick's worked example) and of the low end (Geanakoplos, Mitchell & Zeldes net the legacy debt out of the account return). Feldstein & Samwick also deduct account administration: they assume a 9.0% return against the 9.30% actually reported, i.e. 0.30 points of assets a year for administrative costs. Diamond's $40-50 per worker is a level estimate of the same cost and is not added again. A discussant of the Feldstein & Samwick chapter notes that Latin American account systems cost at least 1% of assets; that higher cost is not modelled in the published family example and is a downside risk to the high end.
policies.grade_reason: The numbers come from published theory quantified in peer-reviewed or academic-press models: Feldstein (1996, AER P&P); Feldstein & Samwick and Kotlikoff (1998, University of Chicago Press/NBER); Kotlikoff, Smetters & Walliser and Cooley & Soares (1999, Review of Economic Dynamics). They are supported by a historical case (Chile 1981; Schmidt-Hebbel 1998 credits the reform with about a quarter of Chile's growth increase). It is not B+ because no peer-reviewed natural experiment measures the gain and turns it into a BCR. The rate-of-return gain is also disputed in peer-reviewed-quality work (Geanakoplos, Mitchell & Zeldes).
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: transition financing of 0.82-1.58% of taxable payroll (Feldstein & Samwick 1998) on 2025 taxable payroll of about $10,670bn (2026 Trustees Report) = $87-169bn a year; the $169bn high end is used. This is the extra amount current workers pay while benefits already promised (closed-group unfunded obligation $55.6 trillion in present value, Trustees Table VI.F2) continue; much of it is saving credited to their own accounts. Administration: Diamond (1999) puts a government-organised account system at $40-50 per worker per year; inflated to 2025 prices and applied to 185 million covered workers this is $14.3-17.9bn a year ($17.9bn used). Private compliance: none identified. GDP loss: no published estimate. cost_bn = 169.0 + 17.9 = $186.9bn a year.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate under the rubric: it needs ordinary federal legislation, and full or partial privatization has precedents (Chile 1981 and other Latin American countries, World Bank 2005). It is politically among the hardest moderate items: the 2005 US personal-accounts proposal never reached a vote, and Cooley & Soares (1999) find no majority supports a transition in its first periods.
policies.who_benefits_reason: In the long run, gains reach all income classes. Kotlikoff (1998) finds poorer classes gain more (about 10.1%) than richer ones (about 8.1%) under consumption-tax financing. The transition generations lose, though: without compensation, the oldest cohorts lose up to about 26% of remaining lifetime welfare, and all those aged 20-65 lose in aggregate (Feldstein & Samwick). Without a progressive floor, the loss of Social Security's progressive benefit formula and coverage gaps (World Bank 2005, Latin America) could make the outcome regressive for low earners.
policies.summary: This policy would replace pay-as-you-go Social Security with funded personal retirement accounts, phasing the old system out. Simulation studies find large long-run gains: about 2% of payroll in accounts eventually replaces the 12.4% payroll tax, and the economy's capital stock and wages rise. Those gains go mostly to young and future workers, while today's workers must also keep paying for benefits already promised. Counting both sides gives roughly $1.00 to $2.00 of benefit per $1 of transition cost, and critics argue that the higher return is mostly a transfer rather than a net gain.

policies.title: Abolish the Income Tax
policies.bcr_basis: The ratio is the benefit to taxpayers per $1 of income-tax revenue given up, assuming the revenue is replaced by cutting government (the 'shrink the size of government' sub-policy) and the forgone spending is valued at $1 per $1: BCR = 1 + DWL/R (deadweight loss removed per $) + C/R (compliance cost removed per $). Revenue at stake is FY2025 individual income tax $2,656bn plus corporate $452bn = $3,108bn, 59% of federal receipts ($5,235bn) or 44% of outlays ($7,010bn) (CBO). C/R counts the full avoided income-tax compliance cost (Tax Foundation 2024, from OIRA/IRS paperwork-burden estimates) plus avoided IRS administration A/R (0.59 x $19.0bn FY2025 IRS operations = $11.2bn). LOW = 1.24: DWL/R = 0.13, the lower bound of Ballard, Shoven & Whalley's (AER 1985) gain from replacing the whole tax system with lump-sum taxes (13-22 cents per $). C/R = $328.9bn income-tax forms (individual $145.4bn + business income-tax returns $118.9bn + depreciation $25.4bn + estates and trusts $20.2bn + QBI deduction $19.0bn) / $3,108bn = 0.106; A/R = 11.2 / 3,108 = 0.004. 1 + 0.13 + 0.106 + 0.004 = 1.24. HIGH = 3.2: DWL/R = 2.0, Feldstein's (1999, REStat) 'nearly two dollars' of deadweight loss per extra $ raised by a proportional rate rise. C/R = $501.3bn (all federal tax paperwork $546.1bn less the $44.8bn employer quarterly return still needed for payroll taxes) / $3,108bn = 0.161; A/R = 0.004. 1 + 2.0 + 0.161 + 0.004 = 3.17, rounded to 3.2. The high end applies a marginal figure to the whole tax (an upper bound). Central: Saez, Slemrod & Giertz's (JEL 2012) illustrative $0.38 excess burden gives 1 + 0.38 + 0.134 (midpoint compliance, $415bn / $3,108bn) + 0.004 = 1.52, between Hendren & Sprung-Keyser's (QJE 2020) MVPFs of 1.16 and 1.85. Corporate sub-policy: Chodorow-Reich, Zidar & Zwick (JEP 2024) find the 2017 cut lowered corporate revenue about 40% (0.63% of GDP a year) and raised long-run GDP about 0.9% and labour income by under $1,000 per worker. Output per $ of revenue: 0.9/0.63 = 1.4 long-run, 0.44/0.63 = 0.7 in the first decade. Shrinking government: Bergh & Henrekson (2011) find that 10 points more government size goes with 0.5-1 pp slower growth in rich countries. If cut spending is worth over $1 per $, the ratio falls toward 1.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed welfare-cost estimates: natural-experiment MVPFs (Hendren & Sprung-Keyser 2020, QJE); a quasi-experimental study of the 2017 corporate cut (Chodorow-Reich, Zidar & Zwick 2024, JEP); Feldstein's TAXSIM deadweight-loss estimate (1999, REStat); and Ballard-Shoven-Whalley general-equilibrium results (AER 1985). These are converted into a BCR and extrapolated to full repeal, which no study observes, so it is not A-range.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Repealing a tax needs no new spending, and revenue returned to taxpayers is a transfer; the fiscal hole is $3,108bn a year (FY2025 individual $2,656bn + corporate $452bn, CBO), closed under the headline sub-policy by shrinking government (44% of FY2025 outlays of $7,010bn). Administration: no new bureaucracy; about $11.2bn a year of IRS income-tax administration is avoided (0.59 x $19.0bn FY2025 IRS operations). No published one-time wind-down cost was found. Private compliance: none created; $328.9-501.3bn a year of income-tax compliance is avoided (Tax Foundation 2024, OIRA/IRS paperwork-burden data). These avoided costs enter the ratio's numerator. If a replacement tax were used instead (a revenue-neutral FairTax needs a 27.8%+ tax-inclusive rate, American Action Forum 2023), its collection and compliance costs would offset part of this saving. cost_bn = 0 + 0 + 0 = $0.
policies.difficulty_reason: Ordinary federal legislation can abolish the personal and corporate income taxes: the 16th Amendment permits an income tax but does not require one, and repealing it would only stop a future reinstatement. Precedents exist in the United States before 1913, in states without an income tax such as Texas and Florida, and in the Gulf states. The difficult part is the size of the change: the tax raises about 59% of federal receipts, so it must be matched by spending cuts of about 44% or by other taxes.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The income tax is the progressive part of the federal system. Tax Foundation finds a FairTax replacement less progressive than current law, and Altig et al. (2001) find that removing progressivity lowers the welfare of the poorest. Chodorow-Reich, Zidar & Zwick (2024) find that most of the corporate cut's gains went to capital, with labour income up under $1,000 per worker. Jokisch & Kotlikoff (2007) find a prebated consumption tax could still leave the poor better off in the long run, so the design of the replacement matters.
policies.summary: This policy would abolish the personal income tax (via repeal of the 16th Amendment) and the corporate income tax, replacing about $3.1 trillion a year mainly by shrinking government. Economists estimate that each dollar of income tax costs between about 13 cents and 2 dollars extra in lost work, saving and investment. Filing and paperwork add another $329-501bn a year (11-16 cents per dollar raised), and the IRS spends about $11bn a year on the income taxes; repeal removes both. Repeal therefore returns about $1.24-3.20 per dollar of revenue given up (central about $1.50). The 2017 corporate tax cut raised investment and long-run GDP by about 0.9%, but recovered little of its revenue cost.

policies.title: Privatize Government Land
policies.bcr_basis: No study computes a welfare BCR for selling all federal land, so the headline range uses published revenue-per-management-dollar ratios for land run for income rather than by federal agencies. Both published ratios count annual management costs but not the one-time cost of transferring title, which is added at the measured 3.3% of sale value (GAO 2008, BLM FLTFA sales: $3.17m administration / $95.7m proceeds). Land value is taken as what a buyer would pay, the present value of net income: V = 12.46 x (R - C) (20 years at 5%). Ratio = 12.46R / (12.46C + 0.033 x 12.46 x (R - C)) = R / (C + 0.033(R - C)). LOW = 1.66: in the peer-reviewed Utah transfer model (Jakus et al. 2017, Land Economics; figures from Stambro 2014), Utah manages 31.2m acres and bears all federal costs; in the high-energy-price case, $422.0m revenue / $248m cost = 1.70 before transaction costs; with them, 422.0 / (248 + 0.033 x 174.0) = 422.0 / 253.7 = 1.66. HIGH = 10.0: in Fretwell & Regan (PERC 2015, 2009-2013 averages), Montana, Idaho, New Mexico and Arizona trust lands earn $14.51 per $1 of management cost, vs $0.73 for the Forest Service and BLM; with transaction costs, 14.51 / (1 + 0.033 x 13.51) = 14.51 / 1.446 = 10.0. Transaction costs lower the high end most because trust-land management costs are small relative to the land's value. Sensitivity at FLTFA's 20% statutory ceiling: 1.49 and 3.9. In the low-price Utah case the ratio is 0.72, shown in the counter list. Spectrum sub-policy (not in the headline because it is extrapolated): Hazlett & Munoz (2009, RAND J. Econ.) estimate that 60 MHz more licensed mobile spectrum in the US cuts prices about 8% and raises consumer surplus about $8.8bn a year. The real cost of freeing spectrum, scaled from the 2021 C-band auction (280 MHz; $3.3bn relocation + $9.7bn accelerated-clearing payments), is 13.0 x 60/280 = $2.8bn per 60 MHz. Ten years of benefit at 5% (annuity factor 7.72): 8.8 x 7.72 = $68bn; 68 / 2.8 = 24. Using only relocation costs ($0.71bn per 60 MHz) gives about 96. Hazlett & Munoz also find consumer-surplus losses from withholding spectrum are 15-20 times the social value of auction revenue (Belgium, Greece). Not netted out in the land ratio: non-market recreation and existence value. Haefele, Loomis & Bilmes (2016) value the National Park Service at $92bn a year, and outdoor recreation is $639.5bn of value added (BEA). Private and trust owners can keep much of this value, but no source measures how much. Tax-finance check: each $1 of public outlay or public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); not applicable here: the title-transfer administration (3.3% of sale value) is paid from sale proceeds under FLTFA, and the management costs in both published ratios are paid from the land's own revenue, so no extra taxes are raised. Additional study (below the range, not used to set it): O'Laughlin (2014, University of Idaho Policy Analysis Group) costs the Idaho Department of Lands' proposed transfer of 6.9m acres of national forest and 9.5m acres of BLM land to the state (Tables 6-7). Low scenario (500m board feet at $150): timber revenue $75m against $186.1m of costs (timber management 40 + other management 1.0 + wildfire 40 + recreation 7 + highways 12 + county payments 33.1 + BLM lands net of grazing and mineral receipts 53) = 0.40; high scenario (1bn board feet at $250): $250m against $225.2m = 1.11, or 250 / (225.2 + 0.033 x 24.8) = 1.11 with transfer costs. Like the Utah low-price case in the counter list, it is a state takeover that keeps federal-style payments to counties rather than a sale to private owners, so it supports the downside case and the range is not extended.
policies.grade_reason: The low end comes from a peer-reviewed fiscal model (Jakus et al. 2017, Land Economics) and the high end from PERC's think-tank comparison of official agency accounts. Property-rights theory of resource management in academic books (Anderson & Leal) and peer-reviewed spectrum welfare estimates (Hazlett & Munoz 2009, RAND J. Econ.; Hazlett 2008, JEP) support them. No study prices full privatization including non-market values, so it is not higher.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: none net; sales raise money (the 2021 C-band auction alone brought $80.9bn in clock-phase bids, MITRE 2021), and the policy ends federal land-agency net losses (BLM/NPS/FWS spent $7.8bn vs $5.2bn revenue in 2010; Edwards & O'Toole 2012). Administration: the measured cost of running federal land sales is 3.3% of proceeds (GAO 2008: BLM FLTFA administration $3.17m on $95.7m of sales). Applied to BEA's $1.8 trillion value of federal land (Larson 2015, 2009 values) this is $59.4bn one-time, or $3.0bn a year over an assumed 20-year disposal programme. Private compliance and GDP loss: no published estimates (null). cost_bn = 0 + 3.0 = $3.0bn a year. Spectrum relocation costs are paid by buyers and sit inside the spectrum ratio.
policies.difficulty_reason: It dismantles the federal land agencies, which manage about one-third of US land, with no modern precedent; Cato's own blueprint phases auctions over 20-40 years (Anderson, Smith & Simmons 1999). The spectrum part alone would be moderate, since the FCC has run auctions since 1994 and has flexible-use licences, but full property rights in all bands, including government bands, would need major legislation.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Under the Anderson-Smith-Simmons (Cato 1999) design, every citizen gets equal 'public land share certificates', spreading the gains. A plain auction would favour wealthy and extractive buyers and could cut free recreational access. Spectrum gains go mostly to consumers through lower wireless prices (Hazlett & Munoz: consumer surplus at least 10 times producer surplus).
policies.summary: This policy would sell or transfer federal land, parks and natural resources to private (or trust) owners and give radio spectrum full, tradable property rights. Land run for income earns far more than federal land: four western states earn $14.51 per $1 of management cost on trust lands, against 73 cents for the Forest Service and BLM. Counting the cost of running the sales (3.3% of proceeds in BLM's recent land sales) as well as management, the ratio is about 1.7 (a Utah takeover bearing every federal cost, high energy prices) to 10. Spectrum liberalization looks even better: 60 MHz more mobile spectrum is worth about $8.8bn a year to US consumers. The main uncounted cost is recreation and conservation value (the national parks alone are valued at about $92bn a year).
policies.selection_method: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World index
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Area 2

policies.title: Tradable Fishing Quotas
policies.bcr_basis: Built from the World Bank's 'Sunken Billions Revisited' (2017) global bio-economic model (5% discount rate, 20 years). Benefit = PV of fishery net benefits on a reform path minus the current path (2012 effort held constant: PV $514bn). Cost = transition losses plus PV of the cost of running a rights-based management regime, which the report puts at 1-14% of the value of landings; optimal landings revenue is $140.6bn a year (Table 3.1), and the 20-year annuity factor at 5% is 12.46. Before tax finance: LOW = 2.8 (moderate path, effort cut 5% a year): PV $1,196bn - $514bn = $682bn gain; first-year loss $0.3bn; management at 14%: 0.14 x 140.6 = $19.7bn/yr x 12.46 = $245bn. 682.3 / (0.3 + 245) = 2.8. HIGH = 16 (rapid path, effort cut sharply until stocks recover): PV $1,465bn - $514bn = $951bn net, after a $44bn cumulative loss in the first four years; management at 1%: $1.4bn/yr x 12.46 = $17.5bn. (951 + 44) / (44 + 17.5) = 16.2. The range keeps the lowest and highest published management-cost shares (1% and 14%); cost_bn uses the median of the published estimates (5.4%). The annual prize is $83.3bn (95% CI $49.7-104.9bn): net benefits rise from $3.0bn to $86.3bn as effort falls about 44%. Corroboration: Mangin et al. (2018, PLOS ONE) compare 2050 profit gains with the extra management cost of reform country by country; moving all fisheries to catch shares has a global benefit-cost ratio of 9.3 (7.0 when costs scale with revenue), and 2.8 even if every country paid the average cost of the five most expensive managers ($489 per tonne), inside this range before tax finance. Cross-checks: Costello et al. (2016, PNAS) find rights-based reform raises 2050 profits by $53bn a year over business-as-usual, with the median fishery recovering in under 10 years. Costello, Gaines & Lynham (2008, Science) find catch-share fisheries were about half as likely to collapse across more than 11,000 fisheries. The World Bank does not prescribe ITQs specifically; it lists catch shares among tools that work, sometimes alongside community management. So this ratio applies to ITQ-type reform as the main route to the effort cut. The ratio is global; US federal fisheries already use catch shares widely, so the US increment is smaller. Combining the worst of each (rapid-path loss with 14% management, no cost recovery, $3.00 per $1) gives (951 + 44) / (44 + 735) = 1.28, inside the range. Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; only the management cost is public, and only the part not recovered from fishers through levies is tax-financed (levies are transfers, so they carry no penalty); the transition loss falls on fishers. LOW: no cost recovery, as in most countries (Mangin et al. 2018), so the tax-financed share of the cost base is 245 of 245.3 (0.999): LOW = 2.78 (682.3/245.3) / (1 + 2.0 x 0.999) = 0.93. HIGH: New Zealand's 63% recovery (Wyatt 2000), the highest published full-programme share, leaves 0.37 of the $17.5bn tax-financed, a share of 6.48 (17.5 x 0.37) of 61.5 (0.105) of the cost base: HIGH = 16.18 (995/61.5) / (1 + 0.34 x 0.105) = 15.6.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed natural comparisons measure the gain from catch shares: Costello, Gaines & Lynham 2008, Science, on collapse across 11,000+ fisheries; Grafton, Squires & Fox 2000, J. Law & Econ., on the BC halibut natural experiment. A peer-reviewed global model gives the size of the prize (Costello et al. 2016, PNAS: +$53bn/yr profit). The BCR itself is built from the World Bank's official model (B- on its own). Mangin et al. (2018, PLOS ONE) add peer-reviewed BCRs for catch-share reform net of extra management costs (global 7.0-9.3; 2.8 in an extreme-cost case) that corroborate the range, but the range itself is still built from the World Bank model, so the grade is left at B+.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, global. Administration, monitoring and enforcement: the median of 14 published estimates is 5.4% of the value of landings (range 0.5-20%, mean 7.1%; GAO, FAO, OECD, Arnason et al., World Bank, Mangin et al.); on the optimal $140.6bn of global landings that is $7.6bn a year, about half of it recovered from fishers through levies (median of published recovery shares) and half tax-financed. Private compliance: no separate estimate (null). GDP loss: temporary catch cuts while stocks rebuild, $44bn over four years on the rapid path = $11.0bn a year during the transition ($0.3bn in year 1 on the moderate path). Public outlay: none beyond management. cost_bn = 7.6 + 11.0 = $18.6bn a year (transitional years; $7.6bn a year thereafter).
policies.difficulty_reason: Ordinary legislation or regulation in one country, with many precedents (New Zealand, Iceland, US catch-share programmes such as BC/Alaska halibut). Globally, though, it requires fishing effort to fall about 44% (World Bank 2017), with 'very high adjustment costs' for displaced fishers.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The World Bank (2017) notes the benefits concentrate on the relatively few fishers who stay in, while displaced vessel owners and crews bear most adjustment costs and the public sector bears much of the management cost. Pinkerton & Edwards (2009) find quota leasing transfers rents from active fishers to quota owners. Auctioned or community-held quotas could make it broad, but the evidence here is for grandfathered ITQs.
policies.summary: Tradable fishing quotas give fishers a secure, sellable share of the total allowed catch, ending the race to fish. Across more than 11,000 fisheries, those with catch shares were about half as likely to collapse. The World Bank estimates that cutting global fishing effort to a sustainable level would raise fishery net benefits by about $83bn a year. Running the system is not free: published management costs have a median of 5.4% of the catch value (about $7.6bn a year worldwide), roughly half recovered from fishers through levies. Counting the temporary catch cuts, those costs and the excess burden of the taxes that pay the public share, each $1 of cost returns about $0.93 to $15.60.

policies.title: End the Fed & Implement Neutral Reserve Currency
policies.short: End the Fed & Implement Neutral Reserve Currency
policies.bcr_basis: Abolish central-bank fiat money and return to a neutral reserve standard (gold, bitcoin or a floating commodity basket) with free banking, adopted by the major economies. All figures are % of US GDP a year; the perspective is global, so the exorbitant privilege the US earns on dollar reserves and lower interest paid to foreign lenders are transfers between countries rather than gains or costs to the world. Benefits come through four channels. (1) Inflation: a sustained 4% inflation costs 0.41% of output a year when money is currency (Dotsey & Ireland 1996, JME); Lagos & Wright (2005, JPE) find 3-5% for 10% inflation, scaled to the Fed-era average of about 3.4% (a 24-fold price rise 1913-2008; Selgin, Lastrapes & White 2012) = about 1.0%; and the interaction of inflation with the tax code adds about 1% of GDP a year going from 2% inflation to price stability (Feldstein 1997, 1999). (2) Banking crises: crises since 1973 have been twice as frequent as under the classical gold standard (Bordo, Eichengreen, Klingebiel & Martinez-Peria 2001); halving the Basel Committee's 4.5% annual crisis probability, at 0.2-0.6% of output per point (BCBS 2010), is worth 0.45-1.35% of GDP. (3) Trade: countries sharing the gold standard traded 18-57% more with each other (Mitchener & Weidenmier 2008, Economic Journal), 60% more in Lopez-Cordova & Meissner (2003, AER), and adopting gold raised trade about 42% (Estevadeordal, Frantz & Taylor 2003, QJE; applying the 1913 standard in 1870 would have raised trade volumes about 30%). On the US trade share of 25.0% of GDP (World Bank 2024), an 18% rise adds 4.5 points of trade and a 30% rise 7.5 points; at Frankel & Romer's (1999) lower bound of 0.5% of income per point, that is 2.25-3.75% of GDP. (4) Borrowing costs: gold adherence lowered sovereign spreads by about 40 basis points (Bordo & Rockoff 1996); on foreign-held federal debt of 29.3% of GDP that is 0.12% of GDP. Cost is the real resource cost of the commodity or free-banking system (Watts & Snyder 2015, Cato Journal): Meltzer 0.5% of GDP; the measured US classical gold standard 1879-1913, 0.249%; White's free banking with 2% gold reserves, 0.05%. Fiat money carries its own resource cost in private gold hoarding (Friedman 1986), measured at 0.014% of GDP a year since Bretton Woods (Watts & Snyder 2015, Table 1), which is netted off. LOW = (inflation 0.41 + crises 0.45 + trade 2.25 + borrowing 0) / (0.5 - 0.014) = 3.11 / 0.486 = 6.4. HIGH = (inflation 1.0 + tax interaction 1.0 + crises 1.35 + trade 3.75 + borrowing 0.12) / 0.05 = 7.22 / 0.05 = 144. With the measured classical gold-standard cost the central case is about 25. Downside risks kept in the counter-evidence: the IMF finds exchange-rate volatility has at most a small effect on trade (Clark, Tamirisa & Wei 2004), which with no trade gain gives (0.41 + 0.45) / 0.486 = 1.8; Friedman's (1960) 2.5%-of-GDP cost for a full 100% commodity standard gives about 0.3; output growth was more volatile under the classical gold standard (Bordo 1981); and countries that left gold early in the 1930s recovered faster (Bernanke 1995).
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed historical estimates of the gold standard's effects on trade (Lopez-Cordova & Meissner 2003 AER; Estevadeordal, Frantz & Taylor 2003 QJE), borrowing costs (Bordo & Rockoff 1996 JEH), crises (Bordo et al. 2001) and inflation (Lagos & Wright 2005 JPE; Lucas 2000 Econometrica). Not tried in a modern economy, and the Depression-era evidence cuts the other way, so B.
policies.cost_basis: Public outlay and administration: $0; closing the Fed needs no budget outlay, supervision passes to existing regulators, and lost seigniorage is a transfer. Private resource cost of holding commodity reserves: Meltzer's 0.5% of GDP (the high end of the estimates reviewed by Watts & Snyder 2015, Cato Journal) x 2025 GDP $30,861bn = $154.3bn a year; the measured 1879-1913 US gold standard cost 0.249% ($76.8bn) and White's free banking 0.05% ($15.4bn). The ratio's denominator uses these same percentages of GDP.
policies.difficulty_reason: It dismantles a major entrenched institution with no modern precedent. No advanced economy has run without a central bank since Canada created the Bank of Canada in 1935 (Bordo, Redish & Rockoff 2015). The competing-currencies sub-policy alone would be moderate (ordinary legal-tender and tax changes; El Salvador 2021 precedents).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Inflation is a tax on all money holders (Lucas 2000). Savers and cash-dependent households gain most; debtors and the Treasury lose the inflation and seigniorage transfer. Banking crises hit output and jobs economy-wide.
policies.summary: This policy would abolish the Federal Reserve and return money to a neutral standard (gold, bitcoin or a basket of commodities) issued by competing banks, the system most major economies used before 1914. Stable money removes the hidden tax of inflation and its interaction with the tax code, banking crises under the classical gold standard were half as frequent as since 1973, and countries sharing gold traded 18-60% more with each other, which raises incomes; governments that kept to gold also borrowed more cheaply. Counting those gains against the cost of holding gold or running free banks gives about $6.40 to $144 of benefit per dollar. The risk is a rigid money supply in a deep slump, as in the 1930s.

policies.title: End Bailouts and Deposit Insurance
policies.bcr_basis: Constructed from published inputs; no published benefit-cost ratio for abolishing deposit insurance exists. Benefit of abolition = crises avoided because guarantees no longer weaken market discipline. Cost = welfare lost from removing depositor protection (more runs and failures). HIGH = 5.5: Demirgüç-Kunt & Detragiache (JME 2002; IMF WP 00/3) estimate that cutting US deposit-insurance coverage to Swiss levels would have lowered the predicted probability of the 1980 US banking crisis from 4.3% to 2.5%, i.e. by 1.8 points a year. Laeven & Valencia (IMF WP 18/206) put the output loss of the 2007 US crisis at 30% of trend GDP. Expected avoided loss = 0.018 x 0.30 = 0.54% of GDP a year (about $167bn at 2025 GDP of $30.9tn, FRED). Cost: Dávila & Goldstein (JPE 2023) estimate that raising coverage from $100,000 to $200,000 was worth $13.2bn a year in 2008 (9.46 bp of $14tn bank assets), i.e. 13.2/14,770 = 0.089% of 2008 GDP; taking this as the welfare value of the first $100,000 of cover gives 0.54/0.089 = 6.1 before administration. Adding the operating cost of private replacement insurance, $2.9bn a year (0.248 NAIC expense ratio x $11.6bn FDIC 2024 assessments), in 2025 dollars (GDP $30,861bn, FRED): benefit 0.0054 x 30,861 = $166.6bn; cost 0.00089 x 30,861 + 2.9 = 27.5 + 2.9 = $30.4bn; 166.6 / 30.4 = 5.5. This is an upper bound: Dávila & Goldstein say marginal gains are highest at low coverage, so full abolition costs more, and DD find the destabilising effect is insignificant where institutions are strong, as in the US. LOW = 0.5: direct resolution costs that guarantees created since 1934, S&L crisis $153bn (Curry & Shibut 2000) + 2008 bailouts ~$500bn (Lucas 2019) + SVB/Signature $16.3bn (FDIC 2023) = ~$669bn over ~90 years = $7.4bn a year, against the same $13.2bn a year plus the $2.9bn private-insurance operating cost: 7.4 / (13.2 + 2.9) = 0.46, rounded to 0.5 (0.56 before administration). The sign is contested: Anginer, Demirgüç-Kunt & Zhu (2014) find deposit insurance raised risk before 2007 and lowered it during the crisis, with a net destabilising effect. Tax-finance check: each $1 of public outlay or public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); not applicable: the $2.9bn administration is the operating cost of private insurers paid from premiums, and there is no public outlay.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed cross-country panel (Demirgüç-Kunt & Detragiache 2002, JME), peer-reviewed historical studies (Calomiris & Jaremski 2019, JF; Calomiris 1990, JEH) and peer-reviewed models (Diamond & Dybvig 1983; Dávila & Goldstein 2023, JPE) quantify each input. The ratio itself is assembled here rather than published, and the inputs disagree on sign, so it cannot rate B+ or above.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Repeal needs no new public spending; the FDIC is premium-funded. Transition to private deposit insurance: private insurers' operating cost at the property-casualty underwriting expense ratio (24.8%, NAIC 2024) on premiums equal to the FDIC's 2024 assessment revenue ($11.6bn) = $2.9bn a year (FDIC's own 2024 DIF operating expenses were $2.43bn; not credited because supervision continues elsewhere). Private compliance and GDP loss: the welfare cost of weaker depositor protection and more runs (depositors lost about 30% in a typical pre-FDIC failure, Correia, Luck & Verner) is the ratio's denominator, not repeated here. cost_bn = 0 + 2.9 = $2.9bn a year.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: it dismantles a major federal institution in place since 1933 and ends the implicit too-big-to-fail guarantee (worth up to $70bn a year to US banks, IMF 2014). No large advanced economy runs without deposit insurance today. New Zealand, the last OECD holdout, introduced a NZ$100,000 Depositor Compensation Scheme on 1 July 2025.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Mixed. Ending bailouts removes transfers that mostly went to bank creditors and shareholders (Lucas 2019: ~$500bn in 2008-09) and the too-big-to-fail funding subsidy to large banks (IMF 2014). Ending deposit insurance shifts risk onto ordinary depositors, who are least able to monitor banks. Neither effect is clearly concentrated on the poor or the rich.
policies.summary: This policy would close federal deposit insurance and bar government rescues of failed banks, so that depositors and creditors carry their own risk. Cross-country evidence finds explicit deposit insurance makes banking crises more likely where institutions are weak, and historical US state schemes encouraged risk-taking that ended in collapse. Bank-run theory and a recent calibrated model, however, find deposit insurance very valuable, especially its first dollars of cover. Putting published crisis costs against the modelled value of insurance gives a ratio of about 0.5 to 5.5 once the running cost of private replacement insurance (about $2.9bn a year) is included, which straddles 1.

policies.title: Free Trade
policies.bcr_basis: Both ends use Copenhagen Consensus estimates of full global liberalisation that include growth (dynamic) effects. LOW = 90: Anderson (2012, CC III), completing the Doha agenda gives PV benefits of $12-64tn against PV adjustment costs below $400bn; Anderson's reported global BCR is 90-180 (140-250 for developing countries), and 90 is the floor. HIGH = 2,800: Anderson (2015 Post-2015 Consensus; Cambridge UP 2018), Doha with growth effects, global BCR 1,300-2,800 at 5% and 3% discount rates (developing countries 2,100-4,700). Anderson & Winters (2008) give 269-1,121 with dynamic gains (17-80 without). The dynamic assumption rests on quasi-experimental evidence: liberalisers grew ~1.5 points a year faster (Wacziarg & Welch 2008), and a 1-point rise in trade share raises income per person 0.5-2% (Frankel & Romer 1999). One country acting alone captures a smaller share of these global gains. The narrow static Halftime estimate (Feyrer et al. 2023: global 11, high-income 5-7) is kept as counter-evidence. Sub-policies, reported but not averaged in: anti-dumping repeal 2-14 (USITC 1995; Gallaway, Blonigen & Flynn 1999 JIE) and trade facilitation 11-640 (Feyrer et al. 2023; WTO 2015 benefits vs OECD costs of EUR 3.5-19M per country). Current US stakes (2026): Tax Foundation (Sept 2026) finds remaining tariffs cut long-run GDP 0.4% (~$120bn a year) and cost $820 per household in 2026. Yale Budget Lab (Aug 2026) finds an average statutory tariff rate of 11.0% (11.8% by end-2026) and household costs of about $1,100 a year. These are recurring losses that repeal removes at near-zero budget cost. Anderson's ratios already put the adjustment costs (the GDP-loss component of cost_bn) in the denominator, and trade-facilitation administration is inside the sub-policy ratio. Tax-finance check: each $1 of public outlay or public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); trade-facilitation administration is $0.02bn of $32.1bn (0.06% of cost_bn); the penalty changes neither end at two decimals and is not applied (negligible).
policies.grade_reason: Peer-edited Copenhagen Consensus benefit-cost estimates (Anderson 2012, 2015; Cambridge UP 2018 chapter) backed by peer-reviewed quasi-experimental and instrumental-variable evidence on growth (Wacziarg & Welch 2008 WBER; Frankel & Romer 1999 AER; Fajgelbaum et al. 2020 QJE). Even the narrowest peer-reviewed estimate (Feyrer et al. 2023, JBCA) is above 1. The sub-policies rate B (anti-dumping: peer-reviewed GE model) and A- (trade facilitation: one peer-reviewed BCA).
policies.cost_basis: Full cost. Public outlay: $0; repealing tariffs and quotas needs no budget outlay, and lost tariff revenue is a transfer. Administration: trade facilitation about $0.02bn a year for the US (OECD, Moise 2013). Private compliance: no published estimate (null). GDP loss: adjustment costs for displaced workers and firms, below $400bn in present value for full global liberalisation (Anderson 2012), annualised over 20 years at 5% = $32.1bn a year (global). cost_bn = 0.02 + 32.1 = $32.1bn a year. These adjustment costs are already the denominator of the Copenhagen Consensus ratios, so they are not added again.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: one country acting alone needs only ordinary tariff legislation, with working precedents in Hong Kong (no tariff on any import or export, HK Trade and Industry Department), Singapore, New Zealand's unilateral tariff cuts and Britain's 1846 Corn Law repeal. Anti-dumping repeal needs Congress to repeal Title VII of the Tariff Act of 1930. Customs reform can be done under existing authority (WTO TFA in force since 2017). In Learning Resources v. Trump (20 Feb 2026) the Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs, but other statutory authorities (Sections 122, 232, 301, 338) remain (Tax Foundation 2026).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Anderson (2015) finds developing-country BCRs of 2,100-4,700 versus 1,300-2,800 globally and ~160 million fewer people in extreme poverty by 2030; Feyrer et al. (2023) find ~100 for low/lower-middle-income countries versus ~5 for high-income; Fajgelbaum et al. (2020) show 2018 US tariffs fell fully on domestic buyers. In the US, tariffs act as a consumption tax (~$1,100 per household a year, Yale Budget Lab 2026), so removing them helps lower-income households most relative to income.
policies.summary: Unilaterally abolishing all tariffs and quotas, repealing anti-dumping duties, and simplifying border paperwork is among the best-evidenced policies in economics. Copenhagen Consensus estimates for full trade liberalisation, counting growth effects, return about $90 to $2,800 per $1 of adjustment cost, and liberalisers grow about 1.5 percentage points a year faster. The sub-policies also pay: anti-dumping repeal returns about 2-14 to 1 and trade facilitation about 11-640 to 1. In 2026 the remaining US tariffs cost households about $1,100 a year (Yale Budget Lab) and lower long-run GDP by 0.4% (Tax Foundation).
policies.selection_method: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World index
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Area 4

policies.title: Energy Without Subsidies
policies.bcr_basis: Annual global flows, $bn. Subsidies removed are transfers counted at $1 on both sides, as in the income-tax entry: taxpayers gain each dollar recipients lose, so the ratio is (subsidies + efficiency gains + other gains - damages) / (subsidies + other costs). Subsidies: $634bn in 2017 (IRENA 2020: fossil fuels $447bn, renewable power $128bn, biofuels $38bn, nuclear $21bn) to $1,447bn (IMF explicit fossil-fuel subsidies in 2022, 18% of $7tn = $1,260bn, plus IRENA's $166bn for renewables and $21bn for nuclear). Net emissions (MtCO2e/yr): ending fossil-fuel subsidies -500 to -2,200 by 2030 (Jewell et al. 2018); ending renewable subsidies, with the $166bn treated as the abatement it pays for, +166/88 = +1,886 at the lowest per-tonne cost ($88/t, Bistline, Mehrotra & Wolfram 2023) to +166/2,138 = +78 at the highest ($2,138/t, Abrell, Kosch & Rausch 2019); open federal leasing +100 (Prest 2022, after leakage); unconstrained LNG exports +22.9 (DOE 2024). Net: +1,509 (low) and -1,999 (high), valued at $66/t (Barrage & Nordhaus 2024) plus $57.5/t of local air-pollution damage (Parry, Veung & Heine 2014) = $123.5/t. LOW: benefits = 634 + fossil-subsidy deadweight loss 44 (Davis 2014, road fuels only) + excess burden of the taxes that fund subsidies 0.17 x 634 = 107.8 (lowest Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985 figure) + federal royalties 5 (Prest 2022) + LNG GDP 13 (NERA 2018, 2040) - emission damages 1,509 x 123.5 = 186.4, total 617.4. Costs = 634 + US GDP loss from ending clean-energy credits 160 (Energy Innovation 2025, 2030, including about 790,000 fewer jobs) + replacement nuclear licensing at the NRC's FY2025 budget 0.995 = 795.0. LOW = 617.4 / 795.0 = 0.78. HIGH: benefits = 1,447 + deadweight loss 0.40 (Davis's 44/110) x 1,260 = 504 + excess burden 0.56 x 1,447 = 810.3 (highest Ballard, Shoven & Whalley figure) + shale-gas welfare 48 (Hausman & Kellogg 2015) + LNG GDP 80 (DOE 2024, 2050) + emission cut 1,999 x 123.5 = 246.9, total 3,136.2. Costs = 1,447 + displaced-worker losses 790,000 x 1.4 years x $49,504 = $54.8bn, / 12.46 = 4.39 + 0.995 = 1,452.4. HIGH = 3,136.2 / 1,452.4 = 2.16. The high end uses 2022 subsidies, a price-spike year. Cross-check: the Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015 assessment rates phasing out fossil-fuel subsidies at 15 per $1, measured against the efficiency and environmental gains only, without counting the subsidy as a transfer. Nuclear licensing reform and lifting development-bank bans on fossil-fuel finance are not priced: no published estimate links either to measured output or emissions. Moss & Leo (2014) find a $10bn gas-only portfolio could connect about 90 million people against 20-27 million for renewables only. Tax-finance check: each $1 of public outlay or public administration costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999); the NRC's tax-financed share is $0.995bn - $0.824bn fee-recovered = $0.171bn of $347.4bn (0.05% of cost_bn); the penalty changes neither end at two decimals and is not applied (negligible).
policies.grade_reason: The priced parts rest on peer-reviewed estimates (Davis 2014 AER; Jewell et al. 2018 Nature; Abrell et al. 2019 J. Public Econ; Prest 2022 JAERE) with a Copenhagen Consensus ratio of 15 for fossil-subsidy phase-out as a cross-check, combined with official and think-tank figures for LNG exports, subsidy totals and the GDP effect of ending clean-energy credits (DOE, NERA, IRENA, Energy Innovation). The ratio is assembled from several separate studies with an assumed equality of renewable subsidies and the resource costs they finance, and two of the four components (nuclear licensing and development-bank finance) are unpriced, so the grade is B rather than B+.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, $bn a year, excluding the subsidies themselves, which are transfers counted at $1 on both sides of the ratio. Public outlay: $0; ending subsidies lowers public spending. Administration: a replacement nuclear licensing system at the NRC's FY2025 budget request, $0.995bn (NRC 2024); no published estimate exists for oil, gas and LNG permitting administration. Private compliance: none estimated. GDP loss: $160bn in 2030 from ending US clean-energy tax credits (Energy Innovation 2025), which includes the loss of about 790,000 jobs; the scenario also rescinds other federal programmes, so it is an upper bound. External damage: the low-end net emission increase of 1,509 MtCO2e a year at $66/t plus $57.5/t of local air-pollution damage, $186.4bn. cost_bn = 0.995 + 160 + 186.4 = $347.4bn.
policies.difficulty_reason: Each country can act alone through ordinary legislation, and fuel-subsidy reform has precedents in Indonesia (2015) and India (2014). Nuclear licensing reform and permitting and leasing changes are ordinary statutes, and lifting development-bank bans on fossil-fuel finance is a decision of each bank's board. No treaty is needed; the obstacle is that most governments must act, after G20 members pledged in 2009 to phase out inefficient fossil-fuel subsidies yet explicit subsidies reached $1.3 trillion in 2022.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Ending subsidies removes transfers that go mostly to better-off households (about 60% of US clean-energy tax credits went to the top income quintile, Borenstein & Davis 2016), and the Copenhagen Consensus finds particularly high benefits for developing countries when revenues are recycled; lifting development-bank bans could connect about 60 million more people per $10bn invested (Moss & Leo 2014). Poor households in subsidising countries lose price support in the short run, and US gas consumers pay about 4% more under unconstrained LNG exports (DOE 2024).
policies.summary: This policy ends subsidies for every energy source, from fossil fuels to renewables and nuclear, speeds nuclear licensing, opens oil, gas and coal permitting, leasing and LNG export approval, and lets development banks finance gas and coal plants in poor countries. Ending fossil-fuel subsidies removes large deadweight losses and cuts emissions slightly, ending renewable subsidies saves money but adds emissions, and more drilling and gas exports add output. Counting the subsidies removed as transfers, each $1 returns $0.78 to $2.16; below 1 when renewable subsidies are treated as cheap abatement and the GDP loss from ending them is counted. Nuclear licensing reform and development-bank lending are described but not priced.
