policies.title: Deregulate the Economy (Top Ten)
policies.bcr_basis: One reform package of ten US deregulation items; the ratio is total yearly benefits over total yearly full costs, $bn, 2025 dollars. LOW pairs the lowest credible benefits with the highest costs; HIGH uses the most favourable credible published estimates (highest benefits, lowest costs). (1) Occupational licensing: consumer costs of $184bn (Kleiner & Vorotnikov 2018) to $203bn (Kleiner 2015); forgone quality from Kleiner & Soltas's (2023, REStud) finding that buyers' willingness to pay offsets 80% of licensing-induced price increases and wages offset 60% of training costs: 184/1.25 = 147.2 and 203/1.67 = 121.6. (2) Minimum wage: reversing CBO's (2019) $15 scenario, families above the poverty line gain about $16bn in real income and families below it lose $8bn (2025); low benefit 0.69 x 8 = 5.5 (Cengiz et al. 2019, QJE). (3) Zoning: Greaney (2026, AEJ: Macro) finds the gain from easing housing constraints about two orders of magnitude smaller than Hsieh & Moretti (2019, AEJ: Macro), 0.037% of GDP or $11.4bn (low). Hsieh & Moretti's headline, with imperfect labour mobility (Table 5, p.27), is US GDP 3.7% higher with New York, San Jose and San Francisco at median regulation, $1,141.9bn on 2025 GDP of $30,861bn; their perfect-mobility case (Table 4, p.26) is 8.9%, 0.089 x 30,861 = $2,746.7bn (high). (4) FDA drug approval: faster reviews under PDUFA added $14-31bn of social surplus (Philipson et al. 2008, J. Public Econ), $3.2bn a year at the low end; Peltzman (1973, JPE) finds the 1962 amendments act like a 5-10% tax on drug purchases, 10% x $467bn of 2024 drug spending (CMS) = $46.7bn. High: Gieringer (1985, Cato Journal) puts the cost of FDA delay at 21,000 to 120,000 lives per decade against about 5,000 (10,000 worst case) casualties per decade avoided by FDA safety review; (120,000 - 5,000)/10 = 11,500 lives a year x $13.1m (HHS value of a statistical life) = $150.65bn, used in place of Peltzman, not added to it. Cost: 0 to $1.0bn a year (upper bound on safety harm, Philipson et al. 2008). (5) Sugar program: consumers pay $2.5bn (GAO low) to $4bn a year (Beghin 2022, AEI: $2.4-4bn); producers lose $1.5-2.5bn; net cost to the economy about $1bn (GAO). (6) Bank compliance: community banks spent $4.5bn on compliance in 2014 (St. Louis Fed/CSBS); high: CEA (2019, pp.14-15) puts the annual net benefits of the 2018 relief act for small banks at almost $5bn (no price year stated, not deflated); CBO scores the 2018 act's crisis risk at $671m over ten years ($0.067bn a year). (7) Jones Act: repeal raises national welfare by $0.656bn (USITC 2002) to $9.8bn a year (USITC range cited by Cato PA 845); about 10,800 displaced workers at BLS median pay of $71,860 lose 1.4-2.8 years of earnings (Davis & von Wachter 2011), $0.087-0.174bn a year over 20 years at 5%. (8) EPA rules that fail their own benefit-cost test: of the EPA major rules issued FY2007-2016 listed in OMB's 2017 report (Table A-2, millions of 2001 dollars), three have agency-estimated costs above even their high benefit estimate: Florida numeric nutrient water-quality standards (2010; benefits 23, costs 111-169), Coal Combustion Residuals (2015; benefits 182-226, costs 399-576) and Cooling Water Intake Structures (2014; benefits 24-27, costs 223-241). Repealing them saves compliance costs of 733-986 and gives up health and environmental benefits of 229-276; at 128.893/74.360 = 1.733 (GDP deflator 2001 to 2025), benefits $1.27-1.71bn and costs (lost benefits) $0.40-0.48bn. Compliance capital already installed is sunk, so the saving is an upper bound. (9) Compulsory collective bargaining (NLRA; national right-to-work and an end to compulsory exclusive bargaining): LOW 0, since Oklahoma's 2001 right-to-work law changed neither employment nor private-sector wages (Eren & Ozbeklik 2016, JPAM). HIGH: the deadweight loss of union wage-setting, 0.11% of wages in 2000 (Rees method; Vedder & Gallaway 2002, J. Labor Research, Table 1), doubled for a labour-supply response as the authors suggest, and scaled from 2000 union density (13.5%, BLS) to 2025 private-sector members as a share of employment (7.4m/146.7m = 5.05%, BLS): 0.0011 x 2 x 0.374 x $12,976bn of 2025 wages and salaries (BEA) = $10.67bn. The union wage premium is a transfer and is left out of both sides; lost worker voice and safety representation are not priced. (10) Antitrust: benefit = enforcement budgets saved, FTC competition mission $239.6m (FY2023 request) + DOJ Antitrust Division $288.0m (FY2025 request) = $0.53bn; HSR filing fees fund these budgets and are not added. Cost (lost consumer savings), high end from the agencies' own performance measures: FTC $3.8bn (FY2018) and $4.8bn (FY2019), mean 4.3 x 1.250 = $5.37bn; DOJ civil $1.65bn and criminal $0.34bn a year (FY2016-23 means), 1.99 x 1.223 = $2.43bn; total $7.81bn. These omit deterrence, which Baker (2003) argues is the larger benefit and which is not priced. Low cost 0: Crandall & Winston (2003, JEP) find no evidence that monopolization, collusion or merger policy has provided much benefit to consumers. Item sums: benefits $213.6bn (low) to $3,148.1bn (high); costs $131.7bn (low) to $167.2bn (high). LOW = 213.6 / 167.2 = 1.28. Item-by-item HIGH = 3,148.1 / 131.65 = 23.9. HIGH from the aggregate study, used because it is the more favourable credible route: Coffey, McLaughlin & Peretto (2020, RED, pp.1, 14) find that federal regulatory growth since 1980 left GDP nearly 25%, about $4 trillion, lower in 2012; 4,000 / 16,254 (2012 GDP) = 24.61% x 30,861 = $7,594.8bn. It replaces the post-1980 federal items it covers (sugar program, bank compliance, EPA rules) and is not added to them. Items outside it (state and local rules and pre-1980 statutes) are added at their high values: licensing 203 + minimum wage 16 + zoning 2,746.7 + FDA 150.65 + Jones Act 9.8 + NLRA 10.67 + antitrust 0.53 = 3,137.35. Benefits: 7,594.8 + 3,137.35 = 10,732.2. The study measures GDP and says it is not a weighing of regulation's benefits, so the non-market benefits of the post-1980 federal rules it removes are counted as a cost, at the lowest credible estimate: (a) 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments: EPA (2011, p.28) finds that even if fine particles and ozone had no effect on premature mortality, non-fatal health and visibility benefits reach $137bn in 2020 (2006 dollars); Cox (2012, Risk Analysis) argues the mortality benefits that make up most of EPA's estimate are unproven; 137 x 128.893/84.071 = $210.0bn. (b) Non-EPA major rules FY2007-2016 (OMB 2017, Table 1-1, low, 2015 dollars): USDA 0.6 + HHS 5.9 + DHS 0.5 + DOJ 1.9 + DOL 9.8 + DOT 22.3 = 41.0, plus DOE 20.3 and joint DOT-EPA fuel-economy rules 44.6 cut to 15%, since Gayer & Viscusi (2013, J. Regulatory Economics) find 85-87% of the benefits of fuel-economy and energy-efficiency rules are buyers' private energy savings (0.15 x 64.9 = 9.7); 50.7 x 128.893/97.316 = $67.2bn. Lost-benefit floor: 210.0 + 67.2 = 277.2. It omits non-EPA rules before FY2007 and rules below the major threshold, so it is a lower bound. Costs: licensing 121.6 + minimum wage 8 + Jones Act 0.087 + 277.2 = 406.9. HIGH = 10,732.2 / 406.9 = 26.37. Cross-checks: with Hsieh & Moretti's 3.7% in place of 8.9%, 22.4 on the aggregate route and 1,543.3 / 131.65 = 11.7 item by item; with Coffey et al.'s $4 trillion deflated (x 1.383 = $5,533bn) rather than scaled to 2025 GDP, 21.3; with agency estimates of lost benefits (1990 CAAA low benefits about 3 x $65bn = $299bn plus non-EPA rules $105.9bn in 2015 dollars = $140bn), 18.9; with no lost benefits at all, which breaks the full-cost rule, 82.8. Wholesale repeal of all 39 EPA major rules of FY2007-2016 in place of item 8 would save $54.1-64.8bn of compliance (2015 dollars; plus the Greenstone, List & Syverson 2012 TFP cost of $20.8bn in 2010 dollars at the high end) and give up $195.8-705.7bn of benefits on OMB's figures, which pulls LOW to 0.26. Not used: Crain & Crain (2023, NAM), $3.079 trillion (2023 dollars) a year, and CEI's Ten Thousand Commandments (2025), $2.155 trillion, are lower than Coffey et al. and count costs only; Dawson & Seater's (2013) counterfactual of 1949 regulation levels covers pre-1980 statutes and its working-paper versions differ widely (output 90% of counterfactual in 2005 in the 2005 draft, 56% in the 2008 draft).
policies.grade_reason: Most items rest on peer-reviewed natural experiments or structural models that measure the gain (Kleiner & Soltas 2023; Cengiz et al. 2019; Hsieh & Moretti 2019; Peltzman 1973; Philipson et al. 2008), with official estimates for the sugar program, bank compliance, the EPA rules and antitrust (GAO, CBO, OMB, FTC, DOJ). The high end rests on a peer-reviewed growth model (Coffey et al. 2020) whose regulation measure has been challenged (Goldschlag & Tabarrok 2018), on Hsieh & Moretti's perfect-mobility case, which a replication and a separate calculation put far lower, and on a 1985 estimate of lives lost to drug delay. The union item rests on a dated deadweight-loss calculation scaled by the author's arithmetic. B+.
policies.cost_basis: Full cost, $bn a year: forgone licensing quality 121.6-147.2 (Kleiner & Soltas 2023 ratios), income lost by families below the poverty line after minimum-wage repeal 8 (CBO 2019), FDA safety bound 0-1.0 (Philipson et al. 2008), sugar producers' lost surplus 1.5-2.5 (GAO), bank-crisis risk 0.067 (CBO 2018), displaced Jones Act workers 0.087-0.174 (USITC 2002; Davis & von Wachter 2011), lost health and environmental benefits of the three EPA rules 0.40-0.48 (OMB 2017, Table A-2), lost consumer savings from antitrust enforcement 0-7.81 (FTC and DOJ performance reports; Crandall & Winston 2003), NLRA reform 0 (wage premium is a transfer; voice effects not priced). Item sums: low 131.7, high 167.2. At the HIGH end the aggregate route replaces the sugar, bank and EPA costs with the lowest credible non-market benefits of all post-1980 federal rules, 277.2 (EPA 2011 non-mortality benefits of the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments; OMB 2017 non-EPA rules, net of private energy savings per Gayer & Viscusi 2013), for a cost of 406.9 against benefits of 10,732.2. Repeal needs no new spending; winding down antitrust enforcement saves $0.53bn of budgets, counted as a benefit.
policies.difficulty_reason: Each item needs ordinary legislation, rule repeal or federal pre-emption of state licensing and local zoning, with strong precedents: the airline, trucking and rail deregulation of 1978-80, Arizona's 2019 universal licence recognition, Auckland's 2016 upzoning, 26 state right-to-work laws, and repeal of rules under the Congressional Review Act. The obstacle is the number of separate laws and entrenched beneficiaries: incumbent homeowners, licensed professions, sugar growers, unions and the regulated industries' competitors.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Zoning and licensing reform favour lower-income entrants and renters; FDA, sugar and Jones Act reform help consumers widely; minimum-wage repeal and NLRA reform lower some wages, and ending antitrust enforcement may raise some prices.
policies.summary: Ten federal, state and local regulations are removed or scaled back: occupational licensing, minimum wages, restrictive zoning, slow FDA drug approval, the sugar program, community-bank compliance rules, the Jones Act's limits on coastal shipping, EPA rules whose own cost estimates exceed their benefits, compulsory collective bargaining, and antitrust enforcement. Licensing sets the low end; at the high end, zoning and an aggregate estimate of the growth cost of federal regulation since 1980 carry the gain, net of the lowest credible estimate of the health and environmental benefits those rules provide. The package gives $1.28 to $26.37 of benefit per dollar of cost.

policies.title: Secure Property Rights
policies.bcr_basis: Copenhagen Consensus analysis of land tenure security in Sub-Saharan Africa (Byamugisha & Dubosse 2023, Journal of Benefit-Cost Analysis; 8% discount rate, 30 years): rural titling benefits $395.71bn against costs $21.72bn (BCR 18); urban titling $236.93bn (average house price) or $159.89bn (population-weighted) against $5.29bn (BCR 45 or 30). Benefits rest on a 15% household wealth effect for rural land and a 25% rise in urban property values. HIGH = (395.71 + 236.93) / (21.72 + 5.29) = 23.4, shown as 23. The paper's headline is 21 (population-weighted urban prices). LOW = 6: urban benefits only, with rural benefits set to zero following the systematic reviews that find no consistent income or productivity effect of rural titling in Africa (Higgins et al. 2018; Lawry et al. 2017; Jacoby & Minten 2007), and all costs kept: 159.89 / 27.01 = 5.9. Quasi-experimental evidence on the mechanism: titling in Peru raised household work hours 17% and cut child labour 28% (Field 2007, QJE); titled families in Buenos Aires built 12% more and their children got 0.69 more years of schooling (Galiani & Schargrodsky 2010); Rwanda's land regularisation raised soil-conservation investment about 10 percentage points, 19 for female-headed households (Ali, Deininger & Goldstein 2014). Other Copenhagen Consensus country studies find higher ratios (Malawi 73, range 18-138). Tax finance: each $1 of public outlay costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), as for the transfer policies; the whole cost behind the ratio is public outlay; LOW = 5.92 (159.89/27.01) / 3.00 = 1.97; HIGH = 23.44 (632.64/27.01) / 1.34 = 17.5. Additional study (above the range, not used to set it): the Ghana Priorities analysis of customary land titling (Adjasi & Adiaba 2020, Copenhagen Consensus Center and Ghana's National Development Planning Commission) values titling as a 25% rise in rural land values and finds a benefit-cost ratio of 91 at its central 25% probability of successful implementation (GHS 86,123m / 942m), 182 at 75% and 5 at 1% (Table 3), with sensitivities from 4 to 219. Like the Malawi study (73) already noted, this single-country result lies above the high end, so the range is not extended.
policies.grade_reason: One peer-reviewed benefit-cost analysis (Byamugisha & Dubosse 2023, JBCA) backed by quasi-experimental and natural-experiment studies (Field 2007; Galiani & Schargrodsky 2010; Ali, Deininger & Goldstein 2014); systematic reviews find mixed income effects, so A-.
policies.cost_basis: $82.4bn over 30 years for Sub-Saharan Africa (rural $68.6bn, urban $13.8bn, undiscounted; Byamugisha & Dubosse 2023, Table 4) = $2.7bn a year, mostly registry operation and upkeep. Per-parcel titling costs of $5-25 have been achieved in Rwanda, Malawi and Tanzania. A global programme would cost more; no sourced global total exists.
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained funding scale-up with working precedents: Rwanda's nationwide land tenure regularisation demarcated 4.8 million parcels in its first year (Ali et al. 2014), and Peru's urban titling programme issued titles to over a million households in the 1990s (Field 2007). The practical obstacles are land administration capacity, elite capture and keeping registries up to date where customary tenure is common.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Targets squatters, smallholders and female-headed households, who gained most in Rwanda; about 1.1 billion adults report insecure land or property rights (Prindex).
policies.summary: Giving the world's poor formal, tradable titles to the land and homes they already occupy lets them invest, borrow against and sell what they own. A peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus analysis for Sub-Saharan Africa finds $18 back per dollar for rural titling and $30-45 for urban titling, at costs of $5-25 a parcel, and field studies find titled families work more, build more and keep children in school longer. Because reviews find weaker effects on rural incomes, the range runs from about $6 to $23 per dollar.

sources.authors: Jayachandran, S.; de Laat, J.; Lambin, E. F.; Stanton, C. Y.; Audy, R.; Thomas, N. E.
sources.title: Cash for carbon: A randomized trial of payments for ecosystem services to reduce deforestation
sources.reported_estimate: RCT in 121 Ugandan villages: tree cover fell 4.2% in treatment vs 9.1% in control villages; no evidence of leakage; value of delayed CO2 emissions 2.4 times programme cost.

sources.authors: Jayachandran, S.; de Laat, J.; Lambin, E. F.; Stanton, C. Y.
sources.title: Cash for Carbon: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Payments for Ecosystem Services to Reduce Deforestation (IPR Working Paper WP-16-25)
sources.venue: Institute for Policy Research, Northwestern University
sources.reported_estimate: Cost at scale ~$0.57 per tCO2 delayed; SCC $39; BCR ~2 in base case, 0.7 if immediate catch-up, 12.3 if permanent delay; take-up 32%; equity caveats (landless households).

sources.authors: Kindermann, G.; Obersteiner, M.; Sohngen, B.; Sathaye, J.; Andrasko, K.; Rametsteiner, E.; Schlamadinger, B.; Wunder, S.; Beach, R.
sources.title: Global cost estimates of reducing carbon emissions through avoided deforestation
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 105(30):10302-10307
sources.reported_estimate: 10% cut in deforestation 2005-2030: 0.3-0.6 GtCO2/yr for $0.4-1.7bn/yr; 50% cut: 1.5-2.7 GtCO2/yr for $17.2-28.0bn/yr.

sources.authors: Assuncao, J.; Gandour, C.; Rocha, R.
sources.title: DETER-ing Deforestation in the Amazon: Environmental Monitoring and Law Enforcement
sources.reported_estimate: IV design using cloud cover: satellite-targeted monitoring and enforcement significantly reduced Amazon deforestation. CPI summary of the research: avoided ~59,500 km2 of clearing 2007-2011; any carbon price above $0.76/tCO2 covers the cost of monitoring and enforcement.

sources.title: Biodiversity: Post-2015 Consensus
sources.reported_estimate: Reduce global forest loss by at least 50%: BCR ~10 (highlight); McVittie's re-estimate $2-3 per $1; Markandya's own assessment $30-100+.

sources.title: Social Cost of Carbon 101
sources.reported_estimate: US IWG interim SCC $51/tCO2; EPA (Nov 2023) $190/tCO2.

sources.title: Action needed to make carbon offsets from forest conservation work for climate change mitigation
sources.reported_estimate: Synthetic-control evaluation of 18 voluntary REDD+ projects (26 sites): only ~6.1% of credits tied to additional emission reductions; 68% of credits from projects with no significant reduction.

sources.title: The Quantification and Tracing of Leakage in the Forest Sector in Nordic Countries
sources.reported_estimate: Reports Gan & McCarl (2007): 'between 42% and 95% of forest conservation efforts within a country or region may be redirected elsewhere'; other studies 50-100% for harvest reductions in the EU and Norway.

sources.authors: International Forest Industries (reporting the Eliasch Review, UK Government)
sources.title: Eliasch Review on international deforestation published
sources.reported_estimate: Capacity building for forest nations estimated at up to $4bn over five years for 40 forest nations; without action, deforestation could add climate damages of $1 trillion a year by 2100.

sources.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Marginal excess burden centres around 33 cents per $1 of revenue, range 17-56 cents (per Fullerton & Henderson 1987, NBER w2353).

sources.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax

sources.title: Biodiversity Perspective / alternative estimate

sources.why_excluded: Falls inside the adopted range; not a separate end point.

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; Prest, B. C.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
sources.reported_estimate: Mean SCC $185/tCO2 (5-95%: $44-413) at a 2% near-term discount rate; used for the cross-check.
sources.why_excluded: Highest published social cost of carbon ($185/t); used only in the cross-check.

sources.title: Do Renewable Portfolio Standards Deliver Cost-Effective Carbon Abatement? (BFI Working Paper 2019-62, revised 24 June 2026)
sources.venue: Becker Friedman Institute / Energy Policy Institute, University of Chicago
sources.reported_estimate: June 2026 revision (SSRN abstract): electricity prices 11% higher seven years after RPS passage; CO2 emissions 8-17% lower; cost per abated tCO2 $86-211. The 2019 working-paper version (EPIC summary, https://epic.uchicago.edu/research/do-renewable-portfolio-standards-deliver): prices +11% after 7 years and +17% after 12; cost exceeds $130/t in all specifications, up to $460.

sources.authors: Abrell, J.; Kosch, M.; Rausch, S.
sources.title: Carbon abatement with renewables: Evaluating wind and solar subsidies in Germany and Spain
sources.reported_estimate: Short-run abatement cost of solar subsidies EUR 411-1,944/tCO2; wind EUR 82-276/tCO2; consumers bear 4-7x larger costs when solar is promoted and benefit when wind is promoted.

sources.authors: Bistline, J.; Mehrotra, N.; Wolfram, C.
sources.title: Economic Implications of the Climate Provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act
sources.venue: Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Spring 2023 (NBER WP 31267)
sources.reported_estimate: Power-sector average abatement cost of IRA tax credits $36-87/tCO2 with discounted costs and undiscounted emissions, $88-94 if both are discounted; 'would be higher if distortions associated with financing the incentives were included'; tax-credit expenditures to 2031 $244bn (lower), $781bn (central), $1,070bn (higher); total fiscal costs $365-1,190bn.

sources.title: Energy: Post-2015 Consensus
sources.reported_estimate: Doubling the share of renewables in the global energy mix: BCR below 1 (excessively costly until intermittency/storage solved); doubling energy RD&D: 11; phasing out fossil-fuel subsidies: 15.

sources.title: The Budgetary Cost of the Inflation Reduction Act's Energy Subsidies (Policy Analysis No. 992)
sources.reported_estimate: IRA energy subsidies $936bn-$1.97 trillion over 2025-2034 ($2.04-4.67 trillion through 2050); CBO/JCT ~$786bn over 2024-2033; also reports Goldman Sachs $1.2T and Penn Wharton just over $1T.

sources.title: 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' Brings Big Changes to Green Energy Tax Credits
sources.reported_estimate: Wind/solar 45Y/48E credits end unless construction begins by July 4, 2026 or in service by Dec 31, 2027; EV credits eliminated after 2025.

sources.title: The Distributional Effects of US Clean Energy Tax Credits
sources.venue: Tax Policy and the Economy 30 (NBER WP 21437)
sources.reported_estimate: Top income quintile received ~60% of clean-energy tax credits, bottom three quintiles ~10%; ~90% of EV credits went to the top quintile.

sources.title: Social Cost of Carbon 101

sources.title: Levelized Full System Costs of Electricity
sources.reported_estimate: Introduces Levelized Full System Costs of Electricity (LFSCOE): the cost of serving an entire market with one source plus storage (abstract, RePEc); in Germany and ERCOT Texas, wind and solar LFSCOE exceed the most expensive dispatchable technology, and even a 90% fall in storage costs does not make them competitive. Fraser Institute commentary (2025) reports from a study in Energy that solar costs rise from $36/MWh to as much as $1,548/MWh and wind from $40 to up to $504/MWh on this basis.

sources.title: Assessing the costs and benefits of US renewable portfolio standards
sources.reported_estimate: Existing RPS: system costs up to $31bn (PV 2015-2050); health benefits $97bn and climate benefits $161bn (central); lower bounds $48bn and $37bn. Expanded RPS: costs $23-194bn, health $558bn, climate $599bn (central). Authors: RPS not the most cost-effective route but cost-effective nationally once externalities counted.
sources.why_excluded: Modelled ex ante by DOE national laboratories (LBNL, NREL), which also carry out DOE renewable-energy programmes; uses projected costs from the laboratories' own capacity-expansion model rather than observed prices, and its ratio is driven by health co-benefits; ex-post studies of the same mandates (Greenstone & Nath) find higher costs per tonne. Kept as the optimistic counter-estimate (8.3; 2.7 with lower-bound benefits).

sources.title: State Electricity Resource Standards: 2025 Data Update
sources.reported_estimate: RPS compliance costs averaged roughly 4% of retail electricity bills across states (less than 1% in 5 states, more than 10% in 3), based on REC prices and utility/PUC data.
sources.why_excluded: DOE-laboratory estimate built from REC prices and utility-reported compliance costs, which omit wider price effects; Greenstone & Nath's observed 11% retail-price effect is used for the private-compliance component (LBNL's 4% would give ~$14.4bn/yr).

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; Prest, B. C.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
sources.reported_estimate: SCC $185/tCO2 (5-95%: $44-413), 2% discount rate.
sources.why_excluded: Highest published social cost of carbon ($185/t); the range uses DICE-2023 ($66/t) as the upper carbon value.

sources.title: Adapt Now: A Global Call for Leadership on Climate Resilience
sources.venue: Global Center on Adaptation / World Resources Institute
sources.reported_estimate: $1.8tn invested 2020-2030 in five areas yields $7.1tn net benefits; BCRs 2:1 to 10:1; 24 hours' warning cuts damage 30%; $800m on EWS in developing countries avoids $3-16bn/yr; EWS benefits at least 10x cost; mangroves avoid >$80bn/yr of coastal flood losses, benefits up to 10x costs.

sources.title: A Cost Effective Solution to Reduce Disaster Losses in Developing Countries: Hydro-Meteorological Services, Early Warning, and Evacuation (Policy Research Working Paper 6058)
sources.reported_estimate: Upgrading hydro-met and EWS in all developing countries: avoided asset losses $0.3-2bn/yr, ~23,000 lives/yr ($0.7-3.5bn), wider benefits $3-30bn/yr; total $4-36bn/yr for ~$1bn/yr; BCR 4-36.

sources.title: Reviewing estimates of the economic efficiency of disaster risk management: opportunities and limitations of using risk-based cost-benefit analysis
sources.reported_estimate: Disaster risk management benefits outweigh costs on average by about four times (risk-based studies); evidence base limited.

sources.authors: Multihazard Mitigation Council, National Institute of Building Sciences
sources.title: Natural Hazard Mitigation Saves: 2019 Report (federal grants - riverine flood)
sources.reported_estimate: Federal riverine-flood mitigation grants: average BCR ~7:1 (~$82bn savings on $11.5bn); all federal mitigation grants since 1995 $27bn saving $160bn, ~6:1.

sources.authors: Hinkel, J.; Lincke, D.; Vafeidis, A. T.; Perrette, M.; Nicholls, R. J.; Tol, R. S. J.; Marzeion, B.; Fettweis, X.; Ionescu, C.; Levermann, A.
sources.title: Coastal flood damage and adaptation costs under 21st century sea-level rise
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 111(9):3292-3297
sources.reported_estimate: Without adaptation 0.2-4.6% of world population flooded annually in 2100 and losses 0.3-9.3% of GDP; dike investment and maintenance $12-71bn/yr in 2100, much smaller than avoided damages.

sources.authors: Narayan, S.; Beck, M. W.; Reguero, B. G.; Losada, I. J.; van Wesenbeeck, B.; Pontee, N.; Sanchirico, J. N.; Ingram, J. C.; Lange, G.-M.; Burks-Copes, K. A.
sources.title: The Effectiveness, Costs and Coastal Protection Benefits of Natural and Nature-Based Defences
sources.reported_estimate: Salt marshes and mangroves are 2-5 times cheaper than submerged breakwaters for wave heights up to 0.5 m; coral reefs and marshes have the highest wave-reduction potential.

sources.title: COP27: $3.1 billion plan to achieve early warning systems for all by 2027
sources.reported_estimate: Early Warnings for All: $3.1bn of new targeted investment 2023-2027 (~50 cents per person per year); countries with limited EWS coverage have disaster mortality 8x higher.

sources.title: Adaptation Gap Report 2023: Underfinanced. Underprepared.
sources.reported_estimate: Adaptation needs of developing countries $215-387bn/yr this decade; finance gap $194-366bn/yr.

sources.title: Section 1215 | Management Costs (Disaster Recovery Reform Act of 2018)
sources.reported_estimate: HMGP management costs: 'not more than 15 percent of the total amount of the grant award', of which not more than 10% by the grantee and 5% by the subgrantee.

sources.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
sources.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Marginal excess burden centres around 33 cents per $1 of revenue, range 17-56 cents (per Fullerton & Henderson 1987, NBER w2353).

sources.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
sources.reported_estimate: Deadweight loss of nearly $2 per extra $1 of revenue from a proportional rise in all personal income tax rates.

sources.title: Does mitigation save? Reviewing cost-benefit analyses of disaster risk reduction
sources.venue: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction 10(A):213-235
sources.reported_estimate: Many results support the economic effectiveness of DRR, but studies often lack sensitivity analysis, ignore climate change and disbenefits, and results are highly context-specific.
sources.why_excluded: Does not give a pooled ratio; used as a caution that published BCRs may be optimistic and context-dependent.

sources.authors: Ward, P. J.; Jongman, B.; Aerts, J. C. J. H.; Bates, P. D.; Botzen, W. J. W.; Diaz Loaiza, A.; Hallegatte, S.; Kind, J. M.; Kwadijk, J.; Scussolini, P.; Winsemius, H. C.
sources.title: A global framework for future costs and benefits of river-flood protection in urban areas
sources.reported_estimate: Dyke investment may be economically attractive in many regions, but not everywhere.
sources.why_excluded: No single global ratio in the abstract; supports the point that some defences fall below 1, consistent with the low end of 2 being an average rather than a floor for every project.

sources.authors: Brander, L. M.; van Beukering, P.; Nijsten, L.; McVittie, A.; Baulcomb, C.; Eppink, F. V.; Cado van der Lelij, J. A.
sources.title: The global costs and benefits of expanding Marine Protected Areas
sources.reported_estimate: Global benefits of MPA expansion exceed costs by a factor of 1.4-2.7, depending on location and extent (six scenarios).

sources.title: Expansion of Marine Protected Areas (Copenhagen Consensus assessment, 'Identifying best buys for Africa')
sources.reported_estimate: Africa, 38 coastal countries: BCR 9.2 for 10% EEZ coverage and 1.16 for 30%; MPA management ~7% of total costs, fisheries opportunity cost ~90%; 5 years to establish, benefits over a further 30 years.

sources.authors: Brander, L.; Baulcomb, C.; van der Lelij, J. A. C.; Eppink, F.; McVittie, A.; Nijsten, L.; van Beukering, P.
sources.title: The benefits to people of expanding Marine Protected Areas (summarised in WWF 'Marine Protected Areas: Smart Investments in Ocean Health')
sources.reported_estimate: BCR 3.17-19.77 across six scenarios; PV costs 2015-2050 $45-47bn (10%) and $223-228bn (30%); PV benefits $622-923bn (10%) and $719-1,145bn (30%); net benefits $490-920bn. Table 14 (PV, 3%, 2013 $bn), P2P30: management 24.374, establishment 7.854, fisheries 195.8, total 228.0, benefits 1,145.2; E2E30: management 23.768, establishment 5.980, fisheries 197.3, total 227.0, benefits 719.2.

sources.authors: Balmford, A.; Gravestock, P.; Hockley, N.; McClean, C. J.; Roberts, C. M.
sources.title: The worldwide costs of marine protected areas
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 101(26):9694-9697
sources.reported_estimate: A global MPA network covering 20-30% of the seas would cost ~$5-19bn/yr to run and support ~1 million jobs.

sources.title: Adapt Now: A Global Call for Leadership on Climate Resilience
sources.reported_estimate: Mangroves avoid >$80bn/yr of coastal flood losses and provide $40-50bn/yr of non-market benefits; preservation and restoration benefits up to 10x costs.

sources.authors: Sala, E.; Mayorga, J.; Bradley, D.; et al.
sources.title: Protecting the global ocean for biodiversity, food and climate
sources.reported_estimate: Only 2.7% of the ocean highly protected; well-placed protection could raise catches by >8 Mt; protecting ~4% would remove 90% of carbon-disturbance risk from bottom trawling.

sources.title: Protecting 30% of the planet for nature: costs, benefits and economic implications
sources.venue: Campaign for Nature / Cambridge Conservation Initiative
sources.reported_estimate: Benefits outweigh costs at least 5:1 for protecting 30% of land and ocean; ~$140bn/yr investment needed by 2030 vs ~$24bn/yr current; +$250bn/yr output and +$350bn/yr ecosystem services.

sources.authors: Edgar, G.J. et al. (via Reef Resilience summary)
sources.title: Global conservation outcomes depend on marine protected areas with five key features
sources.reported_estimate: 87 MPAs in 40 countries: 'Only 9 of the 87 MPAs had 4 or 5 of those characteristics'; 'most of the remainder of MPAs were ecologically indistinguishable from non-MPAs'.

sources.authors: Ovando, D.; Liu, O.; Molina, R.; Parma, A.; Szuwalski, C.
sources.title: Global effects of marine protected areas on food security are unknown
sources.reported_estimate: 'using a more realistic model markedly changes the map of priority MPAs and reduces potential food benefits by 62%'.

sources.title: A path forward for analysing the impacts of marine protected areas
sources.reported_estimate: Sala et al. 'made inconsistent assumptions about how fishing fleets would respond to closed areas'; 'fishing effort moves but does not disappear'.

sources.authors: Hiddink, J. G.; van de Velde, S. J.; McConnaughey, R. A.; et al.
sources.title: Quantifying the carbon benefits of ending bottom trawling
sources.reported_estimate: Sala et al.'s assumptions 'result in an upward bias in the estimated CO2 release by several orders of magnitude'.

sources.title: Capacity shortfalls hinder the performance of marine protected areas globally
sources.reported_estimate: 'Only 9 percent of MPAs reported having adequate staff'; 'only 35 percent of MPAs reported acceptable funding levels'.

sources.title: Carbon Removal Using Coastal Blue Carbon Ecosystems Is Uncertain and Unreliable, With Questionable Climatic Cost-Effectiveness
sources.reported_estimate: Warns of 'potential over-crediting'; median cost about US$560/t CO2e for mangroves and US$469,100/t for saltmarsh (citing Taillardat et al.).

sources.title: Economic impacts of Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument expansion on the Hawaii longline fishery
sources.reported_estimate: For vessels that fished heavily in the area, catch per unit effort fell 7%; 'Revenue per trip decreased by 9%, $3.5 million, during the first 16 months'.

sources.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
sources.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Marginal excess burden centres around 33 cents per $1 of revenue, range 17-56 cents (per Fullerton & Henderson 1987, NBER w2353).

sources.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
sources.reported_estimate: Deadweight loss of nearly $2 per extra $1 of revenue from a proportional rise in all personal income tax rates.

sources.title: Biodiversity: Post-2015 Consensus
sources.reported_estimate: Protect 17% of land and inland water and 10% of coastal and marine areas by 2020: BCR 0.85 ('relatively ineffective or highly uncertain'); stem coral reef loss by 50%: >24.
sources.why_excluded: Combines terrestrial and marine protection in one target, so the 0.85 is not ocean-specific; the coral-reef figure (>24) is for reef-loss reduction generally, not MPAs.

sources.authors: Hiddink, J. G.; van de Velde, S. J.; McConnaughey, R. A.; et al.
sources.title: Quantifying the carbon benefits of ending bottom trawling
sources.reported_estimate: Sala et al.'s trawling-carbon release is 'vastly' overestimated, plausibly by 100-1,000x; of 49 studies, ~60% found no significant effect of trawling on sediment organic carbon.
sources.why_excluded: Not a BCR; it removes most of the seabed-carbon benefit claimed by Sala et al., which is why no blue-carbon credit from trawling bans is added to the range.

sources.title: Policy: Marine biodiversity needs more than protection
sources.reported_estimate: Argues EEZ-wide fisheries management protects biodiversity better than closures; MPAs can displace fishing effort elsewhere.
sources.why_excluded: Qualitative argument without a ratio; fisheries management is outside this policy's scope, but displacement would lower the MPA ratios.

sources.title: Economic Implications of a Phased-in EV Mandate in Canada (Working Paper 2023-01; published Canadian Journal of Economics 2024)
sources.venue: University of Guelph Department of Economics / Canadian Journal of Economics
sources.reported_estimate: CGE results: parity by 2035, deadweight costs 'over $2,700 per tonne', emissions 1.3% below baseline in 2032, real GDP ~1.3% below baseline in 2030; parity by 2050, 'nearly $4,700 per tonne', emissions 3.2% below baseline, real GDP 7.0% below baseline in 2035.

sources.title: Global EV Outlook 2025 (press release: More than 1 in 4 cars sold worldwide this year is set to be electric)
sources.reported_estimate: 2024: >17m electric cars sold, >20% of global sales; China >11m, almost half its market, two-thirds priced below ICE equivalents; BEVs ~20% dearer in Germany and ~30% in the US; >40% share expected by 2030.

sources.authors: Holland, S. P.; Mansur, E. T.; Muller, N. Z.; Yates, A. J.
sources.title: Decompositions and Policy Consequences of an Extraordinary Decline in Air Pollution from Electricity Generation
sources.venue: American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 12(4):244-274 (NBER WP 25339)
sources.reported_estimate: US power-plant damages fell from $245bn to $133bn a year over 2010-2017; EVs are 'now cleaner than gasoline vehicles on average, though substantial heterogeneity remains'. Update to the 2016 estimate; applies to the cleaner US grid, not to coal-heavy Asian grids.

sources.title: The Distributional Effects of US Clean Energy Tax Credits
sources.venue: Tax Policy and the Economy 30 (NBER WP 21437)
sources.reported_estimate: Top income quintile received ~90% of EV tax credits.

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; Prest, B. C.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
Social Cost of Carbon 101
sources.reported_estimate: US IWG interim SCC $51/tCO2.

sources.title: Electric Vehicles for Everyone? The Impossible Dream
sources.reported_estimate: 'Today, the battery adds at least $10,000 to the price of an EV'; battery costs up 20% since 2021; Boston Consulting Group puts utility grid upgrade costs at $1,700-5,800 per EV ($400bn to >$1T for an all-EV US fleet); replacing ~1m US gasoline pumps needs >$100bn of superchargers; IMF projects metals at historic peaks for about a decade; EV life-cycle emissions vary widely with grid and materials.

sources.authors: Holland, S.P.; Mansur, E.T.; Muller, N.Z.; Yates, A.J.
sources.title: Are There Environmental Benefits from Driving Electric Vehicles? The Importance of Local Factors
sources.reported_estimate: Second-best EV subsidy (= environmental benefit of an EV over a gasoline car, CO2 plus local pollution) ranges from $2,785 in California to -$4,964 in North Dakota, mean -$1,095 on the 2010-12 US grid; 91% of EV local pollution damages are exported to other states. Sets the low end.

sources.authors: Ji, S.; Cherry, C.R.; Bechle, M.J.; Wu, Y.; Marshall, J.D.
sources.title: Electric Vehicles in China: Emissions and Health Impacts
sources.reported_estimate: PM2.5 emission factors are generally lower for conventional vehicles than comparable EVs in China; primary PM2.5 health impacts per passenger-km are greater for e-cars than gasoline cars in most cities (3.6x on average).

sources.title: Global Electricity Review 2025: Major countries and regions
sources.reported_estimate: 2024 coal share of electricity generation: China 58%, India 75%, world 34%, US <15%, EU 9.8%.

sources.authors: Hagerty, J.M.; Sergici, S.; Lam, L.
sources.title: Electric Power Sector Investments of $75-125 Billion Needed to Support Projected 20 Million EVs by 2030, According to Brattle Economists
sources.venue: The Brattle Group publication summary (report: Hagerty, Sergici & Lam, 2020)
sources.reported_estimate: $75-125bn of US electric power sector investment needed for 20m EVs by 2030: generation and storage $30-50bn, T&D upgrades $15-25bn, EV chargers and customer-side infrastructure $30-50bn (1-2m public chargers). = $3,750-6,250 per EV (arithmetic).

sources.title: An Electric Vehicle-only approach would lead to the loss of half a million jobs in the EU, study finds
sources.venue: CLEPA (European Association of Automotive Suppliers) press release, 6 Dec 2021
sources.reported_estimate: EV-only phase-out by 2035: 501,000 EU supplier jobs in ICE powertrain at risk (70%, 359,000, lost in 2030-2035); 226,000 new EV-powertrain jobs; net loss 275,000 (-43%) by 2040.

sources.title: Vehicle Scrappage and Gasoline Policy
sources.reported_estimate: Scrap elasticity about -0.7; when new-vehicle standards raise used-car values and delay scrappage, 13-16% of expected fuel savings leak away through the used-vehicle market (Gruenspecht effect).

sources.title: Critical Minerals Market Review 2023: Key market trends
sources.reported_estimate: Broad-based price increases for critical minerals in 2021 and early 2022, especially volatile for nickel and lithium; market for key transition minerals doubled in five years to $320bn in 2022; clean-energy share of demand 56% lithium, 40% cobalt, 16% nickel.

sources.title: Climate Change: The Ultimate Challenge for Economics (Nobel Prize Lecture)
sources.reported_estimate: DICE-2016R3 cost-benefit optimal SCC ~$36/tCO2 (2020); low-end carbon value in the cross-check.

sources.authors: Centre for Economics and Business Research (for the APPG on Fair Fuel), as reported by Forecourt Trader
sources.title: Banning sales of new ICE cars from 2030 will cost five times as much as the benefits, says report
sources.reported_estimate: UK 2030 ban: environmental benefits GBP 76bn vs costs GBP 400bn (ratio ~0.19), incl. GBP 188bn extra vehicle costs, GBP 47bn charging time, GBP 99bn electricity and charging infrastructure. Sets the high end.

sources.authors: Roland Berger for the Clean Freight Coalition (as reported by Trucking Dive)
sources.title: Electrifying trucking would cost nearly $1 trillion, study finds
sources.reported_estimate: Nearly $1 trillion for infrastructure alone: about $620bn for charging and $370bn for utility grid upgrades; about $145,000 of charging per heavy-duty vehicle; vehicle costs excluded.

sources.authors: American Transportation Research Institute (as reported by FleetOwner)
sources.title: Charging Infrastructure Challenges for the U.S. Electric Vehicle Fleet
sources.reported_estimate: All-electric US fleet would need >40% of current US generation; ~13,800 lb payload loss per truck; BEV tractor at least $380,000; 6.3-34.9 years of current world output of key minerals.

sources.title: Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024 (press release)
sources.reported_estimate: Announced projects meet 'only 70% of copper and 50% of lithium requirements in 2035' under national climate pledges.

sources.title: Regulatory Impact Analysis for rescinding the GHG endangerment finding and light-, medium- and heavy-duty vehicle GHG standards (EPA-420-R-26-002)
sources.reported_estimate: Removing the standards, 2027-2055 (2024$): scenario A1 at 3% a net cost of ~$180bn (savings $1,290bn vs costs $1,470bn); net savings of $89-680bn in the other scenario/discount-rate combinations (lower oil prices, consumers valuing only 2.5 years of fuel savings).
sources.why_excluded: Evaluates repeal of a gradual standard rather than a ban, and the visible text does not show whether forgone climate benefits are monetized; shows that the official sign depends on fuel-price and consumer-valuation assumptions.

sources.title: The Cost of Reducing Greenhouse Gas Emissions
sources.reported_estimate: Static cost of battery-EV subsidies $350-640/tCO2e; argues dynamic (learning) costs can be much lower than static ones.
sources.why_excluded: Prices voluntary purchase subsidies, not a binding ban; at $185 SCC it would give 0.29-0.53, inside the adopted range.

sources.title: Zero Emission Vehicle Mandate and CO2 Regulations: Joint Government Response Cost Benefit Analysis
sources.reported_estimate: 80% ZEV cars / 70% vans by 2030: PV benefits GBP 166.5bn, PV costs GBP 127.3bn incl. rebound (GBP 50.4bn excluding it), NPV GBP 39bn (range -40 to +183bn; PV costs 99-138, benefits 98-282); BCR 1.31. Costs: vehicle capital GBP 27bn, chargepoint capital GBP 11bn, opex ~GBP 2bn, congestion GBP 78bn, accidents GBP 7bn, administration <GBP 35m; grid reinforcement inside electricity price forecasts. Benefits include later BEV capital-cost savings; carbon valued at ~GBP 245/t.
sources.why_excluded: Government appraisal of its own mandate; assumes electric cars become cheaper than conventional ones and a near coal-free grid. Its administrative cost share is used in cost_components.

sources.title: Advanced Clean Fleets Standardized Regulatory Impact Assessment (Appendix C)
sources.reported_estimate: Total costs $84.6bn, savings $97.0bn, health benefits $61.7bn, BCR 1.5 (Table 40); GSP -0.12% and employment -43,138 in 2038 (Table 55).
sources.why_excluded: Regulator's appraisal of its own rule.

sources.title: Impact assessment: CO2 emission standards for heavy-duty vehicles, SWD(2023) 88
sources.reported_estimate: Manufacturer cost EUR 6,500-13,100 per vehicle in 2040; first-user net savings EUR 29,100-47,000; GDP +0.06-0.11% in 2040.
sources.why_excluded: Regulator's appraisal of its own rule.

sources.title: Costs and Benefits of the Paris Climate Targets
sources.reported_estimate: Abstract: costs of climate policy, assuming least-cost implementation, 3.8-5.6% of GDP in 2100; benefits 2.8-3.2% of GDP; Paris targets fail the cost-benefit test unless risk aversion is high and the discount rate low. Text (arXiv v1): 2 C target costs just below 4% of GDP and 1.5 C just above 5.5%; benefits ~2.8% (2 C) and ~3.1% (1.5 C) against an SSP5-8.5 baseline, 1.8% and 2.2% against SSP3-7.0; 'simple policy imperfections... would readily double the costs'; citing Riahi et al. (2022), 1.5 C would cost 0.5-6.0% of GDP in 2030 and up to 10% in 2100.

sources.title: Climate Change: The Ultimate Challenge for Economics (Nobel Prize Lecture)
sources.reported_estimate: DICE-2016R3: cost-benefit optimal SCC ~$36/tCO2 (2020), yielding >3 C by 2100; 2 C limits require $158-279/t in 2020; 1.5 C 'essentially infeasible'; abatement ~1% of output for 50% cut, ~3.5% for zero emissions.

sources.authors: Chirakijja, J.; Jayachandran, S.; Ong, P.
sources.title: Inexpensive Heating Reduces Winter Mortality
sources.reported_estimate: The 42% fall in relative natural-gas heating prices in 2005-2010 averted ~11,000 US winter deaths a year; higher heating prices raise winter mortality, concentrated in cardiovascular and respiratory causes.

sources.authors: Parry, I.W.H.; Williams, R.C.; Goulder, L.H.
sources.title: When Can Carbon Abatement Policies Increase Welfare? The Fundamental Role of Distorted Factor Markets
sources.venue: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management (1999); NBER WP 5967
sources.reported_estimate: General-equilibrium models: 'tax interactions significantly raise the costs' of carbon policies; a revenue-neutral carbon tax is efficiency-improving so long as marginal benefits are positive, but policies that do not recycle revenue into cuts in distortionary taxes lose that advantage (a non-auctioned quota needs benefits of at least $25/t carbon just to break even). Mechanism for why re-investing revenue pushes the ratio down.

sources.title: Unpacking the IPCC's Estimated Carbon Prices
sources.reported_estimate: IPCC SR1.5: 1.5 C pathways require carbon prices of $135-5,500/tCO2 in 2030 -- source of the $135 figure.

sources.authors: Parry, I.W.H.; Black, S.; Roaf, J.
sources.title: Proposal for an International Carbon Price Floor Among Large Emitters (Staff Climate Note 2021/001)
sources.reported_estimate: Closest real global proposal: differentiated price floors among large emitters (1.5-2 C requires cutting emissions by a quarter to a half this decade); allows emissions-equivalent alternatives.

sources.title: Fiscal Monitor: How to Mitigate Climate Change (October 2019), Executive Summary
sources.reported_estimate: A $75/tCO2 tax in 2030 is needed for 2 C in large emitters; the global average carbon price is currently $2/t; such a tax would raise electricity prices ~45% and gasoline ~15% cumulatively over 10 years; revenue ~1.5% of GDP in G20 countries in 2030.

sources.title: State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2024 (Executive Summary)
sources.reported_estimate: Carbon pricing covers ~24% of global emissions; prices 'continue to fall short' of Paris ambition; 1.5 C-consistent 2030 prices USD 226-385/t; 2030 range for well below 2 C USD 63-127/t; revenues exceeded USD 100bn in 2023.

sources.title: Carbon Tax and Revenue Recycling: Revenue, Economic, and Distributional Implications
sources.reported_estimate: US $50/t rising 5%/yr: $1.87T net revenue 2020-29; GDP -0.4%, -421,000 FTE jobs in isolation; payroll-tax recycling +102,000 jobs; lump-sum rebate raises bottom-quintile after-tax income 6.8%.

sources.authors: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, ASPE
sources.title: Standard Values for Regulatory Analysis, 2024
sources.venue: HHS Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation
sources.reported_estimate: Value per statistical life for 2024: central $13.1m (2023 dollars).

sources.authors: Visual Capitalist (citing IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2023)
sources.title: Visualizing the $105 Trillion World Economy in One Chart
sources.venue: Visual Capitalist, summarising IMF WEO April 2023
sources.reported_estimate: World GDP ~ $105 trillion in 2023.

sources.title: Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change. Summary for Policymakers
sources.venue: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, AR6 WGIII
sources.reported_estimate: SPM C.12.2: versus continuation of 2020 policies, global GDP in 2050 is 1.3-2.7% lower in 2 C (>67%) pathways and 2.6-4.2% lower in C1 (1.5 C, no or limited overshoot) pathways (models exclude climate damages); Table SPM.2: C1 GHG emissions in 2030 31 [21-36] GtCO2e/yr. SPM C.12: the global economic benefit of limiting warming to 2 C 'is reported to exceed the cost of mitigation in most of the assessed literature (medium confidence)'.

sources.title: Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 121(13): e2312030121
sources.reported_estimate: SCC (2019$/tCO2): C/B optimal $50 (2020), $59 (2025), $125 (2050); 2 C path $75/$89/$213; 1.5 C path $3,557/$4,185/$16,552. 1.5 C limit 'infeasible' (would need emissions near zero in 5 years: 'a deep depression (output declining by around 75%)'). Carbon prices must rise to $115 (optimal), $63 (Paris) and $200 (2 C) by 2050. C/B optimal raises wealth ~$120T, 2 C ~$107T, Paris ~$85T versus current policy; runs 'assume complete efficiency and participation'.

sources.title: What does it cost the IRS to collect taxes?
sources.reported_estimate: IRS cost of collecting $100: 36 cents in FY2024; recent peak 53 cents in FY2010. Used for the administration component (0.53% of revenue).

sources.authors: Baird, S.; Friedman, J.; Schady, N.
sources.title: Aggregate Income Shocks and Infant Mortality in the Developing World
sources.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 93(3):847-856 (near-final version: GWU IIEP WP 2010-7)
sources.reported_estimate: 1.7 million births in 59 developing countries: a one percent decrease in per capita GDP is associated with an increase in mortality of between 0.24 and 0.40 infants per 1,000 children born (abstract; Table 2).

sources.authors: World Bank, World Development Indicators (via FRED)
sources.title: Crude birth rate and total population, low and middle income countries
sources.venue: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (SPDYNCBRTINLMY; SPPOPTOTLLMY)
sources.reported_estimate: 2024: crude birth rate 17.84 per 1,000; population 6,722,971,301; so about 119.9 million births a year in low- and middle-income countries.

sources.title: Death by Regulation: How Regulations Can Increase Mortality Risk (research summary)
sources.venue: Mercatus Center at George Mason University
sources.reported_estimate: Regulations costing more than $99.3 million per life saved can be expected to increase mortality risk (range $75.4m-$123.2m): about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed, through lower income and private health spending.

sources.title: An Updated Analysis of Carbon Dioxide Emission Abatement as a Response to Climate Change (Copenhagen Consensus 2012 challenge paper: Climate Change, Emissions Abatement)
sources.venue: Copenhagen Consensus Center, Copenhagen Consensus III

sources.title: False Alarm: How Climate Change Panic Costs Us Trillions, Hurts the Poor, and Fails to Fix the Planet
sources.reported_estimate: Using DICE, an optimal global carbon tax costs ~$20T and cuts damages from ~$140T to ~$100T (net benefit ~$22T; implied BCR ~2); reduces 2100 warming from ~4.1 C to ~3.75 C (7.4 F to 6.75 F). URL is a secondary summary (Shortform).
sources.why_excluded: Scores the optimal tax (~$36-48/t in 2020-2030), far below $135; a milder policy.

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; Prest, B. C.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
sources.reported_estimate: Mean SCC $185/tCO2 (5-95%: $44-413) at 2% near-term discount rate, 3.6x the prior US value of $51 -- under this SCC a $135/t tax has BCR >1 (counter-evidence).
sources.why_excluded: Marginal-damage estimate at a 2% discount rate under which a $135 tax passes; the main mainstream counter-case, not a full-cost evaluation of a target-driven, non-rebated global tax.

sources.title: Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 121(13): e2312030121
sources.reported_estimate: A 2 C-limited path raises global wealth by ~$107T (present value) versus current policy; 'the 2 C target does pass the cost-benefit test in cases with sufficiently low discounting (2%) or the alternate damage function'.
sources.why_excluded: Reports net wealth, not separate benefits and costs, so no ratio can be taken; assumes 'complete efficiency and participation' and a carbon price path ($200/t by 2050) that reaches $135 later than 2030; the same model finds the 1.5 C path, to which $135 in 2030 corresponds in IPCC SR1.5, infeasible.

sources.authors: C40 Cities; Arup; University of Leeds
sources.title: The Future of Urban Consumption in a 1.5°C World (Headline Report)
sources.venue: C40 Cities report (copy hosted by Arup)
sources.reported_estimate: Ambitious 2030 targets: 0 kg meat and 0 kg dairy per person per year (current C40 averages 58 kg and 155 kg); 3 new clothing items per person per year (progressive: 8); 0 private vehicles (C40 average 240 per 1,000 people; progressive target 190); 1 short-haul (<1,500 km) return flight every 3 years per person (progressive: every 2 years), which cuts C40 residents' flight trips by about 28% against 2017. C40 consumption-based emissions 4.5 GtCO2e in 2017 (about 10% of global); 94 member cities, 523 million people in 2017. Ambitious interventions cut cumulative 2017-2050 emissions by about 32 GtCO2e (Fig. 15, by category: buildings 21->11.9, food 17.7->7.2, clothing 6.8->2.5, private transport 9.9->6.1, electronics 5->3.4, aviation 3.5->1.6). Flights 2% of C40 consumption emissions (aviation fuel combustion 66% of that, fuel extraction 18%). A 'conservative micro-rebound effect' offsets about one third of savings. Wider-benefit claims: 160,000-170,000 diet-related deaths avoided a year; residents 'save $93 billion' on clothing. States it 'does not advocate for the wholesale adoption of these more ambitious targets'. No cost or BCR estimate.

sources.reported_estimate: Randomized-encouragement study of ~30,000 Michigan households: upfront costs (~$4,585 per complier household) are 'about twice the actual energy savings' (~$2,349 PV); model-projected savings more than three times actual; social rate of return about -7.8% a year over 16 years with CO2 at $38/t; net cost ~$201 per ton CO2 at 3% ($285 at 7%).

sources.authors: European Commission (as summarised by the European Clean Hydrogen Observatory)
sources.title: A Renovation Wave for Europe (COM(2020) 662), policy summary
sources.venue: European Clean Hydrogen Observatory (EU) policy page
sources.reported_estimate: EUR 275bn of additional investment a year needed to reach 2030 targets; ~35 million building units renovated by 2030; renovation rate doubled from 1% to 2% a year. Against EU27 GDP of EUR 12,653bn (2020, Ricardo/EC 2021) this is 2.17% of GDP. Commission's own estimate of required spending; used as the compliance cost only, not for benefits.

sources.title: Climate Change: The Ultimate Challenge for Economics (Nobel Prize Lecture)
sources.reported_estimate: DICE-2016R3 cost-benefit optimal SCC ~$36/tCO2 (2020). Used as low-end benefit per tonne.

sources.authors: US Census Bureau (as reported by The Business Standard)
sources.title: World population to be 8.09 billion on 1 Jan 2025
sources.venue: The Business Standard (reporting US Census Bureau population clock release)
sources.reported_estimate: World population ~8.09 billion on 1 January 2025. Used for C40's population share: 523m / 8.09bn = 6.5%.

sources.authors: US Census Bureau (McKenzie, B.; Rapino, M.)
sources.title: Commuting in the United States: 2009 (American Community Survey Reports ACS-15)
sources.reported_estimate: Table 5, workers in metro areas: mean travel time to work 24.2 minutes driving alone, 47.8 minutes by public transportation.

sources.title: The ABC of mobility
sources.reported_estimate: 794 cities in 61 countries (~850m people): 51.4% of urban commutes are by car; 91.9% in the US and Canada; 18.8% in Eastern Asia.

sources.authors: Baird, S.; Friedman, J.; Schady, N.
sources.title: Aggregate Income Shocks and Infant Mortality in the Developing World
sources.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 93(3):847-856 (near-final version: GWU IIEP WP 2010-7)
sources.reported_estimate: 1.7 million births in 59 developing countries: a one percent decrease in per capita GDP is associated with an increase in mortality of between 0.24 and 0.40 infants per 1,000 children born (abstract; Table 2).

sources.authors: World Bank, World Development Indicators (via FRED)
sources.title: Crude birth rate and total population, low and middle income countries
sources.venue: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (SPDYNCBRTINLMY; SPPOPTOTLLMY)
sources.reported_estimate: 2024: crude birth rate 17.84 per 1,000; population 6,722,971,301; so about 119.9 million births a year in low- and middle-income countries.

sources.title: Death by Regulation: How Regulations Can Increase Mortality Risk (research summary)
sources.venue: Mercatus Center at George Mason University
sources.reported_estimate: Regulations costing more than $99.3 million per life saved can be expected to increase mortality risk (range $75.4m-$123.2m): about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed, through lower income and private health spending.

sources.authors: Galdon-Sanchez, J.E.; Gil, R.; Holub, F.; Uriz-Uharte, G.
sources.title: Social Benefits and Private Costs of Driving Restriction Policies: The Impact of Madrid Central on Congestion, Pollution, and Consumer Spending
sources.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 21(3):1227-1267
sources.reported_estimate: Pollution -19% and congestion -16%; consumers affected reduced brick-and-mortar spending in the regulated area by 21%, partly offset by online shopping.

sources.authors: Christensen, P.; Francisco, P.; Myers, E.; Souza, M.
sources.title: Decomposing the Wedge between Projected and Realized Returns in Energy Efficiency Programs
sources.reported_estimate: 9,800+ Illinois homes, 2009-2016: 'approximately 51% of projected savings are realized for the average home'; prior studies find 38% (Michigan WAP, Fowlie, Greenstone & Wolfram 2018), 58% (Wisconsin, Allcott & Greenstone 2017) and 73% (Massachusetts). Engineering-model bias explains up to 41% of the shortfall.

sources.title: Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 121(13): e2312030121
sources.reported_estimate: 'The SCC in the baseline run is $66/tCO2 for the 2020 period (in 2019 international $).'

sources.title: Impacts of active travel interventions on travel behaviour and health: Results from a five-year longitudinal travel survey in Outer London
sources.reported_estimate: Mini-Holland active-travel/LTN schemes in Enfield, Kingston, Waltham Forest: BCR ~50:1 to 200:1 (health), ~GBP 4,800 health benefit per adult over 20 years (per press coverage of the paper) -- counter-evidence for the non-coercive component.
sources.why_excluded: Voluntary low-traffic and active-travel schemes in Outer London (health BCR ~50-200): shows the non-coercive 15-minute-city planning component can pay, but it does not price car bans or consumption caps.

sources.title: Climate Emergency, Urban Opportunity
sources.reported_estimate: Urban low-carbon measures: US$1.83 trillion invested a year 2020-2050 (about 2% of 2018 world GDP), with annual savings of US$2.80 trillion in 2030 and US$6.98 trillion in 2050; NPV US$23.9 trillion at 3.5% (p. 68).
sources.why_excluded: Covers cities' sector (production-side) actions, which are scored under the Green New Deal entry rather than with the consumption caps. Its savings are engineering projections: measured programmes realise about 38-73% of projected energy savings, 51% on average in the largest study (Christensen et al. 2023; Fowlie, Greenstone & Wolfram 2018), and Allcott & Greenstone (2012) find profitable efficiency opportunities much smaller than engineering-accounting studies suggest. At 51% realisation the projected $2.80tn of 2030 savings become about $1.43tn, below the $1.83tn a year of investment, a net cost of about $0.4tn a year; at 38%, savings of $1.06tn leave a net cost of about $0.77tn. McKinsey (2022) puts total net-zero capital spending at $9.2tn a year, $3.5tn above today's, peaking at 8.8% of world GDP in 2030.

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; Prest, B. C.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
sources.reported_estimate: Mean SCC $185/tCO2 (5-95%: $44-413) at 2% near-term discount rate.
sources.why_excluded: Highest published social cost of carbon ($185/t); the range uses DICE-2023 ($66/t) as the upper carbon value.

sources.title: Technology-led Mitigation (Third Copenhagen Consensus: Climate Change Assessment Paper)
sources.venue: Copenhagen Consensus Center; final version in Lomborg (ed.), Global Problems, Smart Solutions: Costs and Benefits (Cambridge University Press, 2013)
sources.reported_estimate: Increased low-carbon energy R&D would yield benefits 'ranging from 3 to 11 times higher than cost, depending on rate of success and time horizon'.

sources.title: op-ed on the Copenhagen Consensus on Climate results (Forbes, 21 Sept 2009)
sources.reported_estimate: Reports Galiana & Green: about $100bn a year of non-carbon energy R&D would yield ~$11 of avoided climate damage per $1 (called conservative); reports Tol: carbon cuts to stay under 2 C avoid ~2 cents of damage per $1 spent; global carbon taxes judged 'very poor'.

sources.authors: Rosegrant, M. W.; Wong, B.; Sulser, T. B.; Dubosse, N.; Lybbert, T. J.
sources.title: Benefit-Cost Analysis of Increased Funding for Agricultural Research and Development in the Global South
sources.reported_estimate: BCR 33; costs $61bn NPV ($5.2bn/yr); benefits $2.1 trillion; +10% ag output, -35% hunger, -16% food prices, +4% per capita income over 35 years.

sources.authors: Alston, J. M.; Andersen, M. A.; James, J. S.; Pardey, P. G.
sources.title: The Economic Returns to U.S. Public Agricultural Research
sources.reported_estimate: Average own-state BCR 21:1, 32:1 including interstate spillovers; real IRR 9-10%.

sources.authors: Glennerster, R.; Emerick, K.; Krahn, A.; et al.
sources.title: The Return to Investing in Climate-Resilient Crops
sources.venue: Market Shaping Accelerator, University of Chicago (draft report)
sources.reported_estimate: Adoption-based advance market commitment (pull prize) for heat-resilient crops: BCR 7.5-22.6 (West African maize), 7.7-25.7 (East African sorghum) across the three adoption/technology scenarios, 24.3 for a $250m multi-target fund.

sources.title: An Analysis of Climate Engineering as a Response to Climate Change (Copenhagen Consensus on Climate: Climate Engineering Assessment)
sources.reported_estimate: Stratospheric aerosol insertion: ~$230bn cost, benefits 'fifteen-times higher' per this summary page, but the paper's own ratio is 'on the order of 25 to 1' (as quoted by Pielke 2009); marine cloud whitening: ~$5.8bn cost, ~$20 trillion benefits, BCR ~3,448:1.

sources.title: Climate Engineering (Third Copenhagen Consensus: Climate Engineering Assessment)
sources.reported_estimate: Climate-engineering R&D program 'on the order of a billion dollars'; each $1 could create ~$1,000 of benefits.

sources.authors: Kremer, M.; Levin, J.; Snyder, C. M.
sources.title: Advance Market Commitments: Insights from Theory and Experience
sources.reported_estimate: $1.5bn pneumococcal AMC: ~150 million children immunized in 73 countries, ~700,000 lives saved, ~$83 per DALY averted; diffusion ~5 years faster than rotavirus vaccine without an AMC.

sources.authors: Brunt, L.; Lerner, J.; Nicholas, T.
sources.title: Inducement Prizes and Innovation
sources.reported_estimate: RASE prizes 1839-1939: doubling a cash prize raised entries 6.4-14% and renewed (high-quality) patents 4-7%; each extra medal raised high-quality patents 20-44%.

sources.title: Innovation Inducement Prizes: Connecting Research to Policy
sources.venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management 31(3):752-776
sources.reported_estimate: Literature review prompted by the America COMPETES Reauthorization Act of 2010 (all federal agencies may offer prizes): success of prizes is hard to judge and 'careful empirical evaluations of innovation inducement prizes are needed'.

sources.authors: Bays, J.; Goland, T.; Newsum, J.
sources.title: Using Prizes to Spur Innovation
sources.reported_estimate: Ansari X Prize: $10M purse induced >$100M in team spending and >$1.5bn subsequent investment; large prizes tripled to $375M over a decade; only 23% of sponsors evaluate impact.

sources.title: McKinsey partners with Stripe, Alphabet, Shopify, and Meta on $925 million carbon removal commitment
sources.reported_estimate: Frontier: a $925M, eight-year advance market commitment guaranteeing future demand for permanent carbon removal to expand supply.

sources.title: XPRIZE Makes History, Awards $100M Prize for Groundbreaking Carbon Removal Solutions
sources.reported_estimate: $100M XPRIZE Carbon Removal (Musk Foundation-funded) awarded in April 2025.

sources.authors: Olson, S. (interview with Erika Wagner, X Prize Foundation)
sources.title: X-Prize director describes incentive prizes
sources.reported_estimate: 'The rough rule of thumb is that the operational costs are equal to the prize costs': a $10M prize implies ~$20M total spending (research, infrastructure, judges, staff, media).

sources.authors: Goes, M.; Tuana, N.; Keller, K.
sources.title: The Economics (or Lack Thereof) of Aerosol Geoengineering
sources.reported_estimate: Complete substitution of aerosol geoengineering for CO2 abatement fails a cost-benefit test over a wide range of scenarios, driven by termination risk and damages from geoengineering itself (as summarised in Bickel & Agrawal 2013).
sources.why_excluded: Peer-reviewed finding that substituting aerosol geoengineering for CO2 abatement fails a cost-benefit test in many scenarios; it concerns deployment, not research, and is answered by Bickel & Agrawal (2013). It is one reason the 1,000:1 research figure is treated as contested.

sources.title: Reexamining the Economics of Aerosol Geoengineering
sources.reported_estimate: Reframing Goes et al.: geoengineering may pass a cost-benefit test over a wide range of the scenarios Goes et al. considered (abstract; no single BCR in abstract).
sources.why_excluded: Reply to Goes et al. finding that geoengineering may pass a cost-benefit test; it gives no research-specific ratio, so it is used only as context.

sources.title: A Perspective Paper on Climate Engineering (Copenhagen Consensus on Climate)
sources.reported_estimate: Reports Bickel & Lane's BCRs as ~25:1 (stratospheric aerosols) and ~5,000:1 (marine cloud whitening); criticises them as 'precision without accuracy', citing Goes et al.'s contrary result.
sources.why_excluded: Critique of the Bickel & Lane ratios ('precision without accuracy'); used as context for the contested geoengineering figure, not as a separate estimate.

sources.authors: Diamond, R.; McQuade, T.; Qian, F.
sources.title: The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality: Evidence from San Francisco
sources.reported_estimate: Treated landlords cut rental supply 15%; tenant mobility down ~20%; NBER version: 5.1% citywide rent rise.

sources.authors: Diamond, R.; McQuade, T.; Qian, F.
sources.title: The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality: Evidence from San Francisco (NBER conference draft)
sources.reported_estimate: Covered tenants gained $7.621bn cumulative 1995-2012 ($423m/yr; $3,100-5,900 per person per year), about one third of it landlord buyout transfers; citywide rent +7% and $5bn welfare loss to all renters, 'almost as large' as tenant gains.

sources.title: Robbing Peter to Pay Paul? The Redistribution of Wealth Caused by Rent Control
sources.reported_estimate: St. Paul 2021 law cut property values 6-7% ($1.57bn); 67% direct capitalisation, 33% (at least $518m) deadweight externalities; higher-income tenants gained most, lower-income owners lost most.

sources.authors: Autor, D. H.; Palmer, C. J.; Pathak, P. A.
sources.title: Housing Market Spillovers: Evidence from the End of Rent Control in Cambridge, Massachusetts
sources.reported_estimate: Decontrol in 1995 added about $1.8bn to Cambridge's housing stock 1994-2004, nearly a quarter of total residential price appreciation, mostly on never-controlled properties.

sources.authors: Glaeser, E. L.; Luttmer, E. F. P.
sources.title: The Misallocation of Housing Under Rent Control
sources.reported_estimate: An economically and statistically significant fraction of New York City apartments is misallocated across demographic groups under rent control; dollar figures are in the NBER working-paper version (w6220), listed separately.

sources.title: Rent control effects through the lens of empirical research: An almost complete review of the literature
sources.reported_estimate: Rent controls are effective at slowing rent growth in controlled units but bring wide-ranging adverse effects for society as a whole.

sources.title: Rent Control (Feb 7, 2012)
sources.venue: Kent A. Clark Center for Global Markets, Chicago Booth
sources.reported_estimate: 0 strongly agree, 1 agree, 3 uncertain, 20 disagree, 13 strongly disagree (33/37 = 89% disagree) that rent limits improved affordable housing.

sources.title: National Rent Caps (Jul 23, 2024)
sources.venue: Kent A. Clark Center for Global Markets, Chicago Booth
sources.reported_estimate: A 5% cap on corporate landlords: 80.5% disagree it would make middle-income Americans substantially better off (2.4% agree); 68.3% agree it would substantially reduce apartments for rent (7.3% disagree). 41 responses.

sources.authors: Elmendorf, C. S.; Nall, C.; Oklobdzija, S.
sources.title: What State Housing Policies Do Voters Want? Evidence from a Platform-Choice Experiment
sources.venue: Journal of Political Institutions and Political Economy 5(1) (SSRN 4811534)
sources.reported_estimate: National survey of ~5,000 urban and suburban voters: homeowners and renters alike support price controls; Cato (Bourne 2024) reports over 85% supported capping rents.

sources.authors: City and County of San Francisco, Rent Arbitration Board
sources.title: Rent Arbitration Board FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26 Budget Memo
sources.venue: City and County of San Francisco
sources.reported_estimate: Proposed FY2024-25 budget $13,827,383 (FY2025-26 $14,386,934); 50 FTE; funded by the Rent Board fee (up to $64/unit proposed for FY2025-26); 219,125 dwelling units and 13,138 SRO guest units billed (projected FY2023-24).

sources.authors: City of Berkeley Rent Stabilization Board
sources.title: FY 2024-2025 Budget, Staffing Model, and Expenditure Level (Item 7C, 20 June 2024)
sources.venue: City of Berkeley Rent Stabilization Board
sources.reported_estimate: FY2024-25 expenditure budget $8,332,918; ~29-30 FTE; registration fee $344 per fully covered unit and $212 per partially covered unit; ~5,700 partially covered units; $6.88m fully-covered fee revenue implies ~20,000 fully covered units.

sources.authors: New York State Homes and Community Renewal, Office of Rent Administration
sources.title: Office of Rent Administration 2025 Annual Report
sources.reported_estimate: ORA has 350 staff across six offices administering 1,064,049 registered rent-stabilized units (registration year 2025); no budget figure published.

sources.title: Quarterly Residential Vacancies and Homeownership, Second Quarter 2026 (press release)
sources.venue: U.S. Census Bureau, Housing Vacancy Survey
sources.reported_estimate: Estimated 46,827 thousand renter-occupied housing units in Q2 2026 (Table 3; MOE +/-335 thousand).

sources.authors: Glaeser, E. L.; Luttmer, E. F. P.
sources.title: The Misallocation of Housing Under Rent Control (NBER Working Paper 6220)
sources.reported_estimate: Best estimate of the cost of New York rent control from misallocating rental apartments: $200 per apartment a year; lower bound from bedrooms and rent/own choice more than $40 per regulated or owned apartment; correcting for unobservables and other attributes gives $200-2,000 per apartment, $300m-$3bn a year for 1.5 million apartments (authors call the top 'perhaps unrealistic'). Data: 1993 NYC Housing and Vacancy Survey vs 1993 American Housing Survey.

sources.title: A Review of Empirical Evidence on the Costs and Benefits of Rent Control
sources.reported_estimate: Table 1: Olsen (1972) NYC 1968 subsidy $406 a year, tenant benefit $213, transfer efficiency 0.52; Mildner (1987 data) landlord cost of subsidy $122/month for controlled units, -$14 for stabilized, efficiency 0.65; other studies 0.45-0.99. Early (2000): controls raise uncontrolled rents 12% and 'the average benefit to tenants in regulated units was negative'. Gyourko & Linneman (1990): Manhattan units under old controls had 'a 9 percent higher probability of being in unsound condition'. Glaeser & Luttmer: misallocation DWL 'from USD 200 to USD 2,000 per apartment per year'.

sources.title: Out of control: What can we learn from the end of Massachusetts rent control?
sources.reported_estimate: As summarised by the NMHC review (Sturtevant 2018): rent control had little effect on new construction but was associated with owners converting rental units to condominiums, keeping thousands of units off the Boston-area rental market; controlled buildings were of lower quality. No dollar estimate used here.

sources.title: Rent Control, Rental Housing Supply, and the Distribution of Tenant Benefits
sources.reported_estimate: As reported by Turner & Malpezzi (2003): using 1996 NYC data, controls raised uncontrolled rents by 12% and the average benefit to tenants in regulated units was negative (abstract not available; figures read from the review).

sources.authors: General Social Survey / ISSP Role of Government (SDA codebook)
sources.title: PRICECONGOVTS: government responsibility to keep prices under control
sources.reported_estimate: 32.1% definitely should, 41.8% probably should (73.9% total), pooled across years.

sources.authors: Favilukis, J.; Mabille, P.; Van Nieuwerburgh, S.
sources.title: Affordable Housing and City Welfare
sources.reported_estimate: Calibrated NYC model: affordability policies (including rent control) have substantial insurance value, and targeting the neediest can yield substantial net welfare gains despite supply and misallocation costs.
sources.why_excluded: A calibrated structural model of well-targeted affordability policy, not an estimate of actual rent caps; its gains depend on targeting that real rent-control programmes lack (see Ahern & Giacoletti on who benefits). Shown as the main counterpoint.

sources.authors: Diamond, R.; McQuade, T.; Qian, F.
sources.title: The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality (NBER w24181 abstract)
sources.reported_estimate: Rent control offered large benefits to covered tenants; welfare losses could be mitigated if rent-increase insurance were provided as government social insurance rather than a landlord mandate.
sources.why_excluded: Supports the tenant-insurance rationale, but the authors' remedy is a different, tax-funded policy; the gross tenant benefits it reports are already in the ratio's numerator.

sources.authors: Albrecht, B. C.; Tabarrok, A.; Whitmeyer, M.
sources.title: Chaos and Misallocation under Price Controls
sources.reported_estimate: 1973-74 US gasoline controls: ceiling 20% below baseline, 9% shortfall; Harberger triangle ~2.0% of spending; misallocation 2.2-17.7% of spending (1.09-8.75x the triangle); cites Frech & Lee and Deacon & Sonstelie finding queuing costs could exceed the entire rent transfer.

sources.authors: Frech, H. E. III; Lee, W. C.
sources.title: The Welfare Cost of Rationing-By-Queuing Across Markets: Theory and Estimates from the U.S. Gasoline Crises
sources.reported_estimate: Estimates the welfare cost of improper allocation across markets in the 1973-74 and 1979 gasoline crises (queuing costs could exceed the transfer, per Albrecht et al.).

sources.title: The Allocative Cost of Price Ceilings in the U.S. Residential Market for Natural Gas
sources.reported_estimate: Allocative cost of natural-gas price ceilings averaged $4.6bn a year 1950-2000 (peak $6.4bn in 1980), roughly tripling earlier net welfare loss estimates; MacAvoy's DWL $10.5bn/yr 1968-77.

sources.authors: Blinder, A. S.; Newton, W. J.
sources.title: The 1971-1974 Controls Program and the Price Level: An Econometric Post-Mortem
sources.reported_estimate: Nixon controls cut the non-food, non-energy price level 3-4% by Feb 1974, but catch-up after April 1974 left it only 0-2% below the no-controls path; decontrol explains most of 1974's double-digit core inflation.

sources.authors: Cavallo, A.; Cavallo, E.; Rigobon, R.
sources.title: Prices and Supply Disruptions during Natural Disasters
sources.venue: Review of Income and Wealth 60: S449-S471
