sources.reported_estimate: About 185 million people paid payroll taxes on covered earnings in 2025; 70 million beneficiaries in December 2025.

sources.authors: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics via Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)
sources.title: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items (CPIAUCSL), annual average
sources.venue: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

sources.authors: Diamond, P. A.; Orszag, P. R.
sources.title: Saving Social Security
sources.venue: Journal of Economic Perspectives 19(2): 11-32 (authors per the Brookings book; the JEP page loaded did not list them) (see also the book Saving Social Security: A Balanced Approach, Brookings 2004/2005)
sources.reported_estimate: Costs are projected to rise by about 2.5% of GDP over 75 years; solvency can be restored with modest benefit cuts and revenue increases, and 'major surgery is neither warranted nor desirable'.
sources.why_excluded: Argues for a progressive pay-as-you-go fix instead of accounts and gives no BCR for privatization. Its main point, that account returns are offset by legacy debt, is already carried into the low end through Geanakoplos, Mitchell & Zeldes.

sources.authors: Orszag, P. R.; Stiglitz, J. E.
sources.title: Rethinking Pension Reform: Ten Myths About Social Security Systems
sources.venue: In Holzmann & Stiglitz (eds.), New Ideas About Old Age Security, World Bank
sources.reported_estimate: Challenges the claims that individual accounts raise saving, returns and labour-market efficiency; argues pension design must fit country circumstances.
sources.why_excluded: A qualitative critique with no quantified welfare estimate to put in the range.

sources.authors: Gill, I. S.; Packard, T.; Yermo, J.
sources.title: Keeping the Promise of Social Security in Latin America
sources.venue: World Bank and Stanford University Press
sources.reported_estimate: Reviews more than a decade of Latin American pension privatizations (two decades for Chile): reforms 'undoubtedly a major step forward' but 'still works in progress'; the full report documents coverage and fee problems.
sources.why_excluded: Evaluates implementation in developing countries with weaker capital markets; gives no BCR comparable with the US models.

sources.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
sources.reported_estimate: Deadweight loss >12x Harberger's classic estimate; raising revenue via proportional rate increases costs ~$2 of deadweight loss per $1 of extra revenue

sources.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
sources.title: The Welfare Cost of Distortions in the United States Tax System: A General Equilibrium Approach
sources.venue: NBER Working Paper 1043 (published as 'General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States', American Economic Review 75(1): 128-138, 1985)
sources.reported_estimate: Marginal welfare loss from raising an additional dollar of revenue 34-48 cents; replacing the existing tax system with lump-sum taxes gains $1.8-3.1 trillion, 13-22 cents per dollar of revenue; a consumption-type VAT yields larger efficiency gains than a proportional income tax.

sources.title: A Unified Welfare Analysis of Government Policies
sources.reported_estimate: MVPFs of top-income-tax-rate changes: 1981 cut infinite (95% CI 0.94-inf; conventional BCR 1.67), 1986 44.27 (CI 2.37-inf), 1993 increase 1.85 (CI 1.19-4.07), 2013 increase 1.16

sources.authors: Saez, E.; Slemrod, J.B.; Giertz, S.H.
sources.title: The Elasticity of Taxable Income with Respect to Marginal Tax Rates: A Critical Review
sources.reported_estimate: Elasticity estimates vary considerably by method and period; frames deadweight-loss calculations (counterweight to high-elasticity estimates)

sources.authors: Chodorow-Reich, G.; Zidar, O.; Zwick, E.
sources.title: Lessons from the Biggest Business Tax Cut in US History
sources.reported_estimate: TCJA corporate provisions: corporate revenue fell ~40% (0.63% of GDP/yr over first decade); corporate investment +8-14%; long-run domestic corporate capital +7%; long-run GDP +0.9% (first-decade average +0.44%); labour income up < $1,000 per worker vs CEA's $4,000-9,000; individual-tax offsets only 1.5-6.3% of the revenue loss.

sources.title: Monthly Budget Review: Summary for Fiscal Year 2025
sources.reported_estimate: FY2025: individual income taxes $2,656bn; corporate income taxes $452bn; payroll taxes $1,748bn; total receipts $5,235bn; outlays $7,010bn; deficit $1,775bn.

sources.title: Tax Complexity Now Costs the U.S. Economy Over $546 Billion Annually
sources.reported_estimate: Total federal tax compliance cost $546.1bn in 2024 (7.92bn hours; $412.8bn time + $133.3bn out-of-pocket), from OIRA/IRS paperwork-burden estimates. Individual income tax returns $145.4bn; business income-tax returns $118.9bn; employer quarterly return $44.8bn; depreciation $25.4bn; estates and trusts $20.2bn; QBI deduction $19.0bn.

sources.title: Government Size and Growth: A Survey and Interpretation of the Evidence
sources.reported_estimate: In rich countries, a 10-percentage-point increase in government size is associated with 0.5-1% lower annual growth; authors warn of pitfalls in a causal reading.

sources.authors: Altig, D.; Auerbach, A.J.; Kotlikoff, L.J.; Smetters, K.A.; Walliser, J.
sources.title: Simulating Fundamental Tax Reform in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Significant long-run output increases for some reforms replacing the income tax (e.g., consumption taxes); smaller gains for reforms protecting low-income and older generations

sources.title: Fair Tax Plan: National Sales Tax (FairTax Act analysis)
sources.reported_estimate: Proposed 23% inclusive (29.8% exclusive) rate falls short of revenue neutrality; Gale estimates at least 44% needed; less progressive than current system

sources.title: Evaluation and Macroeconomic Impact of the FairTax
sources.reported_estimate: GDP +3.1% on average over first 5 years (investment +18.3%, consumption -3.0%); revenue-maintaining tax-inclusive rate 27.8%-68.8%

sources.title: The Constitution of the United States: A Transcription, Article V
sources.reported_estimate: Amendments require two-thirds of both Houses (or a convention) and ratification by three-fourths of the states

sources.title: IRS Budget and Workforce (IRS Data Book, FY2025, Table 6)
sources.reported_estimate: IRS actual expenditures were $19.0 billion for overall operations in FY2025; 95,226 FTE.

sources.authors: Coffey, B.; McLaughlin, P. A.; Peretto, P. F.
sources.title: The cumulative cost of regulations
sources.reported_estimate: Federal regulation added since 1980 cut growth ~0.8 pp/yr; 2012 GDP ~$4T lower.
sources.why_excluded: Measures regulation, not taxes or spending, so it does not price this policy's sub-policies.

sources.title: A Unified Welfare Analysis of Government Policies
sources.reported_estimate: Comparative welfare analysis of 133 US policy changes; direct investments in children's health and education often have very high MVPFs.
sources.why_excluded: Not a separate estimate. It shows that if the 'shrink government' cuts fall on high-MVPF programmes, the ratio could fall below 1; the range assumes cut spending is worth $1 per $1.

sources.title: Comprehensive Tax Reform and U.S. Energy Policy (testimony to the Senate Finance Committee, June 12, 2012)
sources.reported_estimate: Jorgenson-Yun 'Efficient Taxation of Income' would generate growth equivalent to a $7 trillion increase in national wealth (then ~$60 trillion).
sources.why_excluded: Senate testimony, not a study of income-tax repeal; Jorgenson-Yun's reform keeps an income tax. Cross-check only.

sources.title: Divided Lands: State vs. Federal Management in the West
sources.reported_estimate: States earn $14.51 per $1 spent managing trust lands vs $0.73 for USFS/BLM; timber $2.51 vs $0.32-0.38; grazing $4.89 vs $0.10-0.14; minerals $138.08 vs $19.76; recreation $6.86 vs $0.20-0.28.

sources.authors: Jakus, P. M.; Stambro, J. E.; Hogue, M.; Downen, J.; Pace, L.; Grijalva, T. C.
sources.title: Western Public Lands and the Fiscal Implications of a Transfer to States
sources.reported_estimate: States can cover management costs with land-based revenues if they have access to fossil fuel and timber resources at favorable prices; federal lands generate less economic value than private lands.

sources.authors: Stambro, J. E. (with Jakus, P. M. et al.)
sources.title: An Analysis of a Transfer of Federal Lands to the State of Utah
sources.venue: Utah Economic and Business Review 74(3), Bureau of Economic and Business Research, University of Utah
sources.reported_estimate: Managing 31.2m acres would cost ~$248m/yr by 2017 (~$280m with PILT); 2017 revenues $202.7-377.6m (low prices) to $235.1-422.0m (high prices); profitable only if oil/gas prices stay high and Utah gets 100% of royalties.

sources.title: Reforming Federal Land Management
sources.reported_estimate: BLM/NPS/FWS spent $7.8bn vs $5.2bn revenues (2010); Interior deferred maintenance $13.5-19.9bn; BLM revenue almost all from <1 million of 256 million acres.

sources.authors: Anderson, T. L.; Smith, V. L.; Simmons, E.
sources.title: How and Why to Privatize Federal Lands
sources.reported_estimate: Proposes auctioning federal lands (one-third of US land area) over 20-40 years using equal per-citizen 'public land share certificates'.

sources.authors: Anderson, T. L.; Leal, D. R.
sources.title: Free Market Environmentalism for the Next Generation

sources.authors: Hazlett, T. W.; Munoz, R. E.
sources.title: A Welfare Analysis of Spectrum Allocation Policies
sources.reported_estimate: US: +60 MHz cuts prices ~8% and raises consumer surplus ~$8.8bn/yr vs ~$3.0bn tax-efficiency value of licence sales; UK 140 MHz: ~$39bn consumer gains; Belgium/Greece: consumer losses from withheld spectrum 15-20x the social value of revenue; US consumer surplus at least $150bn/yr vs $53bn total licence revenue; estimates are lower bounds.

sources.title: Optimal Abolition of FCC Spectrum Allocation
sources.reported_estimate: Evidence from cellular liberalization shows large efficiency gains from the price system; proposes exclusive frequency rights and abolishing FCC central allocation (no single BCR).

sources.authors: Kahn, C.; Hanson, S.; Giles, S.; Freeberg, C.; Ribeiro, L.
sources.title: The C-Band Spectrum Auction: Retrospective and Prospective Observations
sources.reported_estimate: Auction 107: 280 MHz (3.7-3.98 GHz); $80.9bn clock-phase proceeds plus $9.7bn accelerated clearing payments, $3.3bn relocation costs, $0.3bn assignment premiums.

sources.title: Federal Land Management: Federal Land Transaction Facilitation Act Restrictions and Management Weaknesses Limit Future Sales and Acquisitions (GAO-08-196)
sources.reported_estimate: BLM raised $95.7m mostly by selling 16,659 acres (265 sales, July 2000-May 2007) and spent $3.2m ($3,171,956) on FLTFA administrative expenses to conduct land sales; no more than 20% of proceeds may be used for administration. Derived: 3.3% of proceeds, about $190 per acre.

sources.title: New Estimates of Value of Land of the United States (BEA Working Paper WP2015-3)
sources.venue: Bureau of Economic Analysis Working Paper
sources.reported_estimate: Land in the lower 48 states and DC worth about $23 trillion in 2009; the federal government holds about $1.8 trillion (about 8%).

sources.title: Would a transfer of federal lands to the State of Idaho make or lose money? (Issue Brief No. 16)
sources.venue: University of Idaho, College of Natural Resources, Policy Analysis Group
sources.reported_estimate: Executive summary and Table 7 (p.15): net cash flow to Idaho -$111m/yr (low: 500 mmbf at $150/mbf), -$60m (medium), +$24m (high: 1 bn bf at $250/mbf); Table 6 (p.14): gross timber revenue $75m / $160m / $250m with management costs at 40% of revenue; wildfire $40m, recreation $7m, highways $12m, SRS payments $31.2m, PILT $1.0-1.9m, BLM lands net cost $53m a year.

sources.authors: Haefele, M.; Loomis, J.; Bilmes, L.
sources.title: Total Economic Value of US National Park Service Estimated to be $92 Billion: Implications for Policy
sources.reported_estimate: Survey-based total economic value of NPS lands and programmes about $92bn a year (use plus non-use).
sources.why_excluded: Values parks under current management; it does not estimate how much value would be lost under private or trust ownership, so it cannot enter the ratio. It shows the non-market stakes are large.

sources.title: Outdoor Recreation Satellite Account, U.S. and States, 2023
sources.reported_estimate: Outdoor recreation value added $639.5bn, 2.3% of US GDP in 2023 (non-market value at stake in public-land policy).
sources.why_excluded: Measures the size of outdoor recreation (value added), not the change from privatization.

sources.authors: Stambro, J. E. (with Jakus, P. M. et al.)
sources.title: An Analysis of a Transfer of Federal Lands to the State of Utah
sources.venue: Utah Economic and Business Review 74(3), Bureau of Economic and Business Research, University of Utah
sources.reported_estimate: Low-energy-price scenario: ~$202.7m revenue vs ~$280m cost incl. PILT replacement, ratio 0.72.
sources.why_excluded: A state takeover that keeps federal-style obligations (PILT) under low commodity prices; it is not a sale to private owners, so it is shown as the downside case rather than the low end.

sources.title: The Sunken Billions Revisited: Progress and Challenges in Global Marine Fisheries
sources.venue: World Bank, Environment and Sustainable Development series
sources.reported_estimate: Foregone net benefits $83.3bn in 2012 (95% CI $49.7-104.9bn); net benefits $3.0bn now vs $86.3bn optimal; effort must fall ~44%; PV (5%, 20 yr) $514bn current path, $1,196bn moderate path, $1,465bn rapid path; rapid path loses ~$44bn over 4 years, moderate path $0.3bn in year 1; governance costs 1-14% of landings value; optimal revenue $140.6bn.

sources.title: Giving Oceans a Break Could Generate $83 Billion in Additional Benefits for Fisheries (press release, 14 Feb 2017)
sources.reported_estimate: ~$83bn foregone benefits in 2012; reform could raise sector profits from ~$3bn to ~$86bn a year; report 'does not prescribe a particular reform path'.

sources.authors: Costello, C.; Gaines, S. D.; Lynham, J.
sources.title: Can Catch Shares Prevent Fisheries Collapse?
sources.reported_estimate: Data on 11,000+ fisheries: nearly a third of open-access fisheries have collapsed, about half that rate under catch shares.

sources.authors: Costello, C.; Ovando, D.; Clavelle, T.; et al.
sources.title: Global fishery prospects under contrasting management regimes
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 113(18): 5125-5129
sources.reported_estimate: Rights-based fishery management vs business-as-usual by 2050: +16 MMT catch, +$53bn annual profit, +619 MMT biomass; median fishery reaches recovery targets in under 10 years; 98% of stocks could be healthy by mid-century.

sources.authors: Grafton, R. Q.; Squires, D.; Fox, K. J.
sources.title: Private Property and Economic Efficiency: A Study of a Common-Pool Resource
sources.reported_estimate: BC halibut ITQ natural experiment: efficiency gains in cost, revenue and product form after private harvesting rights, though they take years to appear and are limited by restrictions on transferability and duration.

sources.authors: Mangin, T.; Costello, C.; Anderson, J.; Arnason, R.; Elliott, M.; Gaines, S. D.; Hilborn, R.; Peterson, E.; Sumaila, R.
sources.title: Are fishery management upgrades worth the cost?
sources.reported_estimate: p.14: catch-share reform in the top 25 fishing nations, BCRs 1.7-268 (median ~14); global BCR 9.3 (catch shares) and 9.4 (catch controls); 7.0 and 10.1 when costs scale with revenue. p.15: extreme-cost case ($489/t) global BCR 2.8 for catch shares. Table 2 (p.16): global management cost (72.4% of catch) $7.6bn (2012), $8.0bn (2050 BAU), $15.0bn (2050 catch shares), $30.91bn (extreme). p.3: literature costs 3-28% of landings (Iceland, Newfoundland, Norway), OECD average 6% (0-70%), Australia/UK/US 7-30%, Thailand 0.7-1.64%, Namibia 3.7-5.9%. p.16: 'in most countries, taxpayers end up paying'.

sources.authors: Arnason, R.; Hannesson, R.; Schrank, W. E.
sources.title: Costs of fisheries management: the cases of Iceland, Norway and Newfoundland
sources.reported_estimate: Abstract: management costs as a percent of the gross value of landings are 'by far highest in Newfoundland (15-25%), lowest in Iceland (about 3%), with Norway in the middle (about 10%)'.

sources.title: Individual Fishing Quotas: Management Costs Varied and Were Not Recovered as Required (GAO-05-241)
sources.reported_estimate: Results in Brief: FY2003 management costs of the Alaskan halibut and sablefish IFQ program at least $3.2m, 1.4% of ex-vessel value; surfclam/ocean quahog IFQ at least $274,000, under 0.5%; cost-recovery fee capped at 3% of ex-vessel value; NMFS recovered about $3.2m of halibut/sablefish incremental costs and nothing for the other two programs.

sources.authors: Metzner, R. (comp.); Harte, M. (New Zealand chapter)
sources.title: Report of the Expert Consultation on Low-cost Fisheries Management Strategies and Cost Recovery, Georgetown, Guyana, 4-7 September 2007 (FAO Fisheries and Aquaculture Report No. 853)
sources.reported_estimate: p.134: Nicaragua government fisheries management spending 0.66% of the value of landings (2002-04 average, Table 10); Arnason et al. Iceland 3%, Norway 8%, Newfoundland 20%; Cox (2002) Australian Commonwealth fisheries 7.2%. Harte (pp.147-205), p.155: New Zealand management cost 4% of landed value 'compared to an OECD average of 17 percent'; p.179-180: industry cost-recovery levies predicted to fall to 38% of Ministry of Fisheries expenditure in 2005/06.

sources.authors: Wyatt, N. (Ministry of Fisheries, New Zealand)
sources.title: Why recover costs? Cost recovery and property rights in New Zealand
sources.venue: In Shotton, R. (ed.), Use of Property Rights in Fisheries Management, FAO Fisheries Technical Paper 404/1
sources.reported_estimate: Current costs of fisheries services borne by the Crown and by industry are 'close to $NZ23 million and $NZ39 million respectively', i.e. industry pays about 63%.

sources.title: Ecological indicators display reduced variation in North American catch share fisheries
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 107(2): 754-759
sources.reported_estimate: Catch shares markedly reduced year-to-year variability in exploitation, landings and discards, but average levels of most indicators (except discards) were unchanged.
sources.why_excluded: Suggests the ecological gain is mainly stability rather than better averages, which cautions against the high end. It gives no economic value to put in the ratio.

sources.title: The elephant in the room: The hidden costs of leasing individual transferable fishing quotas
sources.reported_estimate: In the BC halibut ITQ fishery, quota leasing reduces economic benefits to active fishermen and society; challenges theoretical claims for ITQ benefits.
sources.why_excluded: Concerns the distribution of rents (owners vs active fishers) more than total net benefit; used for who_benefits, not the ratio.

sources.authors: Selgin, G.; Lastrapes, W. D.; White, L. H.
sources.title: Has the Fed been a failure?
sources.reported_estimate: Price level: $100 basket in 1790 cost $108 in 1913 but $2,422 in 2008; pre-Fed contractions not more severe than post-WWII and recoveries shorter (7.7 vs 10.6 months); 75-90% of Great Moderation attributed to good luck rather than policy (per Cato summary).

sources.title: Inflation and Welfare
sources.reported_estimate: Welfare gain of reducing inflation from 10% to zero is slightly under 1% of real income.

sources.title: A Unified Framework for Monetary Theory and Policy Analysis
sources.reported_estimate: Going from 10% to 0% inflation can be worth between 3% and 5% of consumption (search-theoretic model), several times Lucas-style estimates.

sources.title: An assessment of the long-term economic impact of stronger capital and liquidity requirements (LEI report)
sources.reported_estimate: Banking crises occur about once every 20-25 years (average annual probability ~4.5%); median cumulative discounted output loss per crisis 19% of pre-crisis GDP (no permanent effect), 63% (all studies), 158% (large permanent effects); each 1-point cut in annual crisis probability is worth ~0.2% (temporary) to ~0.6% (permanent) of output a year.

sources.authors: Bordo, M.; Eichengreen, B.; Klingebiel, D.; Martinez-Peria, M. S.
sources.title: Is the crisis problem growing more severe?
sources.reported_estimate: 120 years of data: crisis frequency since 1973 has been double that of the Bretton Woods and classical gold standard periods, matched only by the interwar years; output losses per crisis not larger.

sources.title: Current Evidence on the Resource Costs of Irredeemable Paper Money
sources.reported_estimate: Gold-standard resource cost Friedman (1960) ~2.5% of national product; Meltzer ~0.5% of GDP; White (1999) ~0.05% with ~2% reserves; measured classical gold standard 1879-1913 0.249% of GDP; Friedman-Meltzer costs $35.4-177bn/yr (2012$).

sources.authors: Bordo, M. D.; Redish, A.; Rockoff, H.
sources.title: Why didn't Canada have a banking crisis in 2008 (or in 1930, or 1907, or ...)?
sources.reported_estimate: Canada's concentrated, branch-banking system avoided crises in 1907, 1930s and 2008 largely without (pre-1935) a central bank; stability attributed to banking structure.

sources.title: Exchange-Rate Regimes and International Trade: Evidence from the Classical Gold Standard Era
sources.reported_estimate: 'two countries on gold would trade 60 percent more with each other'; a monetary union 'would more than double bilateral trade flows'.

sources.authors: Estevadeordal, A.; Frantz, B.; Taylor, A.M.
sources.title: The Rise and Fall of World Trade, 1870-1939
sources.reported_estimate: Going on gold raised trade by about 42%; 'Had the 1913 gold standard been applied in 1870, trade volumes would have been about 30 percent higher'; gold explains about 35% of the 1870-1913 rise in trade/GDP.

sources.title: Does Trade Cause Growth?
sources.reported_estimate: Raising the trade/GDP ratio by one percentage point 'raises income per person by between one-half and two percent'.

sources.title: Trade (% of GDP), NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS
sources.reported_estimate: 2024: United States 25.0%; world 56.7%.

sources.title: The Gold Standard as a "Good Housekeeping Seal of Approval"
sources.reported_estimate: 'the rate on a gold bond would be 40 basis points lower if the country were on the gold standard' (p. 413).

sources.title: The Costs and Benefits of Price Stability (introduction); Capital Income Taxes and the Benefit of Price Stability (NBER WP 6200)
sources.reported_estimate: Net benefit of going from 2% inflation to price stability about 1% of GDP a year (US); Germany 1.4%, Spain 1.7%, UK 0.2%.

sources.title: The Costs and Benefits of Going from Low Inflation to Price Stability
sources.venue: NBER WP 5469; in Romer & Romer (eds.), Reducing Inflation
sources.reported_estimate: 'annual deadweight loss of a two percent inflation rate is a surprisingly large one percent of GDP'.

sources.title: The Welfare Cost of Inflation in General Equilibrium
sources.reported_estimate: A sustained 4% inflation costs 0.41% of output a year (currency) and over 1% (M1).

sources.title: The Resource Cost of Irredeemable Paper Money
sources.reported_estimate: The resource cost of gold and silver in private hoards under fiat 'may have been as great as or greater than it would have been under an effective gold standard' (p. 644).

sources.title: Trade and Empire
sources.reported_estimate: Both countries on gold raised bilateral trade by between 18 and 57 percent (Table 2).

sources.title: A Program for Monetary Stability
sources.reported_estimate: Resource cost of a full commodity standard 'about 2.5 per cent of its national product' (as quoted in Watts & Snyder 2015).
sources.why_excluded: 1960 theoretical estimate for a full 100% commodity standard (2.5% of GDP); later measurement of the actual US classical gold standard found 0.249% (Watts & Snyder 2015), and fiat-era gold hoarding itself costs 0.014-0.022%.

sources.authors: Clark, P.; Tamirisa, N.; Wei, S.-J.
sources.title: Exchange Rate Volatility and Trade Flows - Some New Evidence
sources.reported_estimate: A negative effect of exchange-rate volatility on trade 'would appear to be fairly small and is by no means a robust, universal finding'.
sources.why_excluded: Used for the low end (no trade gain).

sources.title: The Macroeconomics of the Great Depression: A Comparative Approach
sources.venue: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking 27(1):1-28 (NBER WP 4814)
sources.reported_estimate: Over 1932-35 'the cumulative difference in log output levels was .310 ... in favor of countries not on gold'.
sources.why_excluded: Depression-era episode; no published estimate of how often such episodes recur under a modern commodity standard.

sources.title: Does deposit insurance increase banking system stability? An empirical investigation
sources.reported_estimate: 61 countries 1980-97, 40 systemic crises (4.4% of observations): explicit deposit insurance raises crisis probability, more so with wide coverage, government-run funded schemes, deregulated rates and weak institutions. The effect becomes insignificant at high institutional quality. Cutting US coverage to Swiss levels would have lowered the predicted probability of the 1980 US crisis from 4.3% to 2.5% (IMF WP 00/3 version, p.15).

sources.title: Systemic Banking Crises Revisited (IMF Working Paper 18/206)
sources.reported_estimate: 151 systemic banking crises 1970-2017. US 2007 crisis: output loss 30.0% of trend GDP (cumulative over T to T+3), fiscal cost 4.5% of GDP gross (0.6% net), public debt +21.9% of GDP. Median fiscal cost 6.7% of GDP in high-income countries (3.3% net).

sources.title: Stealing Deposits: Deposit Insurance, Risk-Taking, and the Removal of Market Discipline in Early 20th-Century Banks
sources.reported_estimate: Early-1900s state deposit-insurance laws removed the market discipline that had constrained uninsured banks. Insured banks took more insolvency risk during the WWI farm boom, and the insurance systems collapsed with high losses when prices fell.

sources.title: Is Deposit Insurance Necessary? A Historical Perspective
sources.reported_estimate: Antebellum and 1920s US experience: self-regulating mutual-liability schemes succeeded and compulsory state insurance systems failed. Branch banking improved stability.

sources.authors: Anginer, D.; Demirgüç-Kunt, A.; Zhu, M.
sources.title: How does deposit insurance affect bank risk? Evidence from the recent crisis
sources.reported_estimate: Generous deposit insurance raised bank risk and systemic fragility in 2004-06 (log z-score coefficient -0.472) and lowered it during 2007-09 (+0.221). 'The overall effect of deposit insurance over the full sample remains negative' (WB PRWP 6289 version).

sources.title: The Cost of the Savings and Loan Crisis: Truth and Consequences
sources.reported_estimate: Total S&L crisis loss ~$153bn, of which taxpayers ~$124bn (81%) and the industry ~$29bn (19%).

sources.title: Measuring the Cost of Bailouts
sources.reported_estimate: Total direct cost of 2008 crisis-related US bailouts 'on the order of $500 billion, or 3.5% of GDP in 2009'.

sources.authors: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (via Davis Polk client update)
sources.title: FDIC finalizes $16.3 billion special assessment to recover loss from SVB and Signature Bank failures
sources.venue: Davis Polk & Wardwell client update summarising FDIC final rule of 16 Nov 2023
sources.reported_estimate: Estimated Deposit Insurance Fund loss from protecting uninsured depositors of SVB and Signature under the systemic-risk exception: ~$16.3bn, recovered at 13.4 bp a year on uninsured deposits over 8 quarters.

sources.title: Big Banks Benefit From Government Subsidies (IMF Survey, on GFSR April 2014 ch. 3)
sources.reported_estimate: Implicit too-big-to-fail funding subsidy to global systemically important banks in 2012: up to $70bn in the US and up to $300bn in the euro area.

sources.authors: Correia, S.; Luck, S.; Verner, E.
sources.title: Why Do Banks Fail? Bank Runs Versus Solvency (summary of 'Failing Banks', NBER WP 32907)
sources.venue: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Liberty Street Economics
sources.reported_estimate: 5,000+ US bank failures 1865-2023. Insolvency is almost always the root cause, and runs can be ruled out as a plausible cause in >80% of pre-FDIC failures. Depositors lost ~30% in a typical pre-FDIC failure.

sources.title: 2024 Annual Report, Section II: Financial Highlights
sources.reported_estimate: Assessment revenue $11.6bn in 2024; DIF operating expenses $2,433m; DIF balance $137.1bn at 31 Dec 2024; reserve ratio 1.25% (30 Sep 2024).

sources.title: U.S. Property & Casualty and Title Insurance Industries: 2024 Mid-Year Results
sources.venue: NAIC Financial Regulatory Services industry report
sources.reported_estimate: P&C industry underwriting expense ratio 24.8% in the first half of 2024 (25.2% in H1 2023).

sources.authors: Diamond, D. W.; Dybvig, P. H.
sources.title: Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity
sources.reported_estimate: Theory: demand-deposit banks have a run equilibrium. 'there are circumstances when government provision of deposit insurance can produce superior contracts'.
sources.why_excluded: Pure theory with no quantity. Its rationale enters the ratio through the Dávila & Goldstein cost estimate, which is calibrated on this class of model.

sources.title: Optimal Deposit Insurance
sources.reported_estimate: Optimal US coverage in 2008 ~ $381,000. Raising coverage from $100,000 to $200,000 is worth ~$13.2bn a year (9.46 bp of $14tn bank assets). 'the welfare gains from having a deposit insurance system at all are very large.'
sources.why_excluded: Used as the cost input (denominator) of both ends, not excluded. It is listed here because it is the strongest evidence that abolition lowers welfare, and on its own it implies a ratio below 1 for full abolition.

sources.authors: Egan, M.; Hortaçsu, A.; Matvos, G.
sources.title: Deposit Competition and Financial Fragility: Evidence from the US Banking Sector
sources.reported_estimate: Structural model: uninsured deposits flee distressed banks and insured deposits do not. The calibrated model has multiple run equilibria, so banks can be very fragile.
sources.why_excluded: Shows that uninsured funding is run-prone but gives no welfare figure for abolishing insurance, so it cannot be converted into a ratio.

sources.title: Trade Barriers (Copenhagen Consensus 2012 Challenge Paper)
sources.reported_estimate: Doha Development Agenda: PV benefits $12-64 trillion vs costs <$400bn PV; BCR 90-180 globally, 140-250 for developing countries.

sources.title: Post-2015 Consensus: Trade Assessment
sources.reported_estimate: Doha completion: ~$2,000 world benefit per $1 (~$3,400 for developing countries); APEC FTA ~$1,700; TPP ~$1,200; ASEAN+3 ~$1,900; 160 million fewer in extreme poverty by 2030.

sources.title: Does Trade Cause Growth?
sources.reported_estimate: A 1-percentage-point increase in the trade share raises income per person by roughly 0.5-2%.

sources.authors: Fajgelbaum, P. D.; Goldberg, P. K.; Kennedy, P. J.; Khandelwal, A. K.
sources.title: The Return to Protectionism
sources.reported_estimate: 2018 US tariffs: $51bn (0.27% of GDP) loss to US buyers of imports; net aggregate real-income loss ~$7.2bn (0.04% of GDP) after tariff revenue and producer gains; full pass-through to domestic prices.

sources.authors: Hong Kong Trade and Industry Department
sources.title: Hong Kong's Trade Policy
sources.venue: Government of the Hong Kong SAR
sources.reported_estimate: 'Hong Kong is a free port.' 'No tariff is charged on import or export of goods.'

sources.title: Benefits and Costs of the Trade Targets for the Post-2015 Development Agenda
sources.venue: Copenhagen Consensus Center, Post-2015 Consensus Assessment Paper (2015); republished as Chapter 9 in B. Lomborg (ed.), Prioritizing Development: A Cost Benefit Analysis of the UN's SDGs, Cambridge University Press, 2018 (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/prioritizing-development/benefits-and-costs-of-the-trade-targets-for-the-post2015-development-agenda/6C7F2BE259D803132AA9E70957AAEC06)
sources.reported_estimate: Doha completion with growth effects (one-fifth growth boost 2010-15, tapering to comparative-static by 2050): global BCR 1,300-2,800, developing countries 2,100-4,700 (3% and 5% discount rates); FTAAP 800-2,600 global.

sources.title: Trade Liberalization and Growth: New Evidence
sources.reported_estimate: Countries that liberalized grew ~1.5 percentage points a year faster than before; investment rates rose 1.5-2.0 points; trade/GDP rose ~5 points.

sources.title: The Challenge of Reducing International Trade and Migration Barriers (Copenhagen Consensus 2008 Challenge Paper: Subsidies and Trade Barriers)
sources.venue: Copenhagen Consensus Center (also in Lomborg ed., Global Crises, Global Solutions, 2nd ed., Cambridge UP 2009)
sources.reported_estimate: Table 11: Doha liberalisation of subsidies and trade barriers, benefits to 2100 incl. dynamic gains: global BCR 932-1,121 at 3% and 269-363 at 6%; without dynamic gains 17-80; developing countries 692-3,147. Dynamic gains 'many times greater' than comparative-static gains.

sources.title: The State of U.S. Tariffs: August 24, 2026
sources.reported_estimate: Update of 24 Aug 2026: average statutory tariff rate 11.0% (11.8% by end-2026 under current law); consumer price impact ~0.7%; household costs ~$1,100 a year; revenue ~$1.9tn over ten years (somewhat lower after GDP effects).

sources.title: Trump Tariffs: Tracking the Economic Impact of the Trump Trade War (updated 10 Sept 2026)
sources.reported_estimate: Tariffs raised taxes ~$1,000 per household in 2025 and $820 in 2026; $1.4tn revenue 2026-35 conventional (~$1tn dynamic); long-run GDP -0.4%; applied tariff rate 11.8% (1.5% in 2022); -338,000 FTE jobs; retaliation a further -0.1% GDP. The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on 20 Feb 2026 (Learning Resources v. Trump).

sources.title: The Economic Effects of Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Orders and Suspension Agreements (Inv. 332-344, Pub. 2900)
sources.reported_estimate: Removing the 1991 AD/CVD orders gives a net US welfare gain of $1.59bn (0.03% of GDP); losses to petitioning and upstream industries of $320m-$1.09bn vs gains to the rest of the economy of $2.17-2.94bn.

sources.authors: Gallaway, M. P.; Blonigen, B. A.; Flynn, J. E.
sources.title: Welfare costs of the U.S. antidumping and countervailing duty laws
sources.reported_estimate: Collective net economic welfare cost of US AD/CVD orders ~$4bn in 1993, among the most costly US import restraint programs.

sources.title: World Trade Report 2015: Speeding up trade: benefits and challenges of implementing the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement
sources.reported_estimate: Full TFA implementation cuts members' trade costs by 14.5% on average; global merchandise exports +$750bn-1T/yr (CGE); +0.5% GDP growth per annum; gravity model: +$1.8-3.6T exports, LDC exports +13-36%

sources.title: The Costs and Challenges of Implementing Trade Facilitation Measures
sources.reported_estimate: Capital expenditure EUR 3.5-19M per country; annual operating costs no more than EUR 2.5M; costs 'not particularly large and far smaller than the benefits'

sources.authors: Feyrer, J.; Tyazhelnikov, V.; Aleman-Castilla, B.; Wong, B.
sources.title: Benefit-Cost Analysis of Increased Trade: An Order-of-Magnitude Estimate of the Benefit-Cost Ratio
sources.reported_estimate: ~5% rise in global trade (10% tariff cut, 10% lower effective distance, deeper FTAs): benefits $700bn (0.83% of world GDP) vs costs $100bn (0.12%) in year one; BCR ~100 for low/lower-middle income, ~50 upper-middle, ~5 high-income; overall 11 (per Lomborg 2023 intro). Authors say the BCRs are at the low end of the plausible range.
sources.why_excluded: Measures a partial 5% rise in world trade, static and year-one only; authors call their BCRs the low end of the plausible range. Not full free trade.

sources.title: Save 4.2 Million Lives and Generate $1.1 Trillion in Economic Benefits for Only $41 Billion: Introduction to the Special Issue on the Most Efficient Policies for the Sustainable Development Goals
sources.reported_estimate: Halftime 'best buy' list: trade BCR 95 for the poorer half of the world, 11 globally, 7 for high-income; $1.7bn annual cost.
sources.why_excluded: Reports the same partial, static Halftime trade intervention (global 11, high-income 7, poorer half 95); narrower than full liberalisation.

sources.title: How Bad Is Antidumping? Evidence from Panel Data
sources.reported_estimate: Volume and welfare effects of antidumping 1948-2001 are 'negative but quite modest'.
sources.why_excluded: Supports the sign but says the anti-dumping sub-policy's gains are modest. That is consistent with treating it as a small add-on to the free-trade core rather than a driver of the range.

sources.title: The Economic Cost of Global Fuel Subsidies
sources.reported_estimate: 'road-sector subsidies for gasoline and diesel totaled $110 billion in 2012'; 'the total annual deadweight loss worldwide is $44 billion'; 'Incorporating external costs increases the economic costs substantially.' Deadweight loss per $1 of subsidy: 44/110 = 0.40.

sources.authors: Black, S.; Liu, A. A.; Parry, I. W. H.
sources.title: IMF Fossil Fuel Subsidies Data: 2023 Update (IMF Working Paper 23/169)
sources.reported_estimate: 'Global fossil fuel subsidies in 2022: $7 trillion'; 'Explicit subsidies (undercharging for supply costs) share of total subsidy: 18 percent' (0.18 x 7,000 = $1,260bn). Full price reform (including corrective taxes): CO2 '43 percent below baseline levels' by 2030 and '1.6 million local air pollution deaths per year' prevented.

sources.authors: Jewell, J.; McCollum, D.; Emmerling, J.; Bertram, C.; Gernaat, D. E. H. J.; Krey, V.; Paroussos, L.; Berger, L.; Fragkiadakis, K.; Keppo, I.; Saadi, N.; Tavoni, M.; van Vuuren, D.; Vinichenko, V.; Riahi, K.
sources.title: Limited emission reductions from fuel subsidy removal except in energy-exporting regions
sources.reported_estimate: Removing fossil fuel subsidies 'would have an unexpectedly small impact on global energy demand and carbon dioxide emissions'; reduces global CO2 'by only a few per cent by 2030' (editorial summary); 0.5-2.2 GtCO2 a year by 2030, a 1-5% reduction (as reported by Carbon Brief, https://www.carbonbrief.org/?p=28593).

sources.title: Energy: Post-2015 Consensus
sources.reported_estimate: Phase out fossil fuel energy subsidies: benefits 15 times cost; phase out implicit fossil fuel subsidies through energy taxes: 8 (Morris); universal electrification access: $5 per $1; double the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix: under $1 per $1.

sources.title: Energy Subsidies: Evolution in the Global Energy Transformation to 2050
sources.reported_estimate: Direct energy-sector subsidies in 2017 of US$634bn: fossil fuels US$447bn, renewable power US$128bn, biofuels US$38bn, nuclear US$21bn (figures as summarised by Enerdata; the report landing page gives no figures).

sources.authors: Abrell, J.; Kosch, M.; Rausch, S.
sources.title: Carbon abatement with renewables: Evaluating wind and solar subsidies in Germany and Spain
sources.reported_estimate: Short-run abatement cost of solar subsidies EUR 411-1,944/tCO2; wind EUR 82-276/tCO2 (EUR 1,944 x ~1.1 $/EUR = $2,138/t, the upper per-tonne cost).

sources.authors: Bistline, J.; Mehrotra, N.; Wolfram, C.
sources.title: Economic Implications of the Climate Provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act
sources.venue: Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Spring 2023 (NBER WP 31267)
sources.reported_estimate: Power-sector average abatement cost of IRA tax credits $36-87/tCO2 with discounted costs and undiscounted emissions, $88-94 if both are discounted; costs 'would be higher if distortions associated with financing the incentives were included'.

sources.title: Supply-Side Reforms to Oil and Gas Production on Federal Lands: Modeling the Implications for CO2 Emissions, Federal Revenues, and Leakage
sources.venue: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists 9(4): 681-720
sources.reported_estimate: A federal leasing ban 'reduces royalty revenues by $5 billion annually' and, after leakage, cuts emissions by about one-quarter of the amount projected for the Clean Power Plan; RFF summary (https://resources.org/common-resources/economic-and-emissions-consequences-supply-side-reforms-oil-and-gas-production-federal-lands): 'more than 300 million tons of CO2-equivalent' a year on federal lands, 'around 100 million tons in global emissions reductions annually' (2020-2050 averages).

sources.title: Welfare and Distributional Implications of Shale Gas
sources.venue: Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Spring 2015 (NBER WP 21115)
sources.reported_estimate: Between 2007 and 2013 the shale gas revolution increased welfare for natural gas consumers and producers by $48 billion per year; NBER Digest: consumer benefits of $74 billion in 2013.

sources.title: 2024 LNG Export Study: Energy, Economic, and Environmental Assessment of U.S. LNG Exports
sources.venue: U.S. Department of Energy (summaries by Vinson & Elkins, Akin Gump and RFF)
sources.reported_estimate: Model Resolved (unconstrained) vs Existing/FID exports: '$80 billion increase in GDP in 2050' and '$410 billion cumulative increase in U.S. GDP from 2020-2050' (Vinson & Elkins summary); domestic customers pay four percent more in 2050; 'a cumulative increase of about 710 MMT of CO2-equivalent (CO2e) emissions between 2020 and 2050', 'only about 0.05 percent of predicted cumulative global CO2e emissions' (RFF); 0.56% upstream and midstream methane leak rate assumed.

sources.authors: NERA Economic Consulting (for U.S. Department of Energy)
sources.title: Macroeconomic Outcomes of Market Determined Levels of U.S. LNG Exports
sources.reported_estimate: GDP 'exceeds GDP with the lowest level of LNG exports by $13 to $72 billion in 2040'; 'overall U.S. economic output is higher whenever global markets call for higher levels of LNG exports'.

sources.title: Maximizing Access to Energy: Estimates of Access and Generation for the Overseas Private Investment Corporation's Portfolio
sources.venue: Center for Global Development Working Paper
sources.reported_estimate: For a $10 billion portfolio, 'A natural gas-only portfolio could provide electricity access to 90 million people' versus 20-27 million under a renewables-only mix; gas investment could reach roughly 60 million more people.

sources.title: Congressional Budget Justification: Fiscal Year 2025 (NUREG-1100, Volume 40)
sources.reported_estimate: 'The NRC's FY 2025 budget request, including the Office of the Inspector General, is $994,946K'; 2,897.9 FTE; $823,946K recovered from fees; net budget authority $151,000K.

sources.title: National IRA Rollback Update (March 2025)
sources.reported_estimate: Repeal scenario vs current policies: 'GDP drops by more than $160 billion' in 2030, nearly $190bn in 2035; nearly 790,000 fewer jobs in 2030; emissions up nearly 260 million metric tons CO2e in 2030 and more than 530 million in 2035; household energy bills up more than $6bn in 2030. The scenario also rescinds other federal programme funding.

sources.authors: Davis, S. J.; von Wachter, T.
sources.title: Recessions and the Costs of Job Loss
sources.venue: Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Fall 2011 (NBER WP 17638)
sources.reported_estimate: Men displaced in mass layoffs lose 1.4 years of pre-displacement earnings when unemployment is below 6% and 2.8 years when it exceeds 8% (present value, 5% discount rate, 20 years).

sources.title: Occupational Employment and Wages - May 2024 (news release, 2 April 2025)
sources.reported_estimate: All occupations: median hourly wage $23.80; mean annual wage $67,920 (median annual = 23.80 x 2,080 = $49,504).

sources.authors: Parry, I. W. H.; Veung, C.; Heine, D.
sources.title: How Much Carbon Pricing is in Countries' Own Interests? The Critical Role of Co-Benefits (IMF Working Paper 14/174; published in Climate Change Economics 2015)
sources.reported_estimate: 'On average, nationally efficient prices are substantial, $57.5 per ton of CO2 (for year 2010)' for the top 20 emitters, driven mainly by reduced local air pollution from coal plants; used as the per-tonne value of local co-damages.

sources.title: Policies, projections, and the social cost of carbon: Results from the DICE-2023 model
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 121(13): e2312030121
sources.reported_estimate: 'The SCC in the baseline run is $66/tCO2 for the 2020 period (in 2019 international $)'; upper carbon value.

sources.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
sources.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
sources.reported_estimate: Marginal excess burden centres around 33 cents per $1 of revenue, ranging 17-56 cents (as summarised by Fullerton & Henderson 1987, NBER w2353).

sources.title: The Distributional Effects of US Clean Energy Tax Credits
sources.reported_estimate: Top income quintile received ~60% of clean-energy tax credits, bottom three quintiles ~10%; ~90% of EV credits went to the top quintile.

sources.authors: Rennert, K.; Errickson, F.; Prest, B. C.; et al.
sources.title: Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2
sources.reported_estimate: SCC $185/tCO2 (5-95%: $44-413) at a 2% discount rate.
sources.why_excluded: The dashboard values CO2 at $36-66/t (DICE-2016R3 to DICE-2023). At $185/t the LOW-end net emission increase would cost far more and the HIGH-end net reduction would be worth more, widening the range in both directions.

sources.authors: Lee, K.; Miguel, E.; Wolfram, C.
sources.title: Experimental Evidence on the Economics of Rural Electrification
sources.reported_estimate: Randomised grid expansion in rural Kenya: demand for connections 'falls sharply with price'; consumption 'is very low, implying low consumer surplus'; no meaningful medium-run economic or non-economic impacts.
sources.why_excluded: Indicates that grid connections in poor rural areas can return less than their cost, which weighs against assuming large gains from fossil-fuel generation finance; not converted into a figure because the development-bank component is left unpriced.

sources.title: Nuclear Power Learning and Deployment Rates; Disruption and Global Benefits Forgone
sources.reported_estimate: 'Had the early rates continued, nuclear power could now be around 10% of its current cost'; additional nuclear 'could have substituted for 69,000-186,000 TWh of coal and gas generation', 'avoiding up to 9.5 million deaths and 174 Gt CO2 emissions'; in 2015 alone up to 540,000 deaths and 11 Gt CO2.
sources.why_excluded: A historical counterfactual of continued learning rates, not an estimate of the gain from licensing reform today; it does not attribute the cost escalation to regulation, so it is not used in the range.

sources.authors: Kleiner, M. M.; Soltas, E. J.
sources.title: A Welfare Analysis of Occupational Licensing in U.S. States
sources.reported_estimate: Welfare loss 12% of occupational surplus; consumers' WTP offsets 80% of price rise; wages compensate 60% of training cost (item BCR 1.25-1.67)

sources.title: Reforming Occupational Licensing Policies
sources.reported_estimate: Up to 2.85m fewer jobs and $203bn/yr cost to consumers

sources.title: At What Cost? State and National Estimates of the Economic Costs of Occupational Licensing
sources.reported_estimate: Nearly 2m jobs; misallocation ~$6bn conservative, broader measure 'may reach $184 billion or more'

sources.title: The Effects on Employment and Family Income of Increasing the Federal Minimum Wage
sources.reported_estimate: $15 option: real family income in 2025 +$8bn for families below the poverty threshold, about -$16bn for families above it, -$9bn (0.1%) overall (report reposted 7 Nov 2019 with revised income values); median -1.3m jobs

sources.authors: Cengiz, D.; Dube, A.; Lindner, A.; Zipperer, B.
sources.title: The Effect of Minimum Wages on Low-Wage Jobs
sources.reported_estimate: Affected workers' wage +6.8%, affected employment +2.8% (n.s.); used for item low BCR 0.69

sources.title: Housing Constraints and Spatial Misallocation
sources.reported_estimate: Constraints lowered US growth 36% 1964-2009; NY/SJ/SF at median regulation: US GDP 2009 +3.7% (imperfect mobility, Table 5, pp.2, 27) or +8.9% (perfect mobility, Table 4, p.26; $1.95tn on 2009 GDP of $14.5tn, fn.28). HIGH uses 8.9%.

sources.title: Housing Constraints and Spatial Misallocation: Comment
sources.reported_estimate: Cannot replicate HM 3.7%; documents code errors; corrected model gain 'two orders of magnitude smaller' (~0.04% of GDP, author's arithmetic)

sources.authors: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis via Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)
sources.title: Gross Domestic Product, annual (GDPA)
sources.venue: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

sources.authors: Philipson, T.; Berndt, E. R.; Gottschalk, A. H. B.; Sun, E.
sources.title: Cost-benefit analysis of the FDA: The case of the prescription drug user fee acts
sources.reported_estimate: Faster review under PDUFA I-II: social surplus +$14-31bn (PV, 1992$); 140,000-310,000 life-years gained; extreme upper bound on safety harm ~56,000 life-years (WP: ~$4.4bn PV at $100k/LY)

sources.title: An Evaluation of Consumer Protection Legislation: The 1962 Drug Amendments
sources.reported_estimate: Net impact of 1962 efficacy rules 'equivalent to a 5-10 percent tax on drug purchases'

sources.title: National Health Expenditure Fact Sheet
sources.reported_estimate: 2024 prescription drug spending $467.0bn

sources.authors: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics via Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)
sources.title: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items (CPIAUCSL), annual average
sources.venue: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

sources.title: Sugar Program: Alternative Methods for Implementing Import Restrictions Could Increase Effectiveness (GAO-24-106144)
sources.reported_estimate: Program costs consumers $2.5-3.5bn/yr; net cost to economy ~$1bn/yr (citing studies)

sources.authors: Dahl, D. (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis)
sources.title: Compliance Costs Community Banks $4.5 Billion Annually, Survey Shows
sources.reported_estimate: Community-bank compliance cost $4.5bn in 2014 (CSBS survey of 974 banks); 22% of net income

sources.title: Cost estimate: S. 2155, Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act
sources.reported_estimate: Deficits +$671m over 2018-2027; probability of SIFI failure/crisis 'small under current law and would be slightly greater'

sources.authors: Coffey, B.; McLaughlin, P. A.; Peretto, P. F.
sources.title: The cumulative cost of regulations
sources.reported_estimate: Federal regulatory growth since 1980 slowed growth ~0.8 points a year; economy 'nearly 25 percent larger' and GDP ~$4tn higher in 2012 had regulation been held at 1980 levels (abstract p.1; pp.14, 16). Authors: 'this study is not a weighing of the costs and benefits of regulation' (p.2). HIGH: 4,000/16,254 = 24.61% of 2025 GDP.

sources.authors: Grabow, C.; Manak, I.; Ikenson, D. J.
sources.title: The Jones Act: A Burden America Can No Longer Bear
sources.reported_estimate: Cites USITC economy-wide cost estimates of $656 million to $9.8 billion per year; US-flag operating costs $20,053/day vs $7,454/day foreign-flag (2.7x); US coastal ships $190-250m vs ~$30m foreign-built.

sources.title: The Economic Effects of Significant U.S. Import Restraints: Third Update 2002
sources.reported_estimate: Economy-wide welfare gain from Jones Act removal ~$656 million per year (the low end of the USITC range cited by Cato).

sources.authors: Office of Management and Budget, Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs
sources.title: 2017 Draft Report to Congress on the Benefits and Costs of Federal Regulations and Agency Compliance with the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
sources.venue: OMB, Dec 2017 (Table 1-1, PDF p.13; Table A-2, PDF pp.82-90)
sources.reported_estimate: Table 1-1: 39 EPA major rules FY2007-2016, benefits $195.8-705.7bn, costs $54.1-64.8bn a year (2015$). Table A-2 ($m 2001): Florida numeric nutrient WQS benefits 23, costs 111-169 (p.88); Coal Combustion Residuals 182-226 vs 399-576 (p.88); Cooling Water Intake 24-27 vs 223-241 (p.90). Table 1-1 (2015$, low): USDA 0.6, DOE 20.3, HHS 5.9, DHS 0.5, DOJ 1.9, DOL 9.8, DOT 22.3, joint DOT-EPA 44.6. p.12-13: EPA rules over 80% of monetized benefits; air rules over 95% of EPA benefits, 'mostly attributable to the reduction in public exposure to fine particulate matter'; PM co-benefits the majority of MATS benefits

sources.authors: Greenstone, M.; List, J. A.; Syverson, C.
sources.title: The Effects of Environmental Regulation on the Competitiveness of U.S. Manufacturing
sources.reported_estimate: Air-quality nonattainment lowers TFP of polluting plants 2.6% (4.8% corrected); annual cost $11.0bn to $20.8bn (2010$), about 8.8% of manufacturing profits, 1972-1993. Used only in the full-repeal EPA variant.

sources.title: The Transitional Costs of Sectoral Reallocation: Evidence from the Clean Air Act and the Workforce
sources.reported_estimate: Workers in plants newly regulated by the 1990 CAAA lost more than $5.4bn of earnings in aggregate (one-time); small relative to the CAAA's benefits. Cross-check only.

sources.title: Why Is Pollution from US Manufacturing Declining? The Roles of Environmental Regulation, Productivity, and Trade
sources.reported_estimate: Manufacturing emissions fell 60% 1990-2008 despite output growth; the implicit pollution tax doubled; regulation explains most of the decline. Mechanism.

sources.title: The Impacts of Environmental Regulations on Competitiveness
sources.venue: Review of Environmental Economics and Policy 11(2):183-206
sources.reported_estimate: Adverse effects on trade, employment, location and productivity are statistically significant in pollution- and energy-intensive sectors but small relative to general trends. Mechanism.

sources.title: What Do Right-to-Work Laws Do? Evidence from a Synthetic Control Method Analysis
sources.venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management 35(1):173-194
sources.reported_estimate: Oklahoma's RTW law lowered private-sector unionization; total employment rate and private-sector average wages were not affected (union item LOW = 0)

sources.title: The Economic Effects of Labor Unions Revisited
sources.venue: Journal of Labor Research 23(1):105-130 (Table 1 as reprinted in Gallaway & Robe 2014, CEI, p.12)
sources.reported_estimate: Rees-method deadweight loss of unions 0.11% of wages in 2000 (0.08% factor-adjusted); 'could easily double' with a labour-supply response. Table values read from the CEI reprint; the journal article itself was not opened.

sources.title: The Unintended Consequences of Collective Bargaining
sources.reported_estimate: Reprints Vedder & Gallaway (2002) Table 1: deadweight loss 0.34% (1967) to 0.11% (2000) of wages; labour-supply response could double it (p.12-13)

sources.title: Union Members - 2025 (USDL release, Feb 18 2026); Union Members in 2000 (Jan 18 2001)
sources.reported_estimate: 2025: membership rate 10.0%, private sector 5.9%, 14.7m members (about 7.4m private), 146.661m employed wage and salary workers. 2000: 13.5% (https://www.bls.gov/news.release/History/union2_01182001.txt)

sources.authors: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis via FRED
sources.title: Wages and salaries (A576RC1); GDP implicit price deflator (A191RD3A086NBEA)
sources.venue: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

sources.title: What Do Unions Do for Economic Performance?
sources.reported_estimate: Average union productivity effect near zero; unions lower profitability and tax returns on capital, reducing investment and subsequent employment and productivity growth. Mechanism.

sources.authors: Bradley, D.; Kim, I.; Tian, X.
sources.title: Do Unions Affect Innovation?
sources.reported_estimate: Passing a union election lowers patent quantity 8.7% and quality 12.5% three years later (RD design). Mechanism.

sources.authors: Fallick, B. C.; Hassett, K. A.
sources.title: Investment and Union Certification
sources.reported_estimate: A winning certification election cuts next-year investment as much as a 33-point rise in the corporate tax rate. Mechanism.

sources.title: The Effect of State Policies on the Location of Manufacturing: Evidence from State Borders
sources.venue: Journal of Political Economy 106(4):667-705 (Minneapolis Fed Staff Report 205)
sources.reported_estimate: Large abrupt increase in manufacturing activity crossing from a non-RTW to an RTW state (staff-report abstract; the 'one-third' magnitude was not read in the source). Mechanism.

sources.title: Does Antitrust Policy Improve Consumer Welfare? Assessing the Evidence
sources.reported_estimate: No evidence that monopolization, collusion or merger policy has provided much benefit to consumers, nor evidence of deterrence (antitrust item low cost = 0)

sources.title: FY2018 and FY2019 One-Page Performance Snapshots
sources.reported_estimate: Merger and nonmerger actions saved consumers over $3.8bn (FY2018) and over $4.8bn (FY2019); about $66 per $1 of merger-program resources (FY2019). FY2018: https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/documents/reports/2018-one-page-ftc-performance-snapshot/2018_performance_snapshot.pdf

sources.authors: U.S. Department of Justice, Antitrust Division
sources.title: FY 2025 Performance Budget, Congressional Justification
sources.reported_estimate: FY2025 request $288.0m; HSR fees $341.9m offset; consumer savings, civil (merger and non-merger) FY16-23: 2.271, 1.408, 0.928, 3.939, 0.712, 1.567, 0.529, 1.822 $bn; criminal 62, 132, 58, 12, 114, 2,185, 1, 165 $m

sources.title: FY 2023 Congressional Budget Justification
sources.reported_estimate: Program level $490m; Promoting Competition mission $239.6m, 680 FTE

sources.title: The Benefits and Costs of the Clean Air Act from 1990 to 2020: Summary Report
sources.venue: EPA Office of Air and Radiation, March 2011 (pp.22-23, 28)

1.policy: Governments pay landowners, communities or forest countries to keep tropical forest standing instead of clearing it. The payments are results-based: money flows when deforestation falls. The scale evaluated here is a cut of half in global deforestation, funded as public spending with monitoring and administration included.
1.why_on_list: It came first of 18 options in the Peoples' Climate Vote 2021, chosen by 54% of respondents. It also features in the 2025 international survey of climate-policy attitudes by Dechezleprêtre and co-authors.
1.evidence:
Paying people to keep forests standing is often presented as one of the cheapest ways to cut carbon dioxide (CO2). The best evidence is a randomized trial in Uganda. Forest owners in 60 of 121 villages were paid not to clear their land for two years. Jayachandran et al. (2017) report that "tree cover declined by 4.2% during the study period in treatment villages, compared to 9.1% in control villages." They found no sign that enrolled owners moved their clearing to nearby land. Valued at the social cost of carbon, the delayed emissions were worth 2.4 times the programme cost.

That result holds while the payments last. If owners catch up on the clearing as soon as payments stop, the ratio falls to 0.7. If the delay is permanent, it rises to 12.3, a case the authors call a very tentative extrapolation. The harder problem is delivery at scale. Where money buys carbon credits, West et al. (2023) find only about 6.1% of credits from voluntary REDD+ projects (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation) reflect additional reductions. Protection in one country can also push clearing elsewhere. A study summarised by Hu et al. (2024) puts that displacement at 42% to 95% of conservation effort. Combined, these bring the return down to about 9 cents per $1. Halving deforestation would cost about $33 billion a year, including monitoring and administration. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $0.03 to $1.79 per $1.
1.ratio:
**High end: 2.4.** This is the Uganda trial's published central ratio (Jayachandran et al. 2017). The working paper puts total programme cost at scale, payments plus administration, at about $0.57 per tonne of CO2 delayed (Jayachandran et al. 2016). The delayed emissions are valued at a $39 social cost of carbon. The trial's cost already includes monitoring and administration of the programme. Carbon-market certification costs do not apply to a government payments programme. The authors' own sensitivity range runs from 0.7 (immediate catch-up after payments stop) to 12.3 (permanent delay).

**Low end: 0.09.** This is the full-cost case for delivery through credits, with leakage. Payments are counted as programme cost, as Jayachandran et al. do.

1. Cost per credited tonne. Kindermann et al. (2008) give an upper average cost of $18.7 per tonne (28.0 ÷ 1.5). Monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) and certification add $1.46 per tonne (Merger et al. 2012). Total: $20.2 per tonne.
2. Cost per real tonne. Only about 6.1% of credits reflect additional reductions (West et al. 2023). 20.2 ÷ 0.061 = $331 per real tonne.
3. Value per dollar. At the $51 interim social cost of carbon used by the US Interagency Working Group (IWG) (Resources for the Future 2023): 51 ÷ 331 = 0.15.
4. Leakage. Payments flow to countries one at a time, so displacement across borders applies. At the lowest figure of 42%: 0.15 × (1 − 0.42) = 0.09.

**Range: 0.09 to 2.4. Full cost: $32.7 billion a year.**

Cross-checks. If every paid tonne were real, Kindermann's cost range of $6.4 to $18.7 per tonne gives ratios of 2.7 to 8.0 at a $51 social cost of carbon, and 9.9 to 29 at $185 (Rennert et al. 2022). Brazil's satellite-based enforcement system, DETER, breaks even at a carbon price of $0.76 per tonne (Assunção, Gandour and Rocha 2023). The Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015 assessment rated halving forest loss at about 10, while McVittie's re-estimate in the same assessment gave $2 to $3 per $1 (Markandya 2015).

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. The whole cost behind the ratio is public spending. Low end: 0.09 ÷ 3.00 = 0.03. High end: 2.4 ÷ 1.34 = 1.79. **Range after tax finance: 0.03 to 1.79.**
1.cost:
The full cost is $32.7 billion a year. It has three parts.

- **Payments: $28.0 billion a year.** This is the high end of Kindermann et al. (2008), whose range for a 50% cut in deforestation is $17.2 to $28.0 billion a year. The payments equal landholders' opportunity costs: the farm and timber income they give up.
- **Administration: about $4.7 billion a year.** Merger et al. (2012) find MRV and carbon-market compliance costs of up to $1.46 per tonne in Tanzanian REDD+ pilots. At Kindermann's upper volume of 2.7 billion tonnes a year: 2.7 × 1.46 = $3.9 billion. The Eliasch Review put capacity building at up to $4 billion over five years for 40 forest nations, or $0.8 billion a year (International Forest Industries 2008).
- **Private compliance: zero.** The farmers' forgone income is the cost the payments compensate. Counting it again would double count it. Where enforcement replaces payment, as in Brazil, the same cost falls on landholders instead of the budget.

No separate estimate of lost national output was found. Lost farm output in forest countries is the same opportunity cost already counted. The risk of paying for credits that buy little is handled in the low-end ratio, not in the cost.
1.strength: Grade: A. A randomized controlled trial published in *Science* reports a benefit-cost ratio of 2.4, with a range of 0.7 to 12.3. A peer-reviewed study of Brazil's enforcement system and a peer-reviewed global cost curve back it up. The low end rests on a peer-reviewed evaluation of REDD+ credits, also in *Science*. It falls short of the top grade for two reasons. Only one trial computes a ratio, and the evidence on offsets is negative.
1.difficulty: Rating: moderate. The policy needs a sustained increase in funding, but working precedents exist. Norway makes results-based payments. The Amazon Fund is running. Brazil's DETER enforcement system cut deforestation sharply after 2004 to 2008 (Assunção, Gandour and Rocha 2023). No new treaty is needed. Delivery depends on enforcement capacity in tropical-forest countries. Take-up is another limit: in the Uganda trial only 32% of eligible owners enrolled, and 80% of those complied (Jayachandran et al. 2016).
1.who_benefits:
The policy is pro-poor. Payments flow to rural forest-owning households in low-income tropical countries. The climate benefits are global. Taxpayers in funding countries pay.

There is a caveat at village level. In the Uganda trial, forest owners gave neighbours less access to gather firewood. Jayachandran et al. (2016) note that "most of those affected in this manner are the poorest, landless individuals in the community, and the program could have made them worse off." The programme also likely widened inequality within villages, because eligible owners were relatively wealthy to begin with.
1.counter:
The strongest case for the policy is that the high end understates it. The Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015 assessment rated halving forest loss at about 10, and Markandya's own assessment ran from $30 to more than $100 per $1 (Markandya 2015). Even McVittie's more cautious re-estimate of $2 to $3 per $1 sits close to the trial's 2.4. At the $185 social cost of carbon of Rennert et al. (2022), Kindermann's cost range gives 9.9 to 29. These figures are set aside because McVittie falls inside the adopted range and $185 is the highest published social cost of carbon. All of them also assume that every paid tonne is real, which West et al. (2023) find true of only about 6.1% of credits.

The verdict turns on permanence and credit quality. If the delay in clearing proved permanent, the trial's ratio would rise from 2.4 to 12.3; if owners catch up as soon as payments stop, it falls to 0.7. If government payments bought real tonnes at Kindermann's costs, the ratio would be 2.7 to 8.0 at a $51 social cost of carbon, instead of 0.09 for credit-based delivery with leakage. Either change would keep the ratio above 1 after the cost of raising the taxes that fund it, at $1.34 per public $1, and lift the policy out of the Bad tier.

2.policy: Governments pay for wind and solar power through subsidies and tax credits, or require it through mandates such as renewable portfolio standards (RPS), which oblige utilities to buy a set share of renewable power. The policy is evaluated as the subsidy or mandate itself. The question is what each dollar of support buys in avoided carbon dioxide (CO2), compared with what that CO2 is worth.
2.why_on_list: It is one of the most popular climate policies in public surveys. It drew 53% support in the Peoples' Climate Vote and 69.5% in the international survey by Dechezleprêtre and co-authors.
2.evidence: Subsidies and mandates for wind and solar do cut emissions. The question is the cost per tonne, and that varies widely. The most expensive case is solar subsidies in Germany and Spain. Abrell, Kosch and Rausch (2019) use weather-driven variation as a natural experiment and find short-run costs of up to €1,944 per tonne of CO2, or about $2,100. At the former US government carbon value, that returns about 2 cents per $1. Wind did much better, at €82 to €276 per tonne. In the United States, state renewable mandates raised retail electricity prices by 11% seven years after passage and cost $86 to $211 per tonne abated (Greenstone and Nath 2019). Model estimates of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) power-sector credits come to about $88 per tonne when costs and emissions are both discounted (Bistline, Mehrotra and Wolfram 2023). Those authors note the cost would be higher if the distortions from financing the credits were counted. The overall range is about 2 to 75 cents per $1. Counting full costs, the federal credits and the higher bills from state mandates cost about $238 billion a year. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $0.009 to $0.58 per $1.
2.ratio:
The ratio is the social value of a tonne of CO2 avoided, divided by the social resource cost of abating it. The abatement costs used are resource costs: generation, backup, transmission and fuel, or observed changes in retail prices. They already contain the costs borne by firms and ratepayers. Tax credits are transfers, so they are not added again.

**Low end: 0.024.** This uses the highest published cost measured after the fact.

1. Cost. Solar subsidies in Germany and Spain cost €411 to €1,944 per tonne in the short run (Abrell, Kosch and Rausch 2019). Upper end: 1,944 × about 1.1 dollars per euro = $2,138 per tonne.
2. Value. The US Interagency Working Group (IWG) interim social cost of carbon is $51 per tonne (Resources for the Future 2023).
3. Ratio: 51 ÷ 2,138 = 0.024.

**High end: 0.75.** This uses the IRA power-sector estimate on a consistent basis.

1. Cost. Bistline, Mehrotra and Wolfram (2023) put the abatement cost at $88 to $94 per tonne when both costs and emissions are discounted. That is the right comparison with a per-tonne social cost of carbon. Their headline $36 to $87 discounts the costs but not the tonnes.
2. Value. The DICE-2023 model gives a social cost of carbon of $66 per tonne (Barrage and Nordhaus 2024).
3. Ratio: 66 ÷ 88 = 0.75.

**Range: 0.024 to 0.75. Full cost: $237.7 billion a year.**

Intermediate results sit inside the range. State mandates at $86 to $211 per tonne give 0.24 to 0.59 at $51. Wind subsidies at €82 to €276, or $90 to $304, per tonne give 0.17 to 0.57 at $51. The Copenhagen Consensus Center (2015) rates doubling the renewable share of global energy below 1.

Cross-checks. At the $185 social cost of carbon of Rennert et al. (2022), the low end would be 0.087 and the high end 185 ÷ 88 = 2.10; state mandates would give 0.88 to 2.15. Intermittency matters too. In southeastern Arizona, Gowrisankaran, Reynolds and Samano (2016) find "social costs of $138.4/MWh for 20% solar generation, of which unforecastable intermittency accounts for $6.1 and intermittency overall for $46." Idel (2022) finds that the full-system costs of wind and solar serving a whole market are far above the usual levelized cost of electricity (LCOE). These costs are inside the estimates based on observed prices, but can be understated in models that use LCOE.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted, an extra $0.34 to $2.00 (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. The credits are paid from taxes, but the mandates are paid by electricity customers. Only the tax-financed share of the cost carries the extra burden: (197 + 1.0) ÷ 237.7 = 0.833. Low end: 0.024 ÷ (1 + 2.0 × 0.833) = 0.009. High end: 0.75 ÷ (1 + 0.34 × 0.833) = 0.58. **Range after tax finance: 0.009 to 0.58.**
2.cost:
The full cost is $237.7 billion a year.

- **Public outlay: $197 billion a year.** This is the high end of published estimates of the IRA energy subsidies: $1.97 trillion over 2025 to 2034 (Fisher and Loucks 2025). The Congressional Budget Office and the Joint Committee on Taxation put it at about $786 billion over 2024 to 2033. The July 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) ends most wind, solar and electric-vehicle credits, so outlays under current law are lower. The figure is for the policy in full form.
- **Administration: about $1.0 billion a year.** No administration cost specific to the energy credits was found. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) cost of collection at its recent peak, 53 cents per $100, is applied to $197 billion (USAFacts 2025).
- **Private compliance: about $39.7 billion a year.** Ratepayers bear the cost of state mandates. Mandates raised retail prices 11% (Greenstone and Nath 2019). US retail electricity sales in 2024 were 3,975 terawatt-hours at 12.94 cents per kilowatt-hour, or $514 billion (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2025). States with mandates held 70.1% of retail revenue. 0.11 × 514 × 0.701 = $39.7 billion.
- **Lost output: no estimate.** No published economy-wide estimate of output lost to US renewable subsidies and mandates was found.

One friction is not added. Wind developers valued $1 of nonrefundable tax credit at $0.85 of a grant (Johnston 2019). That is a split of the same outlay between developers and investors, not an extra resource cost.
2.strength: Grade: B+. The low end comes from a peer-reviewed natural experiment based on weather variation. The high end comes from a model-based estimate published in *Brookings Papers on Economic Activity*. A quasi-experimental working paper sits in between. All are converted to ratios with published social costs of carbon. Results differ in sign by technology and by carbon value, so the grade stays out of the A range.
2.difficulty: Rating: moderate. The policy needs ordinary budget or tax legislation, or state RPS statutes. Precedent is abundant: the IRA of 2022, feed-in laws in the European Union and Germany, and 29 US state RPS laws. Durability is the weak point. The OBBBA cut back most federal wind, solar and electric-vehicle credits within three years of enactment. Wind and solar credits now end unless construction begins by July 4, 2026, or the facility is in service by December 31, 2027 (Kirkland & Ellis LLP 2025).
2.who_benefits: The policy is regressive. Borenstein and Davis (2016) find the top fifth of US households by income received about 60% of clean-energy tax credits. The bottom three fifths received about 10%. About 90% of electric-vehicle credits went to the top fifth. Mandates raise retail electricity prices by 11% to 17% (Greenstone and Nath 2019), a cost that weighs more on low-income households. Tax credits also favour incumbents, which are more likely to owe taxes than new entrants (Johnston 2019). Health benefits from cleaner air are broad.
2.counter:
The strongest case for renewable subsidies comes from Wiser et al. (2017) at two Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories. They find existing state mandates cost up to $31 billion over 2015 to 2050, against $97 billion in health benefits and $161 billion in climate benefits under central assumptions. That implies a ratio of 8.3, or 2.7 with lower-bound benefits. For an expanded mandate they count $558 billion in health and $599 billion in climate benefits, against costs of $23 to $194 billion. The study is set aside because it projects costs from the laboratories' own model, and studies of the same mandates after the fact find higher costs per tonne (Greenstone and Nath 2019).

Two findings would move the verdict. The first is a higher value of carbon. At the $185 social cost of carbon of Rennert et al. (2022), and before the cost of raising taxes, the source ratio at the high end rises from 0.75 to 2.10, and mandates reach 0.88 to 2.15. The second is a lower cost per tonne. If observed costs matched Wiser's projections, with health gains counted, the ratio would sit at 2.7 to 8.3 rather than below 1, enough to leave the Worst tier even after the cost of raising taxes.
