12.policy: This policy caps prices. It covers two forms: anti-price-gouging laws that apply during emergencies, and general price controls on groceries or the whole economy. The cost is scored on the only economy-wide US precedent, the 1971-74 controls. Disaster-only laws are smaller and sit inside the same range per dollar.
12.why_on_list: Price controls were chosen by public-opinion survey. In April 2026, 65% of 1,085 likely voters backed cracking down on grocery-store price gouging (Data for Progress 2026). In the US General Social Survey's round of the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP), 73.9% say government should keep prices under control (General Social Survey 2024).
12.evidence:
A price cap moves money from sellers to the buyers who still get the good. It also destroys value three ways: trades that no longer happen, goods that go to people and places that value them less, and time burned in queues. The best evidence comes from the US gasoline controls of the 1970s. Station-level data show the 1973-74 ceiling held prices 20% below normal and left a 9% shortfall; the lost trades cost about 2.0% of normal spending, and misallocation cost a further 2.2-17.7% (Albrecht, Tabarrok, and Whitmeyer 2026). Queues were worse still. Deacon and Sonstelie (1989) find: "Rent seeking exhausts an estimated 116 percent of the rent transferred." Buyers lost more waiting in line than they saved at the pump.

Other markets show the same pattern. Price ceilings on US natural gas caused allocative losses of $4.6 billion a year on average over 1950-2000, roughly tripling earlier estimates of the welfare loss (Davis and Kilian 2011). In Poland, controls on colour televisions cost 0.46% of gross domestic product (GDP), about ten times the classic deadweight triangle (Tarr 1994). After the 2010 Chile and 2011 Japan earthquakes, prices stayed stable but the number of goods for sale fell 32% and 17% (Cavallo, Cavallo, and Rigobon 2014). The 1971-74 controls cut the core price level by 3-4% by February 1974, but catch-up inflation after controls ended left it only 0-2% below where it would have been (Blinder and Newton 1981).

Economists are close to unanimous. In 2024, 88% of the Clark Center's panel of leading US economists agreed that widespread price controls create substantial economic distortions (Clark Center 2024). In 2012, 20 of the 29 panel members who took a position opposed Connecticut's anti-gouging bill (Clark Center 2012). The main uncertainty is the size of the misallocation loss. Counting everything, each $1 shifted from sellers to buyers destroys between 44 cents and $1.29 of value. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is −$1.29 to −$0.44 per $1.
12.ratio:
The ratio measures the net value to buyers per $1 taken from sellers: (transfer - queuing - lost trades - misallocation - administration and compliance) ÷ transfer. All terms are in points of normal spending on the controlled good, calibrated to the 1973-74 gasoline controls.

**Step 1: the transfer.** The ceiling was 20% below the normal price and buyers got 91% of the normal quantity. Transfer: 0.20 × 0.91 = 18.2 points.

**Step 2: queuing.** Rent seeking burns 116% of the transfer (Deacon and Sonstelie 1989). Buyers' net gain: 18.2 - 1.16 × 18.2 = 18.2 - 21.11 = -2.91 points. Frech and Lee (1987) likewise find queuing costs could exceed the whole transfer, as summarised by Albrecht, Tabarrok, and Whitmeyer (2026).

**Step 3: lost trades.** The deadweight triangle is 2.0 points.

**Step 4: administration and compliance.** The 1971-74 controls cut the core price level by 3-4%. Applied to 1973 GDP of $1,425 billion, the transfer was at most $43-57 billion a year. Running and complying with the controls cost $0.08 billion plus $2.0 billion a year. Share: $2.08 billion ÷ $42.8 billion = 4.9% of the transfer, or 0.89 points.

**Step 5: misallocation, and the two ends.** Misallocation runs from 2.2 to 17.7 points. It is a separate loss that exists even with zero queuing, so the two are added.
- Low: (-2.91 - 2.0 - 17.7 - 0.89) ÷ 18.2 = -23.50 ÷ 18.2 = **-1.29**.
- High: (-2.91 - 2.0 - 2.2 - 0.89) ÷ 18.2 = **-0.44**. Pairing the measured queuing loss with the lowest misallocation allows for some overlap between the two.

**Result: each $1 moved destroys between $0.44 and $1.29 of value. Full cost: $45.0 billion a year.**

Cross-checks. In 1979 the average pump price was about 80 cents, the market-clearing price about $1.00 and the price including waiting time about $1.20 per gallon (Henderson n.d.). Buyers lost 20 cents against a 20-cent transfer, a ratio of about -1.0. For US natural gas over 1968-77, figures reported by Davis and Kilian (2011) give a $6.9 billion transfer against $9.3 billion of deadweight loss and $5.9 billion of allocative cost: (6.9 - 9.3 - 5.9) ÷ 6.9 = -1.20. For Polish televisions, a rent rectangle of 116 billion zlotys and a triangle of 14 billion give (116 - 116 - 14) ÷ 116 = -0.12, before any misallocation (Tarr 1994). Short, disaster-only laws sit inside the range: a federal gouging law after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita would have caused about $1.9 billion of welfare losses in September and October 2005 (Oil & Gas Journal 2007).

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). As for the other transfer entries, the burden is subtracted from benefits. Only the administration of the Cost of Living Council, $80 million a year or 0.034 points on the 18.2-point scale, is paid from taxes; compliance is private. Low end: (−23.50 − 2.0 × 0.034) ÷ 18.2 = −1.295, still −1.29. High end: (−8.00 − 0.34 × 0.034) ÷ 18.2 = −0.440, still −0.44. **Range after tax finance: −1.29 to −0.44.**
12.cost:
The full cost is **$45.0 billion a year**, for general controls on the 1971-74 model.

- **Public outlay: $0.**
- **Administration: $1.7 billion.** John Dunlop, head of the Cost of Living Council, put the cost to taxpayers at nearly $200 million over about two and a half years (Bleiberg 1974). That is $80 million a year, or 0.0056% of 1973 GDP. Scaled to 2025 GDP of $30.9 trillion (U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis 2026), a factor of 21.65, it is $1.7 billion a year.
- **Private compliance: $43.3 billion.** Dunlop put industry's cost at $721 million to $2 billion for the whole period; other sources put it at about $2 billion a year (Bleiberg 1974). The high end, 0.14% of 1973 GDP, scales to $43.3 billion a year. The low end would be $6.2 billion.
- **Lost output:** shortages, queues and misallocation sit inside the ratio and have no modern economy-wide estimate.

Price cuts from sellers to buyers are transfers, not costs. Total: 0 + 1.7 + 43.3 = $45.0 billion a year. Disaster-only anti-gouging laws would cost a small fraction of this.
12.strength: Grade: **B+**. Peer-reviewed historical natural experiments measure the losses: gasoline queues (Frech and Lee 1987; Deacon and Sonstelie 1989), natural gas (Davis and Kilian 2011), the 1971-74 controls (Blinder and Newton 1981) and disaster pricing (Cavallo, Cavallo, and Rigobon 2014). A 2026 working paper supplies the bounds on misallocation. No published benefit-cost ratio exists. Both ends rest on a peer-reviewed queuing estimate, with the Polish evidence as a cross-check, and expert opinion is strong and one-sided.
12.difficulty: Difficulty: **moderate**. Price controls need only ordinary legislation. Many US states already have price-gouging statutes, and the 1971-74 programme shows economy-wide controls under an act of Congress. No constitutional change is needed.
12.who_benefits: The effect is **broad**, with no clear tilt toward rich or poor. The transfer goes to whoever obtains the capped good, not to the poor in particular. Queues favour people whose time is cheap, misallocation sends goods to people who value them less, and stable prices after disasters came with 17-32% fewer goods on the shelves (Cavallo, Cavallo, and Rigobon 2014). Sellers pay through lower prices, and everyone pays through shortages.
12.counter:
The best counter-evidence comes from Argentina's targeted supermarket controls of 2007-15. Controlled goods stayed available, with no sign of shortages (Aparicio and Cavallo 2021). That suggests mild, negotiated controls do far less harm than the gasoline queues of the 1970s. Rockoff (1984) argues that temporary controls can reduce the unemployment and lost output that usually come with bringing inflation down. Neither gives a welfare estimate per $1 transferred, so neither can set an end of the range. Aparicio and Cavallo also find only a temporary effect on inflation, with firms launching new, higher-priced varieties, and this policy is not tied to a disinflation programme.

The verdict turns on queuing. The range assumes queues and extra purchases burn 116% of the transfer, as Deacon and Sonstelie (1989) measured for US gasoline. If controls caused no queues, as in Argentina, buyers would keep most of the 18.2-point transfer, the high end would turn positive, and the policy would move toward the Bad tier. No measured case shows zero queuing cost, and black markets, which are not priced, push the other way: the wartime Office of Price Administration imposed 259,966 sanctions (Higgs 2009).

13.policy: Open borders means free movement of labor: removing the legal barriers to working and living in another country. Every high-income country would repeal its entry and work restrictions, so people could move to wherever their labour is worth most. It is a change in law, not a spending programme. The main cost is the real expense of moving. The reverse policy, strict border controls in every country, is scored alongside it as the mirror image.
13.why_on_list: Open borders was chosen by public-opinion survey, measured by what people say they want for themselves. In the 2021 Gallup World Poll, nearly 900 million adults said they would like to move to another country permanently. Opinion inside rich countries runs the other way: in the 2024 Cooperative Election Study, 79% of Americans backed more border patrols (Cooperative Election Study team 2025).
13.evidence:
The same worker produces far more in a rich country than in a poor one. Identical low-skill workers from the median country earn at least 3.95 times as much in the United States as at home, a gain of at least PPP$13,600 a year in purchasing-power terms (Clemens, Montenegro, and Pritchett 2019). Removing migration barriers therefore promises the largest gain of any policy studied. Clemens (2011) reviews the models: "For labor mobility barriers, the estimated gains are often in the range of 50–150 percent of world GDP." Removing all barriers to trade in goods, by contrast, yields 0.3-4.1% of world GDP.

The most careful single model is Borjas (2015). With world output of $70 trillion and workers four times as productive in the North as in the South, open borders would raise world output by $40.1 trillion. About 2.6 billion workers, or 5.6 billion people, would move. The key uncertainty is how much of their home country's lower productivity migrants carry with them. If none, the gain is largest; if a quarter, the gross gain falls to $24.2 trillion; if half, the gross gain falls to $8.8 trillion, less than the cost of moving, so the gain net of moving costs turns negative (Clemens and Pritchett 2019). Clemens and Pritchett (2019) find the evidence that migrants carry large fractions of origin productivity unsupported, which bounds that share at about a quarter. Other models agree on the order of magnitude. With estimated migration and visa costs and about 400 million movers, world GDP rises 7.0-17.9% (Docquier, Machado, and Sekkat 2015). Averaged over all workers in 40 less-developed countries, the net gain is $11,046 per worker a year against average income of $8,382 (Kennan 2013).

The restriction side has been measured directly. The 548 miles of US border wall built between 2006 and 2010 cut migration by about 311,000 people. Allen, Dobbin, and Morten (2024) find that "high skill U.S. workers lose $21 (0.04%) a year, whereas low skill U.S. workers gain $9 (0.02%) a year due to the increased scarcity of low-skilled workers." Excluding almost 500,000 Mexican farm workers in 1964 did not raise native farm wages (Clemens, Lewis, and Postel 2018). The gains to protected workers are tiny; the losses to the people kept out are large.

Published models put the gain from open borders at roughly 35-57% of world output before moving costs. Moving billions of people is also very costly, so each $1 spent on moving returns $2.14 to $3.34. Run in reverse, strict border controls everywhere destroy between 97 cents and $1.31 for each $1 of enforcement.
13.ratio:
The benefit is the rise in world output when workers move to where they are most productive. The cost is the real resources spent on moving. Borjas (2015, Table 2) gives both from one model. It assumes world output of $70 trillion before migration, a North/South productivity ratio of 4, and a moving cost of 10 times a Southern worker's starting salary, discounted at 5%.

**High end (migrants carry none of their origin productivity).**
- Gross gain: $40.1 trillion. Gain net of moving costs: $28.1 trillion.
- Moving costs: 40.1 - 28.1 = $12.0 trillion.
- Ratio: 40.1 ÷ 12.0 = **3.34**.

**Low end (migrants carry a quarter of their origin productivity).**
- Gross gain: $24.2 trillion. Net gain: $12.9 trillion.
- Moving costs: 24.2 - 12.9 = $11.3 trillion.
- Ratio: 24.2 ÷ 11.3 = **2.14**.

A carry-over of half cuts the gross gain to $8.8 trillion, less than the cost of moving, so the net gain turns negative in Borjas's table. The evidence reviewed by Clemens and Pritchett (2019) does not support such large carry-over, so a quarter sets the low end.

**Scaling to today.** World GDP in 2025 was $118,350 billion (World Bank 2025). Moving costs: 12.0 ÷ 70 × 118,350 = $20,289 billion a year at the high-cost end and $19,105 billion at the low-cost end. The gross gain is $40.9-67.8 trillion.

**Result: $2.14 to $3.34 per $1. Full cost: $20,288.6 billion a year.**

Cross-checks. Clemens (2011) reports full-removal gains of 50-150% of world GDP before moving costs, consistent with the gross gains here. Docquier, Machado, and Sekkat (2015), using estimated migration and visa costs, find world GDP rises 7.0-17.9% with far fewer movers. Kennan (2013) finds a net gain of $11,046 per worker a year against average income of $8,382 across 40 less-developed countries, a gain larger than current income.

**The mirror image: strict border controls.** The reverse policy is every major destination country enforcing its border on the scale of the 2025-26 US build-up: the July 2025 reconciliation act (H.R. 1) and the 2026 Secure America Act. It is scored per migrant kept out, counting everyone affected, including the people kept out. It is context only and does not change the range above.
- US workers: low-skill workers gain $9 a year across 47.6 million workers; high-skill workers lose $21 a year across 78.7 million (Allen, Dobbin, and Morten 2024; Bureau of Labor Statistics 2010). Over 311,000 migrants deterred, that is +$20,500 and -$79,000 per migrant.
- The migrant's lost earnings: PPP$10,523 a year over a 20-year working life discounted at 3% (× 14.88) = $156,600, or $285,200 at 2024 prices (Clemens, Montenegro, and Pritchett 2019).
- The budget: a $231,000 saving per migrant kept out (Hall 2016, reading National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine 2017) or a forgone contribution of $57,000 (Nowrasteh, Eckhardt, and Howard 2023).
- Enforcement per migrant deterred: $10,600 for the 2006-10 wall, up to $533,400 under H.R. 1 ($170.7 billion ÷ 320,000 fewer residents in 2035; American Immigration Council 2025; Congressional Budget Office 2025).

Case most favourable to restriction: (231,000 + 20,500 - 79,000 - 156,600) ÷ 10,600 = 1.50. Least favourable case: (20,500 - 79,000 - 57,000 - 285,200) ÷ 533,400 = -0.75. Income lost to a policy costs lives: about one statistical death per $99.3 million of cost (Broughel and Viscusi 2017), or $0.132 per $1 at a value of a statistical life of $13.1 million (HHS 2024). The net income change per $1 of enforcement is -21.3 in the first case and -1.64 in the second. Low: 1.50 - 0.132 × 21.3 = -1.31. High: -0.75 - 0.132 × 1.64 = -0.97. Each $1 of enforcement destroys between 97 cents and $1.31, on a cost of about $143.4 billion a year.
13.cost:
The full cost is **$20,288.6 billion a year**, all of it the cost of moving.

- **Public outlay: $0.** Repealing entry restrictions needs no new spending.
- **Administration and private compliance: $0.** Visa processing and employer paperwork would fall, not rise. No published estimate of transition administration exists.
- **Moving costs: $20,288.6 billion.** Borjas (2015) puts moving costs at 12.0 ÷ 70 of world output, where each move costs 10 times a Southern worker's starting salary at a 5% discount. Applied to 2025 world GDP of $118,350 billion (World Bank 2025), that is $20,289 billion a year.

Strict controls instead cost real money. The US build-up runs to about $143.4 billion a year over the 2025 budget: $59.9 billion of public outlay (American Immigration Council 2025; O'Herron 2026), $1.3 billion of administration, and $82.2 billion of lost global output (Edelberg, Veuger, and Watson 2026).
13.strength: Grade: **B**. The range comes from a peer-reviewed general-equilibrium model that prices both the gain and the moving cost (Borjas 2015). Peer-reviewed estimates by Clemens (2011), Kennan (2013) and Docquier, Machado, and Sekkat (2015) confirm the scale. All are calibrated simulations of a policy never tried at world scale. The result also depends on how much productivity migrants carry with them. Both points hold the grade at B. The mirror-image score for restriction rests on a tightly estimated lower bound for the migrant's lost earnings (Clemens, Montenegro, and Pritchett 2019). Its fiscal term relies on think-tank readings of the National Academies model, but that term does not change the sign.
13.difficulty: Difficulty: **hard**. Open borders would require every high-income country to repeal its entry and work restrictions. There is no modern precedent outside regional zones such as the European Union's single market. Restriction is far easier: each country can tighten its own border through ordinary law, and the United States has just done so.
13.who_benefits:
The gain is strongly **pro-poor**. Most of it goes to migrants and their home countries. In Borjas's model, Southern wages rise 143% while Northern wages fall 39.3%, and owners of capital gain $12.0 trillion (Borjas 2015). With smaller flows, natives of sending countries gain 26-79% while natives of the United States gain 0.3% and those of the European Union 2.1%; natives of the Gulf states lose 0.7% (Docquier, Machado, and Sekkat 2015). Kennan (2013) finds the fall in rich-country real wages is small and disappears as capital adjusts. Workers already in rich countries bear most of the risk.

Restriction runs the other way. Would-be low-skill migrants give up at least PPP$10,500-13,600 a year (Clemens, Montenegro, and Pritchett 2019), and their families lose remittances: Mexico received $66.2 billion in 2023 (World Bank/KNOMAD 2024).
13.counter:
The strongest counter-evidence is Clemens and Pritchett (2019), who model productivity carried from home, slow assimilation and congestion. They conclude: "On current evidence about the magnitudes of these parameters, dynamically efficient policy would not imply open borders but would imply relaxations on current restrictions." The study gives no dollar ratio, so it bounds the policy from above rather than setting a number. Moses and Letnes (2004) find full removal is worth 96.5% of world GDP when workers are equally productive everywhere, but only 9.6% when poor-country migrants are assumed far less productive. On public finances, Hall (2016), reading the National Academies model, puts the cost of a nonelderly immigrant without a high school diploma at $231,000 in present value. The range counts real output and moving costs, not tax transfers, so that figure does not enter.

The verdict turns on how much home-country productivity migrants carry with them. With none, the ratio is 3.34; with a quarter, it is 2.14. If migrants carried half, the gross gain would shrink to $8.8 trillion, below the cost of moving, and the net gain in Borjas's (2015) table would turn negative. That would move the policy from the Good tier to the Bad tier. Clemens and Pritchett find the evidence for such large carry-over unsupported, which is why the low end stops at a quarter.

14.policy: Broad student-loan forgiveness cancels federal student debt for most borrowers. The model is the 2022 plan: up to $10,000 per borrower, or $20,000 for those who received Pell Grants. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) put that plan at about $400 billion in present value, roughly $40 billion a year over a decade. It is paid for by taxpayers.
14.why_on_list: Student-loan forgiveness was chosen by public-opinion survey. In the 2024 Cooperative Election Study, a national survey of about 60,000 adults, 55.1% supported forgiving up to $20,000 of student debt per person (Cooperative Election Study team 2025).
14.evidence:
Forgiveness is a transfer. Each $1 of present-value debt cancelled is worth $1 to the borrower, and CBO's present-value scoring already allows for loans that would never have been repaid (CBO 2022). The Penn Wharton Budget Model put the cancellation at $469-519 billion over ten years (Smetters and Chen 2022). The money must be raised by taxes, and taxes cost the economy more than they raise. Central estimates put that extra cost at 33 cents per $1 of revenue (Ballard, Shoven, and Whalley 1985); for a rise in all income-tax rates it is nearly $2 (Feldstein 1999).

Forgiveness can also change behaviour. If students expect more cancellation, they borrow more. For the related SAVE repayment plan, Penn Wharton's ten-year cost rises from $342 billion with no change in borrowing to $475 billion with a medium response and $559 billion with the maximum (Chen and Smetters 2023). In 2024, 48% of student borrowers said they expect their debt to be forgiven (NBC Boston 2024). Much of any extra borrowing ends up in tuition: "We find a pass-through effect on tuition of changes in subsidized loan maximums of about 60 cents on the dollar" (Lucca, Nadauld, and Shen 2019).

Who gains matters too. Measured in present value, full or partial forgiveness is regressive: the top tenth of earners gains as much as the bottom three tenths combined (Catherine and Yannelis 2023). No study publishes a benefit-cost ratio for broad forgiveness. Counting the cost of raising the money, and in the worst case the extra borrowing, each $1 forgiven yields between -1.39 and 0.67 of net value.
14.ratio:
Forgiveness is scored like other transfers on this list: ratio = (value to borrowers - excess burden × net fiscal cost) ÷ net fiscal cost. Value to borrowers is $1 per $1 of present-value debt cancelled.

**Step 1: administration.** Running the programme and lender paperwork add about $0.02 billion a year, 0.05% of the $40 billion annual outlay. Net fiscal cost per $1: 1.0005.

**Step 2: high end.** No extra borrowing, and an excess burden of 33 cents per $1 raised (Ballard, Shoven, and Whalley 1985).
- (1 - 0.33 × 1.0005) ÷ 1.0005 = **0.67**.

**Step 3: induced borrowing.** Penn Wharton's SAVE estimates show how much expected forgiveness adds to cost (Chen and Smetters 2023).
- Medium response: (475 - 342) ÷ 342 = 39%.
- Maximum response: (559 - 342) ÷ 342 = 63%.

**Step 4: low end.** Maximum induced borrowing, and nearly $2 of deadweight loss per $1 raised (Feldstein 1999).
- Net fiscal cost: 1 + 0.63 + 0.0005 = 1.635.
- (1 - 2.0 × 1.635) ÷ 1.635 = **-1.39**.

**Result: -1.39 to 0.67 per $1. Full cost: $120.0 billion a year.**

Sensitivity. With the medium 39% response the low end is (1 - 2.0 × 1.39) ÷ 1.39 = -1.28. With no induced borrowing it is (1 - 2.0 × 1.0005) ÷ 1.0005 = -1.00. Applying a permanent repayment plan's borrowing response to one-off cancellation holds only to the extent that borrowers expect forgiveness to recur. The tuition pass-through found by Lucca, Nadauld, and Shen (2019) is part of the same fiscal leak and is not added again. CBO's $400 billion is a present value, so interest on the borrowing that funds it is not added separately.
14.cost:
The full cost is **$120.0 billion a year**.

- **Public outlay: $40 billion.** CBO put the 2022 plan at about $400 billion in present value, roughly $40 billion a year over ten years (CBO 2022). Penn Wharton's estimate is $47-52 billion a year (Smetters and Chen 2022).
- **Administration: $0.008 billion.** The Education Department's 2024 debt-relief rule put one-time administrative costs at $13.0 million for systems and contractors plus $18.0 million for waiver processing: $31 million for about $147 billion of relief, or 0.021% (U.S. Department of Education 2024). At $400 billion that is about $84 million once, or $0.008 billion a year.
- **Private compliance: $0.012 billion.** The same analysis puts paperwork for guaranty agencies and private lenders at $12.06 million a year.
- **Lost output: $80 billion.** The excess burden of the taxes needed, at nearly $2 per $1: 2.0 × $40 billion = $80 billion a year.

Total: 40 + 0.008 + 0.012 + 80 = $120.0 billion a year. The extra borrowing that expected forgiveness induces enters the ratio, not this total.
14.strength: Grade: **B**. The ratio is built from peer-reviewed estimates of the cost of raising taxes (Ballard, Shoven, and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), applied to official cost estimates from CBO and Penn Wharton. Peer-reviewed work measures who benefits (Catherine and Yannelis 2023). There is no direct benefit-cost study or experiment on broad forgiveness, so B+ or above does not apply. The low end also borrows a think-tank estimate of induced borrowing from a repayment plan and applies it by analogy to one-off cancellation.
14.difficulty: Difficulty: **moderate**. In Biden v. Nebraska (June 30, 2023), the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the HEROES Act does not authorise mass cancellation (Supreme Court of the United States 2023). Broad forgiveness now needs ordinary legislation from Congress. Narrower discharges, such as income-driven repayment and Public Service Loan Forgiveness, show the mechanism already exists.
14.who_benefits: The tilt is **regressive**. Measured in present value, the top income decile gains as much as the bottom three deciles combined (Catherine and Yannelis 2023). Expanding income-driven repayment is cheaper and more progressive than universal forgiveness, though it carries a risk of moral hazard at the school level (Catherine, Perez Clanton, and Yannelis 2024). The main counter-reading comes from Penn Wharton's table based on loan balances for the capped 2022 plan: "About two-thirds of the benefit falls to households making $88,000 or less per year," and the top 5% get almost nothing (Smetters and Chen 2022). Taxpayers carry the cost.
14.counter:
The strongest counter-case is that relief changes lives. Di Maggio, Kalda and Yao (2020) find that borrowers whose private loans were voided by a legal accident cut their debt by 11%, had 24% fewer delinquent accounts, moved and changed jobs more, and earned about $3,000 more over three years. Extra earnings mean extra taxes. The study is not added because it covers a small group of defaulted private borrowers, not a broad federal programme, and the implied revenue is small next to the cost. Evidence from the 2020 payment pause points the other way: borrowers used the extra cash to take on more mortgage, auto and card debt, mostly those who were not behind on payments (Dinerstein, Yannelis and Chen 2024).

Two assumptions set the verdict. The first is the cost of raising the money. At the central excess burden of 33 cents per $1 (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985), with no extra borrowing, the ratio is 0.67; at Feldstein's (1999) nearly $2, it is negative. The second is induced borrowing. If borrowers believed cancellation would never recur, the low end would rise from −1.39 to −1.00. The policy would leave the Worst tier only if the money could be raised at close to the central rate and future borrowing did not respond; even then it would sit in the Bad tier.

15.policy: This policy blocks any rise in the Social Security or Medicare eligibility ages and any cut in scheduled benefits. Under current law the trust funds run short: Social Security's combined funds in the third quarter of 2034, when 83% of benefits would be payable, and Medicare's Hospital Insurance (HI) fund in the second quarter of 2033, at 89% (Social Security and Medicare Boards of Trustees 2026). Paying full benefits after that means new taxes or borrowing.
15.why_on_list: Protecting these programmes was chosen by public-opinion survey, and it is among the most popular ideas tested. In the US General Social Survey's round of the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP), 87.5% say government should provide a decent standard of living for the old (General Social Survey 2024). In a 2024 YouGov poll of 4,038 voters, protecting Medicare and Social Security from funding cuts or higher eligibility ages had net support of +72 (YouGov 2024).
15.evidence:
The gap is large. The 2026 Trustees put the 75-year deficit at 4.42% of taxable payroll for Social Security and 0.56% for Medicare HI, together about 1.67% of GDP, or roughly $535 billion a year (Social Security and Medicare Boards of Trustees 2026). Social Security alone costs 5.3% of GDP in 2026, and its annual deficit rises from 0.8% of GDP in 2026 to 2.4% in 2085.

Benefits are a transfer: each $1 is worth $1 to the retiree who receives it. The cost lies in raising that $1. Taxes cost the economy more than they raise, from 33 cents per $1 in central estimates (Ballard, Shoven, and Whalley 1985) to nearly $2 for a rise in all income-tax rates (Feldstein 1999). Blocking a higher retirement age also forgoes extra work. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) finds that raising the full retirement age from 67 to 70 would cut Social Security spending by about 13% and enlarge the economy by slightly more than 1% in the long run (CBO 2012; Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget 2012). People do respond to such changes. After the 1983 law raised the normal retirement age (NRA), Mastrobuoni (2009) finds: "The evidence suggests that the mean retirement age of the affected cohorts has increased by about half as much as the increase in the NRA."

The range depends on what is blocked and how the money is raised. Blocking an across-the-board benefit cut, financed with low-cost taxes, keeps most of each $1. Blocking an age rise, financed with high-cost taxes, destroys more than it delivers. The ratio runs from -1.27 to 0.66.
15.ratio:
Benefits are scored like other transfers on this list: ratio = (1 - excess burden × net fiscal cost) ÷ net fiscal cost. Net fiscal cost includes administration and the fiscal externality of lower work.

**Step 1: the work effect of blocking an age rise.**
- Raising the full retirement age to 70 cuts Social Security spending about 13%. Social Security costs 5.3% of GDP. Benefits kept by blocking it: 13% × 5.3% = 0.69% of GDP.
- The change would enlarge the economy by about 1%. CBO's rule of thumb returns about 0.25 of extra GDP as revenue (0.5% of GDP on 2% more GDP). Taxes forgone: 0.25 × 1.0 = 0.25% of GDP.
- Fiscal externality: 0.25 ÷ 0.69 = 0.36 per $1 of benefits kept.

**Step 2: administration.** Administration adds 0.53% of benefits.

**Step 3: high end.** Blocking across-the-board benefit-formula cuts, which barely change work (fiscal externality about 0), financed at 33 cents per $1 (Ballard, Shoven, and Whalley 1985).
- (1 - 0.33 × 1.0053) ÷ 1.0053 = **0.66**.

**Step 4: low end.** Blocking an age rise (fiscal externality 0.36, net fiscal cost 1.365), financed at nearly $2 per $1 (Feldstein 1999).
- (1 - 2.0 × 1.365) ÷ 1.365 = **-1.27**.

**Result: -1.27 to 0.66 per $1. Full cost: $1,927.8 billion a year.**

Middle case. Blocking an age rise financed at 33 cents per $1 gives (1 - 0.33 × 1.365) ÷ 1.365 = 0.40. The financing cost is subtracted in the ratio and the work effect enters through the fiscal externality, so neither is counted twice. The choice of cost base (the 75-year gap, the current annual deficit or the post-2034 shortfall) changes the annual cost but not the ratio.
15.cost:
The full cost is **$1,927.8 billion a year**, as a 75-year average.

- **Public outlay: $535 billion.** The 2026 Trustees' 75-year deficits, 4.42% of payroll for Social Security and 0.56% for Medicare HI, come to about 1.67% of GDP (Social Security and Medicare Boards of Trustees 2026).
- **Administration: $2.8 billion.** Social Security spends 0.4% of its cost on administration ($6.95 billion in 2025; Social Security Administration 2026), and Medicare HI about 1.3% ($5.9 billion of $444.2 billion; Congressional Research Service 2026). Splitting the gap 86% to Social Security and 14% to HI: 535 × (0.863 × 0.004 + 0.137 × 0.0133) = $2.8 billion. This is an upper bound, since larger benefits to the same people add little administration.
- **Private compliance:** none identified; payroll reporting does not change.
- **Lost output: $1,390 billion.** First, blocking a rise in the retirement age to 70 forgoes about 1% of GDP, some $320 billion a year at the $32.0 trillion 2026 GDP implied by the Trustees (CBO 2012). This is lost output, not lost welfare, since retirees gain leisure. Second, the excess burden of the taxes needed at nearly $2 per $1: 2.0 × 535 = $1,070 billion.

Total: 535 + 2.8 + 1,390 = $1,927.8 billion a year. Using only the 2026 cash deficit (0.8% of GDP) and the 33-cent excess burden, the total would be far smaller, about $340 billion.
15.strength: Grade: **B**. The ratio combines a peer-reviewed natural experiment on retirement behaviour (Mastrobuoni 2009), CBO's macroeconomic estimates and the Trustees' official fiscal gap with peer-reviewed estimates of the cost of raising taxes. No published benefit-cost ratio exists for keeping current-law benefits. The work feedback comes from CBO's model rather than a measured welfare change, so the grade sits below B+.
15.difficulty: Difficulty: **moderate**. Keeping current benefit rules needs no change at all. Paying full scheduled benefits after 2034 for Social Security and 2033 for Medicare HI needs ordinary legislation to raise payroll taxes or transfer general revenue. Congress has done this before, in the 1977 and 1983 amendments. No constitutional change is needed.
15.who_benefits: The effect is **broad**. Benefits go to nearly all retirees and disabled workers. Elderly poverty moves roughly one for one with benefits, so cuts would raise poverty (Engelhardt and Gruber 2006), which favours the poor. But benefits rise with lifetime earnings, and the cost falls on current workers through payroll taxes. The net effect is broad rather than clearly pro-poor.
15.counter:
The strongest counter-case is that benefits keep older people out of poverty. Engelhardt and Gruber (2006) find that cutting benefits would significantly raise elderly poverty, with poverty moving roughly one for one with benefits. An analysis that weighted income to the poor more heavily would count that as a gain. The ratio here values transfers at $1 per $1 without weights, so the finding informs who benefits rather than the ratio. The work response, the other key input, rests on a Congressional Budget Office (CBO) model rather than a measured change in welfare, although Mastrobuoni (2009) confirms that when the 1983 law raised the normal retirement age, retirement ages rose by about half the increase.

The verdict depends on what is blocked and how the money is raised. Blocking across-the-board benefit cuts, which barely change work, gives 0.66 at the central excess burden of 33 cents per $1. Blocking an age rise at that rate gives 0.40. Only at Feldstein's (1999) nearly $2 of deadweight per $1 does the ratio fall to −1.27. If the shortfall were raised at the central rate, the policy would move from the Worst to the Bad tier. It would need distributional weights, of the kind Engelhardt and Gruber's poverty finding supports, to reach 1.

16.policy: Every major country would require its billionaires to pay tax each year equal to at least 2% of their wealth. Income taxes they already pay count toward the 2%, so only the shortfall is new. The proposal was written for the G20 in 2024 and covers the world's roughly 3,000 billionaires (Zucman 2024). Countries could collect it through a wealth tax, a presumptive income tax or a broader income tax.
16.why_on_list: The tax was chosen by public-opinion survey. In a 2024 Ipsos survey across 17 G20 countries, 68% backed a wealth tax on wealthy people to fund major changes to the economy, and 11% opposed it. Support was 67% in the United States, 67% in France and 68% in Germany (Ipsos for Earth4All and the Global Commons Alliance 2024).
16.evidence:
About 2,800 billionaires owned $14.2 trillion in 2024. Their current tax is equivalent to 0.3% of their wealth, so a 2% minimum adds 1.7% of wealth: $242 billion a year if perfectly enforced, or $193 billion if a fifth is lost to avoidance and evasion (Zucman 2024). That money is a transfer. It leaves billionaires and reaches governments dollar for dollar, so it is neither a gain nor a cost in itself.

The costs come from how people respond. Wealth can be hidden, moved, given away or valued down. A well-designed 1% wealth tax shrinks the declared base by 7% to 17% (Advani and Tarrant 2021). In Switzerland, where banks do not report financial wealth to the tax authorities, a 1-point cut in a canton's rate raised reported wealth by at least 43% after six years (Brülhart et al. 2022). In Denmark the very wealthy held 31% more taxable wealth eight years after their rate was cut from 2.2% to 1% (Jakobsen et al. 2020).

A tax on wealth also means less capital is built, which lowers output and the yield of other taxes. The Penn Wharton Budget Model projects that a US tax of 2% above $50 million and 3% above $1 billion would cut GDP by 1.2% and average hourly wages by 1.2% by 2050 (Huntley and Ricco 2021). Valuing and collecting the tax adds administrative and private costs.

No benefit-cost study of a wealth tax exists, so the tax is scored like the other transfer policies, by the cost of raising each $1 of revenue. A general-equilibrium estimate puts that cost at 34 to 48 cents per $1 (Ballard, Shoven, and Whalley 1985); an estimate that counts tax avoidance puts it at nearly $2 (Feldstein 1999). With 34 cents at one end and $2 at the other, each $1 collected yields between -1.12 and 0.60 of net value. Evidence specific to wealth taxes gives a similar range, -0.55 to 0.72. The published range therefore runs from a $1.12 loss to a 60-cent gain per $1 collected: at its high end the tax returns about 60 cents per $1 it moves; at its low end it destroys more than it collects. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is −$1.20 to $0.59 per $1.
16.ratio:
The revenue is a transfer, so the ratio takes the net-damage form used for the other transfer policies: ratio = (transfer - excess burden - administration - private compliance) ÷ transfer, all per $1 of wealth tax collected.

**Step 1: the tax base.** Billionaires owned $14.2 trillion in 2024 and already pay tax equal to 0.3% of it. The minimum tax adds 1.7% of wealth: $242 billion with perfect enforcement (Zucman 2024).

**Step 2: excess burden.** The same convention as the student-loan and Social Security entries applies, whatever the size of the transfer. The high end uses a marginal welfare cost of 34 cents per $1 of revenue, the bottom of a 34 to 48 cent range (Ballard, Shoven, and Whalley 1985). The low end uses nearly $2 per $1 (Feldstein 1999). Feldstein's measure is built on how the taxable base responds, which is the same channel through which wealth is hidden, moved or valued down, and on the revenue lost as a result. So the wealth-tax base response and the revenue lost from other taxes are not added on top. The revenue is about 0.22% of world GDP, far inside the most that capital taxes can raise, 2.3% of GDP in the US (Trabandt and Uhlig 2011), so the rule that applies Feldstein's figure at both ends of very large programmes does not apply.

**Step 3: administration.** The Wealth Tax Commission costed a one-off 5% UK tax; fixed costs spread over a smaller take are scaled to a 1.7% rate (Advani, Chamberlain, and Summers 2020).
- High end: the central estimate of 1% of revenue × 5 ÷ 1.7 = 0.029.
- Low end: 1.4% of revenue at a £10 million threshold × 5 ÷ 1.7 = 0.041.

**Step 4: private compliance.** Valuation, filing and disputes.
- High end: 0.06% of taxable assets at a £10 million threshold ÷ 1.7% = 0.035.
- Low end: 0.13%, the highest estimate in the Commission's costing, ÷ 1.7% = 0.076.

**Step 5: the two ends.**
- High: 1 - 0.34 - 0.029 - 0.035 = **0.60**.
- Low: 1 - 2.0 - 0.041 - 0.076 = **-1.12**.

**Result: -1.12 to 0.60 per $1. Full cost: $423.6 billion a year.**

Lost output is not subtracted again. Penn Wharton's GDP loss of 1.63 per $1 of revenue is the output counterpart of the excess burden, so it is counted in the full cost and not in the ratio, as in the student-loan, Social Security, Medicare for All and basic-income entries.

Sensitivity. The range can also be built from wealth-tax evidence instead of the income-tax excess burden, with the declared base shrinking as W = W0 × e^(-s × 0.017). At the high end, a 7% fall in the base for a 1% tax (Advani and Tarrant 2021) gives s = 7.26, revenue of $213.9 billion and an average excess burden of 0.064; Penn Wharton's macro feedback, (2,390 - 2,025) ÷ 2,390 = 0.153 (Huntley and Ricco 2021), is lost revenue from other taxes. 1 - 0.064 - 0.153 - 0.029 - 0.035 = 0.72. At the low end, the Swiss response less the 21% of it due to house prices (Brülhart et al. 2022) gives s = ln(1.43) × 0.79 ÷ 0.01 = 28.3, revenue of $149.7 billion and a marginal excess burden of x ÷ (1 - x) = 0.924; in a US growth model, 51% of a capital-tax change pays for itself (Trabandt and Uhlig 2011). 1 - 0.924 - 0.51 - 0.041 - 0.076 = -0.55. With the average excess burden instead, that end is 0.09; with the European self-financing share of 79%, -0.83; with Penn Wharton's full output loss in place of both terms, -0.75. As a cross-check, the Danish long-run elasticity of 1.15 for the very wealthy (Jakobsen et al. 2020), with the net return cut from 7.2% to 5.5%, implies a long-run base of (5.5 ÷ 7.2)^1.15 = 0.73 of its untaxed level.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). As for the other transfer entries, the burden is subtracted from benefits. The wealth-tax revenue is counted in full as the transfer, so the government's cost of running the tax must be paid from other taxes and carries the same burden. Low end: 1 − 2.0 − 0.041 − 0.076 − 2.0 × 0.041 = −1.20. High end: 1 − 0.34 − 0.029 − 0.035 − 0.34 × 0.029 = 0.59. **Range after tax finance: −1.20 to 0.59.**
16.cost:
The full cost is **$423.6 billion a year**, all at full enforcement.

- **Public outlay: $0.** The tax raises revenue, and revenue is a transfer.
- **Administration: $10.0 billion.** The Wealth Tax Commission's highest government cost, 1.4% of revenue at a £10 million threshold, scaled to a 1.7% rate gives 4.1%: 0.041 × 242 = $10.0 billion (Advani, Chamberlain, and Summers 2020). For comparison, the US Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2021 set aside $10 billion a year of extra Internal Revenue Service funding, 70% of it for the wealth tax (Huntley and Ricco 2021).
- **Private compliance: $18.5 billion.** Valuing assets, filing and disputes at 0.13% of $14.2 trillion. At 0.06%, the figure for the £10 million threshold, it would be $8.5 billion.
- **Lost output: $395.1 billion.** Penn Wharton's US tax cuts GDP by 1.2% in 2050 while raising 0.735% of GDP in 2031, so output falls by 1.63 per $1 of revenue: 1.63 × 242 = $395.1 billion (Huntley and Ricco 2021). This is an upper bound, since the revenue share grows as wealth outpaces GDP.

Total: 0 + 10.0 + 18.5 + 395.1 = $423.6 billion.
16.strength: Grade: **B**. The two ends rest on peer-reviewed estimates of the cost of raising tax revenue (Ballard, Shoven, and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), the same as the other transfer entries, applied to the proposal's own revenue estimate. The wealth-tax responses behind the sensitivity come from peer-reviewed natural experiments in Switzerland, Denmark and Sweden and a peer-reviewed review that reconciles them (Brülhart et al. 2022; Jakobsen et al. 2020; Advani and Tarrant 2021). Administration and compliance costs come from a UK commission's costing. No peer-reviewed benefit-cost study of a wealth tax exists, and no country has taxed billionaires at this scale.
16.difficulty: Difficulty: **hard**. The tax needs a binding agreement among many countries. In 2024 the G20 finance ministers committed only to seek to engage cooperatively, with full respect for each country's tax sovereignty, to ensure that the very richest are effectively taxed (G20 Finance Ministers 2024). Twelve OECD countries had net wealth taxes in 1990 and four in 2017, with repeals justified by efficiency costs, capital flight and high administrative costs (OECD 2018). By 2021 only three still levied one (Scheuer and Slemrod 2021).
16.who_benefits: The tilt is **broad**. The tax is paid by about 2,800 billionaires, whose effective tax rate would rise from about 22% to 39% of pre-tax income (Zucman 2024). The $193 billion to $242 billion a year it raises, depending on how much is lost to avoidance and evasion, can fund anything, so its benefits are as broad as the spending. Part of the cost reaches workers: Penn Wharton projects average hourly wages 1.2% lower by 2050 as less capital is built (Huntley and Ricco 2021).
16.counter:
The strongest counter-evidence is Guvenen et al. (2023). When returns differ across investors, a wealth tax falls on idle fortunes and spares productive ones. In their model, replacing the capital income tax with a wealth tax "delivers a significantly higher average welfare." Swedish bunching estimates find small responses, elasticities of 0.09 to 0.27 (Seim 2017), which point to a ratio above the high end. Even Colombia's larger elasticity of 2 (Londoño-Vélez and Ávila-Mahecha 2024) gives 0.89 in the same form. These are set aside. Guvenen et al. study a swap, while the minimum tax is added on top of existing taxes. Bunching captures only people near the threshold and is thought to understate the full response.

The verdict turns on how much wealth is hidden, moved or valued down. The range charges the general income-tax burden of 34 cents to nearly $2 per $1. Built from wealth-tax evidence instead, it would run from −0.55 to 0.72 rather than −1.12 to 0.60, before the cost of raising taxes for administration. The policy would reach the Bad tier only if avoidance sat near the low end of the 7% to 17% base loss for a well-designed tax (Advani and Tarrant 2021). The Danish evidence, a long-run base 0.73 of its untaxed level for the very wealthy (Jakobsen et al. 2020), points against that.

17.policy: Medicare for All replaces private health insurance with one government plan that covers every American. Care is free at the point of use. The federal government pays providers and raises the money through taxes.
17.why_on_list: It was selected by public opinion. In the 2022 Cooperative Election Study (CES), 66% of respondents supported it.
17.evidence: No published benefit-cost study of single payer exists, so the ratio is built from official and academic estimates. They agree on one thing: federal spending would rise by $1.5 trillion to $3.0 trillion a year by 2030 (Congressional Budget Office 2020). They disagree on whether total national health spending would rise or fall. The Urban Institute finds a rise of $720 billion (Blumberg et al. 2019). A Lancet study finds a 13% saving, about $450 billion a year, and adds that "ensuring health care access for all Americans would save more than 68,000 lives and 1.73 million life-years every year compared with the status quo" (Galvani et al. 2020). Most new spending replaces premiums and out-of-pocket costs, so it is a transfer. The damage comes from raising it. New taxes of 5 to 10% of GDP sit at or past the peak of the Laffer curve, where each $1 raised costs about $2 of lost output (Feldstein 1999). Queues add a further cost. Canada's single-payer system had a median wait of 30.0 weeks from referral to treatment in 2024 (Moir and Barua 2024b). Counting lives saved, waiting time and the cost of the taxes, each $1 destroys 57 to 77 cents of value.
17.ratio:
The new federal spending counts as $1 to households per $1, in both benefit and cost. The excess burden of tax financing and the waiting cost are subtracted from benefits. Any rise in national health spending is added to the cost base. Life-years are valued at the Institute for Clinical and Economic Review (ICER 2023) thresholds of $100,000 and $150,000.

**Excess burden.** At the peak of the Laffer curve the United States can raise at most about 7.4% of GDP in extra revenue (Trabandt and Uhlig 2012). The 34-cent burden measured for small tax changes (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985) does not hold at this scale; near the peak the burden can exceed 300% of revenue (Browning 1987). New federal spending of $1.5-2.8 trillion is 5-10% of GDP, so both ends use Feldstein's (1999) $2 per $1.

**Waiting cost.** Canadians lost time valued at C$10.6 billion a year (Moir and Barua 2024a). Scaled per person: C$10.6 billion × (343.0 million ÷ 40.05 million) = C$90.8 billion. At 1.3973 Canadian dollars per US dollar, that is $65.0 billion a year, subtracted at both ends.

**Low end (Urban Institute design).** Federal spending +$2,800 billion; national spending +$720 billion. Life-years: 1.73 million × $100,000 = $173 billion, which generously assumes the Lancet mortality gain.
- Ratio: (2,800 + 173 - 2.0 × 2,800 - 65.0) ÷ (2,800 + 720) = **-0.76**.

**High end (Lancet design).** Federal cost $1,500 billion, the low end of the Congressional Budget Office range. Savings $450 billion. Life-years: 1.73 million × $150,000 = $259.5 billion.
- Ratio: (1,500 + 450 + 259.5 - 2.0 × 1,500 - 65.0) ÷ 1,500 = **-0.57**.

The range is -0.76 to -0.57. The full cost is $5,843.0 billion a year.

Cross-checks. The Congressional Budget Office's five options span national-spending changes of -$0.7 trillion to +$0.3 trillion in 2030, between the two cases. Blahous (2018) puts added federal spending at $32.6 trillion over 2022-31, assuming providers accept payment cuts of more than 40%; that points to the low end. The Council of Economic Advisers (2018) estimates a 9% fall in GDP. That measures the same tax distortion, so it is not added to the ratio.
17.cost:
The full cost is $5,843.0 billion a year.
- Public outlay: $2,940 billion. The Congressional Budget Office's Option 5, the design closest to current bills, adds about $3.0 trillion in 2030 (Blahous 2021).
- Administration: $60 billion, at Medicare fee-for-service's rate of about 2% on $3.0 trillion. The Congressional Budget Office assumes 1.5-1.6%.
- Private cost of waiting: $65.0 billion, from the Canadian analogy above.
- GDP loss: $2,778 billion, the Council of Economic Advisers' 9% applied to 2025 GDP of $30.86 trillion. This is the high-end published estimate.

Sum: 2,940 + 60 + 65.0 + 2,778 = $5,843.0 billion. Provider billing costs sit inside national health spending, already in the ratio.
17.strength: Grade B-. The range rests on official Congressional Budget Office estimates and think-tank models from the Urban Institute and the Mercatus Center. It adds one peer-reviewed modelling study (Galvani et al. 2020) whose savings the official and Urban estimates do not replicate. Coverage does save lives in quasi-experimental work: Medicaid expansion cut mortality among near-elderly adults by 9.4% (Miller, Johnson and Wherry 2021). No peer-reviewed benefit-cost study of single payer exists. The waiting cost is a think-tank estimate for Canada applied by analogy.
17.difficulty: Moderate by the rubric. It needs ordinary federal legislation, and Canada and Taiwan's 1995 single payer are modern precedents. Politically it is near the hard end. It replaces employer insurance for about 150 million people and needs roughly $1.5-3 trillion a year in new federal revenue.
17.who_benefits: Gains go mostly to the uninsured and underinsured, who are disproportionately low-income. Covering low-income adults through Medicaid cut their mortality (Miller, Johnson and Wherry 2021) and cut their medical debt (Finkelstein et al. 2012). Financing through broad taxes is typically more progressive than premiums. Taxpayers and workers pay through the higher tax burden and slower growth.
17.counter:
The strongest counter-case is that single payer saves both money and lives. Galvani et al. (2020) estimate it cuts national health spending by about 13%, more than $450 billion a year, and prevents more than 68,000 deaths a year. Across its options, the Congressional Budget Office (2020) finds national health spending changes by −$0.7 trillion to +$0.3 trillion in 2030. The high end already counts Galvani's savings and lives. The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment found that Medicaid raised use of care and cut medical debt, but a follow-up found no significant change in measured physical-health markers over two years (Finkelstein et al. 2012). Mortality gains as large as Galvani's are therefore uncertain.

The verdict comes from financing. New federal spending of $1.5 to $2.8 trillion is 5% to 10% of US GDP, at or beyond the 7.4% the US can raise at the peak of the Laffer curve (Trabandt and Uhlig 2012). Each $1 is therefore charged nearly $2 of deadweight loss (Feldstein 1999). If the money could be raised at the 34 cents measured for small changes (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985), the high end would rise above 1 and the policy would leave the Worst tier. Two unpriced costs push the other way: health lost to delayed care, and how providers respond to payment cuts of more than 40% (Blahous 2019).

18.policy: A universal basic income (UBI) pays every adult a regular cash amount, with no conditions. The global version sets it at each country's poverty line and funds it permanently through taxes. The International Labour Organization (ILO) puts the cost at about 32.7% of world GDP (Ortiz et al. 2018).
18.why_on_list: It was selected by public opinion, which is split. In Pew's 2020 survey, 45% of Americans favoured a $1,000-a-month UBI and 54% opposed it (Gilberstadt 2020). In Dalia's 2017 poll, 68% of EU respondents said they would vote for one (Basic Income Earth Network 2017).
18.evidence: The best evidence on how people respond comes from a randomized US trial. OpenResearch paid 1,000 people $1,000 a month for three years, against 2,000 controls on $50 a month (Vivalt et al. 2024). The authors report: "For every dollar received, total household income excluding the transfers fell by about 28 cents, and total individual income fell by around 16 cents." Partners cut their hours about as much as recipients did. Delivering the money costs 4 to 25 cents per $1 on top. The deeper problem is scale. A scheme costing a third of world GDP is far beyond what taxes can raise cheaply. At that size each $1 of tax costs about $2 of lost output (Feldstein 1999). A dynamic model finds a labour-tax-financed UBI cuts long-run GDP by 12.9% (Daruich and Fernández 2020). Each $1 paid out returns between minus $1.26 and minus $1.09.
18.ratio:
The ratio is built per $1 paid out. A transfer is worth its face value to the person who receives it, so the benefit is $1. The cost to the public purse is larger than $1, because recipients earn less and pay less tax, and because delivery costs money.

**Formula:** BCR = (1 - excess burden × net fiscal cost) ÷ net fiscal cost.

**Excess burden.** At the peak of the Laffer curve, the United States can raise at most about 7.4% of GDP in extra revenue and the EU-14 about 3.1% (Trabandt and Uhlig 2012). The 34-cent burden measured for small changes (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985) does not apply at this scale; near the peak the burden can exceed 300% of revenue (Browning 1987). A global UBI costs about 32.7% of world GDP, so both ends use Feldstein's (1999) $2 per $1.

**Inputs.** Treated households received an extra $950 a month, or $11,400 a year. Household income excluding transfers fell by $4,215 a year in the raw survey measure (0.37 per $1) and by $3,228 in the preferred adjusted measure (0.28 per $1) (Vivalt et al. 2024). A labour-tax-financed UBI raises the average labour tax from 22% to about 27.8% (Daruich and Fernández 2020). Delivery costs $0.041 per $1 for Mexico's PROGRESA (Caldes, Coady and Maluccio 2004) and $0.25 per $1 for GiveDirectly (GiveDirectly 2024).

**High end:**
- Fiscal externality: 0.28 × 0.22 = 0.062.
- Net fiscal cost: 1.062 + 0.041 = 1.103.
- BCR: (1 - 2.0 × 1.103) ÷ 1.103 = **-1.09**.

**Low end:**
- Fiscal externality: 0.370 × 0.278 = 0.103.
- Net fiscal cost: 1.103 + 0.25 = 1.353.
- BCR: (1 - 2.0 × 1.353) ÷ 1.353 = **-1.26**.

The range is -1.26 to -1.09. The full cost is $56,420 billion a year.

Cross-checks. A universal government scheme would probably deliver nearer PROGRESA's 4 cents, which gives a low end of about -1.13. But a scheme this large needs far higher tax rates than the US scheme Daruich and Fernández model, so the low end's fiscal externality is likely understated. Hendren and Sprung-Keyser (2020) score the randomized US Negative Income Tax experiments at a marginal value of public funds of -0.01. Daruich and Fernández find future generations would give up over 9% of lifetime consumption to avoid a UBI. Both point to net damage.
18.cost:
The full cost is $56,420 billion a year.
- Public outlay: $34,300 billion. The ILO's 32.7% of GDP on world GDP of about $105 trillion (Ortiz et al. 2018; Visual Capitalist 2023). The ILO excludes administration.
- Administration: $8,575 billion, at GiveDirectly's $0.25 per $1 delivered (0.25 × 34,300). GiveWell (2020) finds about 83% of GiveDirectly's spending reaches recipients overall.
- Private compliance: none identified.
- GDP loss: $13,545 billion, a 12.9% fall in GDP on world GDP (Daruich and Fernández 2020). This is the output counterpart of the excess burden already in the ratio, so it is not subtracted twice.

Sum: 34,300 + 8,575 + 13,545 = $56,420 billion. With low-end administration, the total before GDP loss is $35,706 billion.
18.strength: Grade A-. The labour-supply response comes from a modern randomized trial (Vivalt et al. 2024). The cross-check comes from a peer-reviewed welfare analysis of the randomized Negative Income Tax experiments (Hendren and Sprung-Keyser 2020). The excess-burden and dynamic estimates are peer-reviewed (Feldstein 1999; Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Daruich and Fernández 2020). No study scores a global UBI directly, which keeps the grade below A.
18.difficulty: Hard. A global scheme needs binding commitments from many countries. The ILO puts a poverty-line UBI at 32.7-39.4% of GDP on average and 62.3-79.1% of GDP in low-income countries (Ortiz et al. 2018). That is far above the 7.4% of GDP the United States could add at the peak of the Laffer curve.
18.who_benefits: Benefits are broad, not targeted. Payments go to everyone, so most of the money reaches people who are not poor. Financing creates high implicit marginal tax rates on middle earners (Henderson 2019). Daruich and Fernández (2020) find that current adults gain 1.2%, while the long-run losses fall on future generations through lower capital and skills.
18.counter:
The strongest counter-case comes from cash trials in poor countries. In Kenya's GiveDirectly trial across 295 villages, "Labor supply did not change overall, but shifted out of wage employment and towards self-employment" (Banerjee et al. 2023). Net enterprise revenues rose 52%, and depression fell in all arms. One-off transfers into poor Kenyan villages had a local multiplier of about 2.4 (Egger et al. 2022). Finland's pilot for 2,000 unemployed people found a small employment gain and better wellbeing (VATT and Kela 2020). None of these tests a permanent, tax-financed, universal payment. The Kenyan money is donor-funded, with no tax distortion, and the multiplier is a local spending effect, not a welfare ratio.

The verdict comes from scale. A global payment costs about 32.7% of world GDP, more than four times the 7.4% of GDP the US can raise at the peak of the Laffer curve (Trabandt and Uhlig 2012). Each $1 is therefore charged nearly $2 of deadweight loss (Feldstein 1999). If the money could be raised at the 34 cents measured for small changes (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985), with the trial's 28 cents of lost household earnings per $1 (Vivalt et al. 2024), the ratio would turn positive but stay below 1. Only a scheme small enough to be financed at that rate could move from the Worst to the Bad tier.

19.policy: Every country requires its residents to hold and use a government digital identity. The ID would be used to verify people for welfare, work and public services. It is a government rule rather than a spending programme, though building and running the systems costs money.
19.why_on_list: It was selected by public opinion. A September 2025 YouGov poll found 42% of Britons supported the UK plan, with 45% opposed (YouGov 2025). An Ipsos UK poll in 2025 found 57% support for a national ID card.
19.evidence: The best evidence comes from two randomized trials in India, both by Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar. In Jharkhand, biometric checks were made compulsory for food rations. Corruption did not fall: leakage rose by an insignificant Rs 14 per ration card a month. Transaction costs for government, ration dealers and recipients rose by Rs 13.6 per card a month, a 7.8% increase. Nearly 300,000 people lost benefits (Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar 2020). In Andhra Pradesh, a biometric smartcard payment system was rolled out carefully alongside the old one. Recipients' time savings alone, $4.3 million, exceeded the government's cost of $4.1 million (Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar 2016). The two trials point in opposite directions. The authors conclude that results depend on how the mandate and the transition are managed. Each $1 returns between about minus $1.0 and $1.05, before counting privacy and surveillance risks. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is −$1.94 to $0.78 per $1.
19.ratio:
Both ends come straight from the two randomized evaluations.

**Low end (Jharkhand, compulsory authentication for food rations):**
- Benefit: the change in leakage, a rise of Rs 14 per ration card a month.
- Cost: extra transaction costs of Rs 13.6 per card a month.
- Ratio: -14 ÷ 13.6 = -1.03, about **-1.0**.

**High end (Andhra Pradesh biometric smartcards):**
- Benefit: recipients' time savings, $4.3 million.
- Cost: the government's cost of running the programme, $4.1 million.
- Ratio: 4.3 ÷ 4.1 = **1.05**.

The smartcards also cut leakage of employment-scheme wages by $32.8 million a year, eight times the cost. That money mostly moved from corrupt officials back to the state, a transfer, so it is not counted.

The range before tax finance is -1.0 to 1.05. The full cost is $88.8 billion a year.

Platform costs. The Jharkhand low end already counts the extra costs of compulsory authentication to government, dealers and recipients. Adding the platform's own running cost to a negative ratio would pull it toward zero and understate the harm, so it is not done. The Andhra Pradesh high end compares time savings with the smartcard system's full delivery cost. A share of a national ID platform's running cost, 0.06-0.1% of GDP, is not included and would lower the high end somewhat.

Exclusion. In Jharkhand, the 23% of households not linked to the ID system at the start lost Rs 49 a month (12.6%). That averages 0.23 × 49 = Rs 11.3 per ration card a month. The average household's benefits were unchanged, so these losses already sit inside the measured Rs 14 rise in leakage. With an equity weight on excluded poor households, they would be added: -(14 + 11.3) ÷ 13.6 = -1.86.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). High end: the Andhra Pradesh government's $4.1 million implementation and operating cost is all public, so 1.05 ÷ (1 + 0.34 × 1.0) = 0.78. Low end: in the Jharkhand trial the government's share of the Rs 13.6 extra transaction cost is the electronic point-of-sale (ePOS) machines, Rs 6.2 per ration card per month; the rest falls on beneficiaries and ration dealers. Because the low end is negative, the burden is subtracted from the benefit, as for the transfer entries; adding it to the cost would pull a negative ratio toward zero. Low end: (−14 − 2.0 × 6.2) ÷ 13.6 = −1.94. **Range after tax finance: −1.94 to 0.78.**
19.cost:
The full cost is an illustrative global extrapolation of $88.8 billion a year, using the median of published estimates.
- Build and enrolment: $4.8 billion a year. Published costs per registrant are $1.16 for India's Aadhaar (Gelb 2016), about $5 for schemes in poor countries (Gelb and Clark 2013), $7 in Gelb's (2016) model of a low-income country, and $4 to $11, midpoint $7.5 (World Bank 2018). The median is $6.0. For about 8.0 billion people (United Nations DESA 2022), amortised over 10 years, that is $4.8 billion a year. Most people already hold some ID, so this is high.
- Operation and administration: $84 billion a year. Published running costs are 0.06% to 0.1% of GDP, midpoint 0.08% (World Bank 2018); 0.065% for Peru's national registry, RENIEC; and 0.11% in the steady state of Gelb's (2016) model. The median is 0.08%. At world GDP of about $105 trillion (Visual Capitalist 2023), that is $84 billion a year.
- Private compliance: no published estimate.
- GDP loss: none published.

Sum: 4.8 + 84 = $88.8 billion. Budget allocation is the most common way these systems are paid for (Gelb 2016), so the whole public cost is treated as paid from taxes. Cross-check: the UK's Office for Budget Responsibility puts the UK scheme at £1.8 billion over three years, about £0.6 billion a year (Office for Budget Responsibility 2025). Scaled per person, that is about $90 billion a year globally, close to this total. If the ID were also used to track personal carbon allowances, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra 2008) figure of £52 per person a year implies about $420 billion more.
19.strength: Grade B+. Both ends are converted directly from peer-reviewed randomized evaluations that report costs and benefits (Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar 2016, 2025). Applying Indian welfare evidence to a worldwide mandate is an analogy. The two trials point in opposite directions. The cost figures rest on thin data; as the World Bank (2018) notes, "few data points exist and these figures may not apply to different types of systems or to all countries."
19.difficulty: Moderate. Each country can mandate a digital ID through ordinary legislation, and India's Aadhaar shows that more than a billion people can be enrolled. A worldwide mandate still needs action in nearly every country, and rich democracies have retreated. In January 2026, "The government has abandoned its plans to make digital ID compulsory in the verification of right to work" (UKAuthority 2026). In July 2026 the incoming prime minister moved to scrap the UK scheme (ITV News 2026).
19.who_benefits: The policy is regressive. Exclusion risk falls on the poor. About 45% of the poorest fifth in low-income countries lack ID, against 28% of the richest (World Bank ID4D 2019). Between 1.5 and 2 million Indian welfare recipients lost access at some point during the biometric rollout (Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar 2025). Governments and honest recipients gain where a system is run well, as in Andhra Pradesh.
19.counter:
The strongest counter-case is the size of the prize. McKinsey projects that consent-based, privacy-protecting "good" digital ID could unlock value equal to 3% to 13% of GDP by 2030 (White et al. 2019). In Andhra Pradesh, biometric smartcards cut leakage in the rural jobs programme by $32.8 million a year, eight times their cost (Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar 2016). These are left out of the ratio. McKinsey's figure is a consultancy projection of potential, not an evaluation of a mandate. A 2012 appraisal of Aadhaar by India's National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (NIPFP) finds a ratio of 2.55, but its benefits are fiscal savings from less leakage. These, like the Andhra Pradesh leakage savings, are transfers, money moved from corrupt officials to the state.

The verdict turns on how the mandate is introduced. The careful Andhra Pradesh rollout, run alongside the old system, returned 1.05 from time savings alone, or 0.78 once the cost of raising the taxes that pay for it is counted. The abrupt Jharkhand mandate returned about −1.0, and −1.94 after that cost. Even if every country managed the transition as Andhra Pradesh did, the policy would reach only the Bad tier. If the losses of the 23% of households not linked to the system were weighted as harm to the poor, the low end before tax finance would fall to −1.86.

20.policy: Medicare negotiates the prices it pays for some of its highest-spend drugs, under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) runs the process. Negotiated prices for the first 10 drugs take effect in 2026 and for the next 15 in 2027.
20.why_on_list: It was selected by public opinion. In the 2022 Cooperative Election Study (CES), 85.9% supported it, and KFF found 85% support.
20.evidence: Lower negotiated prices mainly move money from drug makers to Medicare and its enrollees. That transfer is not a gain to society on its own. The real gains and losses lie elsewhere. On the gain side, enrollees save $1.5 billion out of pocket in 2026 on the first 10 drugs and $685 million in 2027 on the next 15 (CMS 2024, 2025a). A Quarterly Journal of Economics study finds that Medicare patients facing higher drug costs take fewer medicines and die sooner (Chandra, Flack and Obermeyer 2024). Applied to these savings, that is about 3,583 deaths averted a year. On the loss side, lower prices mean less money for research. The Congressional Budget Office expects 13 fewer new drugs out of about 1,300 over 30 years, about 1% (Congressional Budget Office 2023b). The health gain is an extrapolation, and without it the high end falls below 1. Each $1 returns between 57 cents and $2.80. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $0.54 to $2.79 per $1.
20.ratio:
Benefit: savings to taxpayers and enrollees, plus health gains from lower out-of-pocket costs, minus lost innovation. Cost: manufacturers' revenue loss plus administration.

**Formula:** BCR = (savings + health gains - lost innovation) ÷ (manufacturer revenue loss + administration).

**Inputs.**
- Savings: the Congressional Budget Office puts deficit reduction at $98.5 billion over 2022-31 and $25 billion in 2031 (Congressional Budget Office 2022, 2023a). This is also the manufacturers' revenue loss. In a fully phased-in model, brand revenue falls $10.9 billion a year after manufacturers raise launch prices (Cogan, Heil and Mulligan 2025).
- Administration: the $3 billion appropriation over 10 years is $0.3 billion a year.
- Lost innovation: 13 fewer drugs over 30 years is 0.43 a year. Dubois et al. (2015) find that "$2.5 billion is required in additional revenue to support the invention of one new chemical entity." That gives $1.1 billion a year. Cogan, Heil and Mulligan's own method gives $4.5 billion a year.
- Health gains: Chandra, Flack and Obermeyer (2024) find deaths rise 0.0164 percentage points a month for each $100 a month cut in a patient's drug budget. That is about one death per $610,000 of out-of-pocket cost. Enrollee savings are $1.5 billion + $685 million = $2.185 billion a year. Then $2.185 billion ÷ $610,000 = 3,583 deaths averted a year. At a value of a statistical life of $13.1 million (HHS 2024), that is $46.9 billion.

**Low end** (no health gains, because the Congressional Budget Office has not assessed patients' health outcomes):
- (10.9 - 4.5) ÷ (10.9 + 0.3) = **0.57**.

**High end:**
- (25 + 46.9 - 1.1) ÷ (25 + 0.3) = **2.80**.

The range is 0.57 to 2.8. The full cost is $4.81 billion a year.

Cross-checks. Without the health gains, the high end would be (25 - 1.1) ÷ (25 + 0.3) = 0.94. Valuing a lost drug at the revenue it needs is a floor, since patients usually gain more than the seller earns. Lost innovation is valued as a health harm, so the mortality cost of lost income applies only to the administration cost.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted, an extra $0.34 to $2.00 (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. Only the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' implementation budget of $0.3 billion a year is paid from taxes; manufacturers' reporting cost is private. That is 0.3 of 11.2 (0.0268) of the cost at the low end and 0.3 of 25.3 (0.0119) at the high end. Low end: 0.571 ÷ (1 + 2.0 × 0.0268) = 0.54. High end: 2.80 ÷ (1 + 0.34 × 0.0119) = 2.79. **Range after tax finance: 0.54 to 2.79.**
20.cost:
The full cost is $4.81 billion a year.
- Public outlay: none beyond administration. Price cuts are transfers.
- Administration: $0.3 billion a year, from the IRA's $3 billion implementation fund, with $2.845 billion of outlays over 2022-31 (Congressional Budget Office 2022).
- Private compliance: $0.013 billion a year. Manufacturers report 47,620 hours a year for the 2028 negotiation cycle (CMS 2025b) and 17,000 hours for negotiation data elements (CMS 2023). The 64,620 hours are valued at an assumed $200 an hour, about $13 million.
- Lost innovation: $4.5 billion a year (Cogan, Heil and Mulligan 2025). At the Congressional Budget Office's 13 fewer drugs, it would be $1.1 billion.

Sum: 0.3 + 0.013 + 4.5 = $4.81 billion. Lower prices move about $10.9-25 billion a year from manufacturers to Medicare and enrollees. That is a transfer, not a cost to society. Litigation costs have not been estimated by any source.
20.strength: Grade B-. The high end rests on official Congressional Budget Office and CMS estimates. These are converted with peer-reviewed figures: Dubois et al. (2015) for the value of a lost drug and Chandra, Flack and Obermeyer (2024) for health gains, applied by extrapolation. Chandra and colleagues study a sharp change in coverage at age 65, not a price cut. The low end rests on think-tank modelling. With official estimates as the best sources, the grade is B-.
20.difficulty: Moderate. It needed ordinary federal legislation, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, and CMS now runs it. Adding more drugs, or extending negotiation to commercial insurance, would need new legislation.
20.who_benefits: Benefits are broad. Savings are spread across Medicare enrollees and taxpayers. Part D households save about $51 (middle income) to $65 (upper income) a year, under 0.1% of income (Cogan, Heil and Mulligan 2025). The cost of fewer future drugs falls on future patients generally. Drug makers lose revenue.
20.counter:
The strongest counter-case is lost innovation. Philipson and Durie (2021) find that the drug-pricing provisions of an earlier bill (H.R. 5376) would mean 135 fewer new drugs and 331.5 million US life-years lost through 2039. On their method, lost innovation costs $196.3 billion a year, against savings of $25 billion in 2031, which would make the policy strongly negative. It is not used because it implies about ten times the loss of drugs that the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projects, 13 fewer of about 1,300 over 30 years. Some of that work is also partly funded by the drug industry (Chicago Policy Review 2024). The CBO further expects manufacturers to set higher launch prices, which cuts savings on new drugs.

The verdict rests on health gains. Without them, the high end is 0.94 and the whole range sits below 1, in the Bad tier. With them, it reaches 2.80, or 2.79 after the cost of raising taxes. The gain comes from Chandra, Flack and Obermeyer (2024), who find that Medicare patients facing smaller drug budgets "consume fewer drugs and die more". They study a sharp loss of coverage at age 65, and applying that to lower negotiated prices is an extrapolation. If lost innovation were valued at the Hoover paper's $4.5 billion a year rather than $1.1 billion at the high end too, the ratio would fall further.
