21.policy: Pay for routine childhood vaccines in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and raise coverage to the 2030 targets. The costed package covers nine vaccines in 80 countries: pentavalent, human papillomavirus (HPV), Japanese encephalitis, measles, measles-rubella, meningitis A, pneumococcal, rotavirus and yellow fever. National governments and donors pay, mostly through national immunization programmes and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. The programme cost is about $1.5 billion a year.
21.why_on_list: It is one of the health "best buys" named by the Copenhagen Consensus Center, the Disease Control Priorities project (third edition, DCP3), the World Health Organization (WHO) and GiveWell. All four rank childhood vaccination among the most cost-effective things a health budget can buy.
21.evidence: Few policies have been studied as often, and few studies agree as well. Patenaude, Sriudomporn and Mak (2023) cost a scale-up of nine vaccines in 80 countries for 2023-2030 and find benefits of $762.2 billion against costs of $7.58 billion. That is about $101 of benefit per $1, the figure the Copenhagen Consensus uses. Two earlier studies in *Health Affairs* reach the same verdict with different data. Ozawa et al. (2016) find a net return of about 16 times cost when only treatment costs and lost work are counted, and 44 when the full value of longer lives is counted. Adding back the dollar spent, that is about 17 and 45 of benefit per $1. Sim et al. (2020) report that "using the cost-of-illness approach, return on investment for one dollar invested in immunization against our ten pathogens was 26.1 for the ninety-four countries from 2011 to 2020 and 19.8 from 2021 to 2030." Valuing lives saved, they get 51.0 and 52.2. The pattern is clear: 17 to 26 when only medical costs and lost output count, 45 to 101 when lives are valued. Each vaccine's efficacy rests on randomized trials, so the uncertainty lies in how lives are valued, not in whether the vaccines work. The Copenhagen Consensus package saves about 523,000 lives a year. After adding the overhead of the donor channel, the ratio runs from $14.4 to $94 per $1. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $4.81 to $72.40 per $1.
21.ratio:
The ratio compares the value of illness and deaths averted with the cost of buying and delivering the vaccines. The source costs already include delivery inside each country, so only the overhead of the international funding channel is added.

**Overhead rates.** Gavi's 2023 accounts show $2,025 million of direct country programme spending. Around it sit $86 million of Secretariat implementation, $209 million of partners' implementation and $65 million of overhead.

- All non-direct spending: 86 + 209 + 65 = 360. Share: 17.8%.
- Secretariat implementation plus overhead: 86 + 65 = 151. Share: 7.5%.

**Low end (14.4).** Ozawa et al. (2016) count only the cost of illness and find a net return of 16, so benefits are 16 + 1 = 17 times cost. All of their cost is programme spending, so the full 17.8% is added.

- Ratio: 17 ÷ 1.178 = 14.4.

**High end (94).** Patenaude, Sriudomporn and Mak (2023) value years of life saved, with an 8% discount rate.

- Benefits: $762.2 billion. Costs: $7.58 billion. Ratio: 762.2 ÷ 7.58 = 100.5.
- Programme share of the cost: 1.5 ÷ 1.7 = 0.882. The rest is parents' time, which carries no agency overhead.
- Overhead at the lower rate: 100.5 ÷ (1 + 0.075 × 0.882) = 94.3, rounded to 94.

**Cost.** Programme $1.5 billion + channel overhead $0.27 billion + parents' time $0.2 billion = $1.97 billion a year.

The adjustment touches costs only; benefits are left as published. Other estimates sit inside the range. Sim et al. (2020) give 19.8 and 52.2 for 2021-30. Ozawa et al. (2016) give a net return of 44 on a full-income basis, about 45 of benefit per $1. Copenhagen Consensus 2012 (Jamison et al. 2012) gave 20, and the Post-2015 Consensus panel gave expanded immunization $60 per $1.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted, an extra $0.34 to $2.00 (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. The low end counts all programme spending as public. At the high end, only the programme share of the cost (0.882, plus its 7.5% overhead) is paid from taxes; parents' time is not. Low end: 14.43 ÷ 3.00 = 4.81. High end: 100.5 ÷ (1 + 0.075 × 0.882 + 0.34 × 0.882 × 1.075) = 100.5 ÷ 1.3885 = 72.4. **Range after tax finance: 4.81 to 72.4.**
21.cost:
The full cost is $1.97 billion a year.

- **Programme: $1.5 billion.** The Copenhagen Consensus (2025) puts the package at $1.7 billion a year, of which $0.2 billion is parents' time. Patenaude, Sriudomporn and Mak (2023) cost the vaccines, injection supplies and freight. Their delivery costs include staff, the cold chain, transport, buildings, programme management, training, social mobilization and disease surveillance. Country-level administration is therefore already inside this figure.
- **Channel overhead: $0.27 billion.** This is Gavi's own cost of running the money: Secretariat implementation, technical help from partners and general overhead. At the higher rate: 1.5 × 0.178 = 0.27.
- **Household cost: $0.2 billion.** Parents' time to bring children for vaccination. It is already in the Copenhagen Consensus ratio, so it changes the cost but not the ratio.

As a cross-check, the present-value cost of $7.58 billion for 2023-2030 works out to about $0.95 billion a year in discounted terms. The last children are the most expensive. GiveWell (2025) estimates "about $146 to vaccinate an infant" through cash incentives in northern Nigeria, at about $4,500 per life saved.
21.strength: Grade: A+. Several independent peer-reviewed studies, using different methods, datasets and decades, agree that benefits are many times costs. Patenaude, Sriudomporn and Mak (2023), Ozawa et al. (2016) and Sim et al. (2020) disagree on the size of the return, not its sign. The health effect of each vaccine rests on randomized controlled trials. This is as strong as the evidence for a policy gets.
21.difficulty: Rating: moderate. Nothing has to be invented. The model already works: national immunization programmes backed by Gavi. What is needed is sustained money from donors and governments. The hard part is the last stretch. In 2024, 85% of infants worldwide completed three doses of the diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DTP) vaccine, and measles coverage was 84% for the first dose and 76% for the second (WHO and UNICEF 2025). Coverage has stalled. There were 14.3 million "zero-dose" children who never received a single vaccine, 4 million more than the target for staying on track. Many live in conflict zones and remote areas.
21.who_benefits: Rating: pro-poor. The children left out are the poorest. In the words of WHO and UNICEF (2025): "A quarter of the world's infants live in just 26 countries affected by fragility, conflict, or humanitarian crises, yet they make up half of all unvaccinated children globally." Averted deaths drive most of the benefit, and they are mostly young children in low-income countries (Patenaude, Sriudomporn and Mak 2023). Donors and national taxpayers pay the programme cost. Parents give up a small amount of time.
21.counter:
The case for a lower verdict rests on how lives are valued and where. Counting only medical costs and lost work, Ozawa et al. (2016) find a ratio of about 17, and Sim et al. (2020) find 19.8 for 2021-30, against 101 when lives saved are valued (Patenaude, Sriudomporn and Mak 2023). Two United States studies give lower figures still. Carrico et al. (2022) find 7.5 for society and 2.8 for payers; Zhou et al. (2024) find 10.9 and 3.3. They are left out because they describe a rich country with low child mortality, not an aid-funded scale-up in poorer countries. They still confirm that vaccines pay for themselves even where children rarely die.

The verdict depends on which valuation holds. The low end already rests on the cost-of-illness figure: after overhead and the cost of raising taxes it is 4.81. If that narrower valuation were right, rather than the value-of-life figure of 101, the policy would sit in the Good tier rather than near the top. The other risk is cost. Coverage has stalled at 85% for the third dose of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis vaccine, with 14.3 million infants receiving no dose (WHO and UNICEF 2025). If the children still unreached cost far more to vaccinate than the average child, returns would fall.

22.policy: Scale up cheap generic drugs that prevent and treat heart attacks and strokes in low-income and lower-middle-income countries. The package covers aspirin at the onset of a heart attack, blood-pressure medicines, and combination regimens such as the "polypill", which joins blood-pressure drugs with a statin. Delivery runs through primary care. Governments and donors pay about $2.4 billion a year.
22.why_on_list: It is a health "best buy" for the Copenhagen Consensus Center, the Disease Control Priorities project (third edition, DCP3) and the World Health Organization (WHO) Best Buys list for noncommunicable diseases. Heart attacks and strokes are now among the leading causes of death in many poor countries.
22.evidence: The drugs work, and they cost little. In the TIPS-3 trial, a polypill plus aspirin lowered major cardiovascular events against placebo, with a hazard ratio of 0.69 (Yusuf et al. 2021). Watkins, Ahmed and Pickersgill (2023) rank aspirin for a suspected heart attack as a "best investment", with a ratio above 15 in both low-income and lower-middle-income countries. Their full package of best investments costs $19 billion over 2023-2030, averts 12 million deaths and returns 23 per $1. The Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015 panel put aspirin therapy for heart attacks at $63 per $1, blood-pressure medication at $47 and a combined stroke and heart-attack pill at $7. Nugent (2015) finds 31 to 153 for aspirin, 7 to 34 for hypertension management and 3 to 17 for long-term multi-drug prevention. The range is wide because each study puts a different value on a healthy year of life. At the bottom, WHO (2018) counts only economic output and averted health spending and finds $3.29 per $1 for drug therapy. That figure leaves out the value of lives saved, so it is a floor. After adding the overhead of the donor channel, the ratio runs from $3.1 to $59 per $1. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $1.02 to $44 per $1.
22.ratio:
The ratio compares health and economic gains with the cost of drugs, screening and follow-up. The source costs already include delivery inside each country, so only the overhead of the international funding channel is added. United Nations (UN) agencies charge 8% on earmarked donor funds and 7% on thematic funds (Executive Boards 2018).

**Low end (3.1).** WHO (2018), using the method of Bertram et al. (2018), finds $3.29 per $1 for drug therapy and counselling for people at high cardiovascular risk. It counts only output and averted health spending.

- Ratio: 3.29 ÷ 1.08 = 3.05, rounded to 3.1.

**High end (59).** The Post-2015 Consensus panel put aspirin therapy for heart attacks at $63 per $1. Cheap acute aspirin is the single best item in the package.

- Ratio at the lower overhead rate: 63 ÷ 1.07 = 58.9, rounded to 59.

**Cost.** Programme $2.4 billion + channel overhead $0.19 billion + household cost $0 = $2.59 billion a year.

The adjustment touches costs only; benefits are left as published. Before overhead the components span 3.3 to 63. Routine blood-pressure drugs sit in the middle, at 7 to 47. Multi-drug and polypill regimens sit lowest, at 3 to 17 (Nugent 2015). Nugent and Brouwer (2015) find that tobacco taxes combined with a multi-drug regimen for high-risk people return 7 per $1. The full package of Watkins, Ahmed and Pickersgill (2023) scores 23.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. The whole cost behind the ratio is public spending. Low end: 3.05 ÷ 3.00 = 1.02. High end: 58.9 ÷ 1.34 = 44.0. **Range after tax finance: 1.02 to 44.**
22.cost:
The full cost is $2.59 billion a year.

- **Programme: $2.4 billion.** Watkins, Ahmed and Pickersgill (2023) cost the best-investment package at $19 billion over 2023-2030, about $2.4 billion a year. It is a rough proxy. It includes a few items outside heart disease, such as early breast cancer and epilepsy care, and leaves out the lower-return heart drugs. Their clinical unit costs already carry a 17% markup for programme management above the facility, plus ancillary facility costs (multipliers of 1.17, 1.257 and 1.488 by platform). WHO's $3.29 return uses a costing tool that adds "related health system costs" such as infrastructure and staff to drugs and supplies (WHO and UNDP 2019).
- **Channel overhead: $0.19 billion.** The standard UN cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor money. At the higher rate: 2.4 × 0.080 = 0.19.
- **Household cost: none counted.** Patients' travel and time are not reported separately in these sources.

A larger 70% programme markup used for tuberculosis programmes was not applied, because it belongs to stand-alone disease programmes. Cross-checks: the WHO HEARTS package costs about $18 to $44 per person treated per year (Moran et al. 2022). The Copenhagen Consensus bundle for noncommunicable diseases costs $4.4 billion a year, and Nugent's five interventions about $8.5 billion a year.
22.strength: Grade: A. Several peer-reviewed benefit-cost studies support the policy (Watkins, Ahmed and Pickersgill 2023; Bertram et al. 2018; Nugent and Brouwer 2015). Their effect sizes come from randomized-trial meta-analyses of aspirin, blood-pressure drugs and statins, and from polypill trials such as TIPS-3. It falls short of A+ because the published ratios for each component differ by a factor of ten, and they depend heavily on the value placed on a healthy year of life.
22.difficulty: Rating: moderate. The drugs are generic and cheap. The WHO HEARTS programme already runs in dozens of countries. What is hard is everything around the pill: screening people who feel well, bringing them back, and keeping them on treatment for years. In TIPS-3, about 42% of participants had stopped the polypill regimen by the end of the trial (Yusuf et al. 2021). A sustained scale-up of primary care is needed, not a one-off campaign.
22.who_benefits: Rating: broad. Adults with high blood pressure or heart disease gain, across all income groups in low-income and lower-middle-income countries. Free drugs paid for by governments or donors help poorer patients who cannot buy them. But diagnosis and continuing care tend to reach better-off urban patients first. The sources do not show that the gains are concentrated on the poorest. Donors and national taxpayers pay.
22.counter:
The counter-evidence cuts both ways. Nugent (2015) puts aspirin for heart attacks at 153 per $1. That figure values a healthy year of life at $5,000 with a 3% discount rate, well above the Copenhagen Consensus 2023 values of $995 to $4,440 at 8%, so the panel's 63 is used instead. On the other side, the WHO floor of $3.29 per $1 counts only economic output and averted health spending, not the value of lives saved, so the true low end is probably higher. Adherence pulls the other way: in the TIPS-3 trial, 43% of participants were not taking the polypill by the end (Yusuf et al. 2021), and real-world programmes may do worse.

The verdict depends on the mix of drugs. Aspirin for a suspected heart attack scores 31 to 153 (Nugent 2015), routine blood-pressure drugs about 7 to 47, and multi-drug or polypill regimens 3 to 17. A programme led by acute aspirin and routine blood-pressure drugs would sit well inside the Excellent tier. One built mainly on polypills would sit lower, in the Good tier or below. Real-world adherence below the trial's would pull the result the same way.

23.policy: Expand the three core tools against malaria in Africa. Hand out more insecticide-treated bed nets. Give young children in the Sahel preventive drugs during the rainy season, known as seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC). Subsidize artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) so that sick children get effective treatment. The costed scale-up needs about $1.4 billion a year from donors and governments.
23.why_on_list: It is a health "best buy" for the Copenhagen Consensus Center, the Disease Control Priorities project (third edition, DCP3) and GiveWell. GiveWell's two malaria charities are among its top-rated programmes.
23.evidence: Malaria still killed about 610,000 people in 2024, mostly African children (WHO 2025). The tools to stop it are proven. Bhatt et al. (2015) estimate that control efforts "averted 663 (542–753 credible interval) million clinical cases since 2000," and that insecticide-treated nets "were by far the largest contributor (68% of cases averted)." Shretta and Anye (2023) cost a 10-point rise in net coverage in 29 African countries at $5.7 billion over 2023-2030. It averts 1,337,069 deaths and yields benefits of $275.4 billion, a ratio of 48. Copenhagen Consensus 2012 (Jamison et al. 2012) found that subsidizing treatment returns about 35 per $1. Hallett et al. (2025) find that the best mix of spending on HIV, tuberculosis and malaria returns up to $19 of health value per $1. That covers three diseases at once, so it is a cautious floor for malaria's best tools. GiveWell (2025) puts the cost at about $4,000 per life saved for SMC and $5,500 for nets. The main risk is that rising drug and insecticide resistance could erode these gains. After adding the overhead of the donor channel, the ratio runs from $17.4 to $45 per $1. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $5.81 to $33.60 per $1.
23.ratio:
The ratio compares lives saved, work days regained and health spending avoided with the cost of nets, drugs and their delivery. The source costs already include delivery inside each country, so only the overhead of the international funding channel is added. The Global Fund's operating expenses were 9.0% of grant spending in 2023 and 6.7% in 2024. These are the higher and lower overhead rates.

**Low end (17.4).** Hallett et al. (2025) find up to $19 of health value per $1 across the HIV, tuberculosis and malaria portfolio.

- Ratio at the higher overhead rate: 19 ÷ 1.090 = 17.4.

**High end (45).** Shretta and Anye (2023) cost a 10-point scale-up of nets at an 8% discount rate.

- Benefits: $275.4 billion (lives saved $225.9 billion, productivity $41.7 billion, health-system savings $7.7 billion).
- Costs: $5.7 billion. Ratio: 275.4 ÷ 5.7 = 48.
- Ratio at the lower overhead rate: 48 ÷ 1.067 = 45.0.

**Cost.** Programme $1.4 billion + channel overhead $0.13 billion + household cost $0 = $1.53 billion a year.

The adjustment touches costs only; benefits are left as published. Other estimates fall inside the range. The Post-2015 Consensus panel put "halve malaria infections" at $36 per $1. Copenhagen Consensus 2012 gave the treatment subsidy about 35. Seasonal chemoprevention has no published ratio in these sources, but its cost per life saved is close to that of nets.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. The whole cost behind the ratio is public spending. Low end: 17.43 ÷ 3.00 = 5.81. High end: 45.0 ÷ 1.34 = 33.6. **Range after tax finance: 5.81 to 33.6.**
23.cost:
The full cost is $1.53 billion a year.

- **Programme: $1.4 billion.** The Copenhagen Consensus net scale-up costs $1.1 billion a year (Copenhagen Consensus Center 2025). The treatment subsidy adds about $0.3 billion a year (Jamison et al. 2012). Shretta and Anye (2023) cost the nets, their distribution and the communication that gets people to use them. They do not include active surveillance. Seasonal chemoprevention adds little: about $3.63 per child per season in the ACCESS-SMC programme. GiveWell puts it at about $7 per child protected and about $6 per net.
- **Channel overhead: $0.13 billion.** The Global Fund Secretariat's operating costs. At the higher rate: 1.4 × 0.090 = 0.13.
- **Household cost: none counted.** Time to collect nets is not costed in the sources.

The total funding gap is much larger. WHO (2025) reports $3.9 billion spent in 2024 against a target of $9.3 billion, a shortfall of about $5.4 billion a year. Filling all of it would likely return less per dollar than the costed scale-ups.
23.strength: Grade: A. Peer-reviewed benefit-cost studies (Shretta and Anye 2023; Hallett et al. 2025) rest on randomized trials of nets, seasonal chemoprevention and combination treatment. Large observational studies confirm the effect at scale (Bhatt et al. 2015; ACCESS-SMC Partnership 2020). In seven countries, SMC gave 88% protection in the 28 days after each round. It falls short of A+ because there is essentially one benefit-cost study per tool rather than several independent ones.
23.difficulty: Rating: moderate. The delivery channels already exist: the Global Fund, the US President's Malaria Initiative, national malaria programmes, the Against Malaria Foundation and Malaria Consortium. The obstacle is money. Only 42% of the required funding was found in 2024 (WHO 2025). Scale-up has been done before. SMC grew from 170,000 children per cycle in 2012 to 54 million in 2024, and several countries have been certified malaria-free.
23.who_benefits: Rating: pro-poor. About 95% of malaria deaths occur in the WHO African Region, and about 75% of those are children under five (WHO 2025). The burden falls on the poorest rural households. The gains also reach incomes. Sarma et al. (2019) find that a 10% fall in malaria incidence goes with a 0.27% rise in income per person, and that "greater average income gains would be achieved among poorer and higher endemic countries." Donors and national taxpayers pay.
23.counter:
The narrowest reading of the evidence is the main counter-case. Hallett et al. (2025) find $3.50 of direct economic benefit per $1 when no value is placed on lives saved. It is left out of the range because every other health estimate values lives, but it still shows a positive return on the narrowest test. The larger risk is resistance. The World Health Organization (WHO 2025) reports that cases rose to 282 million and deaths to 610,000 in 2024, and names drug resistance a key threat. If nets and drugs lose power, future returns will fall below the trial-based estimates. That risk has no ratio, so it is noted rather than used to set the range.

The verdict turns on how lives are valued and on the cost of raising the money. The low end comes from Hallett et al.'s portfolio figure of $19 per $1, cut by overhead and by nearly $2 of deadweight for each $1 of tax, giving 5.81. If the direct-economic figure of $3.50 were the right measure, the ratio would drop to the low single digits and out of the Excellent tier. Seasonal chemoprevention could lift it. GiveWell puts its cost at about $4,000 per life saved, against $5,500 for nets, but it has no published benefit-cost ratio.

24.policy: Close the most harmful vitamin and mineral gaps in poor countries. Add iron, zinc and vitamin A to staple foods such as flour, and iodine to salt. Give pregnant women a daily multiple-micronutrient tablet in place of iron and folic acid alone, with calcium. Give young children vitamin A capsules. The costed package, focused on South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, costs about $0.5 billion a year.
24.why_on_list: It is a health "best buy" for the Copenhagen Consensus Center and GiveWell, with support from the Disease Control Priorities project (third edition, DCP3).
24.evidence: Micronutrients cost cents to a few dollars per person a year, and the returns are large. Larsen, Hoddinott and Razvi (2023) find that switching pregnant women from iron and folic acid to multiple micronutrients returns 37.5 per $1 at an 8% discount rate. Adding calcium gives 18.6 to 23.9. Fortifying flour with iron returns 8 at a 3% discount rate and 7 at 6% (Horton, Alderman and Rivera 2008). Iodizing salt returns 30 at 3%, falling to 12 at 6%. Horton and Ross (2003) find a median of 6 across 10 countries for iron fortification when only physical productivity is counted, and 36 when cognitive gains are added. For vitamin A, a Cochrane review found "a 12% observed reduction in the risk of all-cause mortality" for children given supplements (Imdad et al. 2022). GiveWell (2025) estimates about $3,500 per life saved for vitamin A supplements, among its most cost-effective programmes. The main uncertainty is whether old gains still hold where deficiency has fallen. After adding the overhead of the donor channel, the ratio runs from $5.6 to $35 per $1. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $1.85 to $26.20 per $1.
24.ratio:
The ratio compares gains in survival, health and future earnings with the cost of nutrients and their delivery. The source costs already include delivery inside each country, so only the overhead of the international funding channel is added. United Nations (UN) agencies charge 8% on earmarked donor funds and 7% on thematic funds (Executive Boards 2018).

**Low end (5.6).** Horton and Ross (2003) find a median ratio of 6 for iron fortification, counting only gains in physical productivity.

- Ratio at the higher overhead rate: 6 ÷ 1.08 = 5.6.

**High end (35).** Larsen, Hoddinott and Razvi (2023) find 37.5 for multiple micronutrients in pregnancy, at an 8% discount rate.

- Ratio at the lower overhead rate: 37.5 ÷ 1.07 = 35.0.

**Cost.** Programme $0.5 billion + channel overhead $0.04 billion + household cost $0 = $0.54 billion a year.

The adjustment touches costs only; benefits are left as published. Other figures fall inside the range. The Copenhagen Consensus scale-up figures for South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa give iron flour fortification $1,336 million of benefits for $167 million of cost: 1,336 ÷ 167 = 8.0. Salt iodization gives $570 million for $19 million: 570 ÷ 19 = 30. The Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition (GAIN 2019) puts fortification overall at 27 per $1. The whole Copenhagen Consensus nutrition package scores 18.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. The whole cost behind the ratio is public spending. Low end: 5.56 ÷ 3.00 = 1.85. High end: 35.05 ÷ 1.34 = 26.2. **Range after tax finance: 1.85 to 26.2.**
24.cost:
The full cost is $0.54 billion a year.

- **Programme: $0.5 billion.** The sum of the costed parts. Iron flour fortification at 50% coverage costs $167 million a year, and salt iodization at 80% coverage $19 million (Copenhagen Consensus Center, n.d.). Multiple micronutrients for pregnant women cost about $84 million a year and calcium about $216 million (Larsen, Hoddinott and Razvi 2023). Total: 0.167 + 0.019 + 0.084 + 0.216 = 0.486, rounded to $0.5 billion.
- **Channel overhead: $0.04 billion.** The standard UN cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor money. At the higher rate: 0.5 × 0.080 = 0.04.
- **Household cost: none added.** The fortification figures are total resource costs, including the share borne by millers and salt producers.

Fortification is very cheap: about $0.05 per person per year for iodine and $0.12 for iron. Horton, Alderman and Rivera (2008) note that the actual ingredients are "only about 20% of this total"; the rest is equipment and processing. Delivering supplements through antenatal care adds $0.50 to $1.45 per pregnant woman. Two items are not costed: zinc and vitamin A in fortification, and wider vitamin A capsule coverage at about $2 per child per year (GiveWell 2025). Much of the fortification cost falls on millers and is passed on to consumers.
24.strength: Grade: A. Peer-reviewed benefit-cost studies support the policy (Larsen, Hoddinott and Razvi 2023; Horton and Ross 2003). They rest on randomized trials and meta-analyses. The Cochrane review of vitamin A pooled 19 mortality trials with about 1.2 million children and rated the evidence high-certainty (Imdad et al. 2022). It falls short of A+ for two reasons. The largest single vitamin A trial found no significant effect on deaths, and no benefit-cost study covers the exact iron, zinc and vitamin A fortification bundle.
24.difficulty: Rating: easy. A single health ministry or food regulator can require fortification under existing food-standards law. More than 60 countries already have iodized salt in at least 70% of households. Supplements in pregnancy and vitamin A capsules move through existing antenatal care and child-health days, and one donor or ministry can pay for them. The total bill is about $0.5 billion a year.
24.who_benefits: Rating: pro-poor. Deficiency is concentrated in poor households that rely on cheap staples with few nutrients. Eighty percent of undernourished children live in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. Supplements for mothers and children run through public programmes that reach low-income families. Donors and governments pay for supplements. For fortification, millers pay at first and pass a small cost on to consumers.
24.counter:
The largest single trial is the main counter-evidence. DEVTA, which gave vitamin A to preschool children in north India, found a mortality ratio of 0.96, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.89 to 1.03, which is not statistically significant (Awasthi et al. 2013). It suggests the benefit may now be smaller where deficiency and child deaths have fallen. DEVTA is already pooled in the Cochrane estimate of 12% lower child mortality (Imdad et al. 2022), so it lowers the grade rather than setting the range. The Post-2015 Consensus panel put reducing child malnutrition at $45 per $1, but that covers a wider stunting package, including feeding and deworming, not micronutrients alone.

The verdict depends on which nutrients are delivered and what they are credited with. Multiple micronutrient supplements for pregnant women return 37.5 (Larsen, Hoddinott and Razvi 2023), and salt iodization about 30. Iron fortification counted on physical productivity alone returns 6, the source of the low end; with cognitive benefits it reaches 36 (Horton and Ross 2003). If a programme leaned on iron fortification and its cognitive gains did not materialise, the result would fall toward the low end of 1.85, in the Mid tier, after overhead and the cost of raising taxes. If those gains hold, the low end rises with them.

25.policy: Raise excise taxes on cigarettes and alcohol in low-income and lower-middle-income countries. Higher prices cut smoking and heavy drinking, especially among the young and the poor, and raise revenue. This is a rule, not a spending programme. The only real costs are collecting the tax, policing smuggling and marking legal packs.
25.why_on_list: It is a health "best buy" for the Copenhagen Consensus Center, the Disease Control Priorities project (third edition, DCP3) and the World Health Organization (WHO) Best Buys list for noncommunicable diseases.
25.evidence: Price is the strongest lever on tobacco use. Jha and Peto (2014) put the price elasticity of cigarettes at about -0.4: doubling the real price cuts smoking by about a third and still raises revenue. For alcohol, a meta-analysis of 112 studies finds an elasticity of -0.51 (Wagenaar, Salois and Komro 2009). Watkins, Ahmed and Pickersgill (2023) find that tobacco excise taxes return 100 per $1 in lower-middle-income countries and alcohol taxes 53 in low-income countries. In India alone, they estimate $35 billion of benefits and 910,000 lives saved for an implementation cost of $5.7 million a year. WHO (2018) counts only output and averted health spending and finds $7.43 per $1 for tobacco and $9.13 for alcohol. The big uncertainty is how to treat the pleasure smokers give up. Ignoring it, the tobacco ratio reaches 620 to 1,300; counting it, about 100. The low end of 2.9 adds generous costs for collection, enforcement and secure tax stamps, and assumes smuggling eats 10% of the health gain. Even then, benefits exceed costs. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $1.47 to $98.20 per $1.
25.ratio:
The ratio compares health gains with the real resource costs of the tax. Tax revenue itself is a transfer from smokers and drinkers to government, not a benefit or a cost.

**High end (100).** Watkins, Ahmed and Pickersgill (2023), from their replication data, at an 8% discount rate for 2023-2030 across low-income and lower-middle-income countries:

- Tobacco tax benefits: $51.31 billion.
- Costs: implementation $0.045 billion + a charge for pleasure smokers forgo $0.462 billion = $0.507 billion.
- Ratio: 51.31 ÷ 0.507 = 101.2. The published headline, 100, sets the high end.
- Alcohol tax, for comparison: 2.94 ÷ (0.029 + 0.026) = 53.3.

**Low end (2.9).** Start from the same base case and make it harsher.

- Benefits cut by 10% for illicit cigarettes: 0.9 × 51.31 = 46.18.
- Add the upper-bound yearly costs of collection ($0.80 billion), enforcement ($0.45 billion) and secure stamps ($1.21 billion), or $2.46 billion a year, over eight years using an annuity factor of 6.206.
- Costs: 0.045 + 0.462 + 6.206 × 2.46 = 15.79.
- Ratio: 46.18 ÷ 15.79 = 2.9.

**Cost.** Public outlay $0 + administration and enforcement $1.26 billion + industry compliance $1.21 billion = $2.47 billion a year.

Other estimates fall inside the range. WHO (2018) gives 7.43 for tobacco and 9.13 for alcohol. The Post-2015 Consensus panel put "increase tobacco prices 125%" at $22 per $1, and Nugent (2015) gave tobacco taxes 10 to 52. The paper's text describes a larger charge for forgone pleasure than its code applies. Applying a full 90% offset would give 0.1 × 1,134 = 113, still above 101, so the high end is not overstated.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted, an extra $0.34 to $2.00 (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. Consumers' lost enjoyment and the tax stamps the industry pays for are private costs. The public costs are implementation and, at the low end, tax collection ($0.80 billion a year) and enforcement against illicit trade ($0.45 billion a year). They are 0.494 of the cost at the low end and 0.0888 at the high end. Low end: 2.92 ÷ (1 + 2.0 × 0.494) = 1.47. High end: 101.2 ÷ (1 + 0.34 × 0.0888) = 98.2. **Range after tax finance: 1.47 to 98.2.**
25.cost:
The full cost is $2.47 billion a year, an upper bound for low-income and lower-middle-income countries.

- **Public outlay: $0.** The tax raises money rather than spending it.
- **Administration and enforcement: $1.26 billion.** Three parts. First, implementing the tax increases: $0.0739 billion in present value ÷ 6.206 = $0.012 billion a year (Watkins, Ahmed and Pickersgill 2023). Second, collection, using the WHO (2021) ratio for lower-middle-income countries of 1.6 per 100 collected, applied to India's projected $50 billion a year of extra tobacco revenue: 0.016 × 50 = $0.80 billion. Third, enforcement against smuggling at about 0.9% of revenue, the United Kingdom ratio of roughly £90 million a year of enforcement staff against about £10 billion of tobacco revenue (World Bank Group 2019): 0.009 × 50 = $0.45 billion.
- **Industry compliance: $1.21 billion.** Encrypted tax stamps paid by industry. The extra cost per 1,000 packs rises from $0.42 to $8.20 (WHO 2021), applied to about 155.6 billion packs a year. That pack count scales world consumption of about 6 trillion cigarettes by the population share of these countries, 4.065 billion of 7.837 billion.

Each part is an upper bound. Average collection and enforcement ratios overstate the marginal cost of raising an existing tax. India's $5.7 million a year shows how small that marginal cost can be. Alcohol taxes cost less than I$0.10 per person to implement (Chisholm et al. 2018). Many smokers in these countries use bidis or smokeless tobacco, so the stamp cost is also high. Revenue lost to smuggling, $40 to $50 billion a year worldwide, is a transfer and is not counted.
25.strength: Grade: A. Peer-reviewed benefit-cost studies support the policy (Watkins, Ahmed and Pickersgill 2023; Bertram et al. 2018, which underlies the WHO returns). The health effects rest on price elasticities from meta-analyses of many quasi-experimental and econometric studies (Wagenaar, Salois and Komro 2009; Jha and Peto 2014). It falls short of A+ for two reasons. The ratio swings from about 100 to 1,300 depending on how forgone pleasure is treated, and there are no randomized trials.
25.difficulty: Rating: moderate. Each country needs only an ordinary tax law, and there are many precedents. The Philippines, Turkey and South Africa have all raised tobacco excise sharply. The obstacles are political. In 2018 only 38 countries, covering 14% of the world's population, had sufficiently high tobacco taxes (WHO 2021). WHO names tobacco industry interference as a major stumbling block. Fears of smuggling are the other common objection.
25.who_benefits: Rating: pro-poor. The poor quit more when prices rise, so they gain the most health. Among 500 million male smokers in 13 middle-income countries, a 50% price rise would give the poorest fifth 6.7 times more years of life than the richest fifth (Global Tobacco Economics Consortium 2018). It would keep 8.8 million men out of extreme poverty. The same study finds that "the bottom income group would get 31% of the life years saved and 29% each of the averted disease costs and averted catastrophic health expenditures, while paying only 10% of the additional taxes." Poor smokers who do not quit still pay more. As a share of cash spending, the tax falls hardest on them (Remler 2004).
25.counter:
The counter-evidence suggests the ratio could be higher still. Watkins, Ahmed and Pickersgill (2023) report tobacco tax ratios of 620 in low-income and 1,300 in lower-middle-income countries when smokers' lost enjoyment is not counted as a cost. Their own headline keeps that charge, and the range follows them. Remler (2004) raises a different objection: cigarette taxes heavily burden poor smokers who do not quit, whatever measure is used. That does not change the ratio, but it qualifies the pro-poor label. On health gains, the poorest 20% still gain 6.7 times more life-years than the richest 20% (Global Tobacco Economics Consortium 2018).

The low end depends on enforcement costs. It subtracts 10% of the health gain for smuggling and adds upper-bound collection, enforcement and secure-stamp costs of $2.46 billion a year. With only the published implementation costs, the ratio is about 100; with the upper-bound costs it falls to 2.9, and to 1.47 once the cost of raising the taxes that pay for collection and enforcement is counted. Where these costs land decides whether the tax sits in the Mid tier or near the top of the list. A large rise in smuggling would push it lower, but the World Bank Group (2019) finds that "tax increases do not necessarily lead to substantial and sustained increases in illicit tobacco consumption".

26.policy: Give schoolchildren in areas with intestinal worms a cheap pill once or twice a year, delivered through their schools. No child is tested first. Everyone in the school is treated. The aim is to reach most of the 870 million children at risk of worm infection in low- and middle-income countries.
26.why_on_list: It is one of the health "best buys" named by the Copenhagen Consensus Center and by the development-economics handbook Disease Control Priorities, third edition (DCP3).
26.evidence: Intestinal worms sap children's nutrition and keep them out of school. The best evidence comes from the Primary School Deworming Project in Kenya, a randomized trial that phased treatment into schools and then followed the children for two decades. Ten years on, Baird et al. (2016) found that men who had been eligible as boys "work 17% more hours each week, spend more time in non-agricultural self-employment, are more likely to hold manufacturing jobs, and miss one fewer meal per week." The twenty-year follow-up by Hamory et al. (2021) puts the annualised social internal rate of return at 37%. DCP3 reads the Kenyan results as long-run benefits worth more than 100 times the cost (Ahuja et al. 2017). The Copenhagen Consensus best-practice paper is far more cautious: about $6 of benefit per $1 for preschool children (Hall and Horton 2008). The gap between those two numbers is the uncertainty. The wider trial record is disputed, and a Cochrane review finds little effect on short-run nutrition and school outcomes. The ratio therefore runs from a conservative $6 to $100 per $1, on a programme that costs under $0.3bn a year. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $2 to $74.60 per $1.
26.ratio:
Low end. Hall and Horton (2008) find that for pre-school children "each dollar spent results in about $6 of benefits." Ratio: 6.

High end. DCP3 reports the net present value of the long-run educational and economic benefits from the Kenyan trial as more than 100 times the cost (Ahuja et al. 2017). Ratio: 100.

Cost. About $0.30 per child per treatment. Treating most of the 870 million at-risk children costs under $0.3bn a year. No overhead is added, because delivery through schools is already inside the per-treatment cost and the drugs are largely donated.

Result: $6 to $100 per $1, at a full cost of $0.3bn a year.

Cross-checks. Hall and Horton (2008) also say that in high-infection countries the benefits can be up to 60 times the costs. DCP3 gives an annualised internal rate of return of 32% to 51%, depending on whether health spillovers are counted (Ahuja et al. 2017). Baird et al. (2016) estimate a conservative financial internal rate of return of 32%. Hamory et al. (2021) give a conservative annualised social internal rate of return of 37%: 40.7% on earnings gains and 36.7% on consumption gains. At a 10% discount rate, the social net present value is US$ PPP (purchasing power parity) 230.71 on earnings and 467.90 on consumption per child. All of these sit inside the range.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. The whole cost behind the ratio is public spending. Low end: 6 ÷ 3.00 = 2.0. High end: 100 ÷ 1.34 = 74.6. **Range after tax finance: 2 to 74.6.**
26.cost: The full cost is about $0.3bn a year, all of it public outlay. DCP3 puts school-based treatment at about $0.30 per child per treatment, including delivery costs, and estimates that most of the 870 million at-risk children could be treated for less than $300 million a year (Ahuja et al. 2017). The two standard drugs, albendazole and mebendazole, are donated to national health ministries through the World Health Organization (WHO) for all school-age children in endemic countries (WHO 2023). Hall and Horton (2008) give an even lower delivery cost, 15 to 25 cents a round. No administrative overhead or private cost is added.
26.strength: Grade B+. The high end rests on a long-run cluster-randomized trial with peer-reviewed economic returns (Baird et al. 2016; Hamory et al. 2021). The low end rests on a Copenhagen Consensus best-practice paper. The grade is not an A because the wider trial evidence is contested. A Cochrane review of mass treatment finds no clear gain in many short-run outcomes. The long-run Kenyan results are strong but come mainly from one setting.
26.difficulty: Easy. Schools already exist. Treatment happens once or twice a year. The pills are cheap and largely donated. WHO recommends periodic treatment for all at-risk people in endemic areas without testing each person first (WHO 2023). That removes the need to diagnose each child.
26.who_benefits: The gains go to the poor. The children treated live in poor, high-infection areas. In the Kenyan trial the benefits showed up years later as higher earnings and consumption for the same children as adults. Males in treatment schools ate one more meal per week on average (Baird et al. 2016). WHO counts 654 million school-age children living where these parasites are intensively transmitted (WHO 2023). The cost falls on health budgets and donors, and it is small.
26.counter:
The Cochrane review is the main counter-evidence. Taylor-Robinson et al. (2015) conclude that "there is quite substantial evidence that deworming programmes do not show benefit in terms of average nutritional status, haemoglobin, cognition, school performance, or death." The review covers short-run outcomes, so it is left out of the range. It is the reason the low end uses the conservative Copenhagen figure of $6 per $1 for preschool children rather than the long-run trial returns.

The verdict rests on one long-run trial in Kenya. Its 20-year follow-up finds an annualised social return of 37% (Hamory et al. 2021), and benefits more than 100 times the cost (Ahuja et al. 2017). Whether those adult earnings gains repeat in other places, with different worm loads, is the open question. If they did not, the case would fall back on the Copenhagen figure, which is 2.0 after the cost of raising taxes, at the bottom of the Good tier. If they do, deworming stays among the best buys on the list.

27.policy: Fund modern contraception, including pills, injectables, implants, intrauterine devices and counselling, for the roughly 214 million women in poor countries who want to avoid pregnancy but are not using a modern method. The cost is about $3.6bn a year. A sub-policy, paying for girls to finish secondary school, is assessed alongside it but kept out of the headline ratio.
27.why_on_list: It is one of the health "best buys" named by the Copenhagen Consensus Center and by Disease Control Priorities, third edition (DCP3).
27.evidence: Kohler and Behrman (2015) estimate that universal access to contraception would mean 640,000 fewer newborn deaths, 150,000 fewer maternal deaths and 600,000 fewer children losing their mothers each year (Lomborg 2019). Counting health alone, each dollar returns about $40. Adding a demographic dividend from smaller families, worth $288 billion a year, brings the total to $120 per $1. A later peer-reviewed study across 55 low- and lower-middle-income countries, at an 8% discount rate, finds $22 per $1 for family planning alone (Madise et al. 2023). Ghana's national study lands in between: 33.6 for married women and 29.3 for unmarried women (Amporfu et al. 2020). The spread comes from two choices: how much of the demographic dividend to count, and which discount rate to use. Real-world programmes back the mechanism. In Matlab, Bangladesh, an outreach programme cut fertility by about 17% for some two decades, with better health for women and children (Joshi and Schultz 2013). In Colombia, "family planning explains only about 10% of Colombia's fertility decline," yet it let women postpone first births, study longer and work more (Miller 2010). The schooling sub-policy has its own randomized trial in Ghana, where scholarships delayed childbearing and cut infant deaths sharply. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $6.79 to $83.70 per $1.
27.ratio:
Low end. Madise et al. (2023) give a benefit-cost ratio of 22 for the family planning package alone. The programme cost already includes country-level delivery and management, so only the overhead of the international donor channel is added. The United Nations (UN) standard cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor funds is 8% (Executive Boards of UNDP/UNFPA/UNOPS, UNICEF and UN-Women 2018). Ratio: 22 ÷ 1.08 = 20.4.

High end. Kohler and Behrman (2015) give $120 per $1 for eliminating unmet need for modern contraception. The lower UN overhead rate for thematic contributions, 7%, is used here. Ratio: 120 ÷ 1.07 = 112.1, rounded to 112.

Cost. Programme spending: $3.6bn. Donor-channel overhead: 3.6 × 0.080 = $0.29bn. Household cost: not separately costed. Full cost: 3.6 + 0.29 = $3.89bn a year.

Result: $20.4 to $112 per $1, at a full cost of $3.89bn a year. The adjustment changes costs only, not benefits.

Cross-checks. The health-only figure of $40 per $1 and the Ghana results of 33.6 and 29.3 all sit inside the range. The schooling sub-policy returns less. The Ghana trial gives a conservative $4.1 per $1 of long-run government cost (Duflo et al. 2026), and Copenhagen work puts secondary completion at about $4 and girls' schooling and later-marriage programmes at about $5 (Psacharopoulos 2015; Copenhagen Consensus Center 2015). Bundled in at its cost, about $15bn a year, the combined ratio would fall to roughly (3.6 × 22 + 15 × 4.1) ÷ 18.6 = 7.6 at the low end and (3.6 × 120 + 15 × 10) ÷ 18.6 = 31 at the high end. The 10 is the bottom of the 10 to 110 times range reported when scholarships are targeted at girls (Duflo et al. 2024). That is why the sub-policy is kept separate.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. The whole cost behind the ratio is public spending. Low end: 20.37 ÷ 3.00 = 6.79. High end: 112.1 ÷ 1.34 = 83.7. **Range after tax finance: 6.79 to 83.7.**
27.cost:
The full cost is about $3.89bn a year. The $3.6bn comes from Kohler and Behrman, as reported by Lomborg (2019), and rests on the Guttmacher Institute's "Adding It Up" costing. That method adds programme and system costs to the direct cost of services: programme management, staff supervision, monitoring and evaluation, training, outreach, supply systems and health information systems (Sully et al. 2020). Madise et al. (2023) likewise cost staff, consumables, overheads and supervision. The added $0.29bn is the donor channel's own overhead at the UN cost-recovery rate. Users' travel and time are not separately costed in these sources. For scale, donor funding for family planning was about $1.27 billion in 2017 (Lomborg 2019).

The schooling sub-policy is costed apart and left out. Four years of senior high school cost about $505 per girl, including forgone wages, or about $126 a year (Duflo et al. 2024). Across 122 million out-of-school girls (UNESCO 2024), that is about $15bn a year. This is an upper bound, since many of those girls are of primary age.
27.strength: Grade A. The low end is a peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimate (Madise et al. 2023). It agrees with the Copenhagen Post-2015 work and the Ghana study. Quasi-experimental evidence from Bangladesh and Colombia shows that access to family planning changes fertility, health and women's lives (Joshi and Schultz 2013; Miller 2010). The schooling sub-policy rests on a randomized trial of 2,064 youths, now followed for 15 years (Duflo, Dupas and Kremer 2021; Duflo et al. 2026).
27.difficulty: Moderate. The policy needs a sustained scale-up in funding. The target is about $3.6bn a year. Donor funding was around $1.27 billion in 2017, below its 2014 peak of $1.43 billion (Lomborg 2019). Working models exist, such as the Matlab outreach programme in Bangladesh and Profamilia in Colombia. The schooling sub-policy is a larger, budget-heavy build-out, though Ghana's scholarships provide a tested model.
27.who_benefits: The gains go mainly to the poor. Unmet need is concentrated among poorer women in high-fertility, low-income countries. The 55 countries in Madise et al. (2023) are all low- or lower-middle-income. Matlab showed long-run gains for women's and children's health in rural Bangladesh (Joshi and Schultz 2013). In Ghana the scholarships were means-tested. Female recipients earned 20% to 30% more (J-PAL 2024), and the trial reports that "This represents a halving of under-one and under-three mortality in our sample" among their children (Duflo et al. 2026). Governments and donors pay.
27.counter:
Pritchett (1994) argues that women's desired family size, not access to contraception, explains most of the difference in fertility between countries. If so, supplying contraception would do less to cut births, and the demographic dividend would shrink. That dividend is most of the $120 per $1 figure; health benefits alone are worth about $40 per $1 (Lomborg 2019). The study gives no benefit-cost ratio, which is why the low end rests on the much lower 22 of Madise et al. (2023). The Matlab programme in Bangladesh points the other way: fertility stayed about 17% lower for two decades, with better health for women and children (Joshi and Schultz 2013).

The verdict turns on the dividend and on scope. If Pritchett is right and the dividend is close to zero, the health benefit of about $40 per $1 still clears the Excellent threshold before the cost of raising taxes. Bundling girls' secondary education into the policy would lower it, because schooling returns about $4.1 per $1 (Duflo, Dupas, Spelke and Walsh 2026); the combined ratio would fall to roughly 7.6 to 31. Only the narrow family-planning package, valued at an 8% discount and funded at nearly $2 of deadweight per $1 of tax, brings the low end down to 6.79, in the Good tier.

28.policy: Upgrade basic hospitals and health centres in 55 low- and lower-middle-income countries so that every birth has trained staff, clean delivery, drugs to stop bleeding, antibiotics, newborn resuscitation and steroids for preterm labour. Coverage of basic emergency obstetric and newborn care rises from 68% to 90%. The policy covers care at birth in facilities only. Family planning is counted separately under policy 27.
28.why_on_list: It is one of the health "best buys" named by the Copenhagen Consensus Center and by Disease Control Priorities, third edition (DCP3).
28.evidence: Most of the gain is newborn lives. The best estimate comes from a peer-reviewed benefit-cost analysis across 55 low- and lower-middle-income countries (Madise et al. 2023). It finds $83 of benefit per $1 for basic emergency obstetric and newborn care alone. Adding caesarean capability, the comprehensive package, gives $65 per $1. The wider bundle that also includes family planning would avert 161,000 maternal deaths and 1.2 million newborn deaths a year. In that bundle, "Newborn lives saved generates the largest welfare impact by far, with an estimated benefit of $238 billion per year" (Madise et al. 2023). The intervention effects come from the trial-based evidence collected in the Lancet Every Newborn series. That series finds that existing interventions could avert 71% of neonatal deaths, most of them through better care at birth in facilities (Bhutta et al. 2014). The title's 65% target sits inside that evidence: Madise's 1.2 million averted out of 2.16 million neonatal deaths is about 56%, and Bhutta's full coverage reaches 71%. The often-quoted ratio of 87 is left out because it includes family planning and its demographic dividend. The result is a narrow range of 62 to 80. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $28.50 to $66.50 per $1.
28.ratio:
Low end. Madise et al. (2023) give 65 for comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care. The source cost already includes country-level delivery and management, so only the international donor channel's overhead is added. The United Nations (UN) standard cost-recovery charge on earmarked donor funds is 8% (Executive Boards of UNDP/UNFPA/UNOPS, UNICEF and UN-Women 2018). It applies only to the financial share of the cost, 2.8 ÷ 4.9 = 0.571. The rest is mothers' time. Ratio: 65 ÷ (1 + 0.08 × 0.571) = 62.2, rounded to 62.

High end. Madise et al. (2023) give 83 for basic emergency obstetric and newborn care alone. The lower UN rate of 7% is used. Ratio: 83 ÷ (1 + 0.07 × 0.571) = 79.8, rounded to 80.

Cost. Public outlay: $2.4bn. Donor-channel overhead: 2.4 × 0.080 = $0.19bn. Mothers' time: $2.1bn. Full cost: 2.4 + 0.19 + 2.1 = $4.69bn a year.

Result: $62 to $80 per $1, at a full cost of $4.69bn a year. The adjustment changes costs only, not benefits.

Cross-checks. Benefits are valued at $2,983 per statistical life-year, the project standard for these countries. The study uses an 8% discount rate (Lomborg 2023b). If stillbirths averted were valued like newborn deaths, the bundle's ratio would rise to 159 (Madise et al. 2023). Bhutta et al. (2014) put universal coverage at an incremental running cost of $5.65 billion a year, of which $3.66 billion is facility-based care.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted, an extra $0.34 to $2.00 (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. Only the financial share of the cost (0.571, plus its overhead) is paid from taxes; mothers' time is not. Low end: 65 ÷ (1 + 0.08 × 0.571 + 2.0 × 0.571 × 1.08) = 65 ÷ 2.2790 = 28.5. High end: 83 ÷ (1 + 0.07 × 0.571 + 0.34 × 0.571 × 1.07) = 83 ÷ 1.2477 = 66.5. **Range after tax finance: 28.5 to 66.5.**
28.cost: The full cost is about $4.69bn a year. The Copenhagen Consensus puts the maternal and newborn package at $4.9bn a year for 2023 to 2030, including $2.1bn for mothers' time (Lomborg 2023a; Copenhagen Consensus Center 2025). That leaves $2.8bn of financial cost for governments and donors. The package includes family planning. Madise et al. (2023) cost that part at 68.6 million extra women times $6.43 each ($2.89 drugs, $2.14 staff, $0.65 hospital, $0.75 supervision), about $0.44bn a year. Facility care alone is therefore about $2.8bn - $0.4bn = $2.4bn a year. This is approximate, because it mixes 2020 and 2023 dollars. The costing includes staff, consumables, equipment and overheads, a 15% supervision add-on, mothers' travel and demand-generation payments. The $0.19bn is the donor channel's own overhead. Mothers' time, $2.1bn, is an upper bound, since it also covers family planning users.
28.strength: Grade A. The ratios come from a peer-reviewed benefit-cost analysis (Madise et al. 2023), summarised in the same journal issue (Lomborg 2023b). Its intervention effects come from the trial-based Lives Saved Tool evidence in the Lancet Every Newborn series (Bhutta et al. 2014). Two well-defined packages, scored with one consistent method, give a narrow range.
28.difficulty: Moderate. This is a health-system build-out, not a single switch. Birth facilities in 55 countries need staff, equipment and supplies. In the 37 countries where fewer than 70% of births happen in facilities, the costing adds a cash incentive for facility births, modelled on India's Janani Suraksha Yojana programme (Madise et al. 2023). Precedent exists. Sustained government and donor funding is the hard part.
28.who_benefits: The gains go to the poor. The 55 countries carry around 90% of the world's maternal and neonatal deaths (Madise et al. 2023). In 2019, low- and lower-middle-income countries alone saw 2.16 million neonatal deaths and 275,000 maternal deaths. The welfare loss from these deaths is about 5.5% of those countries' gross domestic product (GDP). Mothers and newborns gain most. Governments and donors pay the financial cost, and mothers give time to travel to and stay at facilities.
28.counter:
Broader packages score lower. Madise et al. (2023) find 36 for the entire continuum of care, 7 for antenatal care and 6 for care around conception. Stenberg et al. (2014) find that an extra $5 per person per year across 74 high-burden countries, about $30 billion a year, yields up to nine times its value. Both are left out because they cover far wider scopes than facility obstetric and newborn care. The headline 87 is left out too, because it includes family planning, scored as policy 27, and its demographic dividend. Valuing stillbirths averted would push the other way, raising the bundle's ratio to 159.

No plausible finding moves this policy out of the top tier. Even comprehensive emergency care at 65, after overhead and nearly $2 of deadweight for each $1 of tax, gives 28.5. Only a much smaller health gain than modelled could pull it below 10. The model's gain is not out of line with the wider evidence. Madise's 1.2 million averted newborn deaths are about 56% of neonatal deaths in these countries, below the 71% that Bhutta et al. (2014) find universal coverage of existing interventions could avert.

29.policy: Find and treat far more tuberculosis (TB) cases in low- and lower-middle-income countries. The package follows the Stop TB Partnership's Global Plan for 2023 to 2030: rapid molecular tests, screening of high-risk groups, full treatment courses, prevention for contacts of patients, and work with private clinics. It does not depend on new vaccines.
29.why_on_list: It is one of the health "best buys" named by the Copenhagen Consensus Center and by Disease Control Priorities, third edition (DCP3).
29.evidence: TB still kills over 1.2 million people a year (World Health Organization 2025). Standard diagnosis and treatment work: national programmes already cure 88% of drug-susceptible cases. The problem is reach and money. A peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus study models the full Global Plan against current trends (Pretorius et al. 2023). Incremental costs come to $56.4 billion and benefits to $2,595 billion, in present value at an 8% discount rate, with effects counted to 2050. That gives a benefit-cost ratio (BCR) of 46.0. The plan would avert 27.3 million deaths between 2023 and 2050, about 1 million a year, at $2,063 per death averted. The authors test other baselines, discount rates and cost assumptions and report that these "still yield robustly high BCRs, in the range of 28–84" (Pretorius et al. 2023). An earlier Copenhagen study of a similar target found $43 per $1 (Vassall 2015). After adding donor overhead, the range is 26 to 79. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $9.54 to $61.70 per $1.
29.ratio:
Low end. The lowest case in Pretorius et al. (2023) includes new vaccines and their research and development costs: 27.7. The study's costs already include country-level delivery and programme management, so only the overhead of the international donor channel is added. The rate is the Global Fund's operating expenses as a share of grant spending: 9.0% in 2023 (Global Fund 2025). It applies to the financed share of the cost, 5.2 ÷ 6.2 = 0.839. Ratio: 27.7 ÷ (1 + 0.090 × 0.839) = 25.8, rounded to 26.

High end. The highest case measures the plan against a baseline that includes COVID-19 disruption, at a 5% discount rate: 83.9. The lower Global Fund rate of 6.7% (2024) is used. Ratio: 83.9 ÷ (1 + 0.067 × 0.839) = 79.4, rounded to 79.

Cost. Public outlay: $5.2bn. Donor-channel overhead: 5.2 × 0.090 = $0.47bn. Non-financial "enabler" cost borne by patients and households: $1.0bn. Full cost: 5.2 + 0.47 + 1.0 = $6.67bn a year.

Result: $26 to $79 per $1, at a full cost of $6.67bn a year. The adjustment changes costs only, not benefits.

Cross-checks. Other cells in the study fall inside the range: 55.4 at a 5% discount rate, 36.6 at 12%, 34.0 with research and development costs, and 71.0 against the disruption baseline. Vassall (2015) costed a target of 95% fewer TB deaths and 90% lower incidence at $8.1bn a year, with annual benefits of $344,647 million and a ratio of $43 per $1, saving about 1.3 million lives a year.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted, an extra $0.34 to $2.00 (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. Only the financed share of the cost (0.839, plus its overhead) is paid from taxes; the $1.0 billion of non-financial enabler cost is not. Low end: 27.7 ÷ (1 + 0.090 × 0.839 + 2.0 × 0.839 × 1.090) = 27.7 ÷ 2.9045 = 9.54. High end: 83.9 ÷ (1 + 0.067 × 0.839 + 0.34 × 0.839 × 1.067) = 83.9 ÷ 1.3606 = 61.7. **Range after tax finance: 9.54 to 61.7.**
29.cost: The full cost is about $6.67bn a year. The Copenhagen Consensus lists TB at a total cost of $6.2bn a year for 2023 to 2030, of which $1.0bn is a non-financial enabler cost (Lomborg 2023). Governments and donors must therefore finance $5.2bn a year. This matches the year-by-year costs in Pretorius et al. (2023): $4.4 billion in 2023, a peak of $7.1 billion in 2027, and $5.2 billion in 2030. Those costs include health-system costs and programme costs, with programme costs set as a 70% markup on direct service costs, based on spending data reported to the World Health Organization (WHO). The added $0.47bn is the donor channel's own overhead.
29.strength: Grade A. The range comes from a peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus benefit-cost analysis (Pretorius et al. 2023). It agrees with the earlier Copenhagen estimate of 43 and with the positive, older World Bank estimates. The health effects rest on the trial-established efficacy of standard TB drugs and diagnostics.
29.difficulty: Moderate. The machinery exists. In 2024, 8.3 million people were newly diagnosed and treated, about 78% of those who fell ill (World Health Organization 2025). Money is the gap. As WHO puts it, "only US$5.9 billion was available for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment--just over a quarter of the US$22 billion annual target set for 2027" (World Health Organization 2025). Closing it needs a sustained funding scale-up, not a new invention.
29.who_benefits: The gains go to the poor. TB affected an estimated 10.7 million people in 2024 (World Health Organization 2025). Its deaths are concentrated in low- and lower-middle-income countries, and the roughly 1 million deaths averted each year in the model are all in those countries (Pretorius et al. 2023). Governments and donors pay the financial cost. Patients and families bear the non-financial enabler cost.
29.counter:
The older World Bank estimate is lower. Laxminarayan et al. (2007) found that the benefits of the earlier Global Plan to Stop TB, for tuberculosis (TB), exceeded costs by a factor of 15 in 22 high-burden countries and 9 in the Africa region. It is left out of the range because it covers an older plan with older costs and values benefits differently from the 8% discount standard used across this block. It still confirms that TB control pays. The newer results come from a model, depend on the plan being fully funded, and assume programmes deliver at scale. In 2024 only $5.9 billion was available against a target of $22 billion a year by 2027 (World Health Organization 2025).

The low end, 9.54, sits just below the Excellent threshold. It uses the paper's lowest sensitivity case, 27.7 with vaccine and research costs included, and nearly $2 of deadweight for each $1 of tax. If the main specification of 46.0 held instead, the low end would sit well above 10. If programmes delivered only the older World Bank returns of 9 to 15, before overhead and the cost of raising taxes, the policy would fall to the Good tier.

30.policy: Offer free, voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) to HIV-negative adult men in the Southern African countries with the highest HIV rates. The target is 90% coverage in the five hyperendemic countries, those where more than 15% of adults have HIV: Botswana, Lesotho, South Africa, Swaziland and Zimbabwe. The modelled period is 2015 to 2030.
30.why_on_list: It is one of the health "best buys" named by the Copenhagen Consensus Center and by GiveWell, the charity evaluator.
30.evidence: The core evidence is experimental. Three randomized trials, in South Africa, Kenya and Uganda, found that circumcision cuts a man's risk of acquiring HIV by about 60%. In the South African trial of 3,274 young men, HIV incidence was 0.85 per 100 person-years in the circumcised group against 2.1 in the control group (Auvert et al. 2005). The procedure is done once, lasts for life and costs under $100. A Copenhagen Consensus study values the life-years gained and finds a benefit-cost ratio between 7.4 and 56.4, depending on the discount rate and the value placed on a year of life (Geldsetzer et al. 2015). The Copenhagen summary headline is $28 per $1 (Copenhagen Consensus Center 2015). Savings on future HIV treatment alone exceed the cost. One model found that scaling up across 13 countries would cost $2 billion and save $16.51 billion in averted care (Njeuhmeli et al. 2011). The main uncertainty is that returns fall as HIV incidence falls, and incidence has declined in many places. The range after donor overhead is 6.8 to 53. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $2.26 to $39.40 per $1.
30.ratio:
Low end. Geldsetzer et al. (2015) find 7.4 at a 5% discount rate, valuing a year of life at $1,000. The cost already includes country-level delivery and management, so only the overhead of the international donor channel is added. The rate is the Global Fund's operating expenses as a share of grant spending, 9.0% in 2023 (Global Fund 2025). Ratio: 7.4 ÷ 1.090 = 6.8.

High end. Geldsetzer et al. (2015) find 56.4 at a 3% discount rate, valuing a year of life at $5,000. The lower Global Fund rate of 6.7% (2024) is used. Ratio: 56.4 ÷ 1.067 = 52.9, rounded to 53.

Cost. Public outlay: $0.03bn. Donor-channel overhead: 0.03 × 0.090 = $0.0027bn. Household cost: not costed. Full cost: 0.03 + 0.0027 = $0.033bn a year, about $33 million.

Result: $6.8 to $53 per $1, at a full cost of $0.033bn a year. The adjustment changes costs only, not benefits.

Cross-checks. The other two cells in Geldsetzer et al. (2015) are 11.3 and 37.0, both inside the range. The Copenhagen summary gives annual benefits of $818 million against annual costs of $30 million: 818 ÷ 30 = 27.3, reported as 28. These ratios value only life-years. Haacker et al. (2016) look at money alone: one circumcision at age 20 in South Africa saves a net $617 at a 5% discount rate, a financial rate of return of 14.5%.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. The whole cost behind the ratio is public spending. Low end: 6.79 ÷ 3.00 = 2.26. High end: 52.86 ÷ 1.34 = 39.4. **Range after tax finance: 2.26 to 39.4.**
30.cost: The full cost is about $0.033bn a year. The Copenhagen summary puts the programme at $30 million a year, with $35 million in the outcome document. Geldsetzer et al. (2015) put the additional cost over current coverage at $451.9 million at a 3% discount rate to $524.7 million at 5% over 2015 to 2030, or about $30 million to $35 million a year. Each circumcision costs $65.85 to $95.15 (Njeuhmeli et al. 2011). Those unit costs include direct costs (consumables, staff, training) and indirect costs (capital, maintenance, utilities, support and management overhead), plus waste-management and supply-chain costs. They exclude the cost of creating demand, for which no global estimate was found. The added $0.0027bn is the donor channel's own overhead. Donors such as the United States President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) and the Global Fund currently pay.
30.strength: Grade A. The protective effect comes from randomized controlled trials. In South Africa, "This RR corresponds to a protection of 60% (95% CI: 32%–76%)," where RR is the relative risk and CI the confidence interval (Auvert et al. 2005). The economics come from peer-reviewed evaluations (Njeuhmeli et al. 2011; Haacker et al. 2016; Bansi-Matharu et al. 2023) and a Copenhagen Consensus benefit-cost study. The evidence for the effect is very strong. The size of the payoff depends on local HIV incidence.
30.difficulty: Moderate. The cost is tiny and the model is proven: national VMMC programmes run across 13 eastern and southern African countries (Njeuhmeli et al. 2011). Circumcision "is a one-off intervention that lasts for life," unlike drugs that must be taken continuously (Geldsetzer et al. 2015). The bottlenecks are demand and money. Low demand, especially among older men, is a key reason coverage stays low. International assistance funds 80% of HIV prevention programmes in low- and middle-income countries, and cuts in 2025 put that funding at risk, according to the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS 2025).
30.who_benefits: The gains go to the poor. The target countries are those where HIV is a leading cause of lost life and income. Men gain first. Women gain later, as fewer of their sexual partners are infected and their own infection rates fall substantially (Geldsetzer et al. 2015). Donors and national health budgets pay, and the sums are small.
30.counter:
Falling HIV incidence is the main counter-evidence. Bansi-Matharu et al. (2023) compare five models across sub-Saharan Africa and find continued circumcision cost-effective in 68% of setting scenarios: 62% where incidence is below 0.1 per 100 person-years, rising to 95% above 1.0. The study gives no benefit-cost ratio, so it is left out of the range. It does show that returns fall with incidence, so the high end, based on 2015 estimates, is optimistic for today's lower-incidence settings. Antiretroviral therapy scores 3.0 to 16.6 in the same Copenhagen study, but that is a different intervention.

The verdict depends on where the programme runs and how a year of life is valued. At $1,000 per life-year and a 5% discount, the ratio before overhead is 7.4; at $5,000 and 3%, it is 56.4 (Geldsetzer et al. 2015). In settings where incidence has fallen below 0.1 per 100 person-years, returns sit nearer the low end of 2.26, in the Good tier. Health-system savings alone push the other way: each circumcision at age 20 in South Africa saves a net $617 at a 5% discount (Haacker, Fraser-Hurt and Gorgens 2016).
