31.policy: Replace pay-as-you-go Social Security with funded personal retirement accounts. Each worker saves into an account they own, and the old system is phased out. Benefits already promised to retirees and older workers continue to be paid during the switch.
31.why_on_list: It comes from the Fraser Institute's Economic Freedom of the World index, Area 1, which measures the size of government. A state-run pension paid from current taxes is one of the largest items in that area. Funded accounts move that spending from government into private saving.
31.evidence: The best evidence comes from simulation models of the United States economy, not from field experiments. Feldstein and Samwick (1998) find that, in the long run, accounts funded with about 2.04% of payroll can replace the 12.4% payroll tax. The reason is simple: invested savings earn the return on capital, while a pay-as-you-go system earns only the growth of the wage base. Kotlikoff (1998) finds that the economy's capital stock rises 57%, output 17% and wages 10% in the long run. The catch is the transition. Today's workers must fund their own accounts and also keep paying for benefits already promised, a closed-group unfunded obligation of $55.6 trillion. That burden falls on people now aged 20 to 65, while the gains go mainly to the young and the unborn. Geanakoplos, Mitchell and Zeldes (1998) show that once that legacy debt is paid, the higher return largely disappears. Without extra saving, privatization mostly moves money between generations. The result is a ratio of $1.00 to $2.00 of benefit per $1 of transition cost.
31.ratio:
The ratio compares what later generations gain with what the transition generations pay to keep honouring promised benefits.

**High end (2.0).** Feldstein and Samwick (1998) model a shift to Mandatory Individual Retirement Accounts. In the long run, 2.04% of payroll in accounts replaces the 12.4% tax, and the deadweight loss of taxes falls by 1.57% of payroll. Combined gain: 11.92% of payroll. In the early decades, workers pay an extra 0.82% of payroll in year 1, rising to 1.58% by year 15. Their worked family example uses a 3% discount rate:

- Two 45-year-old parents lose $11,680 in present value.
- Their two children gain more than $23,000.
- Ratio: 23,000 ÷ 11,680 = 1.97, rounded to 2.0.

In their words, "Although the forty-five-year-olds have a combined net present value loss of $11,680 (at a 3 percent discount rate), this is outweighed by the children's gains of more than $23,000" (Feldstein and Samwick 1998).

**Low end (1.0).** Geanakoplos, Mitchell and Zeldes (1998) find that paying the debt to current retirees and workers takes a permanent tax of about 3% of payroll. That cost cancels the higher return on accounts. As they put it, "all of the gains to privatization would disappear in extra taxes to pay off the unfunded liability" (Geanakoplos, Mitchell and Zeldes 1998). Benefits roughly equal costs: ratio 1.0.

**Cross-checks.** Feldstein (1996) puts the net present-value gain of a funded system above $15 trillion, about 3% of future GDP a year. Kotlikoff (1998) measures the pure efficiency gain after fully compensating the transition generations. It ranges from 7.23% of lifetime income (cold-turkey switch) and 4.33% (consumption-tax financing) down to 1.08% (payroll-tax financing). With income-tax financing and strong benefit-tax linkage it becomes a 1.22% loss, so some designs dip slightly below 1. Both ends already net out the transition cost and account administration. Feldstein and Samwick assume a 9.0% return against the 9.30% actually reported, leaving 0.30 points of assets a year for administration.

Final range: **1.0 to 2.0**. Full cost: **$186.9 billion a year**.
31.cost:
The cost is $186.9 billion a year, in two parts.

- **Transition financing: $169.0 billion.** Feldstein and Samwick (1998) require an extra 0.82% to 1.58% of taxable payroll. Taxable payroll in 2025 was about $10,670 billion ($1,322.6 billion in net payroll tax ÷ 0.124, 2026 Trustees Report). Steps: 0.0082 × 10,670 = $87 billion; 0.0158 × 10,670 = $169 billion. The high end is used. Much of this is saving credited to workers' own accounts, so it overstates the true resource cost. It is shown because it is the fiscal burden of the switch.
- **Administration: $17.9 billion.** Diamond (1999) puts a government-organised account system at $40 to $50 per worker per year. Inflated from 1999 to 2025 prices (factor 1.933), $50 becomes $96.6. Across 185 million covered workers that is $17.9 billion a year.

The Social Security Administration's existing administration, 0.4% of total cost, continues and is not new. No separate private compliance cost or output loss has been estimated. Total: 169.0 + 17.9 = $186.9 billion.
31.strength: Grade B. The numbers come from published models in peer-reviewed journals and academic-press volumes: Feldstein (1996), Feldstein and Samwick (1998), Kotlikoff (1998), Kotlikoff, Smetters and Walliser (1999) and Cooley and Soares (1999). Kotlikoff, Smetters and Walliser (1999) confirm the pattern: privatization "can substantially raise long-run living standards," but at the cost of losses to transition generations. A historical case supports the mechanism. Schmidt-Hebbel (1998) credits Chile's 1981 reform with about a quarter of the country's growth increase. It falls short of a higher grade because no natural experiment measures the gain directly, and the rate-of-return gain itself is disputed in serious work.
31.difficulty: Moderate. It needs ordinary federal legislation, and Chile and other Latin American countries have done it. Politically it sits at the hard end of moderate. The 2005 United States personal-accounts proposal never reached a vote. Cooley and Soares (1999) find that every feasible transition uses debt that shifts cost to unborn generations, and that no majority supports a transition in its first periods.
31.who_benefits: In the long run, gains reach all income classes. Kotlikoff (1998) finds poorer households gain more (about 10.1%) than richer ones (about 8.1%) under consumption-tax financing. The transition generations pay. Without compensation, the oldest cohorts lose up to about 26% of remaining lifetime welfare. Feldstein and Samwick (1998) find that the summed present value for everyone aged 20 to 65 at the switch is negative. Without a progressive floor, losing Social Security's progressive benefit formula could leave low earners worse off.
31.counter:
The strongest counter-case is that personal accounts create little new value. Diamond and Orszag (2005) argue that costs will rise by about 2.5% of GDP over 75 years and that modest benefit cuts and revenue increases can restore solvency. Orszag and Stiglitz (2001) challenge the claims that accounts raise saving, returns and labour-market efficiency. Gill, Packard and Yermo (2005) document coverage and fee problems in Latin America, where capital markets are weaker. None gives a ratio. Diamond and Orszag's central point, that account returns are offset by the debt owed to current retirees and workers, is already carried into the low end through Geanakoplos, Mitchell and Zeldes (1998).

How the transition is financed decides the tier. Kotlikoff (1998) finds the efficiency gain, after compensating the transition generations, ranges from 7.23% of lifetime income with an abrupt switch to 1.08% with payroll-tax financing. It turns into a 1.22% loss with income-tax financing and strong benefit-tax linkage. That design would push the ratio below 1, into the Bad tier. Consumption-tax financing, at 4.33%, points toward the high end of 2.0, at the edge of the Good tier. Fees pull the other way: Latin American account systems cost at least 1% of assets a year, far above the 0.30 points assumed.

32.policy: Abolish the federal personal income tax and the corporate income tax. Repealing the 16th Amendment would stop the tax from being brought back. The lost revenue, about $3.1 trillion a year, is replaced mainly by shrinking government.
32.why_on_list: It comes from the Fraser Institute's Economic Freedom of the World index, Area 1, which scores countries on the size of government, including top marginal tax rates. The income tax is the largest single source of federal revenue and the main lever on that score.
32.evidence: Every dollar raised by income tax costs the economy more than a dollar. People work, save and invest less, and they spend time and money on filing. Estimates of that extra loss run from 13 cents per dollar (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1982) to about $2 per extra dollar raised (Feldstein 1999). Paperwork adds another $328.9 billion to $501.3 billion a year, or 11 to 16 cents per dollar raised (Hodge and Rock 2024). Natural experiments on top tax rates point the same way: Hendren and Sprung-Keyser (2020) find that past rate increases cost $1.16 to $1.85 of welfare per $1 raised. On the corporate side, the 2017 tax cut raised investment 8 to 14% and long-run GDP about 0.9%, but recovered little of its revenue cost (Chodorow-Reich, Zidar and Zwick 2024). The key uncertainty sits on the other side of the ledger. Repeal pays only if the spending cut to replace the revenue is worth no more than $1 per $1. The result is $1.24 to $3.20 of benefit per $1 of revenue given up, with a central case near $1.50.
32.ratio:
The ratio is the benefit to taxpayers per $1 of income tax given up. The revenue is replaced by cutting government, and the forgone spending is valued at $1 per $1. Three parts add up:

Ratio = 1 + deadweight loss removed per $ + compliance cost removed per $ + administration removed per $.

**Revenue at stake.** Fiscal year 2025 individual income tax: $2,656 billion. Corporate: $452 billion. Total: $3,108 billion, which is 59% of federal receipts ($5,235 billion) and 44% of outlays ($7,010 billion), according to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO).

**Administration avoided (both ends).** Internal Revenue Service (IRS) operations cost $19.0 billion in 2025. The income taxes' share: 0.59 × 19.0 = $11.2 billion. Per dollar: 11.2 ÷ 3,108 = 0.004.

**Low end (1.24).**
- Deadweight loss: 0.13. Ballard, Shoven and Whalley (1982) find that replacing the whole tax system with lump-sum taxes gains "13 cents to 22 cents per dollar of revenue." The lower bound is used.
- Compliance: income-tax forms only. Individual returns $145.4 billion + business returns $118.9 billion + depreciation $25.4 billion + estates and trusts $20.2 billion + pass-through deduction $19.0 billion = $328.9 billion. Per dollar: 328.9 ÷ 3,108 = 0.106.
- Total: 1 + 0.13 + 0.106 + 0.004 = 1.24.

**High end (3.2).**
- Deadweight loss: 2.0. Feldstein (1999) finds that raising revenue by a proportional rate increase costs nearly $2 of deadweight loss per extra $1.
- Compliance: all federal tax paperwork, $546.1 billion, less the $44.8 billion employer quarterly return still needed for payroll taxes = $501.3 billion. Per dollar: 501.3 ÷ 3,108 = 0.161.
- Total: 1 + 2.0 + 0.161 + 0.004 = 3.17, rounded to 3.2.

The high end applies a marginal figure to the whole tax, so it is an upper bound.

**Cross-checks.** Saez, Slemrod and Giertz (2012) give an illustrative excess burden of $0.38. With midpoint compliance ($415 billion ÷ $3,108 billion = 0.134), that gives 1 + 0.38 + 0.134 + 0.004 = 1.52. This sits between Hendren and Sprung-Keyser's (2020) values of 1.16 and 1.85. For the corporate tax alone, Chodorow-Reich, Zidar and Zwick (2024) find the 2017 cut lowered corporate revenue by about 40%, or 0.63% of GDP a year. Output gained per dollar of revenue: 0.9 ÷ 0.63 = 1.4 in the long run, and 0.44 ÷ 0.63 = 0.7 in the first decade.

Final range: **1.24 to 3.2**. Full cost: **$0 a year**.
32.cost: The full cost is $0. Repeal needs no new spending, and revenue returned to taxpayers is a transfer, not a resource cost. No new bureaucracy is created: about $11.2 billion a year of IRS income-tax administration disappears. No published estimate of one-time IRS wind-down costs was found, and payroll-tax and excise collection continue. No private compliance is created; $328.9 billion to $501.3 billion a year is removed. These savings count as benefits in the ratio, not as negative costs. The $3,108 billion fiscal gap is closed by spending cuts, valued at $1 per $1 inside the ratio. If a national sales tax replaced the revenue instead, its collection and retailer compliance costs would offset part of the saving. Gray and Holtz-Eakin (2023) find such a tax would need a rate of at least 27.8% on a tax-inclusive basis.
32.strength: Grade B+. The welfare-cost estimates are peer-reviewed. They include natural-experiment estimates for top rates (Hendren and Sprung-Keyser 2020), a quasi-experimental study of the 2017 corporate cut (Chodorow-Reich, Zidar and Zwick 2024), Feldstein's (1999) tax-return estimate, and the Ballard, Shoven and Whalley general-equilibrium model. Turning them into a ratio means extending them to full repeal, which no study has observed. That keeps it out of the A range.
32.difficulty: Moderate. Ordinary federal legislation can abolish both taxes. The 16th Amendment permits an income tax but does not require one. Repealing it would only block a future return, and that step needs two-thirds of both Houses of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of the states. Precedents exist: the United States before 1913, states such as Texas and Florida, and the Gulf states. The hard part is scale. The tax raises about 59% of federal receipts, so it must be matched by spending cuts of about 44% or by other taxes.
32.who_benefits: The income tax is the progressive part of the federal system, so repeal is regressive on its face. York and Watson (2023) find that "The FairTax Act would be less progressive than the existing federal tax system as measured by income." Altig et al. (2001) find that reforms which shield the poor and older generations give much smaller output gains. Most of the corporate cut's gains went to capital: labour income rose by less than $1,000 per worker, against the $4,000 to $9,000 once predicted (Chodorow-Reich, Zidar and Zwick 2024). Higher earners and owners of capital gain most. Those who depend on the programmes that are cut pay.
32.counter:
The strongest counter-case is on the spending side. Hendren and Sprung-Keyser (2020) show that some programmes, especially direct investment in children's health and education, return far more than $1 per $1. If the cuts that replace the revenue fall on those programmes, the ratio could fall below 1. The corporate evidence is also sobering: the 2017 investment response "was far too small to offset the direct cost of the reform" (Chodorow-Reich, Zidar and Zwick 2024). Coffey, McLaughlin and Peretto (2020) find large growth costs from regulation, and Jorgenson (2012) large gains from more efficient income taxation. Neither prices repeal of the income tax, so both are left out.

Two assumptions set the tier. The first is the deadweight loss removed. At the 13 cents per $1 that Ballard, Shoven and Whalley (1982) find for replacing the whole tax system with lump-sum taxes, the ratio is 1.24; at Feldstein's (1999) nearly $2, it is 3.2. The illustrative 38 cents of Saez, Slemrod and Giertz (2012) gives 1.52, in the Mid tier. The second is the value of the spending cut. The range assumes each $1 of spending cut was worth $1. If it was worth more, the ratio falls toward 1, and below it where the cuts land on the highest-return programmes.

33.policy: Sell or transfer federal land, parks and natural resources to private owners or to trusts run for income. The federal government owns nearly one-third of the land area of the United States. The policy also gives radio spectrum full, tradable property rights, so owners can use their frequencies for any wireless service.
33.why_on_list: It comes from the Fraser Institute's Economic Freedom of the World index, Area 2, which covers legal systems and property rights. Land and spectrum held and allocated by government are the largest assets outside private ownership.
33.evidence: Land run for income earns far more than land run by federal agencies. Fretwell and Regan (2015) compare 2009-2013 accounts across four western states. State trust lands earned $14.51 for every $1 of management cost; the Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) earned 73 cents. The gap holds across uses: trust lands earned $2.51 per $1 on timber and $138.08 per $1 on minerals. A peer-reviewed model of a transfer to Utah is less generous. Jakus et al. (2017) find a state could cover its management costs only with access to fossil fuels and timber at relatively high prices. Selling land also costs money: BLM spent 3.3% of proceeds to run its recent sales. Spectrum looks better still. Hazlett and Munoz (2009) find that 60 MHz more mobile spectrum in the United States would cut prices about 8% and raise consumer surplus about $8.8 billion a year. The main uncertainty is what the market cannot price: recreation and conservation value, which is large and unmeasured for a sale. The result is $1.66 to $10.00 of benefit per $1 of cost.
33.ratio:
No study computes a full welfare ratio for selling federal land. The range uses published revenue-per-management-dollar ratios for land run for income, then adds the one-time cost of selling it.

**Land value.** A buyer pays the present value of net income: value = 12.46 × (revenue − cost), using 20 years at 5%.

**Transaction cost.** BLM spent $3.17 million to run land sales that raised $95.7 million (U.S. Government Accountability Office 2008). Steps: 3.17 ÷ 95.7 = 3.3% of sale value.

**Ratio.** 12.46 × revenue ÷ (12.46 × cost + 0.033 × 12.46 × (revenue − cost)). The 12.46 cancels, leaving revenue ÷ (cost + 0.033 × (revenue − cost)).

**Low end (1.66).** Utah takes over 31.2 million acres and bears every federal cost (Jakus et al. 2017, with figures from Stambro 2014). In the high-energy-price case:
- Revenue: $422.0 million. Cost: $248 million. Before sale costs: 422.0 ÷ 248 = 1.70.
- Net income: 422.0 − 248 = 174.0.
- With sale costs: 422.0 ÷ (248 + 0.033 × 174.0) = 422.0 ÷ 253.7 = 1.66.

**High end (10.0).** Trust lands earn $14.51 per $1 of management cost (Fretwell and Regan 2015). As the authors put it, "The states examined in this study earn an average of $14.51 for every dollar spent on state trust land management." With sale costs: 14.51 ÷ (1 + 0.033 × 13.51) = 14.51 ÷ 1.446 = 10.0. Sale costs cut the high end most, because management costs on trust land are small relative to its value.

**Cross-checks.** The law behind BLM sales lets up to 20% of proceeds go to administration. At that ceiling the range is 1.49 to 3.9. In Utah's low-price case the ratio is 0.72. Spectrum is kept out of the headline because it is extrapolated, but it points higher. Freeing spectrum, scaled from the 2021 C-band auction (280 MHz; $3.3 billion relocation plus $9.7 billion accelerated-clearing payments), costs 13.0 × 60 ÷ 280 = $2.8 billion per 60 MHz. Ten years of benefit at 5% (annuity factor 7.72): 8.8 × 7.72 = $68 billion. Ratio: 68 ÷ 2.8 = 24. Counting relocation costs only ($0.71 billion per 60 MHz) gives about 96.

Final range: **1.66 to 10.0**. Full cost: **$3.0 billion a year**.
33.cost:
The full cost is $3.0 billion a year, all of it the administration of sales.

- **Public outlay: none net.** Sales raise money; the 2021 C-band auction alone brought $80.9 billion in clock-phase bids (Kahn et al. 2021). The policy also ends federal land-agency losses: in 2010, three land agencies spent $7.8 billion against $5.2 billion of revenue (Edwards and O'Toole 2012).
- **Administration: $3.0 billion a year.** Sales cost 3.3% of proceeds. The Bureau of Economic Analysis values federal land at $1.8 trillion (Larson 2015, 2009 values). Steps: 0.033 × $1,800 billion = $59.4 billion one-time, spread over an assumed 20-year disposal programme = $3.0 billion a year. At the 20% ceiling it would be $18 billion a year.
- **Private compliance and output loss:** no published estimates.

Spectrum relocation costs are paid by buyers and sit inside the spectrum ratio.
33.strength: Grade B. The low end comes from a peer-reviewed fiscal model (Jakus et al. 2017) and the high end from a comparison of official agency accounts by the Property and Environment Research Center (Fretwell and Regan 2015). Property-rights work on resource management (Anderson and Leal 2015) and peer-reviewed spectrum studies (Hazlett and Munoz 2009; Hazlett 2008) support the mechanism. No study prices full privatization including non-market values, so the grade goes no higher.
33.difficulty: Hard. The policy dismantles the federal land agencies, which manage about one-third of United States land, and there is no modern precedent. Anderson, Smith and Simmons (1999) propose auctioning all public lands over 20 to 40 years. The spectrum part alone would be moderate: the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has run auctions since 1994 and already issues flexible-use licences. Full property rights in every band, including government bands, would still need major legislation.
33.who_benefits: It depends on the design. Anderson, Smith and Simmons (1999) would auction land not for dollars but for public land share certificates given equally to every American, which spreads the gains widely. A plain cash auction would favour wealthy and extractive buyers and could cut free recreational access. Spectrum gains go mostly to consumers through lower wireless prices. Hazlett and Munoz (2009) cite evidence that consumer surplus from cellular licences was at least 10 times producer surplus.
33.counter:
The largest uncounted cost is non-market value. Haefele, Loomis and Bilmes (2016) put the total economic value of the National Park Service at about $92 billion a year. Outdoor recreation adds $639.5 billion of value added, 2.3% of GDP (U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis 2024). Neither study measures how much value would be lost under private or trust ownership, so neither enters the ratio. Utah's low-price case is the clearest downside: about $202.7 million of revenue against about $280 million of cost, including payments in lieu of taxes to counties, gives 0.72 (Stambro 2014). That case is a state takeover that keeps federal-style obligations, not a sale to private owners.

Commodity prices and recreation value decide the tier. If oil and gas prices fell to Utah's low case, the low end would drop from 1.66 to 0.72, into the Bad tier. Transfer costs at the 20% legal ceiling, rather than the measured 3.3%, would give 1.49 to 3.9. If buyers kept only part of the recreation value, the loss could outweigh the gains: $92 billion a year from the parks alone compares with $7.8 billion spent by the three main land agencies (Edwards and O'Toole 2012). Spectrum sales, at about 24 per $1 (Hazlett and Munoz 2009), would lift the high end, but are left out because the figure is extrapolated.

34.policy: Give fishers individual transferable quotas (ITQs): a secure, sellable share of the total catch allowed in a fishery each year. A fixed share ends the race to fish first. The total catch is set low enough for stocks to recover, and quota holders can buy and sell shares.
34.why_on_list: It comes from the Fraser Institute's Economic Freedom of the World index, Area 2, which covers legal systems and property rights. Most of the world's fisheries are still open access, with no one owning the right to the catch. Tradable quotas turn that common pool into a defined property right.
34.evidence: Open-access fisheries are overfished, and the losses are large. The World Bank (2017a) estimates that the world's marine fisheries forgo about $83.3 billion a year in net benefits. In the bank's words, reform would boost the sector's profits "from an estimated $3 billion a year to $86 billion" (World Bank 2017b). Getting there requires global fishing effort to fall about 44%. Catch shares are a proven route to that cut. Across more than 11,000 fisheries, those with catch shares were about half as likely to collapse (Costello, Gaines and Lynham 2008). In British Columbia's halibut fishery, private harvesting rights brought gains in cost, revenue and product form, though they took years to appear (Grafton, Squires and Fox 2000). A global model finds rights-based reform would raise annual profit by $53 billion by 2050, with the median fishery recovering in under 10 years (Costello et al. 2016). The main uncertainties are the cost of running the system and how fast effort is cut. The result is $2.80 to $16 of benefit per $1 of cost. Once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, the range is $0.93 to $15.60 per $1.
34.ratio:
The ratio uses the World Bank's (2017a) global model, at a 5% discount rate over 20 years. Benefits are the present value of fishery net benefits on a reform path, compared with the current path. On the current path, with 2012 effort held constant, that present value is $514 billion. Costs are the temporary losses while stocks rebuild, plus the present value of running a rights-based system. The World Bank puts management cost at 1 to 14% of the value of landings; the ends keep those two shares, while the full cost uses the median of published estimates, 5.4%. Optimal landings are worth $140.6 billion a year, and the 20-year annuity factor at 5% is 12.46.

**Low end (2.8): moderate path, effort cut 5% a year.**
- Present value: $1,196 billion − $514 billion = $682 billion net gain.
- Transition loss: $0.3 billion in the first year. Gross gain: 682 + 0.3 = $682.3 billion.
- Management at 14%: 0.14 × 140.6 = $19.7 billion a year × 12.46 = $245 billion.
- Ratio: 682.3 ÷ (0.3 + 245) = 2.8.

**High end (16): rapid path, effort cut sharply until stocks recover.**
- Present value: $1,465 billion − $514 billion = $951 billion net, after a $44 billion loss over the first four years.
- Management at 1%: $1.4 billion a year × 12.46 = $17.5 billion.
- Ratio: (951 + 44) ÷ (44 + 17.5) = 16.2, rounded to 16.

**Cross-checks.** Combining the worst of each end, the rapid path's loss with 14% management, no cost recovery and $3.00 per $1 of tax, gives (951 + 44) ÷ (44 + 735) = 1.28, inside the range. Mangin et al. (2018) compare profit gains in 2050 with the extra cost of management, country by country. Moving all fisheries to catch shares has a global ratio of 9.3, or 7.0 when costs scale with revenue, and 2.8 even if every country paid the average cost of the five most expensive managers, $489 per tonne. The annual prize is $83.3 billion (95% confidence interval $49.7 billion to $104.9 billion): net benefits rise from $3.0 billion to $86.3 billion as effort falls about 44%. Costello et al. (2016) find a $53 billion annual profit gain by 2050, the same order of size. The World Bank does not prescribe ITQs specifically; it lists catch shares among tools that work, sometimes alongside community management. The ratio therefore applies to ITQ-type reform as the main route to the effort cut. It is global. United States federal fisheries already use catch shares widely, so the gain there is smaller.

Range before tax finance: **2.8 to 16**. Full cost: **$18.6 billion a year**.

**After the cost of raising taxes.** Each $1 of public spending costs $1.34 to $3.00 once the excess burden of the taxes that fund it is counted, an extra $0.34 to $2.00 (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). The low end uses the higher burden and the high end the lower one. Only the management cost is public, and only the part not recovered from fishers through levies is paid from taxes; the transition loss falls on fishers. The low end assumes no cost recovery, as in most countries (Mangin et al. 2018), so 0.999 of the cost is tax-financed. The high end uses New Zealand's 63% recovery (Wyatt 2000), which leaves 0.37 of the $17.5 billion management cost, or 0.105 of the cost, tax-financed. Low end: 2.78 ÷ (1 + 2.0 × 0.999) = 0.93. High end: 16.18 ÷ (1 + 0.34 × 0.105) = 15.6. **Range after tax finance: 0.93 to 15.6.**
34.cost:
The full cost is $18.6 billion a year worldwide during the transition, and $7.6 billion a year after it.

- **Management, monitoring and enforcement: $7.6 billion a year.** Fourteen published estimates put this cost at 0.5% to 20% of the value of landings, with a median of 5.4% and a mean of 7.1%. They run from under 0.5% for the US surfclam and ocean quahog quotas and 1.4% for Alaska's halibut and sablefish quotas (U.S. Government Accountability Office 2005), through about 3% in Iceland and 10% in Norway, to 15% to 25% in Newfoundland (Arnason, Hannesson and Schrank 2000). New Zealand spends 4% (Metzner and Harte 2008), and the World Bank range is 1 to 14% (World Bank 2017a). The median on optimal landings: 0.054 × $140.6 billion = $7.6 billion. About half is recovered from fishers through levies, the median of published recovery shares, and half is paid from taxes. Levies are transfers, so they are not counted again. Much of this is already spent under current management, so the true increase is smaller.
- **Lost output during rebuilding: $11.0 billion a year.** The rapid path loses $44 billion over four years: 44 ÷ 4 = $11.0 billion a year. The moderate path loses $0.3 billion in its first year.
- **Public outlay: none beyond management.** Handing out quota is a transfer.

Total: 7.6 + 11.0 = $18.6 billion.
34.strength: Grade B+. Peer-reviewed natural comparisons measure the gain from catch shares directly: Costello, Gaines and Lynham (2008) on collapse rates across more than 11,000 fisheries, and Grafton, Squires and Fox (2000) on the British Columbia halibut natural experiment. A peer-reviewed global model sizes the prize (Costello et al. 2016). The ratio itself is built from the World Bank's official model rather than a peer-reviewed cost-benefit study, which keeps it below A-.
34.difficulty: Moderate. In one country it takes ordinary legislation or regulation, and there are many precedents: New Zealand, Iceland, and United States catch-share programmes such as British Columbia and Alaska halibut. Globally it is harder. Fishing effort must fall about 44%, and the World Bank warns of very high adjustment costs for displaced fishers.
34.who_benefits: The gains are concentrated. The World Bank (2017a) notes that benefits go to the relatively few fishers who stay in. Displaced vessel owners and crews bear most of the adjustment cost, and the public sector bears much of the management cost. Pinkerton and Edwards (2009) find that, in the British Columbia halibut fishery, quota leasing moves income from active fishers to quota owners. Auctioned or community-held quotas could spread the gains more widely, but the evidence here is for quotas handed to existing fishers.
34.counter:
Essington (2010) finds that catch shares in North American fisheries markedly reduced year-to-year swings in exploitation, landings and discards. Yet "The average levels of most indicators were unaffected by catch share implementation", apart from discards. The gain is mainly stability, which cautions against the high end, but the study gives no economic value. Pinkerton and Edwards (2009) find that in British Columbia's halibut fishery, quota leasing reduces the benefits to active fishermen and to society. That bears on who receives the rents rather than on the total gain, so it informs who benefits, not the ratio.

The cost of running the system, who pays for it and the speed of reform decide the tier. The low end assumes management costs of 14% of the value of landings, a moderate path and no cost recovery from fishers, so taxpayers pay at nearly $2 of deadweight per $1: 0.93. The high end assumes 1%, a rapid path and New Zealand's 63% recovery: 15.6. Even the worst combination, the rapid path's $44 billion transition loss with 14% management costs and no recovery, gives 1.28. If fishers paid for management through levies, as for Alaska's halibut and sablefish quotas, the low end would rise back toward 2.8. If taxpayers paid the whole cost everywhere, the policy would slide toward the Mid tier.

35.policy: Abolish the Federal Reserve and central-bank fiat money. Return to a neutral reserve standard, such as gold, bitcoin or a floating basket of commodities, with money issued by competing banks under free banking. Competing currencies become legal tender. The policy assumes the major economies adopt the standard together, as most did before 1914.
35.why_on_list: It comes from the Fraser Institute's Economic Freedom of the World index, Area 3, which scores countries on sound money: money growth, inflation and the freedom to hold other currencies. A neutral reserve currency is the furthest step on that measure.
35.evidence: Money tied to a commodity brought stable prices for a long time. A consumer basket costing $100 in 1790 cost $108 in 1913; prices then rose about 24-fold under the Fed by 2008, an average inflation of about 3.4% a year (Selgin, Lastrapes and White 2012). Inflation is a tax on money holders. A sustained 4% inflation costs 0.41% of output a year (Dotsey and Ireland 1996), and its interaction with the tax code adds about 1% of GDP (Feldstein 1997). Banking crises since 1973 have been twice as frequent as under the classical gold standard (Bordo et al. 2001). Countries sharing gold traded far more with each other: 18 to 57% more in one study, 60% more in another (Mitchener and Weidenmier 2008; Lopez-Cordova and Meissner 2003). Governments that kept to gold also borrowed more cheaply (Bordo and Rockoff 1996). Against these gains sits the real cost of holding gold or reserves, between 0.05% and 0.5% of GDP a year. The main risk is a rigid money supply in a deep slump, as in the 1930s. The result is $6.40 to $144 of benefit per $1 of cost.
35.ratio:
All figures are a percentage of United States GDP a year. The view is global, so the extra return the United States earns on dollar reserves is a transfer between countries, not a gain or cost to the world. Benefits come through four channels.

**1. Inflation.** Low: a sustained 4% inflation costs 0.41% of output a year when money is measured as currency (Dotsey and Ireland 1996). High: Lagos and Wright (2005) find that "going from 10% to 0% inflation can be worth between 3% and 5% of consumption." Scaled to the Fed-era average of about 3.4%, that is about 1.0%. Feldstein (1997, 1999) adds about 1% of GDP a year for the interaction of inflation with the tax code, counted at the high end only.

**2. Banking crises.** The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2010) puts the annual chance of a crisis at about 4.5%. Halving it, as under the gold standard, cuts it by 2.25 points. Each point is worth 0.2% to 0.6% of output. Steps: 2.25 × 0.2 = 0.45% of GDP; 2.25 × 0.6 = 1.35% of GDP.

**3. Trade.** United States trade is 25.0% of GDP (World Bank 2025). Low: an 18% rise (Mitchener and Weidenmier 2008) adds 0.18 × 25.0 = 4.5 points of trade. High: Estevadeordal, Frantz and Taylor (2003) find that applying the 1913 gold standard in 1870 would have made trade about 30% higher, adding 7.5 points. Frankel and Romer (1999) find each point of trade raises income by at least 0.5%. Steps: 4.5 × 0.5 = 2.25% of GDP; 7.5 × 0.5 = 3.75% of GDP.

**4. Borrowing costs.** Gold adherence lowered sovereign spreads by about 40 basis points (Bordo and Rockoff 1996). On foreign-held federal debt of 29.3% of GDP, that is 0.12% of GDP. It is counted at the high end only.

**Costs.** The cost is the real resource cost of the commodity or free-banking system (Watts and Snyder 2015). Meltzer's estimate, as reviewed there, is 0.5% of GDP. The measured United States classical gold standard of 1879-1913 cost 0.249%. White's free banking, with 2% gold reserves, costs 0.05%. Fiat money has its own cost in private gold hoarding, 0.014% of GDP a year since Bretton Woods, which is netted off at the low end.

**Low end (6.4).** (0.41 + 0.45 + 2.25 + 0) ÷ (0.5 − 0.014) = 3.11 ÷ 0.486 = 6.4.

**High end (144).** (1.0 + 1.0 + 1.35 + 3.75 + 0.12) ÷ 0.05 = 7.22 ÷ 0.05 = 144.

**Cross-checks.** Using the measured cost of the classical gold standard, the central case is about 25. Lopez-Cordova and Meissner's 60% trade effect and Estevadeordal, Frantz and Taylor's estimate that adopting gold raised trade about 42% both sit above the 18% used at the low end.

Final range: **6.4 to 144**. Full cost: **$154.3 billion a year**.
35.cost:
The full cost is $154.3 billion a year, all of it the private cost of holding the reserve commodity.

- **Public outlay: $0.** Closing the Fed needs no budget outlay. Lost Fed remittances to the Treasury are a transfer.
- **Administration: $0.** No new agency is created. Bank supervision passes to existing regulators, so no net change is entered.
- **Private resource cost: $154.3 billion.** Meltzer's 0.5% of GDP, the high end of the estimates reviewed by Watts and Snyder (2015), is used. Steps: 0.005 × $30,861 billion (2025 GDP) = $154.3 billion. The measured classical gold standard (0.249%) would cost $76.8 billion; free banking (0.05%) $15.4 billion.

The United States Treasury already holds a large gold stock, which would reduce the one-time cost of acquiring reserves. No published estimate of transition output loss exists.
35.strength: Grade B. The estimates come from peer-reviewed historical studies of the gold standard's effects on trade (Lopez-Cordova and Meissner 2003; Estevadeordal, Frantz and Taylor 2003), borrowing costs (Bordo and Rockoff 1996) and crises (Bordo et al. 2001), and from peer-reviewed models of the cost of inflation (Lagos and Wright 2005; Lucas 2000). No modern economy has tried it, and the Depression-era evidence cuts the other way, so the grade stops at B.
35.difficulty: Hard. It dismantles a major, entrenched institution with no modern precedent. No advanced economy has run without a central bank since Canada created the Bank of Canada in 1935 (Bordo, Redish and Rockoff 2015). The competing-currencies part alone would be moderate: it needs only ordinary legal-tender and tax changes, and El Salvador offers a 2021 precedent.
35.who_benefits: The gains are broad. Inflation is a tax on everyone who holds money (Lucas 2000), and banking crises hit output and jobs across the whole economy. Savers and households that rely on cash gain most. Debtors and the Treasury lose the transfer they now receive from inflation and money creation.
35.counter:
Three findings point the other way. An International Monetary Fund study finds that any harm to trade from exchange-rate volatility "would appear to be fairly small and is by no means a robust, universal finding" (Clark, Tamirisa and Wei 2004). Friedman (1960) put the cost of a full commodity standard at about 2.5% of national product. Most serious, countries that left gold early in the 1930s recovered faster (Bernanke 1995). These are kept outside the range. Later measurement of the actual classical gold standard found a cost of 0.249% of GDP, and the policy uses fractional reserves rather than a full commodity standard. No study estimates how often a 1930s-type episode would recur under a modern commodity standard.

Trade and cost decide the tier. The low end counts a trade gain of 2.25% of GDP. With no trade gain, the ratio falls to 1.8, in the Mid tier. With Friedman's full-commodity cost, it falls to about 0.3, in the Bad tier. In the other direction, with the measured classical gold-standard cost, the central case is about 25. A repeat of the 1930s, when staying on gold deepened the slump, is the largest unpriced risk and would pull every figure down.

36.policy: The United States would close federal deposit insurance and bar government rescues of failed banks. Depositors and creditors would carry their own risk. Banks could still buy private deposit insurance. The change is a law change, not a spending programme.
36.why_on_list: The policy comes from the Fraser Institute's Economic Freedom of the World index, under Areas 3 and 5, which cover money and the regulation of credit. Government guarantees of bank deposits and bank creditors are state involvement in credit, so their removal is on the list.
36.evidence:
The case for abolition rests on market discipline. Demirgüç-Kunt and Detragiache (2002) studied 61 countries from 1980 to 1997, with 40 systemic crises. They find that explicit deposit insurance makes banking crises more likely, and that "the adverse impact of deposit insurance on bank stability tends to be stronger the more extensive is the coverage offered to depositors, and where the scheme is funded and run by the government rather than the private sector." The effect fades where institutions are strong. History points the same way. Calomiris and Jaremski (2019) show that early-1900s state insurance schemes let insured banks take more insolvency risk during the First World War farm boom; when prices fell, the insurance systems collapsed with high losses. Calomiris (1990) finds that voluntary mutual-liability schemes worked while compulsory state schemes failed.

The case against is just as serious. Bank-run theory shows that a sound bank can fail if depositors panic, and that a government guarantee can stop the panic (Diamond and Dybvig 1983). A recent calibrated model finds that the first dollars of cover are the most valuable of all (Dávila and Goldstein 2023). Put the two sides together and the ratio runs from 0.5 to 5.5. It straddles 1. The sign of the effect is contested, and that uncertainty is the whole story of this policy.
36.ratio:
No published study gives a benefit-cost ratio for abolishing deposit insurance. The ratio is built from published inputs. The benefit is crises avoided because guarantees no longer weaken market discipline. The cost is the welfare lost when depositors lose protection and runs become more common.

**High end.**
- Crisis risk: Demirgüç-Kunt and Detragiache estimate that cutting US coverage to Swiss levels would have lowered the predicted probability of the 1980 US banking crisis from 4.3% to 2.5%. That is 1.8 points a year.
- Crisis size: Laeven and Valencia (2018) put the output loss of the 2007 US crisis at 30% of trend GDP.
- Expected avoided loss: 0.018 × 0.30 = 0.54% of GDP a year.
- In 2025 dollars (GDP $30,861bn): 0.0054 × 30,861 = $166.6bn a year.
- Cost of losing cover: Dávila and Goldstein (2023) find that "an increase in coverage of $100,000 is associated with a welfare gain of $13.2 billion for the whole banking sector." That is 9.46 basis points of $14 trillion of bank assets, or 13.2 ÷ 14,770 = 0.089% of 2008 GDP. Taking this as the value of the first $100,000 of cover: 0.00089 × 30,861 = $27.5bn.
- Running cost of private replacement insurance: $2.9bn a year.
- Total cost: 27.5 + 2.9 = $30.4bn.
- Ratio: 166.6 ÷ 30.4 = **5.5**.

This is an upper bound. Gains from cover are highest at low coverage, so full abolition costs more than losing a middle slice. And the destabilising effect of insurance is insignificant where institutions are strong, as in the United States.

**Low end.**
- Direct resolution costs that guarantees created since 1934: the savings and loan crisis, $153bn (Curry and Shibut 2000); 2008 bailouts, about $500bn (Lucas 2019); Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank, $16.3bn (FDIC 2023). Total: about $669bn over about 90 years, or $7.4bn a year.
- Cost: the same $13.2bn a year plus $2.9bn of private-insurance operating cost.
- Ratio: 7.4 ÷ (13.2 + 2.9) = 0.46, rounded to **0.5**. Before administration the ratio is 0.56.

The range is therefore 0.5 to 5.5, with a full cost of $2.9bn a year.
36.cost:
The full cost is $2.9bn a year. Repeal needs no new public spending, because the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) is funded by bank premiums. Even the losses from protecting uninsured depositors at Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank were recovered from banks: by statute the FDIC must recoup such losses through special assessments on insured institutions (FDIC 2023).

The $2.9bn is the operating cost of private replacement insurance. If private insurers wrote cover priced like the FDIC's 2024 assessment revenue of $11.6bn (FDIC 2025), at the property-casualty industry's underwriting expense ratio of 24.8% (National Association of Insurance Commissioners 2024), their costs would be 0.248 × 11.6 = $2.9bn a year. The FDIC's own 2024 fund operating expenses of $2.43bn are not counted as a saving, because much of that work is supervision that would continue at another agency. Premiums are a price for risk, not a resource cost. The welfare cost of weaker protection and more runs sits in the ratio's denominator and is not counted twice. Depositors lost about 30% in a typical failure before the FDIC existed (Correia, Luck and Verner 2024).
36.strength: Grade B. Each input comes from strong work: a peer-reviewed cross-country panel, peer-reviewed historical studies and peer-reviewed models. But the ratio itself is assembled from those inputs rather than published, and the inputs disagree on the sign of the effect. That rules out a higher grade.
36.difficulty: Hard. The policy dismantles a major federal institution in place since 1933. It also ends the implicit too-big-to-fail guarantee, a funding subsidy worth up to $70bn a year to large US banks (International Monetary Fund 2014). No large advanced economy runs without deposit insurance today. New Zealand, the last holdout in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, introduced a NZ$100,000 Depositor Compensation Scheme on 1 July 2025.
36.who_benefits: The effects are mixed. Ending bailouts removes transfers that mostly went to bank creditors and shareholders, about $500bn in 2008-09 (Lucas 2019), and ends the funding subsidy to the largest banks. Taxpayers gain. Ending deposit insurance, though, shifts risk onto ordinary depositors, who are the least able to monitor banks. Neither effect falls clearly on the poor or the rich.
36.counter:
The strongest evidence against abolition is Dávila and Goldstein (2023). They put optimal US coverage in 2008 at about $381,000 and find that "the welfare gains from having a deposit insurance system at all are very large." On its own, their estimate implies a ratio below 1 for full abolition. Diamond and Dybvig (1983) show in theory that government deposit insurance can produce better contracts. Egan, Hortaçsu and Matvos (2017) find that uninsured deposits flee distressed banks while insured deposits stay, so banks can be very fragile. Neither gives a welfare figure for abolition. Dávila and Goldstein's estimate is used as the cost at both ends, so their case sits inside the range rather than outside it.

The verdict depends on how much insurance itself causes crises. The high end of 5.5 assumes that cutting US coverage to Swiss levels lowers the yearly chance of a crisis from 4.3% to 2.5% (Demirgüç-Kunt and Detragiache 2002). The same authors find the effect insignificant where institutions are strong, as in the US. If that held, the benefit would shrink to the direct bailout costs alone, giving about 0.5, in the Bad tier. Correia, Luck and Verner (2024) cut the other way: runs can be ruled out as a plausible cause in more than 80% of bank failures before federal deposit insurance.

37.policy: Abolish all tariffs and import quotas, without waiting for other countries to do the same. Repeal anti-dumping and countervailing duties. Simplify border paperwork so goods clear customs faster. No budget outlay is needed; it is a law change.
37.why_on_list: The Fraser Institute's Economic Freedom of the World index measures the freedom to trade internationally in its Area 4. Tariffs, quotas and border red tape are the main items scored there, so their removal is on the list.
37.evidence:
Free trade is among the best-evidenced policies in economics. The Copenhagen Consensus has asked the same question three times: what is the return on full global trade liberalisation? Each time, counting growth effects, the answer has been in the hundreds or thousands of dollars per dollar of cost. Anderson (2012) puts the present value of benefits from completing the Doha round at $12 trillion to $64 trillion, against adjustment costs below $400 billion. Anderson (2015) finds ratios of 1,300 to 2,800 globally once growth effects are counted.

The growth effect is not just a model assumption. Wacziarg and Welch (2008) find that "countries that liberalized their trade regimes experienced average annual growth rates that were about 1.5 percentage points higher than before liberalization." Frankel and Romer (1999) find that a 1-point rise in the trade share raises income per person by roughly 0.5% to 2%. The costs of protection are also measured directly. The 2018 US tariffs passed fully into domestic prices and cost US buyers of imports $51 billion, or 0.27% of GDP (Fajgelbaum et al. 2020).

The stakes today are real. The Tax Foundation finds that the remaining US tariffs cut long-run GDP by 0.4% and cost $820 per household in 2026 (York and Durante 2026). The Budget Lab at Yale (2026) puts the average statutory tariff rate at 11.0%, rising to 11.8% by the end of 2026, and household costs at about $1,100 a year. The main uncertainty is the size of the growth effect, and how much of a global gain one country captures by acting alone. Even the narrowest peer-reviewed estimate is well above 1. The ratio runs from 90 to 2,800.
37.ratio:
Both ends use Copenhagen Consensus estimates of full global liberalisation that include growth effects.

**Low end: 90.**
- Anderson (2012): "The net present value of the future benefits of a Doha agreement ranges from $12 trillion to $64 trillion. The costs are less than $400 billion in present value terms."
- His reported global benefit-cost ratio is 90 to 180 (140 to 250 for developing countries).
- The floor, **90**, is the low end.

**High end: 2,800.**
- Anderson (2015; 2018) adds growth effects: reform lifts growth rates by one-fifth for a time, tapering back by 2050.
- Global ratio: 1,300 at a 5% discount rate, 2,800 at 3%. Developing countries: 2,100 to 4,700.
- The top, **2,800**, is the high end.

**Cross-checks.** Anderson and Winters (2008) give 269 to 1,121 with dynamic gains and 17 to 80 without. The narrow static Halftime estimate of Feyrer et al. (2023), with a global ratio of 11 and 5 to 7 for high-income countries, is kept as counter-evidence. Two sub-policies are reported but not averaged in. Repealing anti-dumping duties returns 2 to 14 (U.S. International Trade Commission 1995; Gallaway, Blonigen and Flynn 1999). Trade facilitation returns 11 to 640, set against the World Trade Organization's estimated gains (2015) and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development's (OECD) implementation costs of EUR 3.5 million to EUR 19 million per country (Moïsé 2013).

One country acting alone captures a smaller share of these global gains. But the US losses from current tariffs, about $30bn to $120bn a year, are recurring, and repeal removes them at near-zero budget cost. Anderson's ratios already put adjustment costs in the denominator. The range is 90 to 2,800, with a full cost of $32.1bn a year.
37.cost:
The full cost is $32.1bn a year.

- **Public outlay: $0.** Repealing tariffs and quotas needs no spending; resistance to trade reform is almost never about treasury outlays (Anderson 2012). Lost tariff revenue, about $1.4 trillion to $1.9 trillion over ten years, is a transfer from consumers to government, not a resource cost.
- **Administration: about $0.02bn a year** for the United States to implement trade facilitation (Moïsé 2013).
- **Private compliance:** no published estimate separate from trade facilitation.
- **Adjustment costs: $32.1bn a year.** Displaced workers and firms bear costs below $400bn in present value for full global liberalisation (Anderson 2012). Spread over 20 years at 5%: 400 ÷ 12.46 = $32.1bn a year.

Total: 0.02 + 32.1 = $32.1bn a year. These adjustment costs are already the denominator of the Copenhagen Consensus ratios, so they are not added twice.
37.strength: Grade A. The ratios are peer-edited Copenhagen Consensus estimates, published in book form by Cambridge University Press. The growth effect behind them rests on peer-reviewed quasi-experimental and instrumental-variable studies. Even the narrowest peer-reviewed estimate (Feyrer et al. 2023) is above 1. The sub-policies rate a little lower: B for anti-dumping repeal (one peer-reviewed general-equilibrium model) and A- for trade facilitation (one peer-reviewed benefit-cost analysis).
37.difficulty: Moderate. One country acting alone needs only ordinary tariff legislation. There are working precedents. Hong Kong charges no tariff on any import or export (Hong Kong Trade and Industry Department). Singapore, New Zealand's unilateral tariff cuts and Britain's 1846 repeal of the Corn Laws show it can be done. Anti-dumping repeal needs Congress to repeal Title VII of the Tariff Act of 1930. Customs reform can proceed under existing authority, since the Trade Facilitation Agreement has been in force since 2017. The Supreme Court struck down the emergency-powers tariffs in *Learning Resources v. Trump* on 20 February 2026, but other statutory tariff powers remain (York and Durante 2026).
37.who_benefits: The poor gain most. Anderson (2015) finds ratios of 2,100 to 4,700 for developing countries, against 1,300 to 2,800 globally, and 160 million fewer people in extreme poverty by 2030. Feyrer et al. (2023) find a ratio of about 100 for low and lower-middle-income countries, against about 5 for high-income ones. Inside the United States, tariffs work as a consumption tax of about $1,100 per household a year (Budget Lab at Yale 2026). Removing them helps lower-income households most relative to income. The costs fall on workers and firms in protected industries, who bear the adjustment.
37.counter:
Feyrer et al. (2023) give the narrowest estimate. They model a 5% rise in world trade, static and first-year only, and find benefits of $700bn against costs of $100bn, a ratio of 11 globally and about 5 for high-income countries. Lomborg (2023) notes that "almost all costs hit high-income countries." The authors say their ratios sit at the low end of the plausible range. The study is left out because it measures a partial rise in trade, not full free trade. Egger and Nelson (2011) find that anti-dumping duties since 1948 have had negative but modest effects, which makes anti-dumping repeal a small add-on rather than a driver of the range.

The growth effect decides how high the ratio goes, not whether it clears the top tier. Without dynamic gains, Anderson and Winters (2008) find 17 to 80; with them, 269 to 1,121. Even the static figures clear 10. The verdict would fall a tier only if one country acting alone captured a small share of the global gain, and its own gain matched the high-income figure of about 5 in Feyrer et al. (2023). For the United States the stakes are concrete: remaining tariffs cut long-run GDP by 0.4% (York and Durante 2026).

38.policy: End subsidies for every energy source: oil, gas, coal, renewables, biofuels and nuclear. At the same time, reform nuclear licensing and open oil, gas and coal permitting, leasing, pipelines and liquefied natural gas (LNG) export approval. Lift the bans that stop development banks from financing gas and coal plants in poor countries. Every source then competes on its own costs.
38.why_on_list: The Fraser Institute's Economic Freedom of the World index scores the size of government in Area 1, which includes subsidies, and regulation in Area 5, which includes permitting and licensing. Energy subsidies and energy permits sit squarely in both, so the package is on the list.
38.evidence:
The parts of this package pull in opposite directions. Ending fossil-fuel subsidies removes real waste. Davis (2014) finds that road-fuel subsidies totalled $110 billion in 2012, and that "the total annual deadweight loss worldwide is $44 billion." That is 40 cents of pure loss for every subsidy dollar. Yet ending them cuts emissions less than expected: only 0.5 to 2.2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide a year by 2030, a 1% to 5% cut (Jewell et al. 2018). In some models, removing oil and gas subsidies even pushes users toward coal.

Ending renewable subsidies saves money but adds emissions, because the subsidies pay for real abatement. Opening federal leasing, shale gas and LNG exports adds output. The shale boom raised welfare for gas consumers and producers by $48 billion a year (Hausman and Kellogg 2015). The US Department of Energy (2024) finds that unconstrained LNG exports would raise GDP by $80 billion in 2050.

Counting subsidies removed as transfers, each $1 returns $0.78 to $2.16. The result falls below 1 when renewable subsidies are treated as cheap abatement and the GDP loss from ending them is counted. It rises above 2 when subsidies are at their 2022 peak and the taxes that fund them are costly. Nuclear licensing reform and development-bank lending are described but not priced.
38.ratio:
All figures are annual global flows in billions of dollars. Subsidies removed are transfers, counted at $1 on both sides: taxpayers gain each dollar recipients lose. The ratio is (subsidies + efficiency gains + other gains − damages) ÷ (subsidies + other costs).

**Emissions.** In million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year:
- Ending fossil-fuel subsidies: −500 to −2,200 by 2030 (Jewell et al. 2018).
- Ending renewable subsidies, treating the $166bn as the abatement it pays for: 166 ÷ 88 = +1,886 at the lowest cost per tonne ($88, Bistline, Mehrotra and Wolfram 2023), down to 166 ÷ 2,138 = +78 at the highest ($2,138, Abrell, Kosch and Rausch 2019).
- Opening federal leasing: +100 after leakage (Prest 2022).
- Unconstrained LNG exports: +22.9 (U.S. Department of Energy 2024).
- Net: +1,509 at the low end and −1,999 at the high end.
- Each tonne is valued at $66 for climate damage (Barrage and Nordhaus 2024) plus $57.5 for local air pollution (Parry, Veung and Heine 2014): $123.5 a tonne.

**Low end.** Subsidies of $634bn in 2017 (International Renewable Energy Agency 2020).
- Benefits: 634 + deadweight loss 44 (Davis 2014, road fuels only) + excess burden of the taxes that fund subsidies, 0.17 × 634 = 107.8 (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985, lowest figure) + federal royalties 5 (Prest 2022) + LNG GDP 13 (NERA Economic Consulting 2018) − emission damages 1,509 × 123.5 = 186.4. Total: 617.4.
- Costs: 634 + US GDP loss from ending clean-energy credits 160 (Energy Innovation 2025) + replacement nuclear licensing 0.995 (U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission 2024). Total: 795.0.
- Ratio: 617.4 ÷ 795.0 = **0.78**.

**High end.** Subsidies of $1,447bn: explicit fossil-fuel subsidies in 2022 of 18% of $7 trillion = $1,260bn (Black, Liu and Parry 2023), plus $166bn for renewables and $21bn for nuclear.
- Benefits: 1,447 + deadweight loss 0.40 × 1,260 = 504 + excess burden 0.56 × 1,447 = 810.3 (highest Ballard, Shoven and Whalley figure) + shale-gas welfare 48 (Hausman and Kellogg 2015) + LNG GDP 80 (U.S. Department of Energy 2024) + emission cut 1,999 × 123.5 = 246.9. Total: 3,136.2.
- Costs: 1,447 + displaced-worker losses 4.39 + 0.995. Total: 1,452.4.
- Ratio: 3,136.2 ÷ 1,452.4 = **2.16**.

The high end uses 2022 subsidies, a price-spike year. As a cross-check, the Copenhagen Consensus rates phasing out fossil-fuel subsidies at 15 per $1, counting only efficiency and environmental gains and not the subsidy as a transfer (Copenhagen Consensus Center 2015). The range is 0.78 to 2.16, with a full cost of $347.4bn a year.
38.cost:
The full cost is $347.4bn a year, excluding the subsidies themselves, which are transfers on both sides of the ratio.

- **Public outlay: $0.** Ending subsidies lowers public spending.
- **Administration: $0.995bn.** A replacement nuclear licensing system is costed at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's 2025 budget request of $994,946,000, most of it recovered from fees (U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission 2024). No published estimate exists for oil, gas and LNG permitting administration.
- **Private compliance:** none estimated.
- **GDP loss: $160bn** in 2030 from ending US clean-energy tax credits, including about 790,000 fewer jobs (Energy Innovation 2025). The scenario also rescinds other federal programmes, so it is an upper bound. At the high end it is replaced by displaced-worker losses: 790,000 × 1.4 years of earnings (Davis and von Wachter 2011) × $49,504 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics 2025) = $54.8bn in present value, or 54.8 ÷ 12.46 = $4.39bn a year.
- **External damage: $186.4bn.** The low-end net emission increase of 1,509 million tonnes at $123.5 a tonne.

Total: 0.995 + 160 + 186.4 = $347.4bn a year.
38.strength: Grade B. The priced parts rest on peer-reviewed estimates of fuel-subsidy losses, emissions, abatement costs and leasing effects. A Copenhagen Consensus ratio of 15 for fossil-subsidy phase-out serves as a cross-check. But the ratio is assembled from several separate studies. It assumes renewable subsidies equal the resource costs they finance. And two of the four parts, nuclear licensing and development-bank finance, are not priced. That keeps the grade at B rather than B+.
38.difficulty: Moderate. Each country can act alone through ordinary legislation. Fuel-subsidy reform has precedents in Indonesia (2015) and India (2014). Nuclear licensing, permitting and leasing changes are ordinary statutes. Lifting development-bank bans on fossil-fuel finance is a decision for each bank's board. No treaty is needed. The obstacle is that most governments must act. Members of the Group of Twenty pledged in 2009 to phase out inefficient fossil-fuel subsidies, yet explicit subsidies reached $1.3 trillion in 2022.
38.who_benefits: The gains are broad. Energy subsidies flow mostly to better-off households. About 60% of US clean-energy tax credits went to the top income fifth (Borenstein and Davis 2016). The Copenhagen Consensus finds particularly high benefits for developing countries when the savings are recycled. Lifting development-bank bans matters for the poorest: for a $10 billion portfolio, "A natural gas–only portfolio could provide electricity access to 90 million people versus 20–27 million people with a renewables-only portfolio" (Moss and Leo 2014). The losers are poor households in subsidising countries, who lose price support in the short run, and US gas consumers, who pay about 4% more under unconstrained LNG exports (U.S. Department of Energy 2024).
38.counter:
A higher value of carbon cuts both ways. Rennert et al. (2022) put the social cost of carbon at $185 a tonne at a 2% discount rate, against the $66 used here. At $185, the low end's net rise in emissions would cost far more, and the high end's net cut would be worth more, widening the range in both directions. Lang (2017) finds that, had early learning rates continued, nuclear power could cost around 10% of what it does now and could have avoided up to 9.5 million deaths. That is a historical counterfactual, not an estimate of licensing reform today, so it is left out. Lee, Miguel and Wolfram (2020) find that demand for rural grid connections in Kenya fell sharply with price and consumption stayed very low, which weighs against large gains from financing fossil-fuel power in poor countries.

The verdict turns on what renewable subsidies buy. If each subsidy dollar buys abatement at the cheapest estimate, $88 a tonne (Bistline, Mehrotra and Wolfram 2023), ending them adds about 1,886 million tonnes a year, and the low case is 0.78. If it buys abatement at the dearest, $2,138 a tonne (Abrell, Kosch and Rausch 2019), ending them adds only 78 million tonnes, and the high case is 2.16. That one assumption moves the policy between the Bad and Good tiers.

39.policy: Remove ten US regulations together as one package. They are occupational licensing, minimum wages, restrictive zoning, slow Food and Drug Administration (FDA) drug approval, the sugar program, community-bank compliance rules, the Jones Act's limits on coastal shipping, three Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rules whose own cost estimates exceed their benefits, compulsory collective bargaining under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), and antitrust enforcement. The rules sit at federal, state and local level. Repealing them needs no new spending.
39.why_on_list: The Fraser Institute's Economic Freedom of the World index scores the regulation of credit, labour and business in Area 5. The ten rules in this package are regulations of exactly that kind, so the package is on the list.
39.evidence: Most items rest on strong evidence. Occupational licensing costs consumers $184 billion to $203 billion a year (Kleiner and Vorotnikov 2018; Kleiner 2015). Licensing does buy some quality: Kleiner and Soltas (2023) find that higher willingness to pay offsets 80% of the higher prices, and that cost sets the low end. Zoning is the largest and least certain item. Hsieh and Moretti (2019) find US GDP would be 3.7% higher with housing limits eased in New York, San Jose and San Francisco, and 8.9% higher if workers move freely. Greaney (2026) found errors in their code; in the corrected model "the effect is two orders of magnitude smaller than what they report." Across the whole federal rulebook, Coffey, McLaughlin and Peretto (2020) estimate that the economy "would have been nearly 25 percent larger by 2012" had regulation stayed at 1980 levels. That study counts only output, so the health and environmental benefits of those rules have to be set against it. Even after subtracting the lowest credible estimate of those benefits, $277.2 billion a year, it gives the highest ratio. The three items added to the package are small. Ending antitrust enforcement saves $0.53 billion of budgets but loses up to $7.81 billion of consumer savings on the agencies' own figures. The package returns $1.28 to $26.37 per dollar of cost.
39.ratio:
The package is treated as one reform. The ratio is total yearly benefits over total yearly full costs, in billions of 2025 dollars. The low end pairs the lowest credible benefits with the highest costs; the high end uses the most favourable credible published estimates. Benefits and costs for each item:

1. **Occupational licensing.** Benefit: consumer costs removed, $184bn (Kleiner and Vorotnikov 2018) to $203bn (Kleiner 2015). Cost: forgone quality, using the Kleiner and Soltas (2023) offsets: 184 ÷ 1.25 = 147.2 and 203 ÷ 1.67 = 121.6.
2. **Minimum wage.** Reversing the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) $15 scenario, families above the poverty line gain about $16bn in real income and families below it lose $8bn (CBO 2019). Low benefit: 0.69 × 8 = 5.5 (Cengiz et al. 2019). Cost: 8.
3. **Zoning.** Low: Greaney (2026), 0.037% of 2025 GDP of $30,861bn = $11.4bn. Hsieh and Moretti's (2019) headline, with workers only partly mobile, is 3.7%, or $1,141.9bn. High: their case with fully mobile workers, 8.9%: 0.089 × 30,861 = $2,746.7bn.
4. **FDA drug approval.** Low: faster reviews under the Prescription Drug User Fee Act added $14bn to $31bn of social surplus, $3.2bn a year (Philipson et al. 2008). Peltzman (1973) finds the 1962 amendments act like a 5% to 10% tax on drug purchases: 10% × $467bn of 2024 drug spending (Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services 2025) = $46.7bn. High: Gieringer (1985) puts the cost of FDA delay at 21,000 to 120,000 lives per decade, against about 5,000 casualties per decade that FDA review prevents. (120,000 − 5,000) ÷ 10 = 11,500 lives a year × $13.1m per statistical life = $150.65bn. It replaces Peltzman's figure rather than adding to it. Cost: $0 to $1.0bn a year for the upper bound on safety harm.
5. **Sugar program.** Benefit: consumers save $2.5bn (U.S. Government Accountability Office 2023) to $4bn a year (Beghin 2022). Cost: producers lose $1.5bn to $2.5bn.
6. **Bank compliance.** Benefit: community banks spent $4.5bn on compliance in 2014 (Dahl 2015); the Council of Economic Advisers (2019) puts the yearly net benefit of the 2018 relief act for small banks at almost $5bn. Cost: slightly higher crisis risk, $0.067bn a year, from CBO's $671m ten-year score of that act (CBO 2018).
7. **Jones Act.** Benefit: national welfare rises by $0.656bn (U.S. International Trade Commission 2002) to $9.8bn a year (Grabow, Manak and Ikenson 2018). Cost: about 10,800 displaced maritime and shipbuilding workers at median pay of $71,860 lose 1.4 to 2.8 years of earnings (Davis and von Wachter 2011), $0.087bn to $0.174bn a year over 20 years at 5%.
8. **EPA rules that fail their own test.** Three EPA major rules of 2007-2016 have agency costs above even their high benefit estimate (Office of Management and Budget 2017, Table A-2): Florida's numeric nutrient water-quality standards, the coal combustion residuals rule and the cooling-water intake rule. Repeal saves $1.27bn to $1.71bn of compliance a year and gives up $0.40bn to $0.48bn of health and environmental benefits.
9. **Compulsory collective bargaining.** Low: 0, since Oklahoma's right-to-work law changed neither employment nor private-sector wages (Eren and Ozbeklik 2016). High: the deadweight loss of union wage-setting, 0.11% of wages (Vedder and Gallaway 2002), doubled for a labour-supply response and scaled to today's private-sector union share: 0.0011 × 2 × 0.374 × $12,976bn of wages = $10.67bn. Cost: 0; the union wage premium is a transfer.
10. **Antitrust enforcement.** Benefit: enforcement budgets saved, $239.6m at the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plus $288.0m at the Department of Justice (DOJ) = $0.53bn. Cost: lost consumer savings, $0 (Crandall and Winston 2003) to $7.81bn on the agencies' own performance figures (FTC $5.37bn, DOJ $2.43bn).

**Item totals.** Benefits: $213.6bn (low) to $3,148.1bn (high). Costs: $131.7bn (low) to $167.2bn (high).

- Low end: 213.6 ÷ 167.2 = **1.28**.
- High end, item by item: 3,148.1 ÷ 131.65 = 23.9.

**High end from the aggregate study.** Coffey, McLaughlin and Peretto (2020) find that federal regulatory growth since 1980 left GDP about $4 trillion lower in 2012. That is 4,000 ÷ 16,254 = 24.61% of GDP; on 2025 GDP it is $7,594.8bn. It replaces the federal items it covers (sugar, bank compliance and the EPA rules), not adds to them. The state, local and pre-1980 items are added at their high values: 203 + 16 + 2,746.7 + 150.65 + 9.8 + 10.67 + 0.53 = 3,137.35. Benefits: 7,594.8 + 3,137.35 = 10,732.2.

The study measures output, not the health and environmental benefits that rules buy, so those benefits count as a cost of repeal, at the lowest credible estimate:

- 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments: even if fine particles and ozone had no effect on deaths, non-fatal health and visibility benefits reach $137bn a year in 2006 dollars (EPA 2011), or $210.0bn today. Cox (2012) argues the mortality benefits that make up most of the EPA estimate are unproven.
- Other agencies' major rules of 2007-2016: $41.0bn of low-end benefits (Office of Management and Budget 2017), plus 15% of the $64.9bn for energy-efficiency and fuel-economy rules, since Gayer and Viscusi (2013) find 85% to 87% of those benefits are buyers' own fuel savings: 41.0 + 9.7 = 50.7 in 2015 dollars, or $67.2bn.

Lost benefits: 210.0 + 67.2 = 277.2. Costs: 121.6 + 8 + 0.087 + 277.2 = 406.9.

- High end: 10,732.2 ÷ 406.9 = **26.37**.

**Cross-checks.** With Hsieh and Moretti's 3.7% in place of 8.9%, the high end is 22.4. With Coffey et al.'s $4 trillion carried forward by inflation alone ($5,533bn), it is 21.3. With agencies' own lost-benefit estimates ($299bn for the Clean Air Act Amendments and $140bn for other rules), it is 18.9. Leaving out lost benefits entirely would give 82.8, but that ignores what the rules buy. Two other aggregate estimates are smaller: Crain and Crain (2023) put the cost of federal regulation at $3.079 trillion a year, and the Competitive Enterprise Institute (Crews 2025) at $2.155 trillion; both count costs only. The range is 1.28 to 26.37, with a full cost of $167.2bn a year.
39.cost:
The full cost is $167.2bn a year at the low end of the ratio and $131.7bn on the item-by-item high end. Repealing the rules needs no new spending, no administration and no new compliance. The costs are forgone quality, lost health and environmental benefits, lost consumer savings and income transfers:

- Forgone licensing quality: $121.6bn to $147.2bn (Kleiner and Soltas 2023).
- Income lost by families below the poverty line after minimum-wage repeal: $8bn (CBO 2019).
- Lost consumer savings from antitrust enforcement: $0 to $7.81bn (FTC and DOJ; Crandall and Winston 2003).
- Sugar producers' lost surplus: $1.5bn to $2.5bn (U.S. Government Accountability Office 2023).
- FDA safety bound: $0 to $1.0bn (Philipson et al. 2008).
- Lost benefits of the three EPA rules: $0.40bn to $0.48bn (Office of Management and Budget 2017).
- Displaced Jones Act workers' earnings losses: $0.087bn to $0.174bn.
- Bank-crisis risk: $0.067bn (CBO 2018).
- Compulsory bargaining: $0; the wage premium is a transfer, and lost worker voice is not priced.

On the aggregate high end, the sugar, bank and EPA costs give way to the lost non-market benefits of all post-1980 federal rules, $277.2bn, for a total cost of $406.9bn.
39.strength: Grade B+. Most items rest on peer-reviewed natural experiments or structural models that measure the gain directly: licensing, minimum wages, zoning and drug approval. Official estimates from the Government Accountability Office, the CBO, the Office of Management and Budget, the FTC and the DOJ cover the sugar program, bank compliance, the EPA rules and antitrust. The high end leans on weaker ground: a peer-reviewed growth model whose measure of regulation has been challenged, Hsieh and Moretti's fully mobile case, and a 1985 estimate of lives lost to drug delay. Zoning, the largest item, rests on a model that a replication found to overstate the effect about a hundredfold. That keeps the grade below A.
39.difficulty: Moderate. Each item needs ordinary legislation, rule repeal, or federal pre-emption of state licensing and local zoning. There are strong precedents: the airline, trucking and rail deregulation of 1978-80, Arizona's 2019 universal recognition of out-of-state occupational licences, Auckland's 2016 upzoning, 26 state right-to-work laws, and repeal of rules under the Congressional Review Act. The obstacle is the number of separate laws and the entrenched beneficiaries: incumbent homeowners, licensed professions, sugar growers, unions and the regulated industries' competitors.
39.who_benefits: The gains are broad. Zoning and licensing reform favour lower-income newcomers and renters, who are kept out of high-wage cities and protected trades. FDA, sugar and Jones Act reform help consumers and patients widely. The losers are clear too. Minimum-wage repeal lowers income for families below the poverty line by $8bn a year, and ending compulsory bargaining lowers some union wages. Without antitrust enforcement some prices may rise. Licensed professions, sugar growers and maritime workers lose their protection, and people living near the plants covered by the three EPA rules lose some environmental protection.
39.counter: Repealing EPA rules wholesale would lower the ratio, not raise it. On the Office of Management and Budget's (2017) tally, the 39 major EPA rules of 2007-2016 bring benefits of $195.8 billion to $705.7 billion a year against costs of $54.1 billion to $64.8 billion (2015 dollars). Putting all of them in the package would cut the low end to 0.26. Those benefits are open to question: the same report says they are "mostly attributable to the reduction in public exposure to fine particulate matter," and Cox (2012) argues that link is unproven. Even with no mortality benefit, EPA (2011) puts the non-fatal benefits of the 1990 amendments at more than twice their cost. The high end has its own critics. Goldschlag and Tabarrok (2018) find that federal regulation, measured the same way as in Coffey et al. (2020), does not explain the decline in American business dynamism. Glaeser and Gyourko (2018) suggest that 2% of GDP may be an upper bound on the gains from easing land-use rules, and Greaney (2026) finds far less. If the aggregate study and the fully mobile zoning case are set aside, the high end is 11.7 and the package stays Good. If Greaney is right as well, it sits near the low end of 1.28, in the Mid tier, carried by licensing.
